Who We Are 


William Dennis Hendricson 


Synopsis 
Who We Are is a story of nine families that blended through marriage and other relationships 


over the centuries into a current 21" century family, the family of William Dennis Hendricson, 
that’s me, and my wife, Susan Lienau Hendricson. 


As these families evolved over time, they cross paths with the famous and infamous who are 
highlighted in the stories told in this book: Willem Frederic George Lodewijk van der Dussen, a 
founding father of modern genealogy in Europe and first chronicler of Hendricson family 
history; Maarten Schenck Van Nydeggan Hendriksz, one of Europe’s most villainous mercenary 
soldiers and Lambert Barentse Hendriksz, Holland’s most revered naval hero; Peter 
Stuyvesant, peg-legged soldier-politician leader of the New Amsterdam colony; legendary 
pirate of the Caribbean Captain Henry Morgan; ill-fated Miles Morgan, vanished in the 
Carolina’s a decade before the Lost Colony of Roanoke; Molly Reeve Webster, the Witch of 
Hadley, catalyst for the Salem Witch Trials; and her nemesis, scientist, public health champion 
and witchcraft-monger, Cotton Mather; the mystic idealist, William Penn, whose political 
concepts guided Jefferson, Franklin and other founding fathers; George Washington, need | say 
more; Daniel Boone; legendary frontiersman; Molly Pitcher, Revolutionary War heroine; 
General Daniel Morgan, hero of Saratoga and Cowpens in the Revolutionary War; British 
General Charles Cornwallis, the most renowned Redcoat commander of the Revolutionary 
War; Moses Black Harris, famed Mountain Man of the American West; Abner Doubleday, Civil 
War General and rumored founder of baseball; WZ Ripley, a catalyst for 20" century White 
Supremacy dogma; Ernie Davis, Heisman Trophy winning college football player; George 
Preston Marshall, key founder of the National Football League in the U.S. and ardent 
segregationist; Howard Cosell, America’s leading sports journalist in the 1970s; John Lewis, 
prominent U.S. Civil Rights leader; and Shirley Povich, Pulitzer prize winning sportswriter, with 
guest appearances by other notables including Christopher Columbus, on his first approach to 
the Americas, Roger Maris, U.S. baseball legend, the rock band Blood, Sweat and Tears, voting 
rights advocate Evelyn T. Butts, rockabilly and country western star Jerry Lee Lewis, and best- 
selling author of “On Death and Dying,” Elizabeth Kubler-Ross. 


However, Who We Are does not center on these luminaries; they make cameo appearances, 
engaging various family members, past and present, in unique experiences, or serving as 
catalysts for societal phenomenon that influenced the lives of these individuals. Instead, Who 
We Are is about people who did the best they could to build a safe, happy and prosperous life 
‘or themselves in America beginning in the 17" century. The individuals in the nine families 
who first immigrated to America were average folk, working class for the most part, with no 
royal connections or inherited wealth to prop them up. Two of the original immigrants came 
rom merchant families that previously had accrued wealth in Europe, but through misfortune, 
inexplicable decisions, and political turmoil, had drifted so far away from prosperity that 
America was seen as their only recourse. Other original immigrants were from families that had 
known only the meager existence of tenant farm labor for generations. The first immigrants in 
two other families arrived on legal missions as young, unmarried men, and elected to seek their 
ortune in America rather than return to uncertain futures in Europe. Who We Are tells the 
stories of the people in these nine families before and after their arrival in America. All families 
have extraordinary stories, and collectively, these stories shape society. 


About the Cover 


Throughout history, majestic old oaks, with their massive limb structure, have been used to 
visually represent the composition and inter connections of families. | chose an oak for the 
cover art of this family history because of the connection of a particular oak with the early 
development of the Hendricson family in North America. For nearly 200 years, a Great White 
Oak was a principle landmark of the Rutgers University campus in New Brunswick, New Jersey. 
Before its disease riddled demise, the Rutgers Oak was described as majestic and awe-inspiring. 
The Oak appears below in a photo taken by a Rutgers University student in 1963, shortly before 
the centuries old, but much weakened tree, was cut down after several large limbs fell to the 
ground. The Rutgers Oak is generally perceived to be the inspiration for poet Joyce Kilmer’s 
1914 collection of poems known as Trees (i.e., | think | shall never see a poem as lovely as a 
tree), the best selling poetry collection in U.S. history. 


Distant Hendricson ancestors (then Hendrickson with K) played a role in the origins of Rutgers 
University. In the 1700s, members of the New Jersey Hendricksons sold a substantial parcel of 
land, which included the Great White Oak, to the Dutch Reform Church, which founded the 
University and built a campus on this land. Since the opening of the University in 1766, the 
Rutgers Oak served as gathering point at the center of the campus. It was a popular spot for 
student activities, wedding celebrations, picnics, and class reunions. After the first college 
football game between Rutgers University and the College of New Jersey (Princeton since 1896) 
on November 6, 1869, which Rutgers won 6-4, both teams “repaired to the Great White Oak to 
congratulate each other on the competition.” (Rutgers Footballers Carry the Field Over CNJ; 
Daily Targum, November 9, 1869; DeLassus D. Princeton Yearly Results-1869. College Football 
Data Warehouse. Accessed on June 10, 2024 via Internet Archive. www.archive.org).

A side note: “Targum” is an ancient Hebrew word referring to interpretation, translation and 
especially, paraphrasing, of the Old Testament. In the 19" century, Rutgers University students 
used targum as slang for a “crib sheet” (i.e., brief synopsis of a lecture). The student newspaper 
adopted the term to refer to a brief synopsis of campus news.

Prologue 


Genealogy and geriatrics are fellow travelers in the alphabet and in activity. After retirement, 
Individuals who are motivated to explore the evolution of their family have more time, and 
more urgency, to undertake genealogy as a hobby, than during their family and career building 
years. Thus, deep dives into the question of “who and why we are the way we are” are often 
delayed until late in life, when, perhaps, there is too little time left to apply the lessons learned 
from this endeavor for oneself. Yet, many amateur (Do It Yourself; DIY) geriatric genealogists 
aspire to leave behind “take-home messages” that hopefully will be read and pondered by 
unknown others in the future. These take-home messages include: heritage - how did we get to 
be who we are, as individuals, as a family, and beyond that, collectively as a society; legacy - 
what worth are we leaving behind that may benefit others in the future; and, finality - the urge 
to wrap things up. My wife, Susan Lienau Hendricson (1949 - ), is a single child, and there are no 
male grandchildren from our union, so both the Lienau and Hendricson lines will come to an 
end within the 21 century. This sounds dour but it isn’t. New families will emerge from what 
remains of our family. It’s the way of history: lines of families form, are shaped by adversity, 
usually, but not always, adapt and evolve, more often than not flourish, and then scatter into 
new family groupings or insular lives, and the nuclear family fades away. At a micro level, that’s 
the story of families; at a macro level, it’s the story of nations. 


| spent most of my 50-year work career doing precise scientific (biomedical) writing: research 
grants, research reports (chapters and journal articles), and academic governance documents 
needed for accreditation, compliance, strategic planning, institutional assessment, and program 
management. Most of this writing followed a prescribed, or at least an expected (customary) 
format with minimal leeway for variance. Because of my parent’s fascination with genealogy, 
which you will read about later in this book, and my love of history, especially odd and 
unpredictable events and personalities that so often profoundly shaped the path of 
communities and nations, | made an effort over the years to read several family histories that 
my parents used as source materials for their research. | found them to be laudable works, 
undoubtedly the product of massive effort, but tough reading because they largely were 
comprised of long and chronologically organized lists of spousal partners and their many 
children; names, birth and death dates, place of birth, burial sites, but very little, if any, 
information that made these names on a page come alive as real people, and very few pictures, 
even for ancestors who lived in the age of photography, 1850 to the present. Most of these 
genealogies followed a prescribed template for presenting the name, date and place 
information that reminded me of the prescriptive writing | did for much of my career. Much 
factual information is communicated in these family histories, but there is no sense of a 
journey, and no sense of aspirations and their catalysts, or tragedies and their impact. 


After | promised my mother that | would assemble the family history documentation that she 
and my father had assembled over the years, and create a book to be shared within the family, | 
set a goal to produce a history that allowed our ancestors to come alive as real and interesting 
people, to help our current family, and others who might read this book, to appreciate who 
these people of the past were, and why they were they way they were. To make the leap from 
names, dates and places to an enriched history based on stories of our ancestors’ life 
experiences involved three years of deep digging. The detective work needed to assemble a 


historical record of “what came before” was engaging and satisfying in so many ways, akin to 
creating the final chapter of a page-turner novel that pulls diverse story lines together, and it 
fulfilled my lifelong desire to do writing that was allowed to deviate from a prescribed path — to 
chase a story wherever it went, even if it spun off into tangential events, as long as that 
diversion helped explain the life of an ancestor, or the circumstances in which they lived. 


For me, the most exciting outcomes were all the small details and fortunate and unfortunate 
happenstances that comprise history, and often, make all the difference in outcomes. Equally 
compelling are the inexplicable connections between people, dreams and opportunities that 
lead to the events that we call history. In the past three years, | found my self discarding old 
concepts about the formation of our nation that, under inspection, were not sustainable 
against the actual historical record, i.e., the truth of things. | also found myself taking on new 
perspectives about how our nation came to be, and why we are the way we are — divided and 
contentious. In 2025, almost any commentary on the state of our nation begins with the over- 
used and cliché observation that we have become a divided society in recent times, with widely 
disparate interpretations of the past and differing visions of the future. In reality, this is not a 
new phenomenon; this is who we are now, and this is who we have always been. Americans 
never have been “of a single mind.” From the early 1600s to the present day, what we now 
know as America has been the proverbial two-sided coin: inspirational, heroic, innovative and 
persevering on one side, amoral, racist, larcenous, and violent on the other. Just as both sides 
of a nickel create its five cents of worth, both sides of America blend together to create who we 
were, and who we are now; not all admirable and virtuous, not all embarrassing and unsavory. 


Stories 

History comes alive as an added value to our lives through the act of discovery, the search for 
knowing, but more importantly, through the process of making connections among 
circumstances, events, people and beliefs, and then sharing these understandings and 
connections — telling a story. The “Notes On” sections that you will read in this book tell tales, 
albeit in abridged form, of circumstances, events, people and beliefs of which | had no 
knowledge, or just surface awareness as | pursued the task of learning about my ancestors. But 
these circumstances shaped the lives of past generations, and linger with us still, shaping why 
we are the way we are today in 2025. The most exciting days in developing this book, when | 
couldn’t wait to hop up in the morning, grab some coffee, get to the keyboard and start typing, 
were devoted to struggling to write my interpretation of these shaping factors. What | will 
remember the most vividly about the past three years is the challenge of figuring out how to 
capture in words what | had learned about historical figures with multiple defining 
characteristics, admirable and horrific, or, discovered about belief systems and values 
profoundly at odds with my present sensibilities. The daily challenge of creating a story from 
these discoveries and new perspectives drove this book to the finish line. 


The philosophy of Who We Are can be summed up as follows: 

* Much of the true catalysts for societal change move beneath the surface of events. Things 
that happen without noticeable consequence in their own time often shape the lives of 
generations that follow. Accordingly, anonymous people have often moved history. 

+ History is created by two intertwined elements. Knowledge of what actually happened in 
the past, based on evidence derived from sound and objective scholarship, allows 


meaningful assessment of events and trends. However, the ways we remember the past, 
(stories, fables, myths) are often just as powerful as what actually happened, and can 
provide the context to help understand the way we were and the way we are now. 


Book Format 

| organized this book around my pathway of discovery, the starting point of which was learning 
about my parents’ fascination with genealogy. In doing so, | gaining an appreciation for 
genealogy as a passionate pastime for millions of people, as a major industry, and as a social 
status signal. Then, | digested what my parents discovered about the history of the Hendricsons 
and their connections to many other families over the centuries, and read my parents list of 
unknowns, which became the launch pad for my own research. Accordingly, Chapter | 
contextualizes the task of writing a family history, explores the growth of genealogy in the U.S. 
as a hobby, and examines its uses and abuses. Chapter II introduces you to the 150 ancestors 
within nine families who moved the story forward; in essence, if this was a movie script, they 
are the protagonists and antagonists, some were major roles, and others with brief cameos. Yes 
- 150 is a lot of people, but | felt it was important for readers to appreciate the complexity of 
familial growth and see how each family evolved and eventually intertwined. In Chapter III, you 
will learn about the origins of these families in continental Europe and Great Britain with focus 
on the family members who first made the transatlantic leap. Chapter IV, the longest 
component, presents stories of family members in North America who experienced unique 
circumstances or made decisions that profoundly influenced following generations. Chapter V 
brings the Hendricson chronology forward to 2025, and Chapter VI indicates the data sources 
and literature used to write this book. 


For Chapter II, where the cast of players is introduced, | used a template that communicates the 
standard “factoids,” but also provides a synopsis of what | learned about who these people 
were and what they did, sometimes told in just a sentence or two for those in the distant and 
dim past, and in greater detail for more recent or more chronicled ancestors. An example of the 
template appears below. 


Aaron Maris J 1807- Fs winhetd toraar Cane Creek, NC Ea Guilford, NC 
1872 | D: Winfield, Kansas | 1885 Winfield, Kansas 


Aaron and Keziah lived in Parke County, Indiana and in Douglas, Illinois (just south 
of Champaign — Urbana) until 1870. Aaron started out as a farm hand, and eventually 
accumulated enough money to buy farm and pasture property of his own. At age 63, for 
unknown reasons, they relocated to the small community of Winfield in Cowley County, 
Kansas, near Wichita. Aaron died a year after arriving in Kansas and Keziah remained there 
until her death in 1885. Aaron and Keziah appear to have been the last actively practicing 
Quakers in the Maris line. 


Dedication 


This book would not exist without the support, nudging, questions and suggestions 

of my beloved wife and partner, Susan Lienau Hendricson, who provided the space, 

accepted the snail’s pace of research that such a project requires, and tolerated my 
monopolization of the one desktop computer in our home. 


Susan Lienau Hendricson

Chapter I - Context 


What is Genealogy? 

Genealogy is defined as the study of family origins and history. A genealogical study seeks to 
identify the starting point for a line of genetically inter-related people who comprise a distinct 
family, and identify chronological relationships among individuals comprising this family, 
moving from the past to the present. The outcome of this exploration is called a family history. 


Accordingly, this document is a family history for William Dennis Hendricson and Susan Lienau 
Hendricson. For each of the families, identified below, which contributed to our union, | 
worked forward from ancestors as far back in history as could be confidently identified to 
January 2, 1971 when we married. Without DNA analysis, | cannot be 100% certain about 
relationships, but have high confidence in the lineage described in this document, based on 
research over the past three years and research previously completed by my parents. 


Notes on the Concept of History: The modern word “history” is derived from the Greek histor 
(learned, wise person) and historia (investigation leading to an account or narrative), which 
were incorporated into Latin, and centuries later emerged in Old English as istoria and French 
as historie. The concept of history has been defined variously as: 


The memory of things said and done. (Carl L. Becker; Everyman His Own Historian. American 
Historical Review. 1931; 37(2): 221-236. www.historians.org. Accessed: May 19, 2024) 


History is organized memory of past events, and the organization is all-important. History is not 
another name for the past, but rather stories about the past. (Henry Steele Commager; in 
Jumonville N. Henry Steele Commager: Midcentury Liberalism and the History of the Present. 
Chapel Hill NC: University of North Carolina Press. 1999) 


History is understanding the past. Whoever wishes to foresee the future must consult the past; 
for human events ever resemble those of preceding times. Men ever shall be animated by the 
same passions, and thus they necessarily have the same results. (Niccolo Machiavelli; in Black R. 
Machiavelli: From Radical to Reactionary. London: Reakton Books. 2022) 

A chronological record of significant events, such as those affecting a nation, an institution or a 
population of people, often including an explanation of their causes. (Merriam Webster 
Dictionary. www.merriam-webster.com. Accessed: May 20, 2024) 

The study of events that occurred in the past, particularly in human affairs. (Oxford Languages. 
www.languages.oup.com. Accessed: May 20, 2024) 

History is who we are and why we are the way we are. 

(David C. McCullough, from a speech at Wesleyan College on June 2, 1984 and quoted in Canty- 
Jones EE. “History is Who We Are and Why We Are the Way We Are.” The Oregon Historical 
Society Blog — June 2, 2020. www.ohs.org. Accessed: May 20, 2024) 


As readers may have already surmised, David McCullough’s definition is my favorite. 


1D 


The Nine Families 

When Susan and | married in 1971, it was the culmination of the life journeys of 150 people 
over a thousand years in Europe and North America within nine families that comprise four 
paternal or maternal groupings. The contemporary surnames of these families are listed below. 


¢ Hendricson — Morgan — Maris: Bill’s paternal lineage 
¢ Dennis — Goodman: Bill’s maternal lineage 

¢ Lienau —- McManus: Susan’s paternal lineage 

¢  Girault - McAnespy: Susan’s maternal lineage 


Purpose 

The primary goal was to learn the stories of the nine families that brought Susan and | together: 
verifiable truths, probable truths (but not completely nailed down), mysteries, myths, 
exaggerations (tall tales), rumors and speculations — all of what comprises the story, traditions 
and even the mythology of a family. A complimentary goal was to pass the enjoyment of 
discovering and writing these stories on to others who may read this book. Hopefully, other 
genealogists can use bits of this story to build their own family history, or use the format of this 
history to share the story of their families’ journey. 


To tell the story of the origins and history of these nine families, | dug into the stories | had 
heard throughout my life, and attempted to answer the “journalism 6 questions” (who, what, 
when, where, how and as feasible, why), fill-in missing details, and explore rumors and other 
assertions that seemed more like fables than reality, but just-the-same, formed an important 
part of family lore. As | explored these questions, | caught the genealogy bug: the thrill of finally 
understanding the twisty, sometimes hard to believe, improbable, road to the present time, or 
the excitement of learning that a mysterious ancestor shrouded in uncertainty actually was a 
real person who did some of the things that family lore has ascribed to him or her. These were 
the “Wow Moments” that more than compensated for the drudgery of endless document 
checking, the frustration of dead ends, and the futility of false leads. 


Sources 
The sources used to explore our family history are indicated in Chapter VI: Information Sources. 
Citations for a majority of these sources appear within the book. In an era when many 
Americans are comfortable with ignoring or misconstruing well documented historical facts and 
trends, or simply making up new, and | might add, fraudulent, data to support their contentions 
(i.e., alternative facts), | felt it was important to show my cards by prominently displaying the 
sources that were used to document family history and to describe the social, religious, political 
and economic circumstances that these families encountered. Numerous full citations 
admittedly break up the text and may increase the amount of reading, but represent an effort 
to make clear “where the history came from.” | also hope that some of these citations will be 
useful to genealogists in other families who seek to explore the experiences of their ancestors. 


These sources included 22 family histories written between 1843 and 2016 (identified in 
Chapter VI by bold font), data obtained from my parents who devoted more than a decade to 
genealogy research, reports by community historical societies, online genealogical resources, 
and my original research. Many databases were reviewed such as the U.S. Federal Census Data 


12 


1790 to present, the Internet Surname Database, the U.S. Index of Death Certificates 1735- 
1948, colonial and U.S. immigration arrival reports, state, county and church (including Quaker 
Meeting House) reports of births, marriages, deaths and property purchases, property and 
business tax rolls, census reports, prison / reform school records, newspaper articles, 
obituaries, dairies and letters, publications of genealogical societies, and numerous history 
books and historical association websites. In particular, the later two sources enhanced 
understanding of the circumstances that influenced these families and the decisions they made. 


Examples of Hendricson family histories written in the 19" century. The preambles of 19" century 
genealogies sometimes started with vile, racist screed about the superiority of the Teutonic blood 
coursing through the veins of European ancestors. 

A side note: The original Hendricson family surname was Schenck, later morphed to Schenck van 
Nydeck, and ultimately evolving to variations of Hendricks, Hendrickzoon and Hendrickson. It did not 
become Hendricson until 1845. The story of these surname changes is told throughout this history. 


For my Schenck ancestors, a principle source for the history of the family in Europe is a 256 
page hand-written document, with more than 100 pages of accompanying illustrations of 
people and places, researched over three decades and ultimately completed in 1872 by a Dutch 
military officer by the name of Willem Frederic George Lodewijk van der Dussen (1816-1878). 
At the time of his retirement, he was army commandant of the city of Nijmegan. Colonel van 
der Dussen had a deep interest in Dutch and northern German (Cologne area) heritage, leading 
him to investigate and write a number of histories of notable Dutch and German families 
including the Schenck van Nydecks. After retirement from the military, van Dussen became a 
leading genealogist in the Netherlands and established a journal devoted to the science of 
genealogy, which included articles on the histories of numerous Dutch families. Colonel van der 
Dussen’s history of the Schencks was apparently available to other individuals pursuing 
genealogy research in various versions as it evolved during years of writing. Two prominent 
Schenck family historians cited van der Dussen as a source before his tome on the Schencks was 
placed in the Netherlands Genealogical Library at The Hague in 1872. The Library reproduced 


13 


multiple hand written copies of van Dussen’s work and ultimately typeset and printed an 
unknown number of copies, which were slowly added to library collections in Europe and the 
U.S. including the Brooklyn, NY, Museum Libraries and Archives. 


Source: van der Dussen WFGL (Willem Frederic George Lodewijk). Genealogy of the Old and 
Very Illustrious Family of Schenck van Nydeck (Nydegge) Beginning with Year 1368. Nijmegan, 
Netherlands: 256 hand-written pages (self-printed). 1872. Housed at Brooklyn, NY Museum

Notes on The Gilded Age and 19" Century Genealogy: Interest in exploring family history 
exploded in the U.S. during the Gilded Age, which bridged the 30-year span from the end of 
Reconstruction in 1877 to the early 1900s. The label for this era was derived from the novel, 
The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today, co-authored by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, which 
lampooned the “gilding of the lily” extravagance of the wealthy. As depicted in this novel, the 
upper crust of Gilded Age society benefitted financially from political corruption, placed high 
priority on acquiring and protecting elite social status and indulged in flashy displays of newly 
acquired wealth. (Twain M, Warner CD. The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today. Hartford, CT: American 
Publishing Company. 1873) Gilded Age wealth was stimulated in large part by the creation of a 
management class for the nations’ burgeoning “big six industries”: manufacturing, commercial 
and residential construction, real estate (land speculation), municipal infrastructure (i.e., paved 


14 


roads, bridges, tunnels, dams, sewers/drainage systems, train stations and_ ports), 
transportation (i.e., railroads and shipping) and banking/investment. Compensation for 
individuals in managerial or supervisory roles in these industries expanded dramatically, and 
individuals who owned these businesses became obscenely wealthy in comparison to the rest 
of society. Approximately 30% of Gilded Age households reaped the economic benefits of the 
ownership/management class. Forty percent of the public still lived at a basic day-to-day 
subsistence level, primarily as manual laborers, and the remaining 30%, mostly rural and mostly 
southern, attempted to survive punishing levels of poverty with episodic employment. (Calhoun 
C. The Gilded Age: Perspectives on Origins of Modern America. Washington DC: Rowman and 
Littlefield Publications. 2007) 

MARK TWAIN & 
CHARLES DUDLEY WARNER 

THE GILDED AGE Twain’s only novel with a co-author satirized get rich quick land 

a teECeT speculation schemes and political shenanigans in Washington 

D.C. that favored the wealthy at the expense of the poor. 
Although critical reviews at the time of publication were 
middling, the novel was reprinted more than 100 times in the 20" 
century, when it was often used to illustrate the social ill-effects 
of graft, corruption and materialism.

The public’s fascination with genealogy during the Gilded Age was driven by several factors. For 
many, affluence and the advent of the five-day workweek provided more money and time for 
hobbies and leisurely pursuits such as researching family history. The evolution of book 
publication technology made it relatively inexpensive to produce multiple copies of family 
histories for distribution to relatives and libraries, and advances in page printing also facilitated 
inclusion of pictures of current and past family members, a major catalyst for preparing 
genealogy books. Innovations in photography led to affordable personal cameras that created a 
national craze for recreational and vacation photography. The widespread availability of photo 
salons spurred the family portrait industry, and newly emerging photo restoration techniques 
allowed families to restore old tintypes of ancestors and make photographs of portraits that 
had hung on walls for decades, collecting dust. All communities, small and large, had a 
proliferation of newspapers that devoted extensive coverage to marriage and birth 
announcements, social events, family trips, school graduations, business start-ups, award 
ceremonies and obituaries, all of which were primary information staples for family historians 
in the Gilded Age. (O’Hare S. Genealogy and History. Common Place: The Journal of Early 
American Life. www.commonplace.com. 2002: 22(3): 17-31. Accessed: April 26, 2024) 


The growth of the Church of Latter-Day Saints (LDS) and the creation of the Genealogical 
Society of Utah in the 1890s led to many “how to do genealogy” textbooks, and a popular 
journal devoted to genealogical research. Since its establishment in the early 19" century, the 
LDS community has been particularly enthusiastic about tracing family roots. Members of that 
faith believe that all family members will reunite after this life, and thus it is important to be 


15 


familiar with your ancestors so one can establish good relationships in the afterlife. (Powell K. 
Why Mormons Research Their Ancestors. Learn Religions. www.learnreligions.com. Accessed: 
May 1, 2024) In response to the rise of genealogy as a popular hobby, U.S. libraries and 
university's sponsored seminars on genealogical techniques that attracted large and 
enthusiastic crowds, and several genealogical speakers became celebrities. Genealogical and 
historical societies grew in size and scope during the Gilded Age, exerting considerable 
academic, cultural and political influence. For example, the American Historical Association 
(AHA) was established in 1884. The AHA’s largest division was devoted to early American 
genealogy. The New England Historic Genealogical Society and its journal, the New England 
Historical and Genealogical Register were profoundly influential in guiding family history 
research and publication during the Gilded Age (Hjorthen A. Reframing the History of American 
Genealogy: On the Paradigm of Democratization and the Capitalization of Longing. Genealogy. 
2022; 6(1): 21-37. Accessed: May 1, 2024). Membership in these societies was eagerly sought 
as a sign of elite social status, but difficult to obtain. 


By the 1880s, many families had proceeded through multiple generations after immigration 
from other nations, and family founders were now in their 70s or 80s — individuals who may 
have experienced a transatlantic journey first hand, lived thru the turbulent era of Jacksonian 
Democracy, experienced or read about the exciting Frontiersmen era, participated in westward 
expansion, perhaps by wagon train, or survived the Civil War. To capture the oral history of 
these elders, it was fashionable for Gilded Age children or grandchildren to document 
ancestors’ lives to learn family origins before this oral history was lost. In many ways, 
genealogical writing was an extension of nation’s passion for diary writing in the 1880s and 90s, 
much of which was devoted to remberances of ancestors and siblings. (Bunkers S. Midwestern 
Diaries and Journals. What Women Were, and Were Not, Saying in the Late 1800s. In: Studies in 
Autobiography. Olney J. NY: Oxford University Press. 1988) 


Other motives were at play in U.S. genealogy at the end of the 19" century. In addition to 
capturing oral history, a strong motivation was proving linkage to the Revolutionary War Era to 
distinguish the family historically and socially from the mass of 19" century immigrants flowing 
into the U.S., especially those with Mediterranean, Balkan, Irish and South American ancestry. 
(Calhoun, 2007) For example, the Daughters of the American Revolution and the Society of 
Mayflower Descendants were established in this era, as were many regional historical heritage 
societies such as the Daughters of the Republic of Texas. (Des Jardins J. Women and the 
Historical Enterprise in America: Gender, Race and the Politics of Memory, 1880-1945. Chapel 
Hill: University of North Carolina Press. 2003) 


Another genealogy catalyst was the desire to demonstrate that a family’s lineage was 
comprised of pure Teutonic (i.e., White) blood without mongrelization, a crude post-Civil War, 
Jim Crow Era, label for people with multiracial heritage. (DeSantis VP. The Shaping of Modern 
America, 1877-1920. Wheeling, Illinois: Forum Press. 1989) White America in this era was 
profoundly concerned with racial and cultural differences, and overt anti-Black, anti-Semitic 
and anti-immigrant hostility pervaded Gilded Age society. (Foner E. Reconstruction: America’s 
Unfinished Revolution. NY: Harper and Row. 1988)

The tenants of Alfred Schultz’s Race or Mongrel were not considered 
outlandish in the Gilded Age. Schultz contended that: supremacy of 
Northern European Caucasians is indisputable; a nation’s strength 
lies in racial purity; nations decline when Whites marry alien stock; 
and America will sink into decay unless immigration is rigorously 
restrained. Although denounced by some scientists, church leaders 
and pol is at that time, Schultz’s theories were endorsed by 
racist organizations well into the 20" century. These concepts were 
uttered by numerous Republican candidates in the 2024 U.S. 
election cycle. Schultz AP. Race or Mongrel. Boston MA: LC Page Co. 
1908 (3 ed.). Accessed: April 29, 2024 from CURIOSity Collection at 
Harvard University Library (www.CURIOSity.lib.harvard.edu). 


The inter-related pseudo-sciences of phrenology, craniometry and physiognomy contributed to 
the race and class-obsessed environment of the Gilded Age by providing a convenient, if bogus, 
scientific aura for those seeking evidence of the physical, intellectual or moral superiority of 
Caucasians, and support for the presumed social dangers of mongrelization. Phrenology 
involved measuring bumps and indentations in the skull to predict mental capacity and 
psychological traits. Craniometry led to judgments about an individual’s intellectual prowess 
based on the shape, size and weight of the skull, and physiognomy allowed “investigators” to 
judge a person’s character through analysis of facial expressions. Although widely debunked by 
the legitimate 19" century scientific community, phrenology, craniometry and physiognomy 
were held in high esteem among the general public, at least in part because purported research 
derived from these techniques supported assumptions about the racial superiority of those 
with northern European ancestry. For example, one of the popular books in 1885 was: How to 
Read Character: A New Illustrated Hand-Book of Phrenology and Physiognomy, with a 
Descriptive Chart by Samuel R. Wells (New York: Fowler and Wells Publishers; Available from 
APA PsycBooks website www.psycnet.apa.org. Accessed: April 19, 2024).

Toward the end of the Gilded Age, a best selling book by William Z. Ripley spread the 
unfounded theory of a superior sub-set of the Caucasian race, untainted by other bloodlines: 
the Nordic type, and described the attributes of what would eventually be called a Master Race: 
tall, thin, light skin, hair and eyes, long skulls (associated with high intelligence by Craniometry 
advocates) competitive, truthful and individualistic. (Ripley WZ. The Races of Europe: A 
Sociological Study. NY: Appleton and Company. 1899. Accessed via Google Books at 
www.books.google.com on April 18, 2024) 


Notes on WZ Ripley, Author of The Races of Europe: Ripley’s venture into racial anthropology 
was an odd detour from his primary career focus. After earning a PhD from Columbia University 
in economics in 1893, he held a series of academic and governmental appointments over the 
following 40 years related to management of industrial development with emphasis on 
interstate commerce and efficient use of railroads. He was a professor of economics at Harvard 
for decades and also taught at MIT and Columbia. Between 1900 and 1930, he was appointed 
to many federal commissions by Presidents Roosevelt, Taft, Wilson, Coolidge and Hoover to 
develop regulations for interstate transportation by railways, negotiate contracts and policies 
between railroad and coal companies, negotiate settlements for railway strikes, and establish 
protocols and railway worker protections when the eight hour workday was implemented in 


18 


1916. In the 1920s, he created a plan for coordinated and more efficient use of the nation’s 
railways known as the Ripley Plan, which enhanced the influence of the Interstate Commerce 
Commission, on which he served for many years. He became a fierce critic of speculative Wall 
Street investment practices during the Roaring 20s and was a “voice in the wilderness” in 1925 
when he predicted the crash of the stock market. Near the end of his life, he admitted that he 
had limited personal interest in anthropology, but hoped to take advantage of public 
fascination with racial stereotypes by researching and writing the Races of Europe to finance 
the college education of his children. The book was a best seller in the U.S. and England, so that 
goal was accomplished. 


The book was championed in the U.S. by the noted race monger and white supremacist 
eugenicist, Madison Grant, author of The Passing of the Great Race, or The Racial Basis of 
European History (1916; New York: Charles Scribner’s Sons). Grant’s theories spawned 
widespread belief in the replacement theory, which contributed to a virulent anti-immigrant 
environment in the U.S. during and after World War |, and provided support for the racist 
screed of the Ku Klux Klan, which exerted profound social and political influence throughout the 
U.S. in the 1920s. In a different sphere of his life, Grant was an influential conservationist and 
environmentalist who was credited with saving the California redwoods from logging. He led 
efforts to place dozens of animals on endangered species lists and created regulations in many 
states to bar hunting of these animals. Grant was an effective advocate for the national park 
system and was instrumental in creating the Glacier and Denali National Parks. He also was an 
ardent gun control advocate, not a popular position in the gun-crazed culture of the early 20" 
century. (Spiro J. Defending the Master Race: Conservation, Eugenics and the Legacy of Madison 


Given the prevailing racial beliefs at the end of the 1g” century, it is not surprising to read the 
cringe worthy language employed in family history books of that era to establish a Teutonic 
origin story. A Schenck family history by Augustus D. Schenck resorted to such language, per 
excerpts below. 


“It may be of interest to know of what manner of race of people among whom this ancient 
family found its origin. In the dim ages of the past, the races of the Teutonic Aryans swept away 
the weaker nations in their course, or vivifying (i.e., enlivening, animating) them with their fresh 
and vigorous blood. Their bodies were more hardy, their minds more vigorous than those of 
other tribes. Their young men cut neither their hair nor beard till they had slain an enemy.” 


“Physically, they were of vast stature and these gigantic Teutons derided the Roman soldiers as 
a band of pigmies, and excited astonishment by their huge body and muscular limbs, with long 
yellow hair floating over their shoulders, and fierce bright blue eyes and clear blond complexion. 
They were a race remarkable for personal dignity, but with excessive pride, and for a boundless 
spirit of individual enterprise. With these traits, they untied a simplicity and truthfulness, which 
was always observed by strangers.” 


Source: Schenck AD. The Rev. William Schenck: His Ancestry and His Descendants. Washington 
DC: Rufus Darby Publisher. Originally published in 1843 with updates in 1869 and 1883. Re- 


19 


released by Higginson Book Company (www.higginson.com) in 2015 and also available at 
Google Books. (www.books.google.com). Accessed: December 3, 2022. 


A side note: The excerpts above that surmised the Teutonic heritage of the Schenck family line 
did not appear in the original 1843 publication. This language was added in an 1869 update and 
embellished in the 1883 publication. One potential explanation for the insertion of racial 
superiority language in 1869 was the publication of various “Classification of the Races of 
Europe” in the 1860s, which were less vitriolic assertions of northern European prominence than 
Ripley’s theories, but none-the-less, provided an implied ranking of human characteristics and 
capacities that popularized the concept of a Teutonic sub-set within the Caucasian race. Perhaps 
AD Schenck was swayed by these theories, which gained traction in the U.S. during the 
Reconstruction Era after the Civil War. (Gossett TF. The Teutonic Origins Theory in Race: The 
History of an Idea in America. Gossett TF. London and New York: Oxford University Press. 1997) 


In Chapter Ill, Pre-Immigration Family History, a possible alternative background story for the 
Schenck family will be introduced that Augustus Schenck either did not consider, or perhaps 
elected not to mention, given its inconsistency with the concept of Teutonic origin. 


Availability of Information 

Each family has a pre-immigration (Europe) and a post-immigration (North American) history. 
However, the richness of ancestral information varied among the family lines. For several lines, 
the pre-immigration history was limited to names, dates and locations going back to 
approximately 1800. For other families, extensive information was available from a number of 
sources dating back to the medieval period when surnames first emerged, comprising 20 or 
more generations. For eight of the nine families, solid connections existed between the 
European pre-immigration history and the lives of family members in North America. For one 
family line (Dennis), the connection is not yet pinned down. Confidently linking the North 
American phase of a family to the European pre-immigration phase often came down to the 
diligence of a recording clerk at an immigration port of entry in a North American city. Typically, 
these clerks recorded the immigrating families personal and surnames, previous names or 
variations, the wife’s maiden name, number of children (total and traveling with them), dates 
of birth of all family members, port of departure, city of residence before immigration, religion, 
names of immigrants’ parents, parents’ residence and parents’ occupation(s). Clerks indicated 
on the entry ledger if the immigrant had an occupational permit (i.e., equivalent to modern day 
work visa) or other relocation papers, including prison release and subsequent deportation. For 
eight of the immigrating families included in this history, entry clerks managed to capture the 
bulk of this information, which facilitated lineage tracking. For the Dennis family, they did not. 


The growing sophistication of Artificial Intelligence (Al) search resources using Natural Language 
Processing (NLP), such as ChatGPT (Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer), was tangibly 
evident during the period of research and writing for this book. Inquires submitted to Al “ask 
and answer” systems in 2022 typically resulted in generally accurate, in comparison to 
traditional information sources, yet superficial responses, neatly composed in paragraph form. 
However, the Al responses sometimes were comically off base, a reflection of the information 
sources that they had been fed to build memory (i.e., garbage in, garbage out). In spite of these 
limitations, Al responses were sometimes useful as guideposts, indicating where to start a deep

Conflicting or ambiguous descriptions of events abound in the historical literature, especially in 
the histories of folks who were not the VIPs of the society in which they lived. In these 
instances, | used phrases such as “it appears,” “as best as can be determined” or “apparently” 
to indicate that uncertainty exists about a particular incident. Terms such as “probably” and 
“likely” are used to discuss relationships, and my own non-evidenced interpretations are 
abeled as “speculation.” When catalysts for decisions and actions are described, the discussion 
is identified as speculative if only pieces of the story are available, or phrases such as “for 
unknown reasons” are used if | could find no causal factors.

‘amilies in North America. These stories are arranged chronological 
concluding in the 1970s. Well-chronicled historical events involving these family members are 
conveyed in these stories, many of which include interactions with famous individuals or 
involvement in notable events. For example, one family member was instrumental in saving the 
ife of a future U.S. President. No one knows exactly what was said among the participants, or 
the exact, moment-by-moment sequence of events on that freezing cold night in the midst of a 
Revolutionary War battle. The ability to capture an event photographically would not exist until 
80 years after that fateful night, and cell phone cameras and audio recorders would not exist 
or another 230 years. Yet, based on what can be extracted from many published historical 
accounts of the incident, | attempted to reconstruct the event with focus on our family 
member’s actions. Later in Chapter IV, | describe the participation of an ancestor in a 
remarkable dinner conversation/debate with perhaps the most recognizable of the British 
Generals leading the effort to defeat the American Revolutionaries. Although the evening’s 
events have been depicted in books published by historians, books written by two of the 
principle participants in this ig” century dinner party, and also conveyed in a long-running 
regional theatre production, no one alive today knows exactly what was said that evening, or 


21 


the ardor with which thoughts were expressed, which may have been intense, since much of 
the evening was a debate about the defining issue of that era: slavery, the sequela of which we 
are still debating today. 


For yet another ancestor, after several months of research, | was not convinced that this person 
truly existed, and pondered the possibility that this name from the distant past was actually a 
confabulation of several people with similar names, existing in the same time frame with similar 
occupations and parallel movements from nation to nation. But imagine the excitement when 
this ancestor’s name, in his own hand writing, appeared on a port of entry roster bright and 
clear, which led to discoveries of other signatures on employment and entry/exit documents 
that created a paper trail for this distant ancestor that largely matched family rumors — a real 
person who had an amazing life emerged before my eyes. For these and other stories, 
reconstructions of the events were based on interpretation of the available research that | 
perceived to be the most accurate (or most likely to be accurate), often among several accounts 
with minor to major differences. But when you do not witness an event first hand and rely on 
other sources, there is always the potential of error. Additional, in the process of distilling 
complicated events and situations into a hopefully succinct narrative, | may have fallen prey to 
over-simplification, leaving out key details or circumstances, or perhaps failed to recognize 
pivotal contributing factors — errors of summarization and omission.

Foundational Work by Harold and Mildred Hendricson 

My parents, Harold Maris Hendricson and Mildred Dennis Hendricson, devoted extensive effort 
to family history in the pre-internet era of the 1980s. They explored family roots with old school 
detective work: visiting cemeteries to photograph gravestones, and traveling to county offices 
to review birth, death, and marriage records. Working with county clerks, they obtained copies 
of real estate contracts, deeds, employment records, wills, obituaries and census reports to 
uncover facts about our ancestors’ lives. They scoured the records available through the Church 
of Latter Day Saints Genealogical Library and researched books in public libraries written by 
ancestors or genealogical societies. They corresponded by mail with other individuals around 
the nation who were studying Hendricson, Maris, Morgan, Dennis and Goodman histories to 
gain access to documents that played a prominent role in our research. Harold and Mildred also 
accumulated a collection of family photos dating back to the earliest days of photography in the 
1850s. | promised my mother years ago that | would one day take all of their information, add 


22 


new research, incorporate families on Susan’s side, and produce an integrated family history. 
Hopefully, this family history does justice to Harold and Mildred’s vision for this project. 


A few of the dozens of family trees assembled by Mildred and Harold Hendricson in the 1980s. They 
started from scratch as neither the Hendricson or Dennis family were particularly dedicated to 
maintaining family records. Mildred’s parents, Archie and Maude Dennis, were avid photographers, 
and fortunately were diligent in assembling photo albums, which assisted my parent’s efforts to 
identify descendants. However, my father’s parents apparently were not as keen on photography, 
and thus few pictures from the Hendricson side have survived to this day. 


The same phenomenon occurred on Susan’s side. Susan’s mother’s family, the Giraults, were avid 
photographers, and maintained family photo albums that included pictures of people and places 
going back into the 1g century. Few pictures exist from her father’s family, the Lienau’s. The 
Girault’s and Lienau’s were not diligent in maintaining family records, and thus only basic documents 
have survived the years: birth certificates, graduation certificates, and military draft records. 


Fortunately, other data sources existed for the Dennis, Hendricson, Girault and Lienau families, and 
for all the other families included in this family history, which helped to fill-in the stories of these 
families from their European origins to their lives in North America.

Organization 


* Chapter II - Lineage tables for each family. Each table begins with the first ancestor that | 
could confidently identify. The lineage tables allow readers to gain familiarity with the 
names of ancestors in the nine families, and read brief summaries of their lives, which in 
some cases are augmented in Sections III and/or IV. 


¢ Chapter Ill —- European/English pre-Immigration history. This section introduces readers to 
the history of each family before immigration including: (1) origin of the surname, (2) 
geographic origin, (3) first appearance of surname in public records, (4) synopsis of pre- 
immigration history, and (5) names of ancestors that first immigrated to North America. 


¢ Chapter IV — Stories of Family Members on North America. This section tells stories of 
individuals that were influential in family development or experienced pivotal events in our 
nation’s journey to the present. The events depicted in these stories occur during a 350- 
year time span, spanning 1611 to the 1960s. 


* Chapter V — Post Script, San Antonio. This section summarizes our life after Susan and | 
moved to San Antonio, Texas. 


¢ Chapter VI - Information Sources. This section cites databases and published literature used 
to develop this family history. Most of the sources are identified within the text. Prior 
published histories of the nine families are highlighted in bold font within the bibliography.

more yet to be learned about the lives of many other women in these nine families.

Comment on Terminology Used for Native Americans: Except when quoting verbatim from 
historical documents that often used the term “Indian” to refer to the indigenous peoples of 
North America, one of the following identifiers is used: Native Americans, Native Peoples, 
Native Tribes, or the name of specific tribal groups, such as Kiowa or Lenape. 


Comment of Terminology Used for Racial and Ethnic Groups: Except when quoting verbatim 
from historical documents, the current U.S. Census terminology is used for racial and ethnic 
groups with the primary groups being: White, Black, Asian, Native American, Pacific Islander or 
Mixed Race (race), and Hispanic (ethnicity). Occasionally, for clarity, a more precise origin 
identifier is used such as Caribbean Black.

Chapter II — Family Lineage Tables 


The lineage table for each family begins with the first ancestor that could be confidently 
identified. From generation to generation, | only focused on individuals who advanced the story 
toward 1971 when Susan and | were married. For example, one of our ancestors may have had 
six children, but only one of these offspring made relationship decisions that linked them to the 
family as it exists today. The story-advancing individual is identified in bold highlighting in the 
Children box of each generational summary. Across the nine families, 150 individuals are 
identified in the lineage tables. A roster of these individuals appears on pages 29-31. In a few 
instances, the names of spouses are unknown, and these are identified as such. 


The synopsis for each generation provides a brief snapshot of what is reliably known about the 
husband, wife and children comprising that generation, and key events that influenced their 
ife. Where indicated, information provided in the synopsis for some family members is further 
developed in Chapters III and IV. 


Unless otherwise indicated in Chapters II, III, and IV, the primary information sources were: the 
genealogical notebook compiled by Harold and Mildred Hendricson in the 1980s, the published 
amily histories highlighted in the bibliography, and my own research using the online search 
tools and the published works that appear in Chapter VI. A number of publications that might 
be of special interest to readers also are highlighted throughout the book. 


At times in Chapters Il, Ill, and IV, a degree of reasonable speculation was exercised, derived 
rom known facts, when describing family members’ actions and the potential catalysts for 
decisions. As you will read, my ancestors found themselves in remarkable circumstances. The 
available historical record often does not completely connect the dots about what happening 
and in what sequence for some of these events. At times, | had to piece together multiple and 
sometimes varying accounts of events, often with detail gaps. Hopefully, | have faithfully 
identified in the narrative where informed deductions were made in order to communicate an 
understandable story. | take responsibility for any errors, omissions, misinterpretation or 
inconsistencies that may occur in this family history.

The Hendricson family primarily originated in Germany and is comprised of 22 generations, 11 
in Europe pre-immigration and 11 in North America after immigration. As you will note when 
reviewing these generations, the family surname evolved considerably through the centuries. 
The final change in surname did not occur until 1845. 


Wihelmus B: Nydeggan, Mechtildis Schenck | 1220- | B: Nydeggan, Gr

Maiden name

Nydeggan. 

Synopsis: Wihelmus and Mechtildis Schenck van Nydeggan are the first family members in our 
Hendricson line that are mentioned in a public record. After 200 years in the Nydeggan area, 
the Schencks had risen from craftsmen to a position of status in the Duchy of Julich, one of the 
most powerful feudal jurisdictions in the 13" century German Federation. Wihelmus was 
appointed to the influential Pincerna Noster position (i.e., social coordinator, master of 
kitchens, commissary and vineyards) in the hierarchy of the Duchy, and became a confidant to 
Count Wilhelm IV von Julich. As discussed in Chapter III, Pre-lmmigration History, Wihelmus’ 
decision to sell most of the Schenck van Nydeggan property to the Church of Cologne had 
political ramifications and led to the demise of family influence in the Duchy, economic 
hardship for following generations and movement of his descendants to the Netherlands. 
Source: Moller W. West German Noble Families of the Middle Ages. Foundation for Medieval 
Genealogy (www.fmg.ac). Darmstadt: Verlag & Degener. 1995. Available via the Center for 
Medieval and Renaissance Studies. Oxford University Library. Accessed: December 8, 2022.

cluding Rutger Hendrikse. 
Synopsis: Henry and Henrji used Hendrikse as their surname, the first couple to move away 
from Schenck van Nydeck. Schenck family historians speculated that they selected Hendrikse to 
honor Henry’s father, Hendrich, or to recognize their similar first names, Henry and Henrji; | 
found no evidence for either theory. Another speculation is that they desired to distinguish 
themselves for unknown reasons from the Schenck van Nydeck dynasty at Blyenbeck. Both died 
and are buried in Nordheim, Germany, 240 miles away, which lends credence to this theory. 


Notes on Blyenbeck House: Generations 3 — 7 of the Schenck van Nydeck / Hendrikse family, 
spanning 1380 to 1580, were based in the village of Bleijenbeek (modern: Blyenbeck), on the 
Netherlands side of the border with the German Federation. In 1380, Hendrik Schenck van 
Nydeggan and wife Aleide van Rayde van Nydeggan purchased the property in a 14" century 
version of a bankruptcy sale, remodeled the main building and constructed a number of smaller 
homes, which they sold to other family members and local Bleijenbeek residents. Numerous 
family members lived in and around the Blyenbeck House, pictured below, for next 200 years. 


In the 1564, the Dutch soldier of fortune, Maarten Schenck Van Nydeggan Hendriksz, managed 
to swindle a brother of Barent Rutgerse Hendriksz, the rightful owner of Blyenbeck House, out of 
the property by threatening violence (for which Maarten was well known) and legal 
maneuvering. The later was accomplished by kidnapping the daughters of two local magistrates 
and threatening the young women with depravity unless the judges did his bidding, which was 
to evict the owners and deed the property over to Maarten. The Hendriksz family fought back in 
a protracted legal battle that was ultimately settled by the High Court of the Dutch Republic. In 
1571, the Court ordered a battalion of the Dutch army to physically evict Maarten and his family 
from Blyenbeck and required him to pay for damages incurred during his residence. More details 
about Maarten’s life appear in Chapter Ill. During World War II, the German army used the site 
as an operations center during the Battle of Arnheim where the Germans held off a British and 
American advance known as Operation Market Garden. The main structure on the property was 
destroyed in subsequent U.S. bombing raids as the Allies surged into Germany. 


A rendering of the Blyenbeck House painted in 1860 that 
depicts the remodeling by Aelide van Rayde and Hendrik 
Schenck van Nydeggan. The main structure was known as 
Castle Bleijenbeek prior to restoration.

Synopsis: Lambert was one of the most famous and successful of Dutch admirals in the 16" and

anything but beautiful. In contrast, Jennetje was considered to be quite attractive and was the 
subject of many portraits, which were sold commercially and were much sought after as the 
couple’s fame grew. Jennetje’s parents were Spanish, but lived in the Netherlands during the 
decades-long Dutch-Spanish War, known as the 80 Years War (War of Dutch Independence). 
This conflict is discussed in Chapter III, including Mooy Lambert’s pivotal role in the war and his 
other naval exploits.

A portrait of Jennetje Priem Nadal, wife of Lambert Hendriksz, by

read and commented upon popular Dutch fables to auditoriums

brother Hendrick, Ida Ede and husband James started a different familial line, the Way family,

Harold Maris 1919- |B: | B: Walla Walla, WA | Walla, WA | Mildred 1919- | B: | B: Walla Walla, WA | Walla, WA 


Hendricson i 2019 [p: Se WA 


Synopsis: Harold had an adventurous life from an early age. In 1935 at the age of 16, he was 
selected to represent Walla Walla at a National Boy Scout Conference in Washington DC, where 
he came down with a severe case of either measles, mumps or pneumonia (accounts from 
family members differ). Whatever it was, he could not return home with his troop leaders. He 
remained in a DC hotel by himself for several months to recover, eventually returning to Walla 
Walla (Walla’) by train. In 1941, he was a student at Whitman College in Walla? when Japan 
attacked Pear! Harbor, pulling the U.S. into the Second World War (WWII). Harold immediately 
volunteered and based on his academic record and scouting achievements, was selected for 
Officer Candidate School (OCS), which he completed at Forth Knox, Kentucky, ranking 3ina 
class of 167 candidates. Second Lieutenant Hendricson was assigned to the First Armored 
Division in the U.S. Fifth Army, and shipped to Ireland to prepare for the impending U.S. 
landings in North Africa. One month later, Harold was among the first wave of American 
soldiers to go ashore at Oran in Algeria in November 1942 and served in the first American tank 


44 


unit to see combat in North Africa against General Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Corps. He was 
captured during the disastrous (for the U.S.) Battle of Kasserine Pass in February 1943, but 
escaped in a nighttime breakout from a barbed wire pen in which he and several other U.S. and 
British soldiers were held. He was wounded later the same week when his unit repulsed a Nazi 
attack, but his Sherman M4 tank (pictured below) was blown up by a direct hit from a German 
Stuka light bomber, earning the first of six Purple Heart medals during WWII. During 1943, he 
engaged in several tank battles with German forces in North Africa until Rommel’s eventual 
surrender, was promoted to First Lieutenant, was awarded a second and third Purple Heart for 
combat wounds, and became a commander of an Armored Tank Company. 

During WWII, the equipment of an armored tank company consisted of 17 tanks, two jeeps, one 
supply truck, one half-track personnel carrier, and, when available, one tank retriever. The 
personnel included five officers (a 1st Lt. commander and four and Lts) and approximately 100 
enlisted men. Each Sherman tank was staffed by one officer and four soldiers. (Danby J. Men of 
Armor. Havertown, PA: Casemate Publishers. 2022) Harold’s letters to Mildred during WWII 
suggest that at least five of the tanks that he commanded were blown up by German artillery or 
aircraft fire during the North African and Italian Peninsula campaigns. He experienced wounds 
and burns from flying metal debris, aircraft machine gun fire and flaming gas spewing from 
tanks during several of these explosions. The casualty and mortality rate of U.S. tank company 
officers in North Africa and Italy, mostly in their early 20s, fresh out of OCS school, and literally 
learning on the job, was very high (Danby, 2022). 


After Rommel’s surrender in North Africa, Harold was transferred to Sicily to prepare for the 
invasion of Italy. After training under General George Patton, he participated in the Allied 
invasion of Italy commencing with the landing at Salerno, south of Naples, in September 1943, 
and then the landing at Anzio Beach, further north and closer to Rome, an ill-conceived attempt 
to outflank the entrenched Nazi defense in January 1944, where he and thousands of U.S. and 
British soldiers were encircled and trapped for nearly five months. During the battle that finally 
led to the break out from the Anzio beachhead, he was awarded the first of his two silver stars 
for leading an attack on a panzer tank column that stymied a major German counterattack, and 
then opened access to a paved highway that became one of the main route for troops and 
vehicles to flow off the beach. (Bowditch J, Komer R. Anzio Beachhead. Nashville, TN: The 
Battery Press. 1954.) 


After the Anzio breakout, he commanded a tank company (Company B, 1st Battalion, 1st 
Armored Division, a component of the U.S. Fifth Army) for a year as the Americans, British and 
a multi-national force including Italian partisans, a Jewish Brigade, Brazilians, South Africans, 
Moroccans, New Zealanders, Canadians, Polish troops and African-American (Buffalo Soldiers) 
and Asian-American (Nisei Brigade) units fought their way north through the rugged and 
mountainous Italian peninsula. During one of many attacks on Nazi forces, Harold suffered a 
catastrophic head injury when the cement lined turret lid of his tank was accidently slammed 
into the side of his head by a crewmember that did not see Harold stick his head up through the 
hatch. He was evacuated to a recuperation hospital near London for two months. He rejoined 
his unit for the final push through northern Italy that commenced in February 1945. 


On April 23, 1945, near the end of the Italian campaign, now Captain Hendricson was awarded 


45 


a second silver star for leading an attack on a German position at Sorboto that led to the 
capture of 600 soldiers including nine generals and 64 artillery pieces. The attack helped secure 
a bridgehead across the Po River. Two days later, he jumped off his tank to lead a search along 
the banks of the Po River for a missing Lieutenant under his command. During the search, he 
was hit by a German bazooka salvo from the other side of the Po, suffering shrapnel injuries to 
his hands and legs. Harold rejected evacuation so he could participate in the final attack and 
crossing of the Po on April 26, 1945. Three days later he participated in a reconnaissance 
mission into Milan to determine the level of German resistance, which turned out to be 
minimal, and his entire unit, the 1st Tank Battalion, occupied Milan’s central plaza on May 1, 
where they were fed breakfast and lunch by joyous Milan citizens. (Howe G. Capt. Harold M. 
Hendricson, In: Battle History of the 1% Armored Division, “Old Ironsides.” Pgs. 412-430. 
Washington DC; Combat Forces Press. 1954) 


After the German surrender in Italy, Harold was assigned to the U.S. Army of Occupation in 
Germany where he served as provisional mayor of Ulm, a town in Bavaria, for a few months. In 
this transitional governance program, American and British officers managed German cities in 
the immediate aftermath of the war. Finally discharged in 1946, he pondered not returning to 
Walla Walla, but eventually headed back home where he re-united with Mildred. The couple 
had known each other casually before the war. A few months after his return, Harold and 
Mildred married on November 16, 1946. The story of how their relationship endured four years 
of WWII separation is told in Chapter IV via excerpts from their war correspondence. Over the 
next four years, Harold worked in his parent’s grocery business, known as the Community 


Grocery, which primarily served migrant workers in the onion and sugar beet fields near Walla 
Walla. Harold and Mildred lived in an apartment over the grocery store when their first child, 
William Dennis Hendricson, was born in 1948, followed by Shirley in 1950. 


When the Korean War broke out in 1950, Harold rushed to re-activate, which was a challenge 
because he was listed as disabled due to his many WWII injuries. Ultimately, he prevailed and 
after another training stint at Fort Knox, served two years as a tank commander and training 
officer in Korea, earning a Bronze star for his service with the 25" Infantry Division. Harold 
elected to stay in the regular army after returning from Korea. Over the next 20 years, he rose 
to the rank of full Colonel, commanded an armored battalion in Germany, was a brigade 
commander during a second tour in Korea, graduated from the Industrial War College of the 
Armed Forces, completed his bachelors degree in political science at the University of Nebraska 
(the first Hendricson college graduate since Hendrick Hendriksz 300 years earlier), and held a 
managerial position at the Pentagon at the end of his career. Overall, Harold, Mildred, my sister 
Shirley and | were stationed in Kentucky, California, Texas, Virginia (twice) in the U.S., and in 
five towns in Germany during Harold’s two European tours between 1956 and 1965. 


After leaving the army, Harold and Mildred spent a year in a Winnebago evaluating retirement 
spots on the West Coast before purchasing a beachfront home on several acres near the small 
town of Freeland on Whidbey Island, Washington. Harold’s retirement passions were salmon 
fishing, upgrading numerous boats he purchased, creating gemstone jewelry in a rock shop he 
built on the property, rooting for the Seahawks (he and Mildred were season ticket holders 
from the Hawk’s inaugural season) and traveling the country in motor homes.

Shirley Hendricson (1950 - ) 


Shirley Hendricson in a 2007 photo, has lived in 
Germany, Virginia, Maryland, Illinois and 
Whidbey Island, Washington. 


Shirley Hendricson, daughter of Harold and Mildred Hendricson, was born in Walla Walla, 
Washington, on January 8, 1950, the same year that Harold re-joined the military. Shirley’s 
youth, like mine, was characterized by frequent movement from place to place and school to 
school as her father pursued his military career. By the time of their graduation from high 
school, Shirley and | had each attended at least 18 different schools (sometimes several in the 
same year) in such diverse locations as Pacific Grove, California, Lowden, Washington, Killen, 
Texas, Hampton, Virginia, six towns in Germany (Mannheim, Ulm, Goeppingen, Bamburg, 
Nuremburg and Stuttgart) and Fairfax, Virginia. 


As Army Brats with constant 
moving, Hendricson kids spent 
a lot of time together in their 
early years. Shirley may be 
wondering ... “and why do! 
have to stand by the rifle?” 


During the first grade, Shirley bounced back and forth between a school near swank Carmel, 
California on the Pacific Ocean and a four-room school (1% — g grades) in tiny Lowden 
Washington amidst the dry hills of rural eastern Washington. During second grade, Shirley 
attended four different schools in Washington, Texas and Germany. Talk about a unique 
education! Despite all the school switching and the attendant social disruptions, Shirley was an 
excellent student, maintaining strong grades throughout.

Shirley graduated from George Mason University in Virginia and commenced a diverse business 
career, finding success in a number of fields including fashion and design, professional 
associations, the travel industry, continuing education for public school teachers, landscaping, 
and managerial positions for a hardware store, a vineyard and event center, and a Wild Birds 
Unlimited (WBU) franchise. The WBU franchise has been Shirley’s greatest success story. She 
bought a down and out, failing store, and moved the entire operation to a new town (Freeland, 
Washington) in a storefront that she completely remodeled. Starting with almost no customer 
base from the previous owners, Shirley steadily built up her WBU clientele and sales volume 
over a ten-year period to a high level. Accomplishing this in a rural area (located on an island in 
the Puget Sound) with low population density was not an easy task by any means. Customer 
loyalty was critical. Through the opening process and the establishment years for the store, 
Shirley also served as the primary caretaker for her mother, Mildred, who suffered a sequence 
of strokes contributing to dementia, which resulted in several lengthy nursing home 
rehabilitations, adding to Shirley’s range of responsibilities. 


Culminating a long relationship, Shirley married David Putnam Osborne (1946-1996) in 1992 in 
a ceremony at her parent’s Whidbey Island home, exchanging vows with the Puget Sound as a 
backdrop. David was an MIT graduate and also an accomplished yacht restorer on the east 
coast, in constant demand for his craftsmanship. David’s specialty was restoration of 25-40 foot 


51 


Vindo sail yachts made in Sweden with teak or mahogany cabins, decking and interiors. (Mate 
F. The World’s Best Sailboats. New York: W.W. Norton. 2008.) The couple purchased a home in 
Silver Spring, Maryland. Unfortunately, David passed way in 1996.

Mountains. Shirley and Mildred were dedicated gardeners, with a focus on raspberries.

Morgan Lineage Table 


The Morgan family that is linked to our Hendricson family originated in Wales and is comprised 
of 13 generations that were identified with confidence: seven in Europe pre-immigration and six 
in North America after immigration. 


An old Welsh joke goes something like this: “If a Morgan shrugs his shoulders on a street in 
Wales, he will almost certainly bump into two other Morgans.” As subsequently discussed in the 
pre-Immigration history of the Morgans (Chapter Ill), there is a high frequency of the Morgan 
surname in Wales, and marriages among different branches of the Morgan clan were common 
throughout history. Consequently, there has been controversy and inaccuracy in prior 
Hendricson and Morgan histories about designating THE Morgan line in Wales that represents 
the appropriate starting point for tracing Hendricson-related Morgan immigration to North 
America. | am confident that the lineage depicted below represents the Morgan line directly 
associated with the Hendricson family in North America.

Notes on Bosworth Field: This was the final and most significant battle of the War of Roses 
between two houses (lines of noble families) contending for the English throne: the Lancaster’s 
who wore a tunic badge decorated with a red rose and the Yorks, whose tunic badge was a 
white rose. The current king in 1485 (Richard III, a York) was killed early in the battle, and the 
insurgent Lancastrian forces led by Henry Tudor ultimately defeated his army. Henry was 
installed as King Henry VII. The Welsh, led by Sir John Morgan, supported the Lancaster House by 


55 


providing a safe harbor for Henry’s army to land, comprised 25% of the Lancastrian soldiers, and 
fought under the red rose in several battles leading up to Bosworth Field.

Notes on The Book of Llandaff: The Book is an account of people and events in Glamorgan 
County, Wales including Cardiff and Llandaff Village, originated in 1125 by clerics at Llandaff 
Cathedral. The Book reports property and business ownership, acquisitions, sales and taxes in 
Glamorgan with focus on land donated or sold to the Church or to Anglo Saxon Kings beginning 
in the 7" century. The Book also documents marriages, births and deaths, residences, 
construction of buildings and prominent social events over a thousand-year period. The original 
writers used 149 early medieval Welsh records, known as charter scrolls, to document property 
transactions and events in the preceding centuries. The Book also includes biographies of noted 
family groups (i.e., clans such as the Morgans) in the Llandaff area. The Book was updated 
continuously through the 18°" century, and is thousands of pages in length. It has been digitized 
by the National Library of Wales. A 150-page segment of the Book can be viewed at the Llandaff 
Cathedral. Elements of Morgan family history are derived from the Book of Llandaff. (Sims- 
Williams P. The Book of Llandaff as a Historical Source. Suffolk: Boydell and Brewer. 2019)

Synopsis: Morgan graduated from Cambridge University, completing legal training in London
