Notes on David Morgan: David Morgan (1721-1813) was likely adopted by Morgan and 
Catherine Morgan and was probably mixed race, Native American-European. David worked as a 
surveyor early in adulthood. In this capacity, he was employed by notable colonial Virginians 
Patrick Henry, Peter Jefferson (father of Thomas Jefferson) and Thomas Fairfax (Lord Fairfax), 
who owned much of Virginia west of the Shenandoah Valley. Through Lord Fairfax, David was 
hired to train and mentor a 17 year old by the name of George Washington who desired to 
become a surveyor. Between 1749-1752, David and George Washington surveyed the land 
holdings of Lord Fairfax in the western region of the Virginia Colony to establish boundaries 
between Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. During this expedition, they completed surveys 
and maps for nearly 200 parcels of land that now comprise the eastern neck of the state of West 
Virginia. Washington and David Morgan then surveyed and mapped land that Washington had 
inherited on the Ohio River. After Washington departed to join the Virginia Regiment in the 
British colonial Army late in 1752, David mapped the entire course of the Ohio River that now 
serves as the western boundary of West Virginia. During their surveying work, Washington met 
David’s younger brother Zackquill (Zack) Morgan, and established a long-standing relationship. 


David served in a Virginia militia unit of the British Colonial Army as a scout and translator during 
the French and Indian Wars in the 1750s. He was with his brother Zack and George Washington 
during the ill-fated Braddock’s Campaign in Pennsylvania. During the final battle near the 
Monongahela River in 1755, David was wounded by a saber blow to his face when he pulled a 
French officer from his horse. In spite of the wound, he and Zack helped George Washington 
organize a retreat of the surviving troops, saving many lives. Zack, David, Daniel Boone and other 
frontier marksmen kept the French soldiers and their Native allies at a distance as Washington 
rounded up remaining troops, organized litters to carry the wounded, and executed a retreat. 
(Preston D. Braddock’s Defeat: The Battle of the Monongahela and the Road to Revolution. 
Oxford: Oxford University Press. 2015.)

During the Revolutionary War, David served with brother Zack in a Virginia regiment comprised

Sections III and IV), led riflemen units during the Battles of Cowpens, Fort Laurens and Guilford

(WVA), he established several towns including Fort Morgan, PettyJohn and Fairmont, and built

married Hendrickson’s; one son married a daughter of Okey Hendrickson and a daughter

Notes on Levi Morgan: Levi (1766-1828) followed his parents Zack and Drusilla to West Virginia 
around 1780, but soon after moved westward to the newly opened Kentucky Territory, which 
became a state in 1792. Levi staked a claim to 700 acres at the intersection of the Salt River and 
the Ohio River in Northern Kentucky where he farmed for the rest of his life. However, Levi is 
primarily known for his frontiersman and Indian fighter exploits, which earned him considerable 
fame and were detailed in novels and paperbacks about 18" century frontier life. (Eckert A. The 
Frontiersman (7" Ed.). New York: Bantam Books. 1980) This literature, especially the 
paperbacks (heavily illustrated brief novels, similar to modern graphic novels), became wildly 
popular in eastern U.S. cities in the early years of the nation, stimulated interest in frontier life, 
and promoted migration to Kentucky, West Virginia and Ohio. 


Example of a Frontiersman paperback novel. Conway WF. The Incredible 
Adventures of Daniel Boone’s Kid Brother — Squire Boone. 1818. Reprinted - 
Lexington, KY: Squire Boone Village Printing. 1992. Available from Amazon 
Books. As an example of the public’s fascination with accounts of 
frontiersmen heroics, Davy Crockett’s Almanacks, which started in 1832 
before his death and continued annually until 1856, his 1834 autobiography, 
and the touring play based on his myth, The Lion of the West, were the most 
popular paperback series, book and theatrical performance of the 1830s. 
Hutton PA. Davy Crockett, Still King of the Wild Frontier, And a Hell of A Nice 
Guy. Texas Monthly. www.texasmontly.com. November 1986. Accessed: 
March 12, 2023. 


Levi often served with Daniel Boone (1734-1820), Simon Kenton (1755-1836), known as the 
Daniel Boone of Ohio (Eckert, 1980), and once with his uncle David Morgan during territorial 
militia and federal government campaigns against the native Miami, Shawnee and Delaware 
tribes in Ohio and Indiana. These tribes had formed a Confederacy to protect their homelands 
from the disorganized onslaught of European settlers. The entire series of campaigns, which 
occurred between 1788 and 1794, was labeled as the Northwest War. Quite often, militia or 
U.S. army leaders ignored Levi’s advice, which was: show of force first, negotiate second, but if 
necessary to fight, avoid European style tactics. Consequently, federal militia often blundered 
into ill-conceived engagements with the well-organized Tribal Confederacy. 


On November 4, 1791, the most disastrous of these blunders occurred near the Wabash River 
in Ohio (i.e., Battle of the Wabash; St. Clair’s Defeat). A federal army of 1200 soldiers was led by 
General Arthur St. Clair. He was insistent on standard European tactics, which included only 


61 


fighting during daylight and camping in open fields for a more orderly deployment. Despite 
being warned by Levi Morgan that a large force of Miami, Shawnee and Lenape tribesmen was 
beginning to encircle the army’s position, St. Clair failed to relocate the camp to a more 
favorable position in a nearby forest or even to increase the number of sentries. His troops 
were surprised in a pre-dawn attack from all sides by the Confederacy and virtually wiped-out. 
Nearly 700 U.S. soldiers were killed, and another 400 were captured and later ransomed back 
for weapons. It was the most substantial defeat and largest U.S. loss of life in any battle with 
Native tribes, far exceeding Little Big Horn. (Eid LV. American Indian Military Leadership: St. 
Clair’s 1791 Defeat. Journal of Military History. 1993; 57(1): 71-88) 


After this experience, Levi refused further service with U.S. military during the campaign to 
clear tribes from the Northwest Territory. Levi turned his focus to farming and serving as a 
hunting guide, mostly for Easterners and Europeans who wanted to experience the Frontier 
Spirit. However, Levi still managed to get into conflicts with the Miami tribe who claimed he led 
hunting parties onto tribal lands and depleted the wildlife. On one hunting trip, which he 
advertised as a frontier safari in eastern newspapers, several Miami warriors kidnapped Levi 
and brought him to their main encampment near present day Franklin, Ohio. At the camp, Levi 
endured three days of tribal torture rituals including being hung from a horizontal bar by metal 
claws hooked into his chest, as depicted in the 1970 movie, A Man Called Horse, starring 
Richard Harris. The movie, which depicts an Englishman named John Morgan on an American 
Frontier Hunting Safari, is based on Levi Morgan’s experiences with Native Americans. Levi died 
in 1828 while hunting near his farm at Salt Lick when a early fall blizzard surprised him. He 
sought shelter in a hallowed out Sycamore tree, but froze to death over night.

James 1771- B: Bunker Hill, WVA set) 1777- B: | B: Monongalia Va_| Va

Children: James and Dorothy had 13 children including Drusilla Morgan. 

Synopsis: James was less of a frontiersman than his father Zack or brother Levi. He operated 
several businesses in the vicinity of Bunker Hill. Dorothy was a schoolteacher and also 
functioned as an accountant for the family businesses. James was a prominent abolitionist and 
campaigned for WVA admission into the United States as a free state. In June 1855, a gang of 
pro-slavery militia murdered the elderly James as he was gardening at his Bunker Hill home. 
Virtually all of James and Dorothy’s children, including Drusilla Morgan, moved north into the 
free states of Indiana and Illinois between 1810 and 1850. They sought opportunity to be 
productive farmers without competition from large slave plantations that dominated 
agriculture in Virginia, and which they feared would emerge in West Virginia. The efforts of 
James and other abolitionists finally paid off when pro-Union groups rebuffed efforts by pro- 
slavery elements to derail the statehood initiative. WVA was admitted into the Union, after 
extensive political maneuvering, as a border state on June 20, 1863, eight years to the day 
after James’ assassination. Under terms stipulated by President Lincoln, WVA was allowed 
admission to the Union on the condition that the state constitution must include a provision 
calling for gradual elimination of slavery, a demand that was ultimately met.

Synopsis: David Rideout worked as a lumberjack and as a fishing guide at his family’s lodge at

arrival. With Drusilla’s blessing, Amanda directed the creation of the Morgan farm near Albany 
and remained in charge after her marriage to David Rideout. With David’s frequent absences,

Maris Lineage Table 
The Maris surname originated in France, but the Maris line linked to our Hendricson family 
moved to England at some point in the centuries after the Norman Invasion in 1066. The 
circumstances prompting the relocation are not certain, but religious persecution of French 
Protestants (i.e., Huguenots) is a likely cause, especially during the 15" and 16" centuries. The 
Maris line is comprised of 11 generations that could be identified with confidence: two in 
England pre-immigration and nine in North America after immigration.

built a substantial, by early colonial standards, house for his family, which Alice named “Home 
House” that was located on State Road in Springfield, PA, today a suburb of Philadelphia.

Notes on the Maris Home House in Springfield PA: No illustrations could be found, but the 
house was described as having seven ground floor rooms, a cellar and an attic. The original 
Home House stood until 1800 when a Maris descendent replaced the wood structure with a 
two story stone and wood house with five bedrooms that was continuously occupied by the 
Maris family until 1985, when it was remodeled into a office building for three law practices.

Notes on Free States in Northwest Territory: Formally known as the Territory West of the Ohio 
River, the Northwest Territory was established in 1787 by the Congress of the Confederation, 
which existed 1781-1789 during the Articles of Confederation phase of our nation’s history. The 
Northwest Territory comprised the states of Ohio, Indiana, Michigan, Illinois, Wisconsin and a 
portion of Minnesota. The U.S. formally acquired these lands in the 1783 Treaty of Paris 
between Great Britain and the American Colonies. Development of a governance structure for 
this vast swath of land was triggered by the uncontrolled influx of hunters, land speculators and 
homesteaders into the region after the Revolutionary War, leading to constant conflicts among 
these groups, and often deadly conflicts with the native Miami, Delaware, Shawnee and 
Potawatomi tribes. 


The Northwest Territory in 1787. As individual 
regions within the Territory met population and 
governance criteria and were admitted into the U.S. 
as states, the Territory shrunk, and was dissolved as 
a government entity in 1803. McCullough D. The

ry (1787) 


The governing structure for the territory, known as the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 provided a 
Bill of Natural Rights for residents, which included: prohibition of slavery, free public education 
up to age 14, guaranteed freedom of expression and religious practice, trial by peers and a fee 
simple land ownership concept in which property ownership was in perpetuity, rather than a 
term-limited lease system which was the common practice in 18" century colonial America. 


These freedoms proved to be popular, especially with individuals like Aaron and Sarah Maris 
who abhorred slavery and also who could not compete in a slave-powered agricultural economy. 
With a territorial government structure in place to regulate immigration into the region and 
establish cities based on a specified street grid and planning protocol, the European population 
grew dramatically while the Native American population, after a campaign of eviction (i.e., the 
Northwest War) declined precipitously. Pressured by federal and territorial militia, tribes were 
driven north into Canada or west into the Great Plains. Although our Maris line moved 
westward, the majority of other Maris families elected to put down roots within Indiana, Illinois 
and other states evolving from the Northwest Territory.

Notes on the Roger Maris Connection: Like much of the U.S. male population in the 1950s and 
60s, Harold Hendricson was a fan of baseball, especially the New York Yankees. My dad and | 
attended many Yankee games in NYC, and other cities whenever we were in the States, often 
driving long distances to catch Yankee road games in Detroit, Chicago or Washington DC. Part of 
the attraction was Roger Maris, who clubbed 61 homers in 1961 to break Babe Ruth’s long- 
standing record. During that season, Maris and teammate Mickey Mantle smashed equal 
numbers of homers all summer until Mantle developed a serious hip infection, requiring 
drainage, from a botched flu injection and he missed the last two weeks of the season, finishing 
with 54 dingers. Maris became a celebrity and even made a movie with the already iconic 
Mantle. In the 1960s, it was often stated that Roger Maris was a relative via the family line of 
Mabel Maris (Hendricson), a connection that | was happy to mention, erroneously, during 
baseball conversations throughout my life. 


However, Roger was not a member of Mabel’s midwestern Maris 
family. In fact, his real name was not Maris; it was Maras, 
uncomfortably pronounced Mar—-ass. In 1903, Roger's 
grandparents immigrated from Croatia to Minnesota where they 
changed their name to Maris after tiring of taunting about the 
Maras pronunciation. Roger’s parents later moved their family to 
South Dakota where he was a multi-sport star in high school, 
especially excelling in football. In a 1952 game he scored seven 
touchdowns in five ways: kick-off returns (2), punt returns (2), 
interception (1), TD run (1), and a TD pass reception (1), still a 
national record. In the 50s, the big money was in baseball, so he 
turned down 33 college scholarships and signed with the Cleveland 
Indians. Roger was somewhat the rebel, and reverted to using

Notes on Lowden (Frenchtown), Washington and the Battle of Frenchtown: European 
trappers in Canada and Canadian Metis established the community now known as Lowden in 
the 1700s. Metis are the offspring of unions between French/Canadian trappers and Indigenous 
Peoples in the Canadian Provinces of Alberta and British Columbia and the Canadian Northwest 
Territories. By the end of the 1g" century, the majority of trappers, and their families, in 
Washington and Oregon were second or third generation Metis. Beginning in the 1770s, Metis 
trappers started to winter in an area west of Walla Walla attracted by a stream for water and 
bathing, abundant grassland for grazing animals, and substantial wildlife for food supply. A tent 
settlement was established and called Le Village des Canadiens. (Jackson JC. Children of the Fur 
Trade: Forgotten Metis of the Pacific Northwest. Corvallis: Oregon State University. 2007) The 
village stream came to be known as Dry Creek, because that’s what it was in the summer - dry. 
By the 1820s, Metis started to live year-round in Le Village des Canadiens, joined by elderly 
members of the Walla Walla Tribe, creating a community of 500 people. In 1823, the first 
permanent log cabins were built on the western edge of the village by French trapper Michel 
Pellissier and Metis partner, Catherine D’Aubuchan, and by Lizette Walla Walla Lavadour, 
(1817-1891) daughter of a former tribal chief, and French partner Joseph LaRocque. A general 
store, chapel, stable, meeting hall and lodge followed. In 1845, the community was nicknamed 
Frenchtown by wagon train masters who traded with the Metis on their way to Oregon. The 
Frenchtown nickname stuck, even with Metis residents. In the 1850s, substantial numbers of 
White emigrants decided that the Walla Walla area was just as suitable for homesteading as 
western Oregon, leading to pressure on the U.S. Army to clear the land of Indigenous Peoples. 
(Barman J. French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women in the Making of the Pacific 
Northwest. Vancouver, BC: University of British Columbia Press. 2014) 


In 1854, displays of military manpower and firepower, threats of violence and several incidents 
of actual violence failed to induce the Cayuse, Walla Walla, Umatilla, Nez Perce and Yakima 
tribes to vacate their ancestral homelands. Fearing forced removal, the tribes finally agreed to 
negotiate a best conditions obtainable treaty with the U.S. military and the U.S. 
Superintendents of Indian Affairs for the Territories of Washington and Oregon (Trafzer C. 
Walla Walla Treaty Council 1855. Oregon Encyclopedia. Oregon Historical Society 
www.oregonencyclopedia.org. September 26, 2023. Accessed: May 23, 2024) In the resultant 
treaty, the tribes traded 60,000 square miles of their ancestral Washington range for 780 
square miles in northeastern Oregon, two other smaller tracts near Umatilla, Oregon and 
received $200,000 and farming equipment in compensation. (State of Washington. Governor’s 
Office of Indian Affairs www.goia.gov. Treaty of Walla Walla, 1855. Accessed: May 23, 2024) 


| In May 1855, 5,000 members of the Walla Walla 
and four other tribes, led by 15 elected delegates, 
met with the Territorial Governors of Oregon and 
Washington and their Indian Affairs Directors to 
negotiate boundaries for tribal lands in light of 
White settlers’ demands for homesteading rights. 


Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. 
Accessed: 7/18/2024. 


82 


The treaty defined areas in Washington that were off-limits to White settlers, and also allowed 
the tribes to continue hunting and fishing on their homelands. Settlers breached the treaty 
almost immediately by squatting on restricted lands, and violent conflicts occurred when 
tribesmen attempted to hunt and fish on these lands per stipulations of the treaty. After his 
pleas to the U.S. Army and the Washington Territorial Office of Indian Affairs for treaty 
enforcement were ignored, the Walla Walla chief, Peopeomoxmox, formed a homelands 
protection confederation among the Cayuse, Umatilla and Yakima tribes. 


The tribes were provided a fairly lenient timetable for relocation, and not surprisingly, few 
Native families departed voluntarily or promptly. In July of 1855 at the Fort Walla Walla trading 
post, Anglo settlers, Walla Walla tribesmen and several Metis residents of Frenchtown accused 
each other of stealing horses, which led to the inevitable gunplay. Several Natives, Metis and 
settlers were wounded in the exchange of gunfire, and one settler soon after died of his 
injuries. The catalyst for this incident was ambiguous. However, hoping to avoid further 
violence or recriminations against Native Peoples, Peopeomoxmox presented a formal apology 
and provided winter robes and horses as gifts to settlers. In spite of Peopeomoxmoy’s efforts 
to de-escalate the situation, persistent settler agitation led the Territorial Governor to order the 
Metis and Walla Wallians to vacate Frenchtown in 30 days. 


A sketch of Walla Walla Chief Peopeomoxmox (1790-1855), drawn by 
Gustav Sohon, a U.S. Army officer, during the 1855 treaty negotiations 
with the U.S. military and Washington and Oregon Territory 
representatives. 

Image source: Yakima Herald-Republic, www.yakimaherald.com in an article 
titled: Battle of Walla Walla Had A Local Context. December 16, 2022. Accessed: 
7/19/2024. 


Although a few Metis families in Frenchtown headed back to Canada rather than depart for arid 
Oregon, most ignored the evacuation order, as did the Walla Wallians. Fueled by distorted 
accounts of the Fort Walla Walla incident, a militia of 360 white settlers named the Oregon 
Mounted Volunteers (OMV), formed in the Willamette Valley in November 1855 without 
knowledge of the U.S. Army or the Governors of Oregon and Washington. The OMV marched 
toward Frenchtown along the Columbia River with the goal of forcing the Metis and Walla 
Wallians to leave. At Umatilla, members of the Walla Walla tribe along with Cayuse, Umatilla 
and Yakima confederates, numbering around 300 tribesmen, began to follow the OMV, riding 
along a ridgeline about a mile north of the militia unit as it moved east toward Frenchtown 
along the Walla Walla River. (Jackson JC. The First Regiment of the Oregon Mounted Volunteers 
and the Yakima Indian War of 1855-56. Portland: Ye Galeon Press. 1996) 


The OMV reached Frenchtown on December 6, 1855 and the following morning attacked at 
dawn, marching across Dry Creek and into the village during an intense snowstorm. The Metis 
and the tribal confederation counter-attacked, resulting in casualties on both sides. After the 
initial assault and counter-attack, Peopeomoxmox and five elders (i.e., tribal leadership council) 
surrendered to the OMV in hopes of curtailing the violence. One elder was left behind with the 


83 


Metis leaders, which included Lizette Walla Walla’s daughter, Elizabeth. Peopeomoxmox and 
the Council were led away by a group of OMV troops to an abandoned Jesuit mission, where 
they were tortured and then murdered. Their bodies were scalped, mutilated, and thrown onto 
the trail leading into Frenchtown. Predictably, Frenchtown resistance hardened. Three days of 
back and forth battle ensued. The OMV and Metis repeatedly captured and then lost the cabins 
on the western edge of town near Dry Creek, and the OMV failed in attempts to torch the 
community. Although the battle was inconclusive, on the December 11 the Metis leadership 
agreed to cease hostilities and “painfully remove ourselves from our home.” At the time of 
their surrender, Elizabeth and the other Metis leaders did not know that the OMV were also 
planning to withdraw later the same day. The OMV were dismayed by the fierce resistance, the 
heavy casualties within their unit, and were concerned about the repercussions of 
Peopeomoxmox’s murder. And, they were almost out of ammunition. The OMV happily 
accepted the Metis offer, and quickly left the area before a regular Army garrison could arrive 
to investigate. The majority of the Metis in Frenchtown returned to Canada, and most of the 
Walla Wallians reluctantly relocated to the small reservation in northeastern Oregon. The U.S. 
Army conducted an inquiry into the murder of Peopeomoxmox and the elders, but issued no 
findings. No one in the OMV was punished or reprimanded. (Jackson JC. A Little War of Destiny: 
The Yakima/Walla Walla Indian War of 1855-1856. Amazon: CreateSpace Independent 
Publishing Platform (CIPP). March 26, 2011. Amazon merged CIPP into Kindle Direct Publishing 
www.kdp.amazon.com in 2018. Accessed from KDP on May 23, 2024) 


In spite of the urgency to clear the land for white settlement, Frenchtown was largely 
unoccupied until a grain storage facility with a railroad siding was constructed in 1910. Soon 
after, a school, grocery/hardware store, gas station and other businesses were built. The 
community was renamed Lowden in 1916 after Francis Lowden, a local farmer who led the 
revitalization. Archie and Maude Dennis built their home and purchased pasture on the 
western edge of Lowden in 1916-1917. The property borders Dry Creek. The Frenchtown 
homes of Michel Pellissier and Catherine D’Aubuchan and Lizette Walla Walla and Joseph 
LaRocque, both adjacent to Dry Creek, almost certainly existed on this land.

Notes on Manifest Destiny and Displacement of Indigenous Americans 

Archie and Maude Dennis played no role in the removal of the Walla Walla and other tribes 
from the land that became their homestead in Lowden. Yet, they and millions of European 
immigrants to the Eastern Seaboard in the 17" and 18" centuries and westward moving 
settlers in the 19" century, benefitted from the unwavering policy of the U.S. government to 
clear indigenous Americans from their homelands by any means necessary. By 1871, when the 
U.S. Congress prohibited additional treaty-making with Native Americans, 374 treaties had 
been enacted over the previous 100 years, almost all involving land acquisition and population 
relocation. (Pucha FP. American Indian Treaties: History of a Political Anomaly. Berkeley, CA: 
University of California Press. 1997) Politicians who wrote the treaties and the congressional 
acts to remove tribes from land desired by Whites, and the settlers benefitted via inexpensive 
access to property, had no problem with these actions because they considered Indigenous 
tribes, especially those west of the Mississippi River, to be nomads, with no societal 
infrastructure recognizable to Europeans and no legal jurisdiction over lands they hunted or 
occasionally farmed. (Pucha, 1997) 


After 1800, the U.S. government came to understand the great expanse of territory beyond the 
Mississippi that awaited resource harvesting and settlement in spite of an inconvenient 
Indigenous population between 600,000 and 1,200,000. To build a case for westward 
expansion, presidential candidate James K. Polk used the concept of Manifest Destiny in the 
1844 campaign to justify the “obvious (manifest) and certain (destiny) belief” that it was a 
divine and inevitable mission of the U.S. to spread from Atlantic to Pacific, and instill “the 
American Way of Life,” an early expression of American exceptionalism. (Byrnes ME. James K. 
Polk. A Biographical Companion. Bloomsbury Digital Resources. ABC-CLIO. www.abc-clio.com. 
2001) Perceptions of racial dominance were intertwined with territorial lust in Manifest 
Destiny, primarily the notion that the American Anglo-Saxon race was “separate, innately 
superior, and destined to bring good government, commercial prosperity and Christianity to the 
American continent.” (Horsman R. Race and Manifest Destiny: The Origins of American Racial 
Anglo-Saxonism. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press. 1981). From 1600 to 1900, 4.7 
million Native Americans died from warfare with Whites, European diseases and the effects of 
forced displacement. For example, during the Indian Removal Act of 1830, 100,000 Creek, 
Choctaw, Chickasaw and Cherokee were relocated to bleak reservations in Oklahoma. Many 
thousands died during this journey known as the “Trail of Tears.” (Fitzgerald D. The Cherokee 
Trail of Tears. Portland, OR: Graphic Arts Books. 2008) 


The 1830 Indian Removal Act, instigated by President Andrew 
Jackson, allowed land agents to acquire 50 million acres of Native 
American homeland in Alabama, Mississippi and Georgia via bribes, 
false promises of better land, threats and violence. The 1830 Act 
became the model for hundreds of subsequent treaties that 
opened Indian Land to Whites. (Fitzgerald, 2008)

members enjoyed many trips together including: Hawaii, Alaska, Germany, Holland, Italy, 
Cozumel, Catalina Island, Las Vegas, New Orleans, Atlanta, Yosemite, and the Grand Canyon.

Goodman Lineage Table 


The Goodman family that is linked to our Hendricson family had its origins in Northern France, 
with indication that they may have migrated from Denmark. The family moved to England at 
some point after the Norman Invasion (1066) and settled in a rural area of central England. The 
Goodman line is comprised of 13 generations that were identified with confidence: five in 
Europe pre-immigration and eight in North America after immigration. A genealogical website 
known as “Goodman Ancestors of Early Colonial and Pre-Civil War America” supplemented my 
research as an information source for 15""- 19"" century Goodman history.

of which could be leased for vacations, conferences, weddings and other events. British royalty 
used Southill for knighting ceremonies and the following reception and dinner. More details on 
Southill Park appear in Chapter III.

Mary, (together at this point in time), added several more businesses on the new property 
including a silver smith. They built a new home for themselves, constructed several other 
houses that they sold to other families, and expanded the horse breeding operation. 
Essentially, they created a small town, which came to be known as Roundabout Creek. 


One of the children of Robert and Mary Goodman, Benjamin Lewis Goodman (1727-1781), was 
an officer in the Little River, Virginia regiment of the Southern Continental Army under the 
command of General Daniel Morgan (from a different Morgan line). In November 1781, shortly 
after the British surrender at Yorktown, Benjamin, with six other officers and seven enlisted 
men, walked out of a lunch celebrating the Yorktown victory at a tavern in Hayes Station, South 
Carolina. Tory militia, hiding behind surrounding buildings, suddenly attacked the 14 colonial 
soldiers in front of the tavern. Goodman and colleagues fought their way to a blockhouse (a 
fort-like structure used during tribal attacks), where they held off nearly 100 attackers for 
several hours until the Tories tossed burning wood onto the roof, setting the building ablaze. 
With several members of their group badly wounded and smoke engulfing the building, 
Benjamin decided the only recourse was surrender. However, as he and the others exited into a 
mass of taunting militia, the Tory leader, the infamous Bloody Bill Cunningham, directed his 
men to grab tree officers, drag them to a nearby oak tree, and hang them. In short order, 
Benjamin Goodman and two other officers were strung up on a single branch, which snapped 
due to their combined weight, sending the men crashing to the ground. Bloody Bill and several 
Tory followers set upon the three officers with axes, hacking them to death. Bill then ordered 
his followers to turn on the remaining prisoners, and they were clubbed and stabbed to death. 
Bloody Bill and his Tory militia fled the town, soon to continue his killing spree, which included 
assassinations of the Lt. Governor of South Carolina, a state Supreme Court judge and two state 
senators as well as a massacre at Cloud’s Creek where 28 people were murdered. The war in 
South Carolina continued throughout 1782, nearly a year after the Yorktown surrender.

Note on Tory (Loyalist) Militia During the Revolutionary War: Contrary to the impression left by 
basic histories of the American Revolution, such as might be read in high school, there was 
limited support in the colonies for complete separation from Great Britain and establishment of 
an independent nation. Most estimates (there were no opinion surveys in the 1770s) by 
respected Revolutionary historians (i.e., David McCullough) suggest that only one-third of the 
colonial population were enthusiastic about leaving the empire. Support for independence and 
nationhood was particularly weak in the southern colonies, where many residents, particularly 
the landowner (i.e., planter) class, believed that the slavery system would be maintained if the 
British quelled the Revolution. This was an unfortunate misconception. The abolition movement 
in England was already gaining strength fueled by the British High Court’s 1772 decision in the 
Somerset vs. Stewart Case that slavery had no precedent in English law. The ruling held that 
slaves could not be forcibly transported into or out of England, and that slaves escaping from 
English colonies could not be returned for punishment or re-enslavement. After a series of half 
steps, the United Kingdom totally banned slavery with the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act, which 
applied to all of their colonies, much sooner than the U.S. (1865). However, Tories (loyal to the 
Crown) in the colonies did not know or refused to believe the abolition events in England, and 
supported British military efforts to quash the Revolution. (Huzzey R. Freedom Burning: Anti- 
Slavery and Empire in Victorian Britain. Ithaca NY: Cornell University Press. 2012) 


Many Tory militias were formed, primarily in the south, and fought alongside Redcoat units in 
numerous battles. Additionally, Tory militia conducted their own operations, in loose 
coordination with British commanders, aimed at terrorizing individuals and Whig communities 
who supported the independence efforts. Whigs drew their name from the British Whig party of 
that era that condemned British colonial policies, including slavery. One of the most ruthless 
Tory militia leaders were James Lindley, brother of Eleanor Mary Lindley and brother-in-law of 
George Maris that we met previously in the Maris Lineage Table, and the aforementioned 
Bloody Bill Cunningham. In the early years of the Revolutionary War, Lindley and Cunningham 
operated concurrently, which typically involved swooping into a rural Whig village, shooting 
citizens and burning down buildings. Local residents typically mounted a resistance, leading to 
casualties on both sides, and the event earned the label of a battle. (Brown F. Strain of Violence: 
Historical Studies of Violence and Vigilantism. Oxford Press. 1975) 


93 


Lindley, and his 16 year-old teenage son, William, were captured during a larger and more 
conventional battle near Laurens, South Carolina in 1779, tried the next day, and sentenced to 
hang. Both were marched up to the gallows, but after his dad met his fate, William was 
pardoned and released in a show of leniency, apparently assuming he had learned his lesson. 
William instead formed his own Loyalist militia and terrorized villages in the western areas of 
South and North Carolina for two more years until killed ina Whig ambush. 


Cunningham was more ruthless than Lindley as evident by his actions at Hayes Station. Bloody 
Bill originally volunteered for the Continental Army and fought on the colonists’ side in a few 
skirmishes. However, when Bill’s mentally challenged adolescent brother, Wyatt, visited him at a 
winter camp, several colonial officers made fun of the child, making him cry, infuriating Bill. He 
deserted to the Tory side, and formed his own unit after Lindley’s demise. After several years of 
violent raids and assassinations, known as the Bloody Scout in South Carolina newspapers, 
Cunningham achieved his goal of terrifying the state leadership. He became a pop culture figure 
in spite of his violence, and evaded an entire Colonial brigade sent to track him down. After the 
Bloody Scout, he fled to the Bahamas where he robbed banks, looted homes and stole sailboats, 
which he sold at profit in Jamaica. He died from pneumonia during a European vacation after 
years as a successful Caribbean outlaw. (Lewis JD. The American Revolution in South Carolina. 
South Carolina Loyalists in the American Revolution; William “Bloody Bill” Cunningham. 2018. 
www.carolana.com. Accessed: February 20, 2023)

Children: George and Marget were married in 1803 in Kentucky. The couple had six children

Synopsis: After struggling to maintain his father’s (Bartlett Goodman) racehorse farm as a

outnumbered by years in red ink. As other Hendrickson, Morgan and Maris families had 
discovered, small independent farms, operated with paid farm hands, were not competitive 
with much larger slave plantations in Kentucky and Tennessee. The free labor pool was small 
and unskilled, which hindered the scope of non-slave farming. Eventually, George and Marget 
moved north to the free state of Illinois, settling in Hutton, a town in Coles County on the 
eastern side of the state. Coles County was a hotbed of the Illinois abolition movement because 
much of the population had migrated from New England. In Hutton, George worked for an 
agricultural supply company and established a farm where he raised corn. Profitable farming 
was just as challenging in Illinois as in Kentucky during the pre-mechanized era due to limited 
manpower, erratic weather in the growing season and harsh winters, all of which contributed 
to crop failures.

Note on Slavery in America: When Hendrick Willemz Hendrickson (page 38 and pages 215-224) 
arrived in New Amsterdam on the ship Rooseboom (Rose Tree) on June 2, 1663, he and other 
passengers walked down a gangplank to a crude dock where wagons driven by African slaves 
drove them to a building on what is now Wall Street for completion of migrant paperwork. 
Adjacent to the migrant house was the New Amsterdam slave auction. The Dutch West Indies 
Company (DWIC), Hendrickson’s employer, were major players in African and Caribbean slave 
trade in the 1600s. By mid-century 500,000 people worked as slaves in Dutch colonies 
worldwide. The DWIC brought the first shipload of slaves to New Amsterdam in 1655 on the 
ship Witte Paert (White Horse), and by the time of Hendrickson’s arrival, slaves represented 
25% of the city’s population. (Maika DJ. Tale of the White Horse: First Slave Trading Voyage to 
New Netherland. Dutch National Archief (Archive). www.nationalarchief.nl. Accessed October 
14, 2024) DWIC-owned slaves constructed government and commercial buildings, private 
homes, churches, roads, sewers, aqueducts and walls and tilled a tobacco plantation occupying 
what is now Central Park in Manhattan, a pattern that was repeated over the next 200 years in 
literally every major city of the Americas. The DWIC slaves completed many construction tasks 
ahead of schedule. Seeing an opportunity for profit, the DWIC began to sell excess slaves at 
auction to private citizens. For example, on May 16, 1664, the DWIC auctioned 30 male and 
female slaves to 21 citizens at an average price of 400 guilders per slave (roughly $1200 in 
2024). Auctioning surplus slaves became a routine feature of New Amsterdam life, attracting 
large crowds in a carnival-like atmosphere, an activity that would occur in many communities, 
north and south, in the emerging American colonies for two centuries. Boston, Providence, 
Rhode Island, Philadelphia and New York each extracted considerable municipal income from 
slave auctions. (Goodfriend J. Slavery in Colonial New York. Urban History. 2008; 35(3): 485-96) 


Like Hendrick Willemz Hendrickson, other families in our tree who immigrated to America 
before the Civil War (Morgan, Goodman, Maris, Dennis, Lienau) likely pulled into port adjacent 
to slave ships. For example, in 1668, the family of Benjamin Goodman Jr. and Anna Webster 
(Goodman Generation 6) landed at Port Royale on the Rappahannock River, the busiest slave 
offloading and auction site in the Virginia Colony. Overall, between 1619 and 1809, when U.S. 
slave importation was banned, 13 million Africans and Caribbeans disembarked slave ships at 
Port Royale and other coastal sites including New Amsterdam. (Maika, 2024) 


The only person in this family history known to be a slave owner is General Daniel Morgan 
(page 154) of the “close, but not quite” Morgan line discussed later in this book. As a war hero, 
Morgan’s life is documented in historical literature including his slave ownership. Given the 
ubiquity of slave ownership in pre-Civil War America, | suspect other ancestors held slaves. 
Searching for this information is challenging, but new websites are coming online including the 
digitized 1850 Slave Schedules via Ancestory.com. In the 1800s, a form was completed annually 
by slave owners to document slave population because these individuals counted toward a 
states’ population calculation, which determined congressional representation. In 1850, the 
U.S. federal census included a slave schedule among its required forms for the first time. 
Compliance was good and a massive trove of information about acquisition and ownership of 
slaves was obtained, which is now available to researchers.

Notes on Oregon Land Donation Act of 1850. To spur and also to regulate emigration into the 
Oregon Territory, the U.S. Congress passed the Oregon Land Donation Act of 1850. In its original 
form, the law allowed white males and married white women to claim 320 acres of free land. 
Essentially, this allowed married couples to acquire 640 acres of land. The Land Donation Act of 
1850 was also notable in that it was the first Congressional Act in U.S. history that established 
women’s right to own property, thereby creating the precedent for female property ownership 
that continues to this day. (Johansen DO. Empire of the Columbia. A History of the Pacific 
Northwest. 2" edition. New York: Harper Collins. 1967) 

The Land Donation Act was instantly popular, spurring thousands of cross-continent emigrants 
into Oregon, so much so that Congress halved the land donation to 320 acres by the time that 
the Goodman family reached Oregon. The territorial government maintained an inventory of 
available plots, which settlers could review or even personally inspect, with the most prized 
plots located near the Columbia River and in the Willamette Valley. Settlers submitted a rather 


97 


elaborate application, designed in part to prove that they were literate and had capacity to 
complete business management forms. On the application, prospective claimants designated 
the acreage plots they desired to acquire, and then waited in settler camps for up to a year for 
the territorial government to approve their application, or negotiate alternative property if there 
were several claimants for the same plot. 


To gain permanent title to the land, claimants had to reside full-time on the property (i.e., no 
absentee ownership) for four years and make tangible improvements: access roads, fencing, 
wells, residence structures, crops planted and harvested. The Donation Act was amended 
several times in the 1850s to allow widows to claim property and later to allow “American half- 
breed Indians above the age of 18” (actual language) to claim acreage. The later amendment 
was notable in that it was the first time Congress approved the concept of Native Americans 
owning property (but not Indigenous Canadians). It also was the first time Congress 
acknowledged that some of the population was of mixed race and allowed these individuals to 
own property. In the Pacific Northwest (i.e., Washington and Oregon), the mixed race 
population was substantial by 1860, a by-product of frequent common-law marriages and other 
relationships among Native Americans and the many European trappers and explorers living in 
the region during the 1830s and 1840s. Although Oregon was granted statehood in 1859 as a 
Free State, many populations were denied access to land donations and citizenship: U.S. born 
Blacks, Africans, Hawaiians, Filipinos, others from the Pacific region and a long list of Canadian 
Indigenous Tribes. 


Much of what | learned about the Oregon Land Donation Act 
and its impact on the Native Peoples of Oregon came from

Ronde Community. Although the campaign to clear Native 
Peoples from land desired by White settlers was less violent 
than in the Northwest Territory (Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, etc.), 
it was just as effective in removing unwanted Natives from 
their ancestral homelands. Lewis DW. Tribal Histories of the

Lienau Lineage Table 


The Lienau surname has been prevalent in the German state of Schleswig-Holstein near the 
Denmark border for many centuries. Denmark and the German Federation fought over this 
region politically and militarily for centuries. The first Lienau family member that | could 
confidently identify was born in Uetersen located north of Hamburg, the largest city in the 
region, in the 17th century. Little is known about the initial four generations of the Lienau line 
who all lived in or near Uetersen. Histories of Schleswig-Holstein (see: Carr. Schleswig-Holstein 
1815-1848 in the Information Sources chapter) indicate that its proximity to the Baltic Sea (east 
of the Denmark Peninsula) and the North Sea (west of the Denmark Peninsula) and the Elbe and 
Trave Rivers dictated the occupations of 17 — 19" century men in this region. Commercial 
fishing, the whaling industry and boat building were the three primary sources of income. Men 
who were not in these industries were agricultural workers, primarily involved in dairy farming 
with the region’s famous Holstein cattle. A village with the name Linau has existed about 40 
miles from Uetersen since the medieval era. The spelling of the surname Linau by generations 1 
and 2 in the following lineage table suggests that unknown ancestors prior to the 17" century 
may have lived in this village, before their descendants relocated to Uetersen. 


In the late feudal period, farmers with some degree of affluence (i.e., owned parcels of farm 
land or owned land with access to the Elbe or the oceanfront) were known as Bonden and paid 
taxes to whatever Danish or German nobility controlled the land at any point in time. Bonden 
also contributed a portion of their crops or fish catch to the Lord’s commissary. The Bonden had 
some rights, such as trial by peers, and an administrative unit known as the Ding, by which they 
could make infrastructure decisions for the common good of the Bonden class, such as road 
construction, refurbishing docks, or building fishing boats to be shared by the community. 
Common serfs (indentured workers) toiled on the farms or fishing boats of the Bonden in 
exchange for shelter, plots to raise subsistence vegetables and animals or fishing rights. The tax 
rolls of 17" — 19" century Schleswig-Holstein and the ten-year census did not indicate 
occupation with the consistency of the British tax and census reports of that era. The Schleswig- 
Holstein rolls did indicate property ownership, number of people in households, spouse names, 
and participation in Ding and peer courts, which provided evidence of economic status.

ren: Charles and Laura married in 1935, and had one child, Susan Elizabeth Lienau. 


Synopsis: To help with family finances, Charles Jr. joined the workforce full-time when he was 
14 years old after completing gi grade. He was particularly attracted to the new world of 
electronic communication, and by the age of 17, Charles was working as a radio salesman for 
Center Music on 6"" Street in Manhattan. The first commercial radio station, KDKA in Pittsburgh, 
started broadcasting on November 2, 1920 with a full evening of live reports on the Harding- 
Cox Presidential election. As the NY Times proclaimed in a headline announcing the first 
broadcast: Things Will Never Be the Same Again. Radio took 1920s America by storm. 

Owning a radio was perceived as a symbol of progress, upward mobility, and openness to 
innovation. Charles did well as a radio salesman, supplementing his parent’s income and 
making enough money to live on his own. By the mid-1930s, his focus had shifted to another 
new technological breakthrough: high fidelity, stereo turntables; i.e., Hi-Fi. Music in the 1930 — 
1950 era was the dominated by the Big Band Sound - Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, Artie 
Shaw, Duke Ellington, Fats Domino, Glenn Miller and many others. People were eager to play in 
their own home the music they heard in concerts, nightclubs, movies, and on the radio (but 


with low fidelity). Hi-Fi equipment (turntables, amplifiers and speakers, and later stereo- 
capable radios) was purchased as soon as it hit the showroom floor. 


Charles anticipated the Hi-Fi market, and broke away from Center Music to form his own 
company in the 1940’s: Lienau Associates. He secured vendor contracts with Garrard 
Turntables and with the Fisher Company that made the highest rated stereo console in that era, 
and became a distributor for both companies. People who wanted cutting edge sound systems 
in their homes often purchased a combined Fisher-Garrard Home Hi-Fi Stereo System. 

Working out of their apartment in Brooklyn, Charles and Laura experienced success, but 
competition was intense in the Hi-Fi industry in metropolitan New York. In 1947, Charles and 
Laura decided to stake out a new turf in the Washington DC area. Starting out in an office/store 
room beneath a delicatessen in Silver Spring, Maryland with a drippy ceiling, Charles gradually 
acquired the capital to build his own office complex. In the late 1950s, Charles anticipated 
another emerging market and expanding his product line to include 8 track cartridges and 
players, which he handled through a second business known as Lawrence Associates. Shortly 
after establishing Lawrence Associates, he built a warehouse for the cartridge arm of his 
business to handle the massive demand for 8-track music. Over a 50-year career in the 
technology end of the communication and music industries, Charles literally worked his way up 
from store clerk to being a major high fidelity distributor on the East Coast. 

In addition to success in business, Charles loved high performance sports cars, especially Ford 
Thunderbirds, enjoyed traveling with family and friends, took great pleasure in family vacations 
at their Bethany Beach, Delaware cottage, and was an ardent fan, and season-ticket holder, of

the Washington Redskins. Horse racing also was one of Charles’ favorite pastimes. Charles’

mathematical odds of placing winning bets. Blanche wrote a popular book on race track betting 
titled “Off To The Races. Horse Sense and Track Logic,” and he even appeared on the television 
quiz show, What’s My Line? Charles and Ernie enjoyed betting on the horses at D.C. area tracks,

Notes on Radio in the 1920s and 1930s: By 1925, the question, do you own a radio in your 
home, was included on many state census surveys, and it appeared for the first time on the 1930 
U.S. national census. By 1930, there were more radios in American than people, and the major 
networks broadcast a full slate of half-hour or full hour programming every evening: news and 
political commentary, dramas (Perry Mason, the Shadow, the Lone Ranger, Green Hornet), 
comedies (Our Miss Brooks, Fibber McGee and Molly, Amos and Andy), musical variety, game 
shows (i.e., the original What’s My Line?) and broadcasts of sporting events, most notably 
boxing matches, but also baseball, rowing competitions and college football. In the 1930s, over 
70% of American households listened to the broadcasts of the heavyweight fights between the 
American Joe Louis (the Brown Bomber) and German Max Schmeling, which had massive U.S. 
versus Nazi Germany symbolism. Broadcasts of the powerhouse gridiron teams of the 1920's, 
the University of Illinois (with star Red Grange, the Galloping Ghost), Notre Dame, Centre 
College, Michigan and Georgia Tech are widely credited with raising public awareness of post 
secondary education. Many families’ first visit to a college campus was to attend a football 
game. Programming that dominated the local airways included gospel music, church services 
and bible hours, broadcasts of famous tent evangelists of the era (Billy Sunday, Sister Aimee), 
agricultural talk shows, and white nationalist social commentary. 


A side note: The KKK owned more than 50% of the small town, 100 watt, daylight hours radio 
stations in the South and Midwest, and one 50,000 watt station in Washington DC. (Harcourt F. 
Ku Klux Kulture. America and the Klan in the 1920s. Chicago: University of Chicago Press. 2017) 


108 


Radio was a completely new communication concept that literally appeared out of the blue and 
provided a forum where much of the nation for the first time could participate in momentous 
events simultaneously, and “call-in” to share their opinions about controversies. Radio was 
particularly popular in rural areas as a way to combat isolation and to stay up-to-date with 
national and international news. Demand for radio in rural areas is credited with speeding up 
the pace of electrification. 


| remember my mother describing the excitement in Lowden when my grandparents (Archie and 
Maude Dennis) purchased the first radio in the community. Twenty or more neighbors would 
squeeze into their living room to listen to popular comedy shows, the Lowell Thomas with the 
News of the Day program and Walter Winchell’s animated news and entertainment industry 
(i.e., Hollywood) broadcasts. Then everyone retired to the kitchen for desserts, and for some in 
attendance, adult beverages — a “Radio Night in America” tradition.

Girault Lineage Table 


The Girault surname originated in France, and for centuries has been prevalent in the Ardennes 
region of northeastern France, of which Reims is the principle city. The first Girault family 
member that was confidently identified was born near Reims in the early 19" century. 


Charles 1740- B: Merfy, France (FR) Jeanne 1746 | B: Chalons-Sur- 
Girault 1804 Barbier 1812 | Marne, FR 
D: Merfy, FR D: Merfy, FR 


Children: Married in 1772, Charles and Jeanne had six children during their 32-year 
relationship 

Synopsis: In the Ardennes regional census reports of 1770 and 1780, Charles was listed as a 
shop owner and livery driver, and Jeanne was listed as a papiers (i.e., documents) aide for the 
Deputy Intendant of Reims. In 18" century France, an Intendant was the Crown’s chief 
administrative officer for an assigned town or rural region. An Intendant functioned as the city 
manager in an urban area or a county commissioner in a rural or suburban area. The 
Intendant’s office for a major city like Reims contained a substantial infrastructure of 
administrative personnel similar to what exists today for municipal government in U.S. cities. 
Intendants were employees of the large civil service system in France, and were rotated from 
city to city every 3 years to prevent corruption. Jeanne’s role as a document aide within the 
Reims Intendant office is not defined, but suggests that she might have been well connected 
and well educated by the standards of that era for females. 


Jeanne’s great-grandmother, also named Jeanne Barbier (1653-1718), was a Fille du Roi 
(Daughter of the King) immigrant to Canada, as described on the next page. After arriving in 
Quebec, Canada in 1670 at the age of 17, great-grandmother Jeanne signed a marriage contract 
with Bernard Champlain, but quickly arranged to have that union dissolved based on his public 
infidelity. Within a few months, she married Julien Plumereau, who was killed soon after during 
a tavern altercation. Not deterred, Jeanne’s great-grandmother next married Francois Blain, 
who was a seaman. He died 11 years later during a geographic charting expedition to South 
Africa and was buried near present day Cape Town, leaving his spouse and children stranded in 
Quebec. 


After receiving word of Jacques’ death more than a year after the incident, Jeanne successfully 
petitioned the Quebec Intendant, Jean Talon, for permission to leave the colony, one of only a 
few Fille du Roi allowed to depart. Jeanne and her children returned to Reims in 1683 and later 
settled in Merfy. She had several relationships after returning to France, one of which led to 
the birth of Jeanne’s grandmother, Suzanne Habelin (1690-1764), who, in turn, gave birth to 
Jeanne’s mother, Marie-Josephe (1716-1779), who adopted the Barbier surname, perhaps to 
honor her Fille du Roi ancestor. Marie-Josephe was married and widowed twice, but 
unattached when Jeanne Barbier (wife of Charles Girault; | know, its confusing!) was born. 


115 


Notes on the Fille du Roi: Unlike colonization of the Dutch and English settlements in America 
where approximately 40% of the early immigrants were female, the population of New France 
(present day Quebec, Canada) in the 17" century was 95% single males, who were mostly fur 
trappers and soldiers, and well known for rowdy behavior. Efforts to attract families to this 
rough frontier colony were not productive. French King Louis XIV (i.e., the fabled Sun King) 
desired to make the struggling colony conducive to families to promote community 
development. He also saw the need to evolve the economic base of the colony from singular 
dependence on fur trapping and trading toward family-owned agriculture. Abandoning efforts 
to attract family units to New France, the Sun King decided to send young females with 
“demonstrated capacity for fertility,” to the Quebec colony in an immigration program he 
named Daughters of the King (Fllle du Roi). The fertility capacity was defined as the ability to 
bear ten children, however that was measured in the 1600s. An aggressive recruitment 
campaign targeted teenage females from poor families and young females “already turned out 
by their families and living sordidly on the streets” (i.e., likely references to banditry and 
prostitution). Fille du Roi participants were offered a substantial dowry of 300 livres (roughly 
$22,000 in 2023) to make the transatlantic journey to Canada. Between 1663 and 1678, 
approximately 1,500 French females agreed to become Fille du Roi and boarded ships bound 
for New France including great grandmother Jeanne Barbier. Many of the Fille du Roi 
candidates were personally “screened” by the Sun King. Approximately 20% of the young 
women died during the journey, mostly due to ships lost at sea, not uncommon for the 
notoriously unseaworthy French cargo ships of that era, and also due to infectious disease that 
spread rapidly in the squalid below deck areas assigned to the Fille du Roi. 


Upon arrival in Quebec, Fille du Roi were assigned in groups of 25 to a Guardian, who arranged 
temporary housing, “promoted chastity and piety prior to marriage by limiting pre-match 
contact with gentlemen of the colony”, and, critically, functioned as the matchmaker. Young 
female immigrants matched to a suitor signed a marriage contract, which they had to honor 
within 30 days or risk loss of their dowry. However, Fille du Roi were allowed to back-out of the 
marriage for reasonable cause within the initial three months after exchanging vows. Of the 
Fille du Roi who reached New France, 90% married within a year of arrival, which stimulated 
dramatic population growth within the colony, so much so that the program was terminated 
after 15 years due to excess population growth in relation to resources.

Jeanne Barbier’s likely grim teenage existence in France probably led her to apply and be 
selected for the Fille du Roi. There is evidence that she blossomed considerably in her 13 years 


116 


in New France. During her final five years in the colony, she sat on the Colony Commission, a 
30-member body equivalent to what would be called a city council today, as one of the three 
appointments reserved for females. Her dossier (area of responsibility) was community health 
education, and it is known that she functioned in previous years as curator of records for the 
Quebec Intendant’s office. These assignments suggest that she was literate and was held in 
esteem within the colony. A historical novel by Suzanne Desrochers describes the Fille du Roi 
experience in the New France colony.

Alexander | 1811- a Reims, FR Ee Theodora | 1841- | B: Skye, Scotland 
Girault 1882 enn | ENG McGreal 1876 [. London, ENG

Synopsis: Thomson Cunningham’s will allocated financial support for Alexander’s education. 
Alexander attended and graduated from University College London, and soon after entered 
London’s thriving banking industry. During the 1830s, he joined the London Joint Stock Bank as 
an accounts manager and by the 1840s, had been promoted to a managing partner. The 
London Joint Stock Bank was a new concept in banking in England. Prior to the 1830’s, all 
banks were privately held by affluent families or consortiums of merchants or nobility, or 
combinations thereof. These banks functioned as private repositories and investment vehicles 
for the wealthy. Average citizens could not access private banks. In contrast, a joint stock bank 
was owned and controlled by a group of shareholders, who, although wealthy, came from 
more diverse backgrounds. Joint stock banks also accepted deposits from anyone who met 
reasonably attainable financial criteria, and offered what we today call savings accounts and 
Certificates of Deposit (CDs) with small, but steady investment returns. (Michie RC. British 
Banking: Continuity and Change from 1694 to the Present. New York and London: Oxford 
University Press. 2016) 


Alexander’s banking career was rewarding, leading to a posh lifestyle in an upscale area of 
London. Sara, at age 18, was 31 years younger than Alexander when they married. They met 
three years earlier when Alexander was on a hiking vacation in the Hebrides. Before and after 
their marriage, the couple traveled abroad extensively including visits to Athens, Rome, Cairo, 
Damascus, Baghdad and Istanbul, and often spent their August holiday in Turkey. The couple’s 
first child, Emily Alexanderine Girault (1860-1947), was born in that nation several months 
after their marriage in Corum, a major Hittite Empire archeological site with a hot springs 
resort where the couple owned an apartment. Like many affluent Londoners in the 19" 
century, Alexander had a deep interest in Middle Eastern archeology. He was a financial 
supporter of The Royal Geographic Society and one of the original investors in the Corum 
Archaeological Museum. His passion for archaeology likely explains the many visits to Corum, 
although the hot springs may have added to the appeal. The story of Alexander, Sara and their 
youngest son, Theodore Stefano, is further developed in Chapters III and IV.

Synopsis: Theodore’s life in many ways epitomizes the rags to riches American Dream

Hendrickson, a Long Island architect, and potentially a relative of Cornelius and Hendrick 
Hendrickson at some level. However, this possibility has not yet been investigated.

Synopsis: James appears to have come from a long line of Irish tenant farmers who raised crops

countrymen, James immigrated to North America as a young man, landing in Quebec in 1821,

growing season of New Brunswick, James and Emily managed to operate a relatively successful 
farm that served as the family home for several generations.

Hendricson 


Origin and evolution of surname 

The original family name when it was first appeared in medieval records in the 12" century was 
Schenck, not Hendrikse, Hendriksz, Hendrickzoon, or Hendrickson, which would not occur until 
the 1500s in The Netherlands. The name would not become “Hendricson with C and no K” until 
1845 in the United States. There are three theories about the origin of the Schenck name. Only 
one of these theories fits with the Teutonic saga depicted by Augustus Schenck, author of the 
original published history of the Schenck family (1843) that was discussed at the beginning of 
this book. One of the origin theories, discussed below, may have Augustus spinning in his grave. 
(Schenck AD. The Rev. William Schenck: His Ancestry and His Descendants. Washington DC: 
Rufus Darby Publisher. Originally published in 1843 with updates in 1869 and 1883. Re-released 
by Higginson Book Company (www.higginson.com) in 2015 and also available via 
www.books.google.com) 


A side note: Family histories that served as foundational sources for the pre-immigration origins 
of the Hendricson family are listed on pages 145-147. These sources are 50 to 180 years old. 
Although much of the basic information communicated in these histories appears to be 
fundamentally accurate, research over the past three years, using modern data sources and 
search techniques that my genealogy-minded ancestors could not imagine in a wild 
hallucination, has added layers of detail, and additional or different plausible interpretations of 
our predecessors’ journey through life. 


The most prominent origin theory for the Schenck surname is that it likely evolved from the 
Germanic tribal names of Scenko or Scenken, which were used as far back as the 4" century to 
designate an innkeeper or the person who brought liquor to military encampments. (Hanks P, 
Hodges, F. A Dictionary of Surnames. London: Oxford University Press. 1989) Roman writers of 
that era used both Scenko and Scenken to refer to operators of village taverns and the wagon 
drivers who transported libations to military camps in Germania. As with Scenko and Scenken, 
when surnames began to emerge in pre-medieval times in Europe (i.e., the 5" through 10" 
centuries following the collapse of Roman influence), they were often derived from a role or 
function played by individuals or a craft historically associated with a particular family. As the 
population increased and relocated from isolated farms and villages to much larger feudal 
estates or cities in the 11 through 15‘ centuries, the family’s habitation (i.e., location: town, 
nearby castle, estate or church) was typically added to the occupational/functional title to 
further distinguish one individual from others, as in Johannus Steinmetz van Fulheim (in other 
words: Johannus, a stone cutter, from the town of Fulheim). 


A second theory, that Augustus Schenck likely would have endorsed, is that the word Schenck is 
derived from a Norse practice that was passed on to Germanic tribes when Scandinavians 
migrated south into present day Germany and Poland seeking tillable lands in the 8” and 9" 
centuries. (Green DH. Language and History in the Early Germanic World. New York and 
Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 1998) The Norse used hallowed out pig and boar shank 
bones as spouts for leather bags that stored wine and mead. With social intermingling, this 
practice was adopted by Germanic tribes in the post-Roman Era. In German, Shank was 


133 


pronounced and eventually, several centuries later, spelled as Schenck. The word came to 
mean pourer or provider, as in pouring wine, providing meals, or leading the service of a meal 
for a large group. Schenck was used as the title for an individual in a tribal leaders’ retinue who 
supervised food, wine and ale preparation, and coordinated the pre-meal tasting to detect 
poison or spoiled food, the later being fairly common, and a far more frequent threat to health 
than murder by poison. This role usually, where feasible, passed from father to son, ensuring a 
continuation of family social status and influence within the tribes’ hierarchy. (Blark G. 
Surnames and the History of Social Mobility. Princeton NJ: Princeton University Press. 2014) 


A third theory is that the surname Schenck and the similar surnames Shenk, Schenk and 
Schenke were derived from the Ashkenazi Jewish culture in northern Europe. (Malkiel D. 
Reconstructing Ashkenaz: The Human Face of Franco-German Jewry, 1000-1250. Palo Alto, CA: 
Stanford University Press. 2016) Variations of Schenck were commonly used in Ashkenazi 
communities in northern Europe during the s through 10" centuries. Similar to the Germanic 
tribes, individuals with the name Schenck in Jewish communities were often owners or 
operators of inns for lodging, taverns, communal gathering halls and campsites for food, 
beverage and entertainment, and also were food and liquor wholesalers. For example, during 
the eight through tenth centuries, only Ashkenazi Jews were allowed to brew and sell liquor in 
eastern Russia and adjoining lands including what is now Poland and Belarus. (Ehrlich AM. 
Encyclopedia of the Jewish Diaspora: Origins, Experiences and Culture. Camden, UK and NY: 
Bloomsbury Publishing USA. 2008) 


Notes on Ashkenazi Jews Migration to Northern Europe: The Ashkenazi are one of two primary 
ancestral groups within the Jewish faith. The majority of Ashkenazi migrated from the Middle 
East to Italy during the first century AD, but many others relocated, voluntarily and 
involuntarily, to the Balkans (present day Bulgaria, Albania, Croatia and Serbia), the Aegean 
Islands, Greece, Turkey and even to southern France. Many Ashkenazi arrived at these locations 
as slaves of Roman families, or in various forms of indebted servitude as tutors, scribes, nannies 
and domestic workers. The other ancestral group was the Sephardic Jews that primarily 
migrated from the Middle East and North Africa to Spain and Portugal. Sephardic Jews also 
were enslaved or survived with limited rights and protections on the fringes of Roman society 
during the first through fifth centuries, even after Catholicism became the official state 
theology of Rome in 380 AD, and persecution of Jews was outlawed, at least theoretically. 


As Roman military power, economic influence and infrastructure declined in the fourth and fifth 
centuries, many Jewish slaves escaped or were released from their servitude when Roman 
towns, agricultural communes and military outposts collapsed or were abandoned in the 
outlying regions of southern France, Greece, Turkey and the Balkans. These individuals joined 
with Ashkenazi communities in Italy who were migrating north to escape persecution and 
disenfranchisement. (Malkiel D. 2016) 


During the fifth through eighth centuries, bands of Ashkenazi Jews moved into Germania where 
they established functional relationships with the indigenous tribes of northern Europe, who 
were undergoing considerable change themselves: slowly converting to Christian theology or a 
transitional pagan-Christian hybrid, developing agrarian versus nomadic economies and 


134 


lifestyles, and building fixed communities linked to early versions of protective castles. (Mosk C. 
Nationalism and Economic Development in Modern Eurasia. NY: Routledge. 2013) 
Demonstrating adaptability, the Ashkenazi incorporated elements of tribal languages, social 
customs, attire and religious practices to their culture and identity, and established a niche 
within these Germanic communities as merchants (i.e., pre-medieval import-export 
businesses), owners of hospitality sites such as taverns, halls, inns, and gaming sites (i.e., camps 
where tournaments of military skills and holiday festivals were held) and functioning as 
“learneds” who could read, write and communicate in several languages, and thus translate, 
negotiate and write documents. After Charlemagne expanded Frankish rule and stabilized much 
of Europe in the late eighth century, Ashkenazi groups moved into present-day Poland and 
gradually gained economic influence, particularly in an area of eastern Poland known as Silesia. 
The Ashkenazi in Poland spoke a unique language that incorporated Hebrew, Slavic and ancient 
Germanic tribal words, creating an early form of Yiddish, and also practiced a hybrid religion 
based in traditional Hebrew beliefs, but blended with Christian practices (i.e., Roman Catholic) 
and lingering vestiges of non-Christian tribal rituals. Until the 11" century, Ashkenazi 
communities were generally well accepted in Silesia, but increasingly frequent eruptions of 
anti-Semitism in that region may have made Silesia a less attractive location. (Ehrlich, 2008; 
Elukin J. Living Together, Living Apart: Re-thinking Jewish-Christian Relations in the Middle Ages. 
Princeton NJ: Princeton University Press. 2007) 


| don’t know which of the origin theories is most likely correct, and suspect, given the 
similarities in these origin stories, that all three may have played a role in the establishment of 
the Schenck surname for the familial line that eventually, over centuries, morphed into the 
Hendricksons, and then, fairly recently, into the Hendricsons, with a “C and no K”. We do know 
that the Schenck title became important within the feudal system that dominated medieval 
society for several centuries. 


The Schenck title (Latin: Pincerna Noster; cup-bearer, or less frequent: sommelier, bartender, 
food arranger; www.latin-dictionary.net) was prized in feudal courts, as it was often a stepping- 
stone to a nobility title. During the height of the feudal system in Germany, the Schenck had a 
complex job description. The person in this role was hand picked by the Count (next to the 
Emperor, the top nobility position in German feudal pecking order) and thus had to be 
someone the boss trusted. The Schenck coordinated social activities for the Count, including 
banquets, ceremonies and festivals, home and on the road, (there could dozens of these 
annually), coordinated daily meal preparation, supervised the estate vineyards, wine cellar, 
vegetable fields and managed the commissary (food storage). The Schenck also functioned as a 
stand-in for the Count during meet-and-greets with village mayors and craft guilds, represented 
the Count at secondary conferences, and coordinated the tasting of all wine, ale and food that 
was provided for the Count and his entourage. Typically, the Schenck did not do this himself — 
he was too important to the estate to take a chance on severe Gl distress or even death. 
(Luthern A. Testing for Poison Still a Profession for Some. Smithsonian Magazine. June 26, 2009. 
www.smithsonianmag.org. Accessed May 9, 2024) Generally, the Schenck requested the 
individuals who prepared and delivered the meal and spirits to consume the product of their 


135 


labors during the Tasters Meal before the nobility and their retinue arrived. (O’Brian P. 
Feudalism in Medieval Europe. NY: Cavendish Square. 2016) 


Depiction of a Taster’s Meal by a late medieval 
artist. The designated taster at the left prepares 
to consume the meal while the Schenck, second 
from left, supervises, and the servers await the 
outcome of the tasting. 

Image source: Wikimedia Commons. 
www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. Accessed: 8/10/2024. 


Typically, the Schenck served in this demanding position for 4-5 years, and assuming successful 
performance, was rewarded with a lower level nobility title, usually Lord, and assigned other 
duties within the Count’s realm. Frequently, a high performing Schenck moved up to be one 
the Count’s inner circle of advisors for financial, real estate, agricultural, political or military 
matters. Because each feudal district, known in the German system as a Duchy, employed a 
Schenck, individuals with this title adopted the name of their Duchy as part of their name. For 
example, as we will see in the next section: Wihelmus Christianhus Schenck Van Nydeggan. 


Geographic origin 

The Hendricson line has been traced in several family histories to the small town of Nideggen 
(medieval: Nydeggan) in western Germany 25 miles from Cologne (Koln) and 30 miles from 
Aachen in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Nydeggan/Nideggen was the ancestral home of 
the family throughout the medieval period until the 1400s when the Schenck Van Nydeggan 
family moved to nearby Holland after their financial status diminished. 


The present-day village of Nideggen is located near the 
border of Germany and Holland.

First appearance of surname in public records 

The original Schenck family surname first appeared in tax rolls around the year 1000 in the 
region of present day Poland known in medieval times as Silesia. The region derived its name 
from the Silingi tribe, a sect of the larger Vandal culture. Silesia centered on the modern day 
city of Wroclaw, located on the Oder River in Eastern Poland. For centuries, the Silingi and 
other Germanic tribes fought turf battles within Silesia until the newly formed Polish state 


136 


finally gained control late in the tenth century, establishing a feudal order modeled on the 
Germanic system and installing the Roman Catholic Church as state theology. (Harc L. Cuius 
Regio? Ideological and Territorial Cohesion of the Historical Region of Silesia, circa 1000-2000. 
Wroclaw, Poland: www.ebooki.com.pl) At least one distant Hendricson ancestor apparently was 
assigned the Pincerna Noster (Schenck) role within the Piast Duchy of the new Polish nation, 
which may account for the Schenck surname, although other factors, previously discussed, 
likely played a role in the Schenck surname derivation. 


The highlighted area indicates the location of the medieval 
geographic region known as Silesia in eastern Poland. Distant 
Schenck ancestors departed Silesia and moved 500 miles 
west to the Nydeggan area around the year 1000. 

Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 8/10/2024 


For unknown reasons, the Schenck family left Silesia, possibly because tribal attempts to regain 
control made it a dangerous place. In addition to tribal revolts and the ensuing social instability, 
if the Silesian Schencks were Ashkenazi, waves of anti-Semitism, which escalated after Roman 
Catholicism was installed, also may have made the region less attractive. The Schencks moved 
westward a few hundred miles, settling in Nydeggan early in the a century. This rural 
community, nestled in a forested valley, was part of the vast Duchy of the Count of Julich during 
the medieval period. Nydeggan featured a picturesque castle high on a hill overlooking the 
village that was completed in 1190. The Nydeggan castle and surrounding structures including a 
chapel have been fully restored, and are a significant tourist attraction today. If the Schencks 
who departed Silesia were Ashkenazi, they apparently shed their Hebrew identity entirely and 
adapted to the reality of an intensely Christian environment in Nydeggan. 


Nydeggan Castle between Cologne (Koln) and

Schenck van Nydeggan / Hendricson line.
