Synopsis of pre-immigration history 

The Counts of Julich were among the most powerful feudal leaders in the late Holy Roman 
Empire (HRE) of the 11" — 16" centuries. The HRE included present-day Germany and Austria, 
and parts of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, the Netherlands, Belgium, France and Italy. It 
was comprised of dozens of territorial governance units known as duchies and principalities 
that underwent constant mergers and separations. The history of the HRE is complex and often 


137 


confusing. A book by Barbara Stollberg-Rilinger, The Holy Roman Empire: A Short History, 
explains the evolution of the constantly shape-shifting HRE without a deep dive into the 
intricate political, economic and military alliances that held the empire together. (Barbara 
Stollberg-Rilinger. The Holy Roman Empire: A Short History. Princeton NJ: Princeton University 
Press. 2018) 


After relocating to Nydeggan, members of the Schenck family rose substantially in stature over 
a two hundred-year period comprising roughly 1000-1200. During these centuries, the family 
climbed in social rank over the course of many generations, working as skilled craftsman with 
titles in the Julich estate records such as blacksmith/sharpener, machinist, armsman 
(weaponry), vintner (winemaker) and pleader. A pleader was a literate person who served as a 
representative for small villages in dealings with the Duchy over property disputes, village 
boundaries, and tax issues (i.e., pleading the village’s case before the Count or a judicial court) 
and also developed contracts, invoices, receipts and deeds for the village leaders who likely 
were illiterate. The Schenck family’s rise in social standing culminated with the appointment of 
two consecutive family members to the prized Pincerna Noster position within the Julich Duchy. 


The first was Christianhus Schenck van Nydeggan (1197-1246), (also listed as Christianhus 
Pincerna in duchy records) and the second was his son, Wihelmus Christianhus Schenck van 
Nydeggan (1218-1292). Christianhus was appointed as Pincerna Noster in 1246 and served less 
than a year before his death in the same year. We know little about his life, other than he 
previously worked as the platzwart (groundskeeper) for the Julich vineyards, which were said to 
be among the largest in Germany at that time. His son, Wihelmus Christianhus, was appointed 
to the role in 1247 and appears to have served as Pincerna Noster longer than usual, at least 
eight years, suggesting successful performance and a good relationship with the Count. Of 
course, Christianhus and Wihelmus already used Schenck as a surname, possibly a linkage to 
Ashkenazi heritage and/or an occupational role in Silesia, so maybe the Count (William Julich IV; 
1210-1278) concluded that they had Pincerna skills in their blood. Given Wihelmus’s long 
tenure, it appears that the Count was correct. 


Even before Christianhus Schenck van Nydeggan was appointed Pincerna Noster, the family had 
sufficient resources to start buying property of their own. Julich records of deeds and 
transactions indicate that the Schenck van Nydeggans acquired more than 10 estates (typically 
a residence with farm, pasture or game lands) within and adjacent to the Julich Duchy. In 1255, 
at the close of Wihelmus Christianhus’ tenure as Pincerna Noster, the Count of Julich awarded 
him a title, which was Lord of Blyenbeck and Afferden, representing the areas within the Duchy 
where the family owned the bulk of their property. In exchange for this title, the family also 
gained the privilege of paying dramatically higher taxes and supplying soldiers and equipment 
in times of conflict. The papers that document the conferral of this title directly identified the 
names of the new Lord, Wihelmus Christianhus Schenck van Nydeggan, and his wife, 
Mechtildis Schenck van Nydeggan (1220 — 1278). As far as | can determine, this is the first time 
that specific members of the family were identified by full name in a public record. (House of 
Julich. Wikipedia. www.wikipedia.org. Accessed: December 3, 2022) 


Wihelmus Christianhus apparently was a good businessman, and made the Schenck Van 
Nydeggan estates profitable, which pleased the Count (more taxes). After serving as the 


138 


Pincerna Noster, Wihelmus appears to have become a court favorite and chief advisor to the 
Count. However, for unknown reasons, in 1279, Wihelmus sold virtually all of his property to 
the Electorate of Cologne, a theological principality of the Holy Roman Empire (HRE), which was 
the political, financial and military arm of the Church of Cologne led by an Archbishop who was 
also one of the most powerful princes in the HRE. (de Quetteville H. History of Cologne. The 
Catholic Encyclopedia. November 28, 2009. www.catholic.com/encyclopedia. Accessed: 
December 3, 2022) The Electorate allowed the Archbishop to wield both theological and feudal 
power. Previous Schenck family historians conjectured that Wihelmus was heart-broken over 
the recent death of his wife, Mechtildis, who was said to be quite devout, and sold the 
properties to the Church in her honor, or he may have owed considerable money to the 
Electorate of Cologne, which also served as a medieval investment banker. Whatever the 
reason, the sale highly displeased the Count of Julich, who was engaged in a long-standing 
political struggle with the Electorate of Cologne. Wihelmus and the family soon became 
persona non-gratis, leading his descendants to scramble toward a new financial model — 
entrepreneurship, a new homeland and a new name. 


The next several Schenck Van Nydeggan generations retained small portions of the family’s pre 
1279 property holdings, but crops were increasingly unproductive, failing to produce revenue 
to keep up with taxes, further displeasing the Count, and the buildings on the estates needed 
restoration. In 1376, Hendrick Schenck van Nydeggan, the great grandson of Wihelmus, married 
Aleide van Rayde from a successful mercantile family in Holland, who was wealthy in her own 
right, owning several properties and a castle at Waldeck. Hendrick and Aleide modified their 
surname to van Nydeck (combining Nydeggan and Waldeck), possibly to sound more Dutch or 
maybe to create a more catchy business name. 


Under the name Nydeck, the couple found success with a business that renovated old castles 
and designed manor houses — the country residential estates that began to replace stone and 
mortar fortress castles. In the 1400s, Hendrick Schenck van Nydeck’s son and grandson added 
Hendrikse (possibly to indicate son of Hendrick, but perhaps for other reasons) to their name 
(Henry Hendrikse Schenck van Nydeck). In following generations, Schenck and van Nydeck were 
slowly dropped in favor of the surnames Hendrikse, Hendriksz or Hendrikzoon (depending on 
personal preference), which served as the primary surnames for family members who enjoyed 
successful in business, the military, exploration and cartography over the next 200 years. 


Two brothers led especially notable lives during the Netherlands phase of the Hendricson family 
history: Maarten Schenck Van Nydeggan Hendriksz (1539-1589), and Lambert Barentse 
Hendriksz (1549 — 1625). Maarten and Lambert were actually half-brothers (same father, 
different mothers), and had high levels of public notoriety for different reasons. The brothers 
also had different approaches to formulation of their name. 


Notes on Dutch Surnames in the 16" century: In a period of considerable flexibility and 
experimentation with surnames, Maarteen and Lambert occasionally used, or were referred to 
by others as “Hendrikzoon”, another form of “son of Hendrick”. For reasons that will soon 
become apparent, Maarten preferred to retain the ancestral Schenck van Nydeggan, whereas 
Lambert did not. Surnames unrelated to occupation or habitation were a new concept in 


139 


England and Europe in the 16" century. It was considered stylish and modern among people 
with status to develop unique surnames with personal meaning, while the less affluent (i.e., 
craftsmen and laborers) continued to use occupation and/or residence as a basis for a surname. 
(Patrick H. Dictionary of Family Names. Volume 2. London & Oxford: University Press. 2003) 


Maarten Schenck van Nydeggan Hendriksz 

Maarten was the illegitimate son of Barent Hendriksz (1519-1571) who was also Lambert’s 
father. Maarten was born near the family’s ancestral home in Nydeggan, Germany. Maarten’s 
mother, Anna van Beslaer, brought him to Nijmegan in the Netherlands when he was two years 
old, and shortly thereafter married Dederick Hendriksz, who was a cousin of Barent Hendriksz. 
After Anna and Dederick started to have children of their own, Maarten appears to have 
become inconvenient. When he was 12, his mother and stepfather essentially paid the 
mercenary knight Christoffel van sselstein (1521-1593), to take Maarten off their hands. (van 
der Broek, 2016; citation below) 


For the next 10 years, Maarten functioned as the page, assisting the knight in tournaments of 
military skills (archery, swordplay, horseback riding, and the new skill of pistol shooting) and 
supporting him in military campaigns throughout Europe. Mercenary knights contracted with 
nobles and local governments to represent them at tournaments, provide security and function 
as soldiers during hostilities. When he was 22, van Ysselstein arranged for Maarten to join the 
army of William of Orange, the leader of the Dutch revolt against the Spanish rulers of the 
Netherlands in the late 1500s, known as the 80 Years War (War of Dutch Independence). 
Maarten led a unit of 20 men who undertook sabotage missions behind enemy lines and 
conducted commando operations at sea in small boats to sink Spanish gunships. Maarten 
apparently was an incessant braggart and not well liked by his Dutch military colleagues, who, 
he claimed, blocked his promotion to a higher rank. During his tenure with the commando unit, 
Maarten also swindled a relative out of a castle (the Blyenbeck estate; see page 36). Maarten 
lost much of his financial assets and prestige when his relatives took the case to the Dutch High 
Court, and won a settlement, which led to Maarten’s eviction from the estate. 


Maarten’s military career was the topic 
of Dr. Olga van den_ Broek’s, 
dissertation, which was later published 
in The Netherlands. Van den Broek 
describes her subject as “fearless, cruel, 
genius and beastly”. He was a clever 
strategist, but never shied away from 
violence to intimidate foes. (van den 
Broek 0. Maarten Schenck van 
Nijdeggen: Career in War _ Time. 
Boxmeer, NL: Van Dinter Media. 2016) 


Maarten Schenck van Nydeggan Hendriksz, Dutch soldier of fortune. 
Image source: Wikimedia Commons. www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. Accessed: 2/11/2023. 


140 


Disgruntled, Maarten approached the Spanish for a high level military position, which they 
granted. For the next 10 years, he served as a general in the Spanish Army of Flanders, 
defeating the Dutch in several battles. In 1580, discouraged by a perceived lack of respect from 
his Spanish superiors, he again switched teams, jumping back to the Dutch army, serving once 
more as the leader of a commando team. After complaining about low pay, he resigned his 
position with the Dutch military and formed his own mercenary unit as a private enterprise. His 
services were in high demand and he led successful military operations all over Europe for 
many clients, one of which was the Electorate of Cologne, the same organization that received 
the property of Wihelmus Christianhus Schenck Van Nydeggan three hundred years earlier. 


On August 10, 1589, in a raid to kidnap the leader of a political group in conflict with his current 
employer (a Dutch ally of English Queen Elizabeth |), Maarten and 20 commandos boarded five 
skiffs and floated down the Waal River into Nijmegan; ironically, his hometown. Their plan was 
to float to the home of the targeted individual that literally overhung the river, climb through 
windows to enter the home, grab their prey, jump back into the boats, and make an escape. 
Heavy rains the day before swelled the river with a strong current that pushed four of the skiffs 
beyond the designated home. Maarten and the remaining men in his skiff proceeded with the 
plan anyway. With difficulty due to the swirling current, his band clambered off the boats, 
climbed up and through the windows into a house where they found a heavily attended 
wedding party in full swing: musicians, dancing, a 16" century version of an open bar, and 
dozens of people celebrating. While fighting the current, Maarten tied up to the wrong house! 


Surprisingly, the wedding guests rushed to repel Maarten and his men, and an alarm was 
sounded to alert the local militia who soon arrived. In the ensuing chaos, Maarten dove through 
a window to escape, missed the skiff below and landed in the river. The rapid current was too 
much for him and he drowned. His body was retrieved downstream the next day. It was 
decapitated and quartered. The head was presented to the bride and groom who placed it on a 
spike in front of their house. The Nijmegan mayor came by a week later to retrieve the head, 
which he hung from the front gate of the walled section of the city. Several weeks later, 
Maarten’s remains were assembled into an elegant coffin purchased by his wife Maria Van 
Geire, and a funeral service, “with friends, neighbors and colleagues in admiration’, was held at 
St. Stephen’s Church in Nijmegan. Apparently, the citizens of Nijmegan forgave quickly.

Lambert Barentse Hendriksz (Hendrikzoon) 

Lambert Barentse Hendriksz was Maarten’s younger brother by a different mother. Unlike 
Maarten, Lambert was born in the Netherlands in the town of Brielle, experienced a traditional 
childhood in a stable home, and was happy to include reference to his father, Barentse, in his 
name, whereas Maarteen, for obvious reasons, was not. It is not known if Lambert ever met 
Maarten. It seems likely they would have met considering that they had the same father who 
lived until the siblings were adults, and they both pursued military careers in roughly the same 
time frame. Yet, no evidence of their interaction was found. Lambert attended a Dutch naval 
academy and served as a cadet/apprentice on commercial (East Indies Company) and military 
ships. His travels included Ireland, Iceland and the North Atlantic, the Mediterranean, east and 
west coasts of Africa, and islands in the Indian Ocean. After receiving an appointment to the 
regular Dutch Navy, Lambert slowly moved upward through officer ranks over a long active 
duty career, ultimately becoming the Rotterdam harbormaster and then naval commander for 
the principle Dutch fleet that was stationed at Rotterdam. 


In recognition of his burly physique, rugged features, and “general lack of handsomeness” as 
one of naval colleagues noted, his ironic nickname in the navy became “Mooy Lambert” 
(Lambert the Beautiful). At the height of his fame, he was commonly referred to by that name 
in the Netherlands. When researching his life, it was noted that several historians used Mooy 
Lambert as if it was his actual name. 


Lambert Barentse Hendriksz (Hendrikzoon), often referred to as 
Mooy Lambert, was one of Holland’s greatest naval heroes. Lawrence 
C. Origins of the Cult and Iconography of Dutch Naval Heroes. 
Netherlands Quarterly of the History of Art. 1992; 21(4): 265-295. 

Image source: Wikimedia Commons. www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. 

Accessed: 2/13/2023. 


Although the Rotterdam fleet was a main focus of Lambert’s career, his notoriety primarily 
comes from his actions away from Rotterdam. He first rose to public awareness at the naval 
Battle of Dunkirk in 1605 when he led a Dutch fleet that defeated a much larger pirate fleet 
composed of a coalition of Irish privateers, Dutch dissidents, and the Dunkirk Corsairs, who 
were state-sponsored French pirates. The pirate fleet had raided coastal towns in England, 
France and the Netherlands and disrupted shipping in the English Channel for 10 years before 


142 


Mooy Lambert destroyed much of the fleet and captured the commander of the pirate 
confederation, Adriaan Dirksen. After Dunkirk, Lambert became an anti-pirate specialist for the 
Netherlands in the English Channel and later in the Mediterranean. 


In 1607, Lambert served as Vice Admiral and ship commander during a surprise Dutch attack on 
the principle Spanish fleet in the Bay of Gibraltar. After blocking the narrow outlet of the bay 
with six ships to prevent Spanish escape, the Dutch commander, Jacob van Heemskerk, 
attacked straight into the Spanish fleet with 20 ships. In the first exchange of fire from both 
sides, a Spanish cannonball tore through Heemskerk’s right leg, severing it, and he bled to 
death in the first minutes of the battle. Mooy Lambert took command of the Dutch forces on 
his ship, de Tygre, and focused the attack on the three largest Spanish galleons, which all 
exploded and sank when powder magazines were hit. Demoralized, Spanish officers and crews 
fled ten other large galleons and 15 smaller gunships, which were quickly sunk. Eight other 
galleons and corsairs under construction were also destroyed. The battle resulted in the 
complete destruction of Spain’s primary fleet. The Dutch victory led to the Twelve Years Truce 
between Spain and the Netherlands, and Spanish recognition of the legitimacy of the Dutch 
Republic that was formalized in a treaty known as the Peace of Munchen. 


From 1615-1623, Mooy Lambert commanded the Dutch Fleet of the Mediterranean District to 
protect merchant shipping from the Barbary Pirates based in Tunisia and the Algerian Corsairs. 
In a major, multiple day battle in 1618, Mooy Lambert’s fleet defeated a combined Barbary- 
Algerian Fleet, destroyed their primary harbor, and freed several hundred Dutch hostages. 


Lambert Hendriksz is the father of the North American explorer Cornelius Lambert Hendriksz 
(Hendrickson). Lambert’s grave can be visited at the Saint Laurens Church in Rotterdam. A 
naval museum nearby has an extensive collection of Mooy Lambert artifacts including a model 
of de Tygre. 


Notes on the 80 Years War (Dutch War of Independence): From 1278 through 1740, the 
monarchy known as House of Habsburg, based in Austria, was the most powerful political, 
economic and military entity in Europe. For example, all of the Kings of the Holy Roman Empire 
from 1440-1740 were Habsburgs. Through a combination of marriage, political maneuvering, 
financial mergers, and warfare, members of the Habsburg royal line, and their entourage of 
administrators, ruled a number of European nations including Spain in the 16" century. Holland 
did not exist as a distinct nation at this point in history. Instead it was a loosely affiliated group 
of 17 provinces, called the Low Countries, including Holland, present day Belgium, Luxemburg 
and parts of Germany and France. Throughout the medieval period, these provinces were ruled 
by a variety of German duchies or French provinces. 


Stimulated by the Protestant Reformation spreading through Europe in the early 1500s, seven 
provinces that comprise what we today know as The Netherlands, broke away from the other 
Low Country provinces that were less enamored by the Reformation. Shortly after, the seven 
provinces came under the rule of the Spanish Habsburgs via marriage when a daughter of 
Isabella and Ferdinand of Spain (sponsors of Christopher Columbus) married a Dutch Duke. The 
Catholic Church urged the Spanish monarchs to suppress the Reformation Movement in the 
newly acquired Dutch territory. A harsh Spanish Governor was sent to the Dutch provinces with 


143 


a military force, known as the Army of Flanders, and violence quickly ensued, provoking a Dutch 
separatist movement, leading to a sequence of Dutch revolts and Spanish reprisals. 


By 1568, the Dutch separatists, with external help from England and non-Catholic groups in 
France, organized a relatively formidable army and a naval force that was smaller than the 
Spanish fleet but better managed. Fighting raged on and off, with several multi-year lulls until 
1648 when the Peace of Munster formally recognized the seven provinces as the Dutch 
Republic. However, Spain and the Habsburgs retained the other 10 Low Country provinces, 
known as the Catholic Netherlands. During the 80 Years War, the Dutch East and West Indies 
Companies thrived. The Companies honored their contracts with Habsburgs by annually 
distributing a share of their profits to the Spanish monarchy in spite of the conflict. War and 
business do make strange bedfellows. (Hart M. The Dutch Wars of Independence. Warfare and 
Commerce in the Netherlands, 1570-1680. New York: Routledge. 2014) 


First family member to Immigrate to North America 

Hendrick Willemz Hendrickson (1636-1706), grandson of Dutch explorer Cornelius Lambert 
Hendrickson, (1572-1650) was the first member of our family to immigrate and live 
permanently in the New World. He arrived in New Amsterdam (present day Manhattan and 
Brooklyn) in 1663 on board the ship Rooseboom (Rosetree), with 18 families (76 adults and 
children), one other single man and two single women.

Hendrick became embroiled in the affairs of the Dutch colony, including an investigation of 
black market beaver pelt smuggling, and the transfer of the colony to the English. The story of 
Hendrick Hendrickson’s early years in North America, focusing on the fall of New Amsterdam to 
the British and the Hudson Valley beaver pelt industry is told in Chapter IV. 

Although Hendrick Hendrickson was the first person in the line to establish permanent 
residence in North American (he lived the last 43 years of his life in New York and New Jersey), 
his grandfather Cornelius Lambert Hendrickson lived onboard ships and camped on shorelines 
of Long Island, New England, New Jersey, Delaware and Pennsylvania from 1611 to 1616 as he 
mapped these regions for the Dutch West Indies Company. He is recognized as the first 
European to enter Pennsylvania, and is considered one of the most important early explorers of 


144 


North America. The story of Cornelius Hendrickson’s travels in North America appears In the 
Chapter IV. 


Notes on 17™ Century Transatlantic Travel to New Amsterdam: Hendrickson’s one-way adult 
transatlantic ticket on the Rooseboom cost 36 Dutch guilder, equivalent to $2160 in 2020. 
Children over three years traveled half-price at 18 guilder ($1080), infants traveled free, and 
married couples received a reduced rate of 25 guilder each, or 50 guilder total ($3000). Adding 
up these fees, a Rotterdam to New Amsterdam trip for a family of two adults and two children 
cost $5160 in present day dollars. For point of reference, the annual income of pastors, 
attorneys and physician / surgeons in 17" century Netherlands was roughly 600 guilder 
($36,000), skilled tradesmen (guild craftsmen) averaged 500 guilder ($30,000), and outdoor 
laborers earned approximately 300 guilder ($18,000). In contrast, high-level military leaders 
were paid 1,200-1,500 guilder ($72,000-$90,000) annually. Thus, travel to North American was 
not out of the economic reach of the upper level of professions in the Netherlands, and even a 
moderate-income family likely could scrimp and save for several years to generate the funds 
required to transport the family across the Atlantic. Actually, New Amsterdam was eager to 
have laborers immigrate to the colony to build the houses, churches and other community 
facilities needed to accommodate the influx of new residents arriving every month. The colony 
provided financial subsidies and housing to low income laborers as an incentive. (Reden C. How 
Transatlantic History Shaped the World as We Know It: The Transatlantic Crossing. 
www.royalcaribbean.com. April 25, 2022. Accessed May 17, 2024) 


Passengers were required to bring their own bedding, two changes of clothing, eating utensils, 
personal hygiene supplies, and had tight limits on the amount of baggage stored in the hold. 
There were no first class accommodations on the Rooseboom or any of the other passenger 
ships sailing the North Atlantic. Everyone traveled in open bays one or two levels below deck, 
lying on the floor or on racks hung on the inside of hulls. Passengers were allowed topside only 
a couple of hours per day at scheduled times to minimize deck crowding. Two meals a day of 
meager rations were provided. Communicable and hygiene-related illnesses were rampant by 
the end of the journey. On the return trip to the Netherlands, the ship was loading with beaver 
pelts, lumbar, mail from colonists, government officials and occasionally, private passengers 
disgruntled with life in the colony. 


Between 1630-1667, at least one passenger ship like the Rooseboom departed a Netherland 
port each month with 70-100 passengers and at least one ship returned east with cargo for 
European markets. The passage routes became sufficiently routine that inbound and outbound 
ships sometimes rendezvoused mid-journey to exchange news about the colony or back home 
in the Netherlands, balance out provisions and even exchange passengers who changed their 
minds about their destination. (Dobson D. Transatlantic Voyages, 1600-1699. Baltimore: 
Genealogical Publishing Co. 2009; Jacobs J. New Netherland: A Dutch Colony in Seventeenth 
Century America. Leiden: Brill Academic Publishers. 2005)

Morgan 


Reminder - Morgan / Hendricson Connection 

After members of both families immigrated to North America, the Morgans and Hendricsons 
paralleled each other in their westward movement through New Jersey, Delaware, West 
Virginia, Kentucky, the Northwest Territory and Oregon. Through the generations, there were 
extensive interactions among members of these families and at least six marriages, leading to 
other Hendricson-Morgan family lines in New Jersey, Illinois, Ohio, Wisconsin and Minnesota. 
The sixth marriage was pivotal in advancing the story toward the union of Susan and Bill 
Hendricson. | would not be writing this history if a member of the Morgan family had not made 
a fateful decision in 1851 that ultimately led to the sixth Morgan-Hendricson marriage. 


In the spring of 1851 at age 56, Drusilla Morgan Price (1795-1870), was pondering the 
opportunity to join a wagon train composed of more than 80 Morgan family members that was 
being organized in Danville, Illinois. Drusilla was in a tough situation. She had been widowed 
four times overall and twice within the past three years. Oddly, her third and fourth deceased 
husbands were both named James Price, and both had left her with substantial debts. She was 
attempting to manage a failing farm that was not capable of supporting the numerous adult 
sons and daughters, spouses and grandchildren residing with her. The destination of the wagon 
train was Oregon more than 2,000 miles to the west, where the territorial government was 
offering land donations of 320 acres as settlement enticement to family units and widows. 
Other members of the Morgan entourage at her farm were eager to attempt the journey but 
could not afford it on their own. Wagon train participation criteria required a head of 
household for each traveling family who would be responsible for paying for any repairs or 
extra supplies during the trip and settling up any debts upon arrival in Oregon. 


Drusilla Morgan Price, at approximately age 65 in an 1860 
photo, taken in Albany, Oregon nine years after leading a 
band of 13 Morgans to the Willamette Valley from 
Illinois. 


Although prospects in Danville were grim, a five-month journey across the continent, walking 
the entire way, to an unknown future in far-off Oregon was not an attractive alternative. The 
deadline was fast approaching for acquiring the covered wagon, oxen, other livestock, 
equipment, food and supplies that were required in order to join the wagon train. When 
Drusilla decided that she could not afford the trip to Oregon, her 19-year old daughter, Amanda 
Morgan, recently jilted by a fiancé and hoping for a new start, launched what must have been 
an impressive campaign to change her mind. Two days after almost continuous debate with the 
fiery Amanda, Drusilla approached the wagon master and paid a holding fee to reserve a spot in 


148 


the Morgan wagon train for her family. She was informed she had two months to get 
organized. Drusilla hired a broker to sell her farm “as promptly as can be arranged”, used the 
proceeds to prepare for the trip, and headed west. Traveling with Drusilla were her brother 
Nathan, also a widower, eldest daughter Mary (Polly) with her husband Martin Price, grandson 
Nimrod with his two children, teenage daughter Amanda, three of Drusilla’s other adult 
children and a niece and her husband. The Morgan wagon train reached Oregon in the fall of 
1851. All 13 members of the Drusilla’s group survived the trip. 


Soon after arriving in Oregon, Amanda Morgan met a young man, David Rideout, who also 
came to Oregon seeking a fresh start after failing at several enterprises in Maine, 
Massachusetts and California. They married in 1852 and their third child, Mary Eleanor (Ella) 
Morgan Rideout was born in 1856. In 1880, Ella married a young sheriff from Colfax, 
Washington with the unlikely name of Omar Pasha (OP) Hendricson (1854-1913), who was 
Bill’s great-grandfather. OP was named after a Turkish general who gained notoriety during the 
Crimean War. 


Origin and evolution of surname 

The Morgan surname is of Welsh and Celtic origin. The name evolved from the Old Welsh and 
Celtic word Morcant, which had meanings related to oceans: of the sea, sea chief, sea captain, 
and sailor. Use of the surname Morgan has been extremely common throughout the history of 
Wales. The 1811 census of England and Wales found that more than 25% of Welsh property 
owners went by Morgan or derivatives (Morgen, Morgane, Morghan, Morghann, Morghyn). 


Morgan is one of the oldest Welsh names on record, stretching back to the legends of King 
Arthur, who, according to Malory’s 15" century novel Le Morte d’ Arthur, was based in Wales 
near present day Cardiff in the 4" or 5" centuries. In Malory’s telling of the Arthurian saga, 
Arthur was defeated in a battle, and fearing for the safety of his wife, Queen Guinevere, 
secretly moved her to the safety of a secluded coastal town in Wales. Arthur’s youngest son 
was born in this hide-away and was named Morgan — “he who came from the sea”. The name 
of Glamorganshire (Glamorgan County) in Wales is derived from this tale. The oldest village in 
Glamorganshire is Caerfyrddin, which dates back to the 2" century, and still exists today. It is 
mentioned in Le Morte d’ Arthur as the secluded hide-away and is considered to be the 
hometown of the earliest Morgan ancestors. The Morgans were members of a tribe that the 
Romans called Demetae (Latin: wealth from sheep. It is generally thought that Arthurian sagas 
were inspired by the efforts of the Demetae to drive the Romans from Wales. The people of 
Cornwall in the southwest corner of England have a different Arthurian saga, featuring the 
sorcerer Merlin, as will be seen later in this family history. (Vinaver E. The Works of Sir Thomas 
Malory. Oxford University Press. 1990. Johnson B. Camelot, Court of King Arthur. www.historic- 
uk.com. The History and Heritage Accommodation. June 21. 2015. Accessed: May 7, 2023) 


Geographic origin 

The individual who is recognized as the first leader of the geographic entity known as Wales 
was Morgan Mwyn Fawr who lived in the 700s. He was nicknamed Morgan the Generous for his 
civil treatment of enemy tribes he defeated in battle. The area of Wales where he lived was 
known as Morganwg and is the modern day Glamorgan County, which includes Cardiff, the 


149 


most prominent city in Wales. Virtually all of the pre-immigration Morgan ancestors were born 
in the village of Llandaff, now a district within Cardiff, or a nearby estate known as Tredegar. 


England, Scotland and Ireland with Wales highlighted in red. 
Cardiff/Llandaff is at southeastern corner of Wales. 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 5/8/2023. 


At the time of the Norman Conquest in 1066, the leader of the now civilized Demetae tribe was 
Cadivor-Fawr Morgaine (1030-1091) and his wife was Elan Llawen (dates unknown). Cadivor- 
Fawr was a farmer and the Mayor of his village, which unlike other villages, was cooperative 
with the invading Normans. The Normans rewarded Cadivor-Fawr with a large track of land in 
Glamorganshire, which they converted into a successful agricultural and coal mining operation. 


The evolution of the Cadivor-Fawr Morgaine/Elan Llawen household into the Morgan family is 
documented in family histories written in 1938, 1950 and 1966. These Morgan histories relied 
considerably on information available in the Book of Llandaff (see page 58). These Morgan 
histories describe ten marriages between 1081 when Cadivor-Fawr and Elan’s son Bleddri was 
married, through the year 1323 when a Llewelyn Morgaine of Kilsaint, a many generations 
distant great grandson, married Anghard Morgan, the daughter of the lord (owner) of a country 
manor known as Tredegar, in the neighboring county of Monmouthshire. Llewelyn and Anghard 
elected to use Morgan as their surname, perhaps because Anghard was the financial 
heavyweight in the relationship; her dad owned the estate. The important point for our family 
genealogy is that from 1323 forward, the line of Morgans that included Hendricson-linked 
family members that immigrated to North American, was known as the Tredegar Morgans. The 
original Tredegar House, built around 1300, still exists. A village, also known as Tredegar, 
developed near the estate, comprised of families that leased tracts of land for farming. 


Tredegar house in Monmouthshire, Wales was 
constructed in the 1300s, and expanded in the 
16", 18 and 20" centuries. Newman J. 
Buildings of Wales: Gwent & Monmouthshire. 
London: Penguin Books. 2000. 

Image source: Wikimedia Commons. 
www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. Accessed: 7/16/2024. 


First appearance of surname in public records 
A great-great grandson of Llewelyn and Anghard Morgan by the name of Jevan Evan Morgan 
(1405-1448) was the first family member to formally use the surname Morgan in a marriage 


150 


certificate, a property deed, and a will. Jevan married Denise Thomas (1404-1464) in 1429. She 
was identified as Denise Thomas Morgan on their marriage certificate. 


Synopsis of pre-immigration history 

Throughout their pre-immigration history, the Morgans of Tredegar were landed gentry, not 
nobility, although a few family figures were knighted for deeds in service of the crown, or for 
being a close friend of the King. In the 300 years from Llewelyn and Anghard’s marriage in 1323 
to when the first Morgans landed in North America, the family’s economic basis was diverse 
including income from agricultural crops, leasing farm land to tenants, leasing pastures for 
sheep grazing, leasing forest acreage to clubs for hunting, leasing water front property to 
tenants for fishing lodges, operating mills on rivers flowing through their lands, and coal mining 
operations. Many Morgans also had professional jobs: attorneys, architects and politicians, and 
in particular, sheriffs. In medieval Wales, the sheriff was the tax collector for the county, but 
also had similar duties as a county sheriff today in the U.S.: investigating crimes and complaints, 
jailing suspected perpetrators and enforcing regulations. 


First Morgan family member to Immigrate to North America — Sorting Out the Truth. 
Triggered by the economic chaos of the English Civil War in the 17" century, members of many 
Morgan lines in Wales, including the Tredegars, fell into hard times, and looked to the New 
World for a fresh start. Given the proliferation of similar names among the various Morgan 
lines, it is understandable that prior family historians, including Harold and Mildred Hendricson, 
encountered difficulty in sorting out, who did what and when. The Tredegar Morgan 
immigration story that captured the imaginations of several prior family historians involved the 
arrival of three Morgan brothers, James, Miles and John, in Boston in 1636 on the ship Mary. 


The three brothers were among the seven legitimate children of a Welsh attorney, Sir Thomas 
William Morgan (1571-1649), who used William as his first name, perhaps to distinguish himself 
from his prominent father, Thomas Henry Morgan (see Morgan lineage table, page 56). William 
Morgan was the King’s Attorney for Wales from 1637 until his death in 1649. In addition to his 
legal prominence, William was a successful merchant, Parliament Member (PM), active 
participant in London’s high society, and a close confident of King Charles |, who knighted him 
for his legal work in Wales. However, Sir William is best known for numerous extramarital 
affairs, well chronicled at the time, which produced at least four illegitimate children. 


His extracurricular activities were a basis for a popular Oliver Goldsmith play, She Stoops to 
Conquer featuring the immortal line, “Ask me no questions, and I'll tell you no lies.” (Clarke N. 
Brothers of the Quill: Oliver Goldsmith in Grub Street. Cambridge MA: Harvard University Press. 
2016) One of these child-producing entanglements involved a liaison with Sybil Wayte, a 
seamstress and also a housekeeper for a PM colleague of Sir William. When Sir William refused 
to recognize two of Sybil’s children as his offspring and thus deserving of Morgan inheritance, 
Wayte sued him. In an unusual ruling for that era, the court ruled in her favor! Sir William 
Morgan was ordered to reach a settlement with Wayte that involved a house, a monthly 
stipend and recognition of the children’s’ status as members of the Morgan Tredegar family. 


In 1636, Sir William sent his three sons to the Virginia colonies to explore business 
opportunities that might resurrect the families’ financial standing, which had been battered by 
questionable investments. They departed on the Mary with intention to return to England the 


151 


following year. The Mary was one of a flotilla of five ships heading from Bristol, England to the 
Virginia colonies with each ship carrying approximately 80 passengers, mostly young married 
couples seeking a better life. The flotilla encountered a North Atlantic hurricane, which sank 
two of the ships with extensive loss of life, and damaged a third to the extent that it returned to 
England. The Mary was driven off course and ultimately found its way to the coast of 
Massachusetts, where it was grounded. The fifth ship, the Sarah, continued to Virginia. After 
clamoring off the Mary onto a rocky beach, the Morgan brothers made their way to Boston 
where James and Miles liked what they saw and decided to make a go of it in New England. The 
third brother, John, was repelled by religious intolerance in Massachusetts and went to Virginia 
to pursue his father’s goal of North American business development. 


James Morgan (1607-1685), who was an attorney, ultimately moved to the area of Groton and 
New London, Connecticut, where he was instrumental in the development of both 
communities. He was appointed as the first commissioner of New London and supervised the 
planning and construction of the city. He played the same roles for Groton, where he also 
served as mayor, city council member and city attorney for many years. James bought land 
throughout Connecticut, typically 800-acre parcels, and sold it to developers who desired to 
create other towns. One of these towns was Wallingford, Connecticut. James served on a 
committee that established the framework of the original colonial government in Connecticut, 
known as The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut, and was chair of one of the Colonial 
Assemblies in the formative years of the Colony. 


Miles Morgan (1616-1699) relocated to western Massachusetts, where he was instrumental in 
establishing Springfield and played a key role in the defense of the town during Prince Philips’ 
war, a Native American uprising that led to the deaths of 25% of New England colonists and a 
higher percentage of the region’s Native Peoples. A statue of Miles Morgan stands in the 
historic district of Springfield. Neither James nor Miles ever returned to England. Their brother 
John did not either. He married in Virginia and established a Morgan line in the southern 
colonies that produced notable descendants including Daniel Morgan, the Revolutionary War 
General, who defeated the British in important battles including Saratoga in New York and 
Cowpens in North Carolina. 


This is quite an illustrious group of Morgan first immigrants, all born in Wales. But, alas, it is, for 
the most part, NOT the Morgan line most directly connected with our Hendricson family. There 
are undoubtedly many U.S. families who can claim the philandering Sir William Morgan, the 
three Morgan Brothers of the Mary, and the heroic General Daniel Morgan as ancestors. 
However, Sir William and his sons are not the Morgan Tredegar line that contributed to our 
family history. Close, but not quite. As indicated in the Morgan lineage (generations 4-8, pages 
57-58), the genealogical challenge is the fact that there were two brothers born to Thomas 
Henry Morgan and Elizabeth Bodenham: Henry William Morgan (1567-1653) and Thomas 
William Morgan (1571-1649). Both elected to use William as their first name after entering 
professional life, one in London, and the other in Wales. Thomas William is the illustrious Sir 
William Morgan. His less well-known brother, Henry William, is the actual link. 


The first family member related to the Hendricson-Lienau line to immigrate to North America, 
and survive (see note below) was Morgan Wilm Morgan (1687-1767) who arrived in the 


152 


Delaware Colony in 1713. He was born in Llandaff, Glamorganshire to Charles Morgan (1635- 
1720), Henry William Morgan’s grandson, and Susan Powell Morgan (1646-1697). Charles and 
Susan farmed Tredegar lands and sold produce at farm to market shops in Tredegar village, 
Llandaff and Cardiff. Their agricultural work was not as glamorous as other Tredegar Morgans, 
but it was sufficient to ensure that their son Morgan was well educated. He graduated from 
Cambridge, attained legal training by apprenticeship with a senior London barrister, and also 
was an ordained clergymen of the Church of England, all by age 26. We do not know why 
Morgan Morgan elected to immigrate to North America. There are ruminations in prior Morgan 
histories that he was sent to Delaware as a Crown Council (i.e., attorney representing the royal 
court) to investigate financial mismanagement in the colony. The story of Morgan Morgan’s life 
in the colonies and his role in the establishment of West Virginia appears in Chapter IV. 


In addition to being Morgan Morgan’s father, Charles Morgan also was the twin brother of the 
legendary pirate of the Caribbean Captain Henry Morgan (1635-1688). We do not know why 
Henry turned to piracy given the Morgan’s financial history. It has been conjectured that the 
social upheaval of the English Civil War, which occurred when he was a teenager, may have 
been a catalyst. In spite of his baby-faced appearance and preference for flamboyant apparel, 
Henry Morgan was ruthless as he prowled the Caribbean for 25 years from his base at Port 
Royal, Jamaica. Henry was knighted for his disruption of Spanish and Dutch shipping, and for 
destroying Caribbean seaports that traded with Spain and Holland. His pirating made him 
wealthy, allowed him to build a huge privateer fleet, and to acquire vast property in Jamaica. 
Henry retired to life as a sugar plantation owner and politician in Jamaica, eventually serving as 
governor, one of the few Caribbean pirates who outlived his profession. 


This portrait of Captain Henry Morgan was produced in 1681. He

often wore during naval battles, made him fearful to the staid Dutch and

Notes on the First Morgan Immigration to North America: Some historians contend that 
another Miles Morgan (1536-1578; born 80 years before the Miles Morgan associated with 
Springfield, MA), who was a brother of Thomas Henry Morgan, was actually the first Morgan to 
reach North America. Miles was among a group of investors intent on colonization, which 
included the privateers and explorers Walter Raleigh, Humphrey Gilbert (Raleigh’s half-brother) 
and Richard Grenville, as well as Henry Knollys, London’s leading financier of that era, and 
Queen Elizabeth herself. This group combined efforts to raise funds and assemble a fleet to 
explore sites for a colony on the outer banks of North Carolina. Among this impressive group, 
Miles was the least among equals, more noted for his sibling connection to the respected 
Thomas Henry Morgan and the Tredegar Morgan estate, than for his accomplishments. Up to 
this point, Miles was mainly known for his active engagement in London social life, although he 


153 


was considered a worthy seaman, and he owned a 110 ton ship, a major plus in the eyes of the 
other investors. 


Gilbert, the senior seaman in the group, led a flotilla of seven ships that set sail in November 
1578 from Plymouth to scout for colony sites. Miles Morgan captained his ship, Red Lion of 
Newport, with a crew of 48 men and the investor Knollys who traveled with his own entourage 
of five militia, in case of “engagement with hostiles upon landfall.” One of the other ships, the 
Ann Ager, was captained by Raleigh, and Gilbert captained the flagship Falcon, contributed by 
the Queen. Grenville and three of his most experienced captains helmed the other four ships. 
Early in the voyage, Miles ran afoul of Knollys who felt that Miles had deceived him about the 
profits to be accrued from the colony. Insult led to insult, culminating with Miles flattening 
Knollys with a punch to the head. Knollys had his personal militia arrest Miles and chain him to 
the hull below deck. A crewmen on the Red Lion signaled Gilbert’s ship about the altercation. 
Gilbert hustled over in the Falcon to stop the dispute, promised Knollys a more substantial cut 
of any profits, and transferred the irascible investor to the Falcon. 


Six weeks out, storms enveloped the fleet, damaging several, and causing all of the ships to 
return to Plymouth except the Red Lion. The last flag signal Gilbert received from Miles Morgan 
on the Red Lion indicated that they were pressing ahead. The Red Lion was never seen again. 
For such occurrences, the 16'" century default convention was to assign the disappearance to 
“storm at sea; ship and crew perished”. However, historians searching for evidence pertinent to 
the fabled Roanoke colony, which occurred subsequently, have found items south of Roanoke 
Island that may be associated with the Miles Morgan expedition. The most telling of the 
recovered items are several coins that Miles’ printed to commemorate the trip with his motto: 
Now or Never. 


A current theory is that Miles and shipmates may have indeed reached North Carolina, lost the 
Red Lion in a mishap as they approached shore or at anchorage, and realizing no rescue was 
forthcoming, attempted assimilation with the Secotan tribe in the area, which may or may not 
have been successful. Accounts by Raleigh, Grenville and other investors’ involved in the 
unsuccessful efforts to establish the Roanoke Island Colony 12 years later, describe the 
Secotan’s capacity to communicate in English and their familiarity with Europe. As discussed on 
pages 203-205, this was not an uncommon phenomenon for early European colonists. It is 
unknown if the Secotan tribe’s English language skills came from interactions with Miles 
Morgan and his crew, or from interactions with other English speaking fishermen who may 
have came ashore on the outer banks of North Carolina. (O’Brien H. Miles Morgan, Intrepid 
Explorer from Tredegar House. www.walesonline.com.uk. October 15, 2015. Accessed: February 
21, 2023. Gabriel-Powell A. Richard Grenville and the Lost Colony of Roanoke. Jefferson, NC: 
McFarland Co. 2016)

Reminder - Maris / Hendricson Connection 

In 1911, William Firman Hendricson (1883-1948), the oldest son of Ella Morgan Rideout 
Hendricson and Omar Pasha Hendricson, married Mabel Julia Maris (1887-1981) in Spokane, 
Washington. The couple moved to Walla Walla shortly after their marriage. William and Mabel 
had two children: Yvonne Eleanor Hendricson (1913-1993) and Harold Maris Hendricson (1919- 
1992) who was my father. 


Origin and evolution of surname 

The Maris surname is of French origin from the region of Normandy in northern France. The 
name appears to have evolved from the French words “Mariess” and “Marais”, which were 
used in medieval times to describe a marshy area of land. 


First appearance of surname in public records 

In England after the Norman Invasion, the name Maris appeared in the Domesday Book Census 
of 1086 as Richard de Maris in Kent, a county in the southeastern region of England. This 
individual was a tenet farmer on lands of a nobleman, but apparently had some property of his 
own because his name appears on recordings of deeds in the County Kent ledger of the 
Domesday. It is known that many of the invading army of approximately 8,000 Norman soldiers 
that accompanied William the Conqueror (William |) to England in 1066 settled in Kent after the 
hostilities concluded. In France, the surname Maris first appeared in Normandy in the 1180 
population survey known as the Magni Rotulli Scaccarii Normaniae sub Regibus Angliae (Great 
Rolls of the Board of Normandy and the Kings of England). In this census, four Maris brothers 
were identified as Normandy landowners: Ivo, Drogo, Gilbert and Roberto de Maris. 


Notes on the Domesday Book (1a century title — “Doomsday”): The Domesday Day Book is 
Great Britain’s earliest public record of towns, population, public and private lands, and names 
of property and business owners. The survey was commissioned in 1086 by William | (William 
the Conqueror) for purposes of reforming taxation in England after the Norman Conquest. It is 
the most complete record of pre-industrial medieval society assembled anywhere in the world, 
and is remarkable in its level of sophistication and detail. (Domesday Book Census of 1086 
(Great Survey; Liber de Wintona). London: National Archives. 1° published 1783; published 
online in contemporary English 2011. Archives.gov.uk. Accessed: March 9, 2023) 


Notes on the Magni Rotulli (Great Rolls Survey): This document was a French version of the 
Domesday Survey, but less sophisticated. However, the Great Rolls Surveys were administered 
on a regular basis from approximately 1150 to 1833, and thus provide considerable information 
about the evolution of society in the province of Normandy. (Stapleton T. Magni Rotuli Scaccarii 
Normaniae sub Regibus Angliae (Great Rolls of the Board of Normandy and the Kings of 
England) Volumes | and II. London: Society of Antiquaries. 1841) 


It also has been suggested in genealogy investigations of other Maris lines that many individuals 
in England with a Maris surname were French Huguenots (French Protestants who adhered to a 
Calvinist or Reformed Christianity orthodoxy) that moved across the English Channel to escape 


156 


government persecution and anti-Protestant violence. As we saw in the Chapter II Maris 
Lineage Table, the backstory of the first confidently identified Maris in England is consistent 
with the Huguenot theory. 


Geographic origin 

The de Maris brothers and other individuals with the surname Maris were born in a village 
known as Le Marais-la-Chapelle in the Calvados Department (i.e., county) of Normandy, which 
lies on the coast of the English Channel. The most prominent city in this region is Caen. 
Consistent with the definition of Mariess and Marais, the area has many salt marshes and soft 
wetlands near the coastline. Members of the Maris family that immigrated to North America in 
the 17" century lived in England, suggesting that the migration of Normandy residents to 
England between the 11" and 16" centuries included individuals with the Maris surname. 


Notes on French Huguenots: The name derives from the Swiss politician Besancon Hugues who 
was Catholic and led persecution of Reform Protestants. So, in other words, Hugue-nots were 
everything that Hugues was not. French Huguenots were Protestants who believed in a strict 
interpretation of the Bible, had ambiguous perceptions of free will versus predetermination as 
per the Calvinist dilemma over these concepts, believed that God only saved those that 
deserved to be saved, opposed art, music and pageantry in religious services, advocated 
conservative dress and behavior in public (no provocative attire, dancing, singing, gambling, 
swearing or drinking), and prohibited the naming of children after Catholic saints and images of 
Christ on a cross. The Saint Bartholomew’s Day Massacre in August 1572, triggered by a 
Protestant Huguenot wedding in Catholic Paris, was directed by the French royal family. The 
massacre led to a series of attacks on Huguenot leaders and communities throughout France 
resulting in 15,000 deaths. (Diefendorf BB. The St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre: A Brief History 
with Documents. Bedford: St. Martin’s Press. 2008) Surviving Huguenots either converted to 
Catholicism or fled France, with many immigrating to England. The massacre reinforced 
Protestant perceptions in England and elsewhere in Europe that the Catholic Church was 
murderous and treacherous. (Cottret B. Huguenots in England. Immigration and Settlement. 
Cambridge & Paris: Cambridge University Press. 1991)

Synopsis of European / English pre-immigration history 

The first record | found of a Maris family in England was Richard Dunwall de Maris (1568-1641) 
and wife Agnes Griffin (1572-1640). Richard, likely born in France, probably was brought to 
England as a young child by his parents in the aftermath of the Saint Bartholomew’s Day 
Massacre. Little is known about the lives of Richard and Agnes, but considerable information 


157 


exists about their grandson, George Edward Maris Jr. (1632 — 1706), and his wife Alicia Wilsmith 
(1632-1699). George and Alicia lived in Worcestershire (Worcester County) in central England, 
just south of Birmingham. They practiced the Quaker faith and were shoemakers. As Quakers, 
George and Alice experienced persistent harassment from local government officials. George 
was imprisoned for nine months in 1670 and again in 1674 for failure to show proper deference 
to representatives of the crown (i.e., failure to “bow and doff the hat in tribute”) and was jailed 
for brief periods several times in the following years for “suspicious means of piety and prayer”. 
After the Worcester County Sheriff imposed penalty taxes on George and Alice’s cobbler 
(shoemaker) shop, claiming it doubled as a “house of pagan worship,” George and Alice decided 
that William Penn’s Great Experiment in Freedom (see pages 161-162) across the sea in 
America offered the prospect of a better life consistent with their Quaker ideals. 


Notes on Quaker Beliefs and Practice in 17" Century England: Quakerism emerged around 
1650 in England among conservative Protestant groups dissatisfied with the Church of England. 
Led by George Fox (1624-1691) and his wife, Margaret Fell, followers of this movement, 
originally named Religious Society of Friends, believed it was desirable for individuals to have a 
personal Christian experience, based on private conversations with God, without the leadership 
of ordained clergy who told people what to believe, without ritualized religious services and 
without a designated worship site, in other words, without a church. The term Quakers evolved 
from George Fox’s concept that people should “tremble at the word of the Lord” (i.e., quake), 
and not at the word of clergy”. It was originally a dismissive nickname used by critics of Fox, but 
it caught on among the Friends Society. Fox, Fell and their followers, which included William 
Penn, emphasized an individual’s unique interaction with the Christian faith, and perceived that 
their mission was to restore a pure Christian church, where individuals could focus on 
emotional and behavioral purity, and shape their own relationship with God, without all the 
pomp, ceremony and elaborate cathedrals. (/ngle L. First Among Friends. George Fox and the 
Creation of Quakerism. New York & London: Oxford University Press. 1996) The movement was 
popular; there were an estimated 60,000 Quakers in England by 1675. Early Quaker practices 
which continue to this day include: teetotalism, plain dress, refusal to participate in war, no 
profanity, silent prayer, not using the words church or cathedral to describe worship sites 
(because prayer can occur anywhere), opposition to slavery and allowing women to speak 
during prayer services and to lead such services. Substantial numbers of the Maris, Dennis and 
Goodman families brought their Quaker faith with them to the New World. 


First family members to immigrate to North America 
In 1683, George Edward Maris and Alice Welsmith Maris immigrated to Penn’s colony in 
Pennsylvania with their six children from Bromsgrove, Worcester County, England.

Reminder - Dennis / Hendricson Connection 

In 1916, Archibald (Archie) Dennis (1889-1976) and Maude Odessa Goodman (1895-1979) were 
married in Walla Walla, Washington. Archie and Maude had two children, Lloyd Neal Dennis 
(1917-1992) and Mildred Marietta Dennis (1919-2019). Mildred married Harold Maris 
Hendricson in 1946. Mildred and Harold were the parents of Shirley and |. Archie and Maude 
were our maternal grandparents. 


Origin and evolution of surname 

The Dennis surname is of French origin from the Normandy region in northern France. The 
name appears to have evolved from the French Le Denys, which was used in medieval times to 
refer to the residents of Denmark (Danes). This suggests that members of the family originally 
may have relocated to Normandy from Denmark. This would have not been unusual in 
Normandy, which was ruled for centuries by Vikings beginning with Rollo Normand in the hi 
century, or in England during the Danelaw era where Vikings governed much of present day 
England for almost 200 years. In France and England, the surname name evolved to Denys or 
Denis by the 12th century, and by the 16"" century, Dennis was commonly used. 


First appearance of surname in public records 

A Denis of Normand appears in the 1180 Normandy population survey, Magni Rotulli Scaccarii 
Normaniae sub Regibus Angliae, with the notation that this individual had been granted roughly 
130 acres of property and a residence in the Cornwall region of England by King William | 
(William the Conqueror). Cornwall comprises the peninsula jutting into the Atlantic Ocean at 
the southwestern corner of England. The principle Cornwall city is Plymouth. 


The Cornwall region of England is highlighted in red. Wales 
(Morganshire) and Cornwall have competing Arthurian legends, 
and each claim castles as the theoretical sites of the saga.

Geographic origin of family 

No origin site has been identified for the Dennis family in the Normandy region of France to the 
best of my knowledge. A previous account of Dennis family genealogy suggested that the small 
medieval village of Saint Denis de Mere in the Calvados Department (county) of Normandy may 
be the origin site, but research for this book found no evidence to support this assertion. 


The first direct connection to a specific person of pertinence to our family history is a Thomas 
Denis who obtained permits to repair “un-tended family fields and a manor in much decay” in 
the village of Lesnewth in Cornwall in 1325 (language from tax rolls; see Gilbert. Project 
Gutenberg E-Book of Cornwall. 2017). These were the 130 acres awarded to Denis of Normand 
145 years earlier, which apparently were not well managed. Over several decades, Thomas

revitalized the property for sheep grazing and subsistence farming, and supervised the 
restoration of the manor, which served as the home base of the Dennis family of Lesnewth 
from the 1300’s to 1642, when it was acquired by the “Lesnewth Hundred” (i.e., county/parish 
voting council) and converted into a religious facility. (Gabriel M. 17” Century Hundred of

Synopsis of European / English pre-immigration history 

As best as can be determined, the ancestors of Thomas Denis effectively managed the lands in 
Lesnewth, earning income from pasture and farming leases, and from rental of the manor as a 
medieval event center. The Dennis family was described in Lesnewth parish records as “proper 
upper class groundsmen.” The family was sufficiently successful in business endeavors to 
pursue property acquisitions on the Cornwall peninsula, including a tract of land in Ashburton, 
near Plymouth, which they subsequently sold to a real estate syndicate led by Sir Francis Drake. 


Aside note: When he was on dry land, and not privateering and exploring, Drake was very much 
a Chamber of Commerce booster for his hometown of Plymouth. He promoted and often funded 
what we what would now call downtown (urban) renewal to make Plymouth more competitive 
with Bristol and Cardiff as a commercial seaport, tourist attraction, and as a place to live. He 
served as Mayor and on the city council for many years and represented Plymouth in 
Parliament. The Ashburton track included a small but picturesque abbey that Drake hoped to 
develop into a pilgrimage destination because 16" and 17" century religious tourism was a 
major source of municipal income. Drake’s efforts led to quality of life enhancements for 


160 


Plymouth, but the city never challenged Bristol or Cardiff as a seaport or holiday destination. 
(Sugden J. Sir Francis Drake. London: Henry Holt & Company. 1991) 


First family members to immigrate to North America 

The Denis (now Dennis) family of Lesnewith was evidently caught up in the political, social, 
religious and economic disarray of the 17" century. A Thomas Dennis of Lesnewth (1580-1653), 
a great? (G-5) grandson of the Thomas Denis who restored the Manor, immigrated to Boston in 
1630 with two of his four sons. The other two sons joined the Dennis clan in Boston a few years 
later. Thomas and his sons stayed 18 years in the vicinity of Boston working as stonemasons 
and carpenters before returning to Wales. Based on their glowing reports about America, other 
Lesnewth Dennis families made the journey across the Atlantic as conditions grew chaotic in 
Cornwall in the aftermath of the English Civil Wars of 1642-1649. Most of the Dennis families 
ultimately made their way to Pennsylvania, likely because they were Quakers, or were attracted 
to the religious beliefs of the Quakers. The Genealogical Society of Chester, Pennsylvania 
tracked early immigration into William Penn’s colony, and identified 47 families with the Dennis 
surname residing in the colony by 1700, roughly 15 years after it was opened for settlement. 
he fact that so many Cornwall Dennis families came to Pennsylvania is not surprising. Between 
650 and 1850, more than 25% of Cornwall’s population immigrated to North America. 


T 
al 

These early arrivals established a pipeline for Lesnewth Dennis immigration to Pennsylvania. 
The Lesnewth immigrants who are directly connected to our North American Dennis family 
were Jowan and Tamsyn Dennis, who arrived in Philadelphia in 1829 from Lesnewth with four 
children. Port of entry records indicate that Jowan was 26 on arrival and Tamsyn was 22. We 
know very little about Jowan and Tamsyn’s life in Lesnewth, and few details exist about their 
existence in Pennsylvania other than they lived in a small town north of present-day Harrisburg. 
Their son, William Albert Dennis (1829-1893) was born three years after they arrived in PA. As 
previously described in the Dennis linage table on page 75, William met Maria Mary Fox (1831- 
1923) soon after she immigrated to Philadelphia from Ireland in 1856, and they were married 
the following year. William and Maria were the great grandparents of Archie Dennis. 


Notes on William Penn and the Pennsylvania Colony: William Penn (1644-1718) was an Oxford 
educated nobleman from a wealthy and politically prominent family, a practitioner and 
outspoken advocate of the Quaker faith in England, and an ardent pacifist and abolitionist. 
Penn published many papers in praise of Quaker ideals, arguing for greater personal liberty in 
religious behavior, and espousing what would now be recognized as the basic tenets of a 
democratic society. His papers and speeches often lambasted the Church of England and the 
Crown for denying religious and personal freedom, and questioned the need for a monarchy. 
For these positions, Penn was arrested and jailed in the Tower of London multiple times, but he 
was always released after a brief internments due to his family’s influence in the royal court. 

His father, Sir William Penn Sr., (1621-1670) was an admiral in the English navy, who gained 
notoriety, both pro and con, during his naval career. He had flexible political views to say the 
least; he managed to fight for both sides in the English Civil War. Later in his career, Admiral 
Penn developed the first manual of naval warfare tactics for the English navy that guided 
engagement strategy for 200 years. In 1681, King Charles II awarded a huge tract of North 
America comprising modern day Pennsylvania, Delaware and parts of New York and New Jersey 


161 


to William Penn Jr. to pay off a debt of 16,000 pounds that the King owed to Penn’s father, and 
also to encourage Penn Jr., his Quaker / democratic ideals and his followers, to leave England, 
thus ridding the King of a political headache. Penn Jr. obliged by traveling to North America in 
1682 to explore his new domain and begin planning a colony based on democratic concepts, 
which he proposed to name Sylvania, which means “a pleasant forested area” in Latin. The first 
General Assembly for the new province amended the name by adding “Penn” to Sylvania to 
honor Penn Sr. and Penn Jr. (Hull WI. William Penn and the Dutch Quaker Migration to 
Pennsylvania. Baltimore, MD: Genealogical Publishing Company. 1970)

society that democratically elects leaders and values personal freedom deeply influenced 
Thomas Payne, Ben Franklin and Thomas Jefferson who liberally incorporated ideas and almost 
verbatim phrasing from the Frame of Government into Revolutionary Era documents. He was 
the earliest advocate for unification of the colonies into an independent nation, and also 
advocated for a Union of European States ruled by democratically elected leaders, which he 
called the European Union. For this proposal, he was once again tossed into the Tower for 
several months. Upon release, he commented, “I spend much time here, | should purchase it 
and make accommodations sensible to my comforts.” Interestingly enough considering his 
Quaker beliefs, Penn was flamboyant with a lavish lifestyle, excessive spending habits, and 
unusual, mystical, beliefs. He was profit-oriented and saw himself as business genius; kind of a

Origin and evolution of surname 

The surname Goodman originated in England and Scotland in the medieval period. The name is 
derived from the Middle English “Gode” (Good) and “Mann” (Man), which combined refer to 
the head of a household, or master of the household, usually in a broader context of being a 
manager of an estate or other large parcel of property. In Scotland and throughout the 
northern counties of England, the term Godemann also referred to a landowner who received 
or purchased land, not from the crown, but from a member of the non-royal landed gentry 
class (i.e., wealthy merchants or professionals — attorneys, sheriffs, architects, politicians, etc.). 
In class-conscious medieval England, Godemann was also a status signal surname, indicating a 
person with supervisory responsibilities, and thus was at a higher social level than laborers or 
household employees. By the 15" century, Godemann had evolved to Goodman. 


First appearance of surname in public records 

The first Goodman that | could identify who was linked to the family line leading to Maude 
Goodman was an Alexander Goodman (1449 — 1516) and wife Mary Hughes Goodman (1461 — 
1519). Alexander and Mary lived in a rural area of England known as the West Midlands near 
the border with Wales. Property deeds indicate that Alexander and Mary owned three plots of 
land of unknown size and a village market, but little else is known about them. 


Geographic origin of family 

Alexander and Mary lived near or in the village of Chelmarsh in the county of Shropshire. The 
next several generations of Goodman’s after Alexander and Mary Goodman continued to live in 
Chelmarsh, and were involved in agricultural work.

Synopsis of European / English pre-immigration history 

By the mid 1600s, this line of the Goodman family had moved to the town of Southill in 
Bedfordshire, located closer to London. The Goodman family in Southill worked as property 
managers and groundskeepers at an estate in the area known as Southill Park. Opened in 1597, 
Southill Park included private and public gardens, public parkland with trails and cabins, a 40- 
acre lake with public access and woodlands that could be leased for gaming (i.e., hunting). The 
focal point of the park was a restored manor house from the 14" century, which was used as 
residence by the park owners and also was leased out for events. Southill Park still exists today 
and continues many of the same functions. It is now owned and operated by the largest hotel 
and resort chain in England. (Historic England. SOUTHILL PARK HOUSE. Southill, Bedfordshire. 
National Heritage List for England. https://historicengland.org.uk. Accessed February 4, 2023)

First family members to immigrate to North America 

Benjamin Goodman Sr. (1633-1735) was working in an administrative position (Head, 
Properties) at Southill Park in the mid-1600s when the chaos of the English Civil War forced the 
closure of Southill Park, apparently throwing the family into a financial crisis. Benjamin Sr. 
appears to have bounced around after his departure from Southill Park, both in his professional 
life and personal life. He had relationships with several women leading to an entourage of 16 
children. By 1668, the situation in Southill was sufficiently dire that he packed up his current 
wife, Anna Webster Goodman (1640-1719), her parents and the youngest 11 of his 16 children, 
traveled to Bristol, and boarded a ship bound for the Virginia Colony in the Americas. Thus, 
Benjamin Goodman Sr. and Anna Webster Goodman, were the first Goodman adults to 
immigrate to North America.

Notes on the English Civil War: The English Civil War of 1642-1649 (there were two phases o' 
the war: 1642-1645, and 1647-1649), an overlapping conflict known as the Wars of the Three 
Kingdoms (1638-1651) and the ensuing economic fall-out were principle catalysts for the 
massive migration from England and Wales to North American in the 17" century, which 
included members of the Morgan, Maris, Dennis and Goodman families. The initial decades in 
17" century England (i.e. 1600-1640) were an era marked by extreme economic and socia 
tension (class and culture warfare), political polarization, and religious unrest. A non-roya 
merchant class was becoming wealthy and competing successfully with nobles in many areas o 
aj" century business enterprise, which challenged the traditional class pecking order. The 
crown became heavily reliant on the business sector for funding of almost any enterprise the 
King desired to pursue. Concepts of individual autonomy and personal freedom were spreading 
through the population, which spawned the Quaker movement and other anti-royal societies 
that questioned the role of a monarchy and the church in an increasingly merchant-led 
entrepreneurial society. 


The King at the time, Charles I, sought to firmly re-instate the divine right of kings and moved 
toward royal absolutism. He reduced the decision-making authority of Parliament, and then 
threatening to abolish Parliament completely, the key element in the constitutional monarchy 
that England slowly had built over the previous 200 years. Charles | also wanted to replace the 
Church of England (Protestant theology) with the Catholic Church. Parliament, comprised of 
wealthy businessmen, landowners and Protestant nobles, formed an army in 1642 and sought 
to depose Charles |. 


At play in the conflict were royal absolutism versus a constitutional parliament (i.e., shared 
governance), national theology — Catholic versus Protestant, and other issues too complex to 
summarize here (i.e., Irish, Scotch and Welsh sovereignty). Seven years of violent civil war 
ensued between the Roundheads, the Parliamentarian army (name derived from their bowl 
haircuts) and the Royalist army, known as the Cavaliers (derived from their flamboyant attire). 
After dozens of battles, the military outcome was inconclusive, but the nation was devastated: 
each side experienced more than 150,000 deaths (in a nation of 3.4 million people at the time), 
and 500 villages and towns were completed destroyed. Farm to market and port to market 
distribution systems were devastated leading to severe food shortages. Conscription of 
farmers, loggers and fishermen for military service hindered economic productivity. King 
Charles | was eventually captured in 1649 after being on the run for much of the war. He was 
promptly tried and executed by the Roundheads. 


Beginning in 1649, Oliver Cromwell, a leading Roundhead and arch Protestant conservative, 
served as the head (Lord Protector) of a constitutional republic, but in reality, his tenure was a 
brutal dictatorship. Catholics, the Irish, Quakers and other perceived non-conformists were 
ruthlessly persecuted. Much violence and social upheaval ensued for another decade, further 
damaging the economy. Cromwell unexpectedly died in 1658, and within two years, the 
Royalists rebounded and installed Charles Il as king. Charles II introduced reforms to restore a 
constitutional monarchy where the crown and parliament shared decision authority, and 
repealed many of Cromwell’s puritanical social regulations. 


165 


Yet, religious conflict continued for the rest of the century leading to another overturning of the 
crown in the Glorious Revolution of 1688. However, the events of 1688, which led to the 
installation of William of Orange and his wife Mary as King and Queen, finally led to 
development of a meaningful Bill of Rights for citizens, enhancement of the Prime Minister’s 
power and significant expansion of Parliament’s authority so that the crown could only make 
decisions with the approval of Parliament. The English economy finally began to rebound by 
1700, but by then, many members of the Morgan, Maris, Dennis and Goodman families had 
already immigrated to the North American colonies.

Lienau 


Origin and evolution of surname 

The surname Lienau is a habitational name for individuals who lived in medieval German 
communities with a similar name. The village of Linau has existed since the 12% century in far 
northern Germany. As we saw in Chapter II, Susan’s ancestors spelled their surname as Linau 
until approximately 1775. Given the frequent use of habitational surnames during this period, it 
could be conjectured that Susan’s Lienau line originated in this village. As described below, a 
nearby town is most directly associated with Susan’s ancestors. In 2025, Lienau is a rare 
surname in Germany; less than 250 people use the name. Lienau is more common in North 
America; roughly 700 people have the surname. 


Geographic origin of family 

In the search for ancestors of Susan’s father, Charles Lienau (1903-1969), virtually every source 
led to a small town in present-day Germany that is a suburb of Hamburg in northern Germany. 
This town is Uetersen in Pinneberg County in the German state of Schleswig-Holstein near the 
border with Denmark. Uetersen dates back to the 11" century when King Frederick Il made 
Hamburg, on the Elbe River 50 miles from the Baltic Sea, a major seaport. Uetersen lies on one 
of the main branches of the Elbe, and its economy benefited during the Middle Ages from river 
traffic, but that faded away as shipping services were concentrated in Hamburg. In a bit of irony 
considering the Lienau family history in America, Uetersen and Pinneberg (the main city in the 
county of the same name) were both sister cities of Rockville, Maryland in the 1950s and 1960s. 


‘eUetersen 
Uetersen lies near several major Baltic Sea ports in the far north of 
Germany. The village is a suburb of Hamburg and has the highest 
concentration of people with the Lienau surname in Germany. 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 7/29/2024. 


As noted above, there are few Lienau’s in Germany currently, and few individuals with that 
surname appear in the historical record. However, of the Lienau’s that | identified over the past 
200 years, virtually all of them were born in Uetersen. For example, Johann Jacob Lienau 
(1798-1884) was one of the most prominent individuals in the history of the major northern 
German port city of Lubeck, which is 40 miles from Uetersen. Johann Lienau acquired wealth as 
a grocery store owner and then as a grain wholesaler. He owned a fleet of eight ships that 
exported grain throughout Europe and Scandinavia. He channeled much of his profits into 
public works for Lubeck including construction of hospitals, churches, schools and parks. The 
main street in Lubeck is Lienau Strasse, a major park along the Trave River is named for him, 
and the area of the city known for galleries, restaurants and theatres is recognized as the 
Lienau Arts District. Johann Lienau was born in Uetersen. A biography by one of his sons, cited 
below, mentions the “several branches of the Lienau clan from Uetersen who are all related in 
one way or the other, and held family days in Uetersen and at Oldesloe Lake.” Several other 
prominent Germans from the 18" and 19" centuries were from Uetersen including Robert Emil 


167 


Lienau (1838-1920), Johann’s son, a major music producer and publisher in Europe, Martin 
Michael Lienau (1786-1861), a wine merchant, referred to as the “father of the modern German 
wine industry” and Detlief Lienau (1818-1887), a well known architect, who moved to New York 
and became a founder of the American Institute of Architects. (Lienau RE. Pictures and Figures 
From My Life. Berlin: Lichterfelde Archive. 1949.)
