First appearance of surname in public records 

The earliest reference to a Lienau in public records that | found referenced a Provintmeister 
Barthalome Lienau. He worked in the 15° century for a Count of Holstein, the northernmost 
Duchy in the German Federation, which encompassed lands and villages north of Hamburg, 
including Uetersen. A Provintmeister served as the payroll master and chief employment officer 
in a German feudal duchy, and sat on the Count’s main advisory council. 


Synopsis of European / English pre-immigration history 

| used Schleswig-Holstein tax rolls and census records to trace Susan’s ancestry back to a 
Wilhelm Linau (1674-1743) and Gesche Boot Fesefeld Linau (1678-1749), a married couple 
from Uetersen. Four generations later, | came across a Johann Lienau (1808-1876), also from 
Uetersen, who led an adventurous life at sea, and who was Susan’s Great-Great-Great (G’) 
Grandfather. Information gleaned from tax rolls and the Schleswig-Holstein census suggest that 
Lienau families in the 17" and 18" centuries were economically secure. The family appears to 
have owned farmland, which passed from generation to generation, and probably were 
involved in the dairy business. We do not know why Johann Lienau elected to go to sea versus 
working in the family’s agricultural business. Histories of Schleswig-Holstein describe a 
catastrophic flood, known as the Great Halling Flood (Gross Hallingflut) of 1825, that destroyed 
a coastal island, Halligen, and ravaged the region, destroying villages, causing thousands of 
deaths, decimating livestock and wiping out dikes and docks on the Elbe. The region was soon 
after afflicted with a deadly malaria epidemic, attributed to the flood’s aftermath: miles of 
brackish water that served as perfect breeding grounds for malaria mosquitoes. It’s not known 
if the 1825 storm influenced Johann’s plans, but he would have been a 17 year old that year, 
considering career options, and the storm and following epidemic may have obliterated his 
family’s dairy business. (North Sea Flood. Encyclopedia Britannica Online. www.britannica.com. 
January 24, 2023. Accessed: May 27, 2024) 


First family members to immigrate to North America 

Johann Lienau (1808 — 1876) was the first member of the Uetersen Lienau family to immigrate 
to the U.S. In the 1830 Schleswig-Holstein census, Johann at age 22 was listed as cadet seaman 
(apprentice) with residence in Hamburg, Germany’s largest port. On the 1840 census, Johann’s 
occupation was Seaman/Harbor Pilot with residence in Neustadt, a suburb of Lubeck, 


168 


Germany’s second largest port. This suggests that Johann had developed his seaman skills 
considerably between 1830 and 1840. Ships entering and exiting Lubeck had to navigate the 
narrow and curving Trave River channel with extensive lock systems. Ship captains turned the 
helm over to local harbor pilots, such as Johann, for that portion of the journey. In 1847, 
Johann’s name appeared as an occupational immigrant to England with employment listed as 
seaman. The designation of occupational immigrant means that he had a secured employment 
with a company operating out of Great Britain. | don’t know why Johann immigrated to 
England, but assume that it was career advancement. (United Kingdom Merchant Navy Seaman 
Records, 1835-1941. Database and Images. Findmypast. http://findmypast.com. The National 
Archives of the UK. Kew, Surrey. 2023. Accessed: May 27, 2024) 


The next time Johann Lienau’s name appeared in a public record was in 1854 in Puerto Rico, 
where he again was listed as an occupational immigrant, now using the name John Lienau. 
Between 1847 and 1854, John was a seaman for Royal Mail Steam Packet Company that 
transported mail and travelers between England and the Caribbean with stops in Cuba, Puerto 
Rico, Jamaica, Panama and Nicaragua. John’s home residence was San Juan, Puerto Rico. By 
1854, he had risen up the seaman ranks to chief mate, responsible for supervising the other 
crewmembers. (United Kingdom Merchant Navy Seaman Records, 1835-1941. 2023) 


During 1854 in San Juan, John changed employers by securing a position as a sailor mate, a drop 
in rank, on the Star of the West, one of the largest steamships in the world at the time, which 
was owned by Cornelius Vanderbilt. The steamship, depicted below, was nearly 100 yards long 
(almost a football field), had two masts, a giant paddlewheel mid-ship, and space for 1000 
passengers, including 200 in private cabins. The main purpose of the ship, however was to 
transport mail and packages between New York and the Caribbean. The first time John Lienau 
set foot in the U.S. was when he disembarked from the Star in the harbor of New York City in 
September 1854 at age 46. Soon after docking, John Lienau appeared at the immigration office 
in lower Manhattan. The story of John’s adventures on the Star during a pivotal event in 
American history is told in Chapter IV.

Girault 


Reminder - Girault / Lienau Connection 

In 1935, Laura Pearl Girault (1908-1982) married Charles William Lienau (1903-1969) in 
Hastings-on-the Hudson, New York at the home of her parents, Theodore Stephano Girault 
(1873-1943) and Bessie Pearl McAnespy Girault (1874-1946). Laura and Charles were Susan’s 
parents, and Theodore and Bessie were her maternal grandparents. 


Origin and evolution of surname 

The surname Girault evolved from the ancient Germanic word Gibeault, which referred to a 
person with power or authority. By the 16th century, Gibeault evolved into two primary 
variations: Giroux, commonly seen on the Atlantic (western) side of France, and Girault 
(sometimes spelled Garault), commonly seen in southern and eastern regions of France. 
Throughout French history, the Giroux / Girault surnames appear frequently in public records. 
Today, Girault is among the 50 most common surnames in France. 


Geographic origin of family 

The Girault surname first appeared in property deeds and court records in the region of France 
known previously as Languedoc. From 1229-1791, Languedoc existed as a province and was 
ruled by a Director-Governor appointed by the King. As indicated in the map below, Languedoc 
comprised much of Southern France. The capital city was Toulouse and the largest city was 
Marseilles. During the 1600s, the branch of Giraults that are linked to Susan’s grandparents 
and mother migrated north from Languedoc to the area of northeastern France known as the 
Champagne — Ardennes region. The reason for the northward migration is not known. The 
primary city in the Ardennes is Reims. By 1750, Susan’s Girault line had settled in the small 
town of Merfy, a suburb of Reims. 


The Languedoc province is indicated in red. The province 
existed until the French Revolution in the 1790s. The Girault 
family was prominent in this province for several centuries. 
After northward migration, Girault became a common surname 
in Merfy and throughout the Champagne-Ardennes region, 
below.

170 


First appearance of surname in public records 

The earliest reference to a Girault in public records that | could find described a Philippe Girault 
who was an officer during the 1680s in the French Royal Army of King Louis XIV (1638-1715), 
also known as the Sun King (i.e., Louis the Great). Girault, who was born in Reims and died in 
Merfy, served as the aid-de-camp to Francois Henri de Montmorency-Bouteville, Grand 
Marshall of the Royal Army and Duke of Luxemburg, one of the most experienced and 
successful military commanders of that era. Philippe Girault is often mentioned in 
Montmorency-Bouteville biographies. (Chisholm H. Francois Henri de Montmorency-Bouteville, 
Duke of Luxemburg. In: Encyclopedia Britannica. 11" ed. Cambridge University. 1911. Accessed 
via www.wikisource.org on February 15, 2023) Like Philippe Girault, many Giraults were 
professionals, serving in the military and as judges, attorneys, and mayors of large towns 
including Reims, Nancy and Strasbourg, and functioning in other administrative roles such as 
town and province commissioners. Several were members of the French Parliaments, a system 
of regional law courts responsible for converting royal decrees and tax levy’s into law. At the 
onset of the French Revolution in 1789, the parliamentary Giraults mostly sided with the 
Royals, which led several of them to the guillotine in the 1790s, and one, an Etienne Girault, 
fleeing from a mob, took his own life by leaping from a spire of a Catholic Church. (Etienne 
Girault, French Politician, 1756-1793. www.fr.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed May 27, 2024) The 
earliest Giraults that could confidently be linked to Susan were a Charles Girault and wife 
Jeanne Barbier Girault who lived in Merfy in the mid-1700s. 


Synopsis of European / English pre-immigration history 

Pierre-Louis Girault (1785-1820) was one of the sons of Charles and Jeanne Girault. We know 
little about Pierre-Louis other than that he was born in Merfy, had an illegitimate son named 
Alexander (1811-1882), who was Susan’s great grandfather, and his early demise stemmed 
from a war injury. Pierre-Louis joined a French Royalist Brigade upon Napoleon Bonaparte’s 
return to France from exile in Elba in 1815. The Royalist Brigade fought during the ensuing 100 
Days War (March—July 1815) with the Seventh Coalition Army (Great Britain, Prussia and several 
states of the German Federation) that formed to oppose Napoleon’s return to power. Pierre- 
Louis suffered crippling injuries at the Battle of Wavre (fought concurrently with the Battle of 
Waterloo on June 18-19, 1815) that apparently contributed to his early death at the age of 35. 
Alexander’s mother, Mary Eugenia Thomas, was an English citizen and took Alexander to 
England after the events of 1815. See pages 117-118 in the Girault Lineage Table for details. 
(Chandler D. Waterloo, The Hundred Days War. Oxford: Osprey Publishing. 1981) 


Little is known about his childhood, but Alexander Girault thrived in England. He was college 
educated and had a lucrative career within the British banking system. He married Sara 
Theodora McGreal (1842-1876) from the Hebrides Islands of Scotland in 1860 in Corum, Turkey, 
and the couple honeymooned there for nearly six months. Alexander and Sara lived in an 
upscale neighborhood at 11 Sydney Street in Chelsea, London, which now serves as a luxury 
boutique hotel, known as the Sydney House Chelsea. They had three children: Emily 
Alexandrine Girault (1861-1947), Louis Alexander Girault (1863-1933) and Theodore Stefano 
Girault (1874-1943). Theodore was Susan’s grandfather. Considering the story that is about to 
unfold, It is important to note that Alexander Girault was 31 years older than Sara when they 
were married and 63 years old when Theodore was born. 


171 


Contemporary photo of Girault home at 11 Sydney Street in London 
Image source: Wikimedia Commons. www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. Accessed: 5/17/2023. 


Sara McGreal Girault died in 1876 from unknown causes leaving Alexander, at age 65, with two 
teenagers and a two year old. Despite his wealth and likely access to childcare services, 
Alexander elected to place young Theo in an orphanage for pauper children run by the Parish of 
Saint Pancras in London. For the next 11 years, the child was transferred among several 
orphanages in England, eventually winding up in 1887 at the Barton Regis Rural Work Home for 
Delinquent and Pauper Boys near the city of Bristol with an already lengthy record of 
misbehavior. Not long after being transferred to this rural work farm, Theo, now 13, along with 
two other teens named Henry Mitchell and George Harvey, were caught during an attempted 
escape via a stolen donkey and wagon. They were brought before the Board of Governors of 
the Bristol Emigration Society for orphans and given a choice: stay in England and enter the 
juvenile penal system, or register as volunteers for the British Home Child Service (BHCS). If 
they volunteered for BHCS, they were told that the destination would be Canada, where they 
would be placed on farms as laborers, but provided housing, meals and medical care. Theo, 
Henry and George all agreed that BHCS was the best option. In September of 1887, the three 
teens boarded the steamship, Lake Nepigon, bound for Canada, along with 10 other teenage 
boys who also chose the BHCS over juvenile prison.

First family member to immigrate to North America 

In October 1887, Theodore Stefano Girault, Henry and George arrived in Halifax, Nova Scotia 
and were soon transported to three adjoining farms owned by William Oliver (Will) McAnespy 
(1858-1917), only 29 years old himself, and his brother and brother-in-law near Portage Vale, 
New Brunswick. Soon after arrival, Theo undoubtedly took notice of William’s 14-year old 
sister, Bessie Pearl McAnespy, who lived at the farm with Will after her mother apparently 


172 


abandoned the family following the death of her husband. | found site visit reports from the 
New Brunswick Provincial Immigration and Re-Settlement Office, which included assessments 
by both Will McAnespy and Theo in 1889 when Theo was 15 and two years later when he was 
17. Both parties were pleased with the situation. Will indicated that Theo was a bit 
independent-minded and sometimes uppity, but a great worker, had leadership talents, and he 
fit in well. Theo observed, “like it here well better than England,” when he was 15, and “it's 
such a good place to be,” when he was 17. 


Theo worked at the McAnespy farm for 13 years, rising to the position of foreman (manager| 
for all three farms, and, this is not a surprise, married Bessie in 1901. Bessie is Susan’s materna 
grandmother. One of Theo’s BHCS pals, Henry Mitchell, ultimately joined the Royal Canadian 
Navy and made it a career. George Harvey moved to Manitoba when he was 19, but | could find 
no further information about his life. Theo and Bessie’s subsequent careers and family are 
described in Section IV, Post-Immigration History of the Girault family. 


Notes on the British Home Child Service (BHCS): In the second half of the 19" century, rural 
families in England, Ireland and Scotland flocked to urban areas seeking newly emerging 
industrial jobs, contributing to massive over-crowding in London, Birmingham, Manchester, 
Liverpool, Edinburgh, Belfast and other cities. Metropolitan areas had inadequate housing and 
minimal social support services such as hospitals and schools for the population onslaught. 
Multiple families crowded into hastily constructed and often squalid apartments or lived in 
abandoned buildings. Factory jobs were readily available but paid poorly, not enough for the 
basic needs of a family with children. Youngsters were increasingly seen as extra mouths to 
feed, and were abandoned to orphanages or the streets in shocking numbers. 


City leaders were desperate to ease overcrowding in British orphanages and pauper homes, 
and to combat child homelessness (and associated child labor and sexual abuse). In 1870, a 
group of 54 British juvenile protection and emigration agencies under the leadership of Annie 
McPherson, an early advocate of social work as a profession, banded together to create the 
British Home Child Service (BHCS). (Parker R. Uprooted: Shipment of Poor Children to Canada, 
1867-1891. Bristol: Policy Press. 2010) McPherson conceptualized the BHCS as a child 
resettlement program to reduce child deprivation in Britain and improve children’s lives abroad 
with a fresh start. The purpose of BHCS was to gather, assess and immigrate wards of the state 
(such as Theo, Henry and George), and other neglected or unwanted children to other nations 
in the British Empire who were under-populated and seeking immigrants, especially teenagers 
who could function as farm workers or domestics. There was no guarantee of schooling or 
adoption for BHCS participants, just room, board and health care in exchange for gainful work. 


Between 1870 and 1930, 120,000 children were sent to Canada under the BHCS for placement 
with rural families who needed extra hands or with urban families who needed support for the 
elderly, childcare (nannies) or domestic servants. In Canada today, nearly 15% of the overall 
population is descended from a British Home Child. An 11-year-old British Home Child on Prince 
Edward Island inspired the Anne of Green Gables novels by Lucy Maud Montgomery.

Unfortunately, McPherson’s fresh start resettlement was erratically implemented. Many BHCS 
children were not treated nearly as well as Theo Girault. Audits found that BHCS children in 
Canada were traded or sold among families as needs arose or were simply told to leave and 
fend for themselves. Many were not provided adequate shelter, regular meals or medical care. 
Beginning around 1900 the Canadian government started to weed out agencies and families 
who abused the system. Mounting criticism led to the termination of the BHCS in Canada in 
1932, although World War II stimulated under the table re-settlements of English orphans with 
rural Canadian families. 


Although Theodore Girault benefitted from his BHCS

McAnespy 

Reminder - McAnespy / Lienau Connection 

In 1901, Bessie Pearl McAnespy (1873-1946) married Theodore Stefano Girault (1874-1943) in 
Portage Vale, New Brunswick. William Oliver McAnespy (1857-1917), a key figure in both of 
their lives, served a dual role of walking the bride down the aisle (as her older brother) and 
serving as Theo’s best man (as his mentor and father figure). Bessie and Theo Girault had three 
children: Evelyn Elizabeth Girault (1902-1984), Theodore Alexander Girault (1904-1980), and 
Laura Pearl Girault (1908-1981). In 1935, Laura married Charles William Lienau (1903-1969). 
The couple had one daughter, Susan Elizabeth Lienau (1949 - ). Thus, Bessie and Theodore 
Stefano Girault were Susan’s grandparents on her mother’s side. 


Origin and evolution of surname 

The surname McAnespy is an Anglicized version of the Scottish, Gaelic and Irish Mac An 
Easpaig, meaning son of a bishop. Prior to the 20" century, the name was sometimes written as 
Mac Anespy. McAnespy is today a rare surname in Great Britain. Less than 100 people have the 
name in Ireland, all of whom live in Northern Ireland. Less than 20 each in Scotland and England 
have the McAnespy surname. The rarity of the name appears to be consistent throughout the 
past 200 years. Griffith’s Primary Valuation of Ireland (a 19" century national tax survey of 
households, property and business owners) conducted every 10 years starting in 1817 listed 
from 49 to 64 McAnespy’s or Mac Anespy’s on each survey. (Griffith’s Valuation — A Mid 19" 
Century Gem. Irish Genealogy Toolkit. www.irish-genealogy-toolkit.com In: Santry C. The Family 
Tree Irish Genealogical Guide. www.books.google.co.uk. 2017. Accessed: May 28, 2024) 


Geographic origin of family 

Given the rarity of the McAnespy surname, it was easy to identify Loughgall (in Irish: Loch gCal), 
a rural community of less than 300 residents in the Northern Ireland parish of Armagh as the 
likely geographic origin of the name. Loughgall sits adjacent to a loch (lake) from which it 
derives its name. The community was established in the bh century when a Gaelic clan 
constructed a crannog (a wood and stone fort in the middle of a lake) in Loughgall Loch. In the 
search for potential ancestors of the New Brunswick McAnaspy’s, virtually all individuals with 
that name, currently and in the past, were associated with Loughgall or Armagh Parish. 
Loughgall sits near the border with the Republic of Ireland amidst lakes and rolling hills. In spite 
of its bucolic setting, it has been the scene of numerous religious and sectarian battles 
throughout its history, including a bloody shootout in 1987 between the Irish Republican Army 
and a British Special Forces Unit resulting in many fatalities. 


Location of Loughgall in Armagh Parish near the border of 
Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 8/2/2024.

First appearance of surname in public records 

The surname McAnespy appears in the aforementioned Griffiths Survey throughout the 19" 
century including James McAnespy (1796-1862) and wife Emily Morton McAnespy (1795- 
1844). James and Emily lived in Loughgall and were William Oliver McAnespy’s grandparents. 
The survey indicted that James was a farm laborer and Emily worked as a shopkeeper and 
domestic (i.e., cook and housekeeper). 


Synopsis of pre-immigration history 

As best as can be determined, residents of Loughgall primarily have been sheep grazers and 
small plot farmers throughout history. Farmers either owned small farm-to-market shops in the 
village or had contracts to supply produce to designated vendors. The largely absentee English 
owners of Irish estates took a substantial percentage of the profits from sales of crops and 
livestock as well as charging lease fees to the tenants. 


First family members to immigrate to North America 

James and Emily McAnespy, with three of their eventual six children, immigrated to Canada in 
1821, settling in New Brunswick. | don't know for sure, but a best guess might lead to the 
conclusion that James and Emily were part of the Great Irish Wave that immigrated to Canada 
between 1820 and 1860, triggered by the Irish Potato Famine that reached its peak during 1845 
to 1852. Over these seven years, Ireland lost 50% of its population — one million people died of 
famine and associated diseases, and one million people left for North America, Australia or New 
Zealand. Even before the peak of the famine, another million people had already immigrated to 
other nations, hoping to leave behind the massive poverty that engulfed Ireland in the 19" 
century. (Elliot BC. Irish Immigrants in the Canadas: A New Approach. McGill: Queen’s University 
Press. 1988) 


Substantially under-populated, the Canadian government actively encouraged and incentivized 
Northern European, and particularly, Irish relocations in the 19" century. Family units were 
offered at least partial payment for transatlantic passage, temporary, albeit shabby, housing 
after landing at a Canadian port-of-entry, assistance in locating tracks of inexpensive farmland 
to purchase, and transportation to purchased property. Between 1820 and 1860, more than 
60% of all immigrants to Canada were Irish, a total of 700,000 people. By the year 1920, 30% of 
all Canadian residents were born in Ireland, and the percentage was much higher in the eastern 
provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. 


176 


The journey from Ireland to Canada was arduous. Immigrants crossed the ocean in hastily and 
crudely constructed cargo ships, primarily designed to haul lumber on the return trip to Great 
Britain to meet the building and refurbishment demands of the rapidly expanding British navy. 
Over 75% of the wood used in the 19" century British fleet was from Canadian forests. On 
board conditions for passengers likely were no better than experienced by the first immigrants 
to New Amsterdam 200 years earlier. Mortality rates were high, exacerbated by the poor 
health of many Irish immigrants before they boarded ships in Bristol or Belfast. In the 1840s, 
nearly 2,000 Irish children annually, whose parents had died during the voyage or soon after, 
were placed for adoption or entered into a Canadian branch of the British Home Child Service. 


Beginning with James and Emily McAnespy in 1821, members of the McAnespy family have 
operated farms, dairies and other agricultural businesses in New Brunswick to this day, more 
than 200 years. Signs for McAnespy agricultural businesses are evident as one drives through 
rural New Brunswick near the Bay of Fundy. However, as described in the McAnespy lineage 
table on page 128, William Oliver McAnespy chose a different path and moved to Hartford, CT 
to become a book publisher.

McManus 


Reminder - McManus / Lienau Connection 

In 1901, Mary Theresa McManus (1884-1940) married Charles William Lienau Sr. (1876-1940) in 
Brooklyn, New York. Mary and Charles W. Lienau Sr. had two children: Charles William Lienau 
Jr. (1903-1969), and Helen Lienau (1908-1987). In 1935, Charles William Lienau Jr. married 
Laura Pearl Girault in Hastings-on-the-Hudson, New York. The couple had one daughter, Susan 
Elizabeth Lienau (1949 - ). Thus, Mary and Charles William Lienau Sr. were Susan’s grandparents 
on her father’s side. 


Origin and evolution of surname 

McManus is an Irish surname, first appearing in the 1500s, derived from the ancient Gaelic Mac 
Maghnais, McMaghnais or McMaghnuis, which means Son of Magnus. The name McMaghnuis 
first appeared in Ireland in the 12" century. Turlough Mor O’Conor (appr. 1100-1166) was a 
leader of the powerful O’Conor clan, based in Connaught (present day Galway) on Ireland’s 
west coast. One of his sons was named Maghnais O’Conor (1123-1181). As a young man, 
Maghnais gained his father’s disfavor for an unknown transgression and broke away from the 
Galway base. Maghnais and a few supporters established a new Sept (i.e., family line) in an area 
known as Roscommon in central Ireland. The eldest son of McMaghnais, who went by Turlough 
McMaghnais, founded the principle town in the Roscommon region, Kilronan, and built a castle 
and a church, the requisite first constructions of any medieval community. By the 1500s, when 
surnames started to be used in Ireland, McMaghnais had evolved to McManus, and this 
surname has been prevalent in Roscommon throughout the ensuing centuries. (Byrne V. The 
Hidden Annals: A Thousand Years of the Kingdom of Connaught. Universal Publishers. 2003) 


Geographic origin of family 

The ancestors of Mary Theresa McManus were traced back to John James and Theresa 
McManus who lived in a pastoral village by the name of Ballyfarnon, in the Roscommon District 
in the early 1800s. 


Ballyfarnon is located in the Roscommon District of Ireland, a few 
miles from the Kilronan Castle. 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 8/2/2024. 


178 


First appearance of surname in public records 

Like many residents of Ballyfarnon, John and Theresa were decidedly not wealthy. John’s name 
appears on several tenant leases in the 1840s, which allowed use of plots of land on a local 
estate for farming. There is no record that they owned property of their own or owned a home. 
The couple do not appear to have been involved in the sheep grazing industry as were many 
others in Roscommon. The 1837 and 1847 Griffiths Irish Census listed John as a farm worker 
and woodsman, and Theresa as a domestic at the nearby Kilronan Castle. By the 19" century, 
the castle built by Turlough McMaghnais already had been converted into a rural lodge and 
venue for weddings and other celebrations. Today, it is a five star hotel, restaurant, spa, and 
event center with two 18-hole golf courses. 


Kilronan Castle in 2023 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 8/4/2024. 


Synopsis of pre-immigration history and first family members to immigrate to North America 
John and Theresa McManus from Ballyfarnon were born around 1810, married in 1837 and 
passed away in 1863 and 1864 respectively. Their only surviving son, John James McManus 
(1854-1915), arrived in New York as an immigrant in 1865 at age 11. Port of entry records do 
not indicate the circumstances of his arrival. For example, did John James travel alone or did an 
adult accompany him? Irish immigration records (i.e., port exit) indicate that a substantial 
number of Roscommon women and children, incarcerated in female prisons or pauper child 
reformatories, were relocated to New York in 1865 and subsequent years as part of a 
nationwide program to reduce overcrowding in the Irish penal system. (Maxwell-Stewart H. 
Convict Transportation from Britain and Ireland 1615-1870. History Compass. 8(11): 1221-1242. 
2010) | do not know if John James was involved in this mass relocation, but the dates of his 
parents’ deaths indicate that he may have been left on his own at a young age, not an 
uncommon experience for a child in mid-19"" century Ireland. (Lancour H. Passenger Lists of 
Ships Coming to North America, 1607-1825. New York: Bulletin of the New York Public Library. 
Summer, 1937) 


A Mary Maria McNellis (1853-1925) arrived at the port of New York from Belfast on the same 
day as John James McManus (April 15, 1865; the day of Abraham Lincoln’s assassination) at the 
age of 12 accompanied by two older sisters. Seventeen years later, John James and Mary Maria 
were married in Brooklyn. The couple had four children, one of whom was Mary Theresa 


179 


McManus, who married Charles Lienau Sr. in 1901 at the age of 17. Thus, John James and Mary 
Maria were Susan’s great grandparents, and Mary McManus was her paternal grandmother. 


Notes on the Surname McNellis: The surname McNellis is the Anglicized form of the Gaelic Mac 
Niallghious, which combines Mac (son of) with a common Gaelic personal name, Niall (modern 
day: Neal) and with a descriptive adjective, ghuis, that refers to a vigorous or energetic person. 
Mac Niallghious is thus a complimentary personal name meaning: “son of the Niall, the 
vigorous one.” McNellis, or McNelis was a frequently used surname in medieval Scotland and 
Ireland. The surname first appeared in public records of the Island of Bara in the 11" century, 
the southernmost island in the Outer Hebrides chain off the northwest coast of Scotland. The 
name has remained popular in the Hebrides ever since. As evident in the image below, the 
Hebrides and Northern Ireland are not far apart, especially for two seafaring populations (in 
2023, a four hour ferry ride). Throughout history, there has been considerable back and forth 
travel and inter-marriage between the populations of Ireland and the Hebrides chain. 


This map shows the geographic relationship of Hebrides Island 
chain to Northern Ireland. 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 8/4/2024. 


Mary Maria McNellis and her sisters were born in Colonsay on one of the Inner Hebrides 
Islands. After deciding to immigrate to North America, it is possible that they traveled to Belfast 
because it was the closest embarkation port. We know Mary Maria’s parents, Ralph McNellis 
and Isabelle Brennan, were born in the Hebrides around 1830, but it is also possible they may 
have relocated to Ireland with their daughters prior to 1865. | was not able to determine why 
the McNellis sisters (ages 12, 15 and 16) immigrated to New York without their parents.

Chapter IV — Stories of Family Members in North America 
Overview 
The Hendricson, Morgan, Maris, Dennis and Goodman families shared common experiences: 


(1) immigration to North American in the 17" century fleeing the economically and socially 
disastrous English Civil War and ensuing religious persecution during the Cromwell era; 


(2) additional emigration within the colonies and the fledgling United States in the 17) 18" and 
19" centuries, moving westward to West Virginia, Kentucky, states in the Northwest Territory, 
and to the Pacific Northwest to escape slave powered agriculture with which they could not 
compete given the skimpy infrastructure, manpower shortages and Midwestern climate; 

(3) desire to live in a non-slave free state with other guaranteed benefits and liberties including 
opportunity to acquire acreage of fertile lands at no cost, in-perpetuity land ownership, female 
land ownership, free public education and religious freedom; 

(4) all but one family (Maris) reached the West Coast by wagon train; and, 

(5) each family finally gained financial stability in Oregon and Washington. 

The Lienau, McManus, Girault and McAnespy families immigrated to North America up to 200 
years later, in the 19" century, also seeking economic stability and upward social mobility. 
These families did not seek farming careers, instead gravitating to metropolitan New York for 
contemporary urban careers in publishing, the music industry and the financial sector. 


Chapter IV is comprised of stories of individuals in these families whose experiences capture 
aspects of the American journey from the 1600s to the mid 20" century. Connections to our 
ancestors primarily survive through stories about unique moments in their lives, what they did, 
and who they were ... not the dry facts of their existence: birth and death data, places of 
residence, spouses and children’s names, occupations, and so on. All families need stories that 
are bridges to the past, allowing ancestors to come alive as real people with real problems. 


Timeline - North American Stories 
The timeline is based on the date of birth of the family member involved in the story.

Finding America - Cornelius Lambert Hendrickson (1572-1651) 


Portrait of Cornelius Lambert Hendrickson created in 
celebration of his selection for the Netherlands Geographic 
and Scientific Academy, a forerunner of the Royal Dutch 
Geographic Society. Many of his maps, terrain sketches and 
notebooks are on display at the Society Library located at the 
University of Amsterdam. 

Image source: Wikimedia Commons. www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. 
Accessed: December 17, 2022. 


Cornelius Hendrickson was the son of Lambert Barentse Hendriksz (Mooy Lambert), Royal 
Dutch Navy Admiral, and one of the nation’s greatest hero’s in the 80 Years War with Spain. 
Cornelius was the grandfather of Hendrick Willemz Hendriksz (Hendrickson), the first member 
of our Hendricson family to reside permanently in North America. Cornelius literally grew up on 
the water, accompanying his father on North Atlantic fishing trips, on naval training exercises in 
the North Sea and, in particular, a trip to Iceland that peaked his interest in geography. After 
graduation from Leiden University in 1594 and working in Denmark to chart the numerous tiny 
islands in the Kattegat Strait, Hendrickson was hired and trained by the Dutch East India 
Company (DEIC) as a cartographer (mapmaker) and linguist, the later an important skill when 
exploring new lands with indigenous populations. Early in his career with the DEIC, he 
participated in exploration and mapping expeditions to the East Coast of Africa, islands in the 
Indian Ocean and Indonesia. In 1610, Hendrickson was hired as a cartographer for the newly 
formed Dutch Republic. He would soon be a key participant in two North American exploration 
and trade expeditions. 


A side note: The Dutch West India Company was created in 1621 to develop Holland’s land 


claims in the western hemisphere, open trade with indigenous peoples in North and South 
American and hinder Spanish and British trading in the Caribbean. 


Notes on Historical Sources for 17" Century Dutch Exploration in North America: Much of 
what is known about Cornelius Hendrickson’s explorations are based on expedition reports, 
maps, sketches and logs (diaries) that he submitted to the DEIC and to the Dutch Royal 
Government, principally, the States General of the Netherlands, which was the legislative 
branch, roughly equivalent in composition to the U.S. Congress. These documents are 
maintained in Amsterdam Municipal Archives and/or the Dutch National Archives known as 
Archives of the States General. In Chapter VI: Information Sources, see: Sainsbury N. Dutch 
National Archives. Archives of the States General - Calendar of Dutch State Papers, Reports, 
Notes and Archives; the Colonial Series, 1574-1660. Historians of the Dutch colonial experience 
in North America relied on these original sources for their research. A number of historical 
accounts of early 17" century Dutch exploration in North America are identified in the 
information sources for this family history (See the Howe, Spijkerman and Weslager citations), 


187 


which describe Cornelius Hendrickson’s explorations. Overall, the most detailed account of the 
voyages of Block and Hendrickson was provided in 1848 by Edmund Bailey O’Callaghan, which 
includes verbatim excerpts from the reports of both explorers to the Dutch States General, as 
well as the legislator’s reactions to these reports. (O’Callaghan EB. History of New Netherland, 
or New York Under the Dutch. NY: Appleton & Company; 1848. Available from Internet Archive. 
www.archive.org. Accessed: January 20, 2023) 


In general, the explorations of Cornelius Hendrickson have not been as well reported as those 
of Henry Hudson or Adriaen Block, who aggressively self-promoted narratives of their voyages 
after returning to Europe. However, a recent dissertation and ensuing articles in historical 
journals have focused more attention on Hendrickson’s North American adventures, and the 
educational activities of his wife, Sennetje Rutgers. (Parmenter JW. Separate Vessels. The 
Worlds of the Seventeenth Century Hudson Valley and Other Lands to the South. Binghamton, 
NY: SUNY Press. 2014) 


Block’s Expedition of 1611-1613 

On his first North American assignment, Cornelius served as the cartographer on an expedition 
to expand fur trade with Native Peoples, search for locations of potential trading posts and map 
unknown lands. The expedition was led by the controversial Adriaen Block (1567-1627), a 
merchant who was not above freelance privateering when opportunity arose. Block’s strengths 
in the eyes of the Dutch government were his navigation skills and knowledge of North 
American coastlines. Block had already completed three trips back and forth between 
Rotterdam and present day New York harbor, which Block named New Netherland in 1609. 


A side note: Despite his pivotal role in the early exploration of New England, Long Island and 
present day New York Bay, no definitive biography of Adriaen Block was ever written. A chapter 
in Henry Howe’s 1969 book on New England settlement and two online resources provide 
summaries of Block’s maritime career and New World explorations: 

Howe H. Adriaen Block Explores New England. In: Prologue to New England. Port Washington 
NY: Kennikat Press. 1969. Available via Internet Archive. www.archive.org. Accessed: June 7, 
2023. 


Rattiner D. An Amazing Journey: How Adriaen Block Discovered Montauk for Europe. History of 
Eastern Long Island. www.danspapers.com. December 14, 2018. Accessed: June 3, 2023. 


Stapler M. 1614 - Adriaen Block. Society of Colonial Wars in the State of Connecticut. 
www.colonialwarsct.org. 2011. Accessed: June 9, 2023. 


Cornelius Hendrickson arrived in New Netherland in April 1611 onboard Block’s flagship, the 
Tyger, named in honor of Mooy Lambert’s ship at the Battle of Gibraltar. The meticulous Dutch 
transatlantic voyage documentation noted that the Hendrickson transported a thousand 
pounds listed as barter material for native negotiation including 100 pairs of bedroom slippers, 
50 gentleman’s dress hats, 50 bonnets, 50 sketch pads, 50 kettles, 50 hand mirrors, and seven 
casks of beer. Block’s flotilla included three 12-foot skiffs suitable for shallow rivers that 
remarkably, were towed behind Tyger across the Atlantic without damage, a cargo ship, 
Fortuyn, for hauling beaver pelts back to Holland owned by Block’s second in command, 
Hendrick Christiaensen, and a third ship, owned by Block, that appears to have played no role in 


188 


the subsequent explorations. On the way to New Netherland, the Fortuyn was anchored in a 
cove at Cape Cod, near where the Pilgrims landed nine years later. The Fortuyn already had a 
reputation in Holland and New Netherland as a contraband (smuggling) ship. Block and 
Christiaensen likely feared that the ship’s appearance in New Netherland would raise suspicions 
about the intent of the expedition. The ship was guarded for two years at Cape Cod by four 
Dutch sailors and two English soldiers of fortune (presumably included for military expertise) 
that were supported by four Faroe Island fishermen and trappers. Block had recently recruited 
the Faroe Islanders from a fish camp on the Nova Scotia coast. This group of ten guarded 
Fortuyn and traded with local natives until Block’s group returned for the trip back to Holland. 


While waiting for Block and Christiaensen to re-appear, the stay-behind Fortuyn crew fished, 
hunted and interacted extensively with the Wampanoag tribe across the bay on the mainland. 
These interactions produced two children, and also may account for the ability of Massasoit, 
chief of the local village of the Wampanoag Nation and other tribesman to greet the Pilgrims in 
1620 by speaking English and Dutch and showing them a bible, possibly obtained from the 
Fortuyn stay behinds. This initial interaction stunned and befuddled the new European arrivals. 
Of course, the presence of Tisquantum (popularly known as Squanto in the Plymouth Pilgrim 
mythology) within Massasoit’s band likely also contributed to their European language capacity. 
In 1614, Squanto was kidnapped and taken to England, where he remained for several years 
working as a carriage driver for an English merchant named Thomas Dermer. By the time 
Squanto returned to Massachusetts with Dermer in 1619, he was said to be “much proficient in 
the British language, appearance and ways.” (Halsall P. Modern History Sourcebook: Excerpts 
from William Bradford, History of Plymouth Plantation. www.sourcebooks.fordham.edu. 1998. 
Accessed: 7/27/2024) 


Adriaen Block made four trips to North America to build 
trade networks with Native Peoples. In 1615, he 
commanded three warships and 11 whalers that illegally 
hunted whales near the Spitsbergen Islands of Norway to 
the dismay of the Norwegians who had no capacity to 
stop him. Block repeated the whale piracy for three years 
until Norway coaxed the English into interceding. The 
English sent warships to chase off Block in 1618, and he 
then returned to more conventional privateering. Stapler, 
2011. Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. 
Accessed: 7/27/2024. 


By September 1611, Block was ready to commence his intertwined missions of establishing fur 
trading networks with Native Tribes, buying pelts (with beer and European clothing) for 
transport to Holland, and geographic exploration and charting. Block’s goal was to convince the 
Dutch States General to grant him an exclusive charter for fur trading with Native tribes for all 
of the lands that were charted on this mission and subsequently displayed via maps. 
Hendrickson, with his charting training and experience, was to play a major role in achieving 
this goal. 


189 


Block, Cornelius Hendrickson, Hendrick Christiaensen and 12 seamen devoted 18 months to 
exploring and mapping what we now know today as Manhattan and the southern shore of Long 
Island. They verified that Manhattan is indeed an island, at least technically, drew the first 
definitive maps of surrounding waterways, and explored the north end of Manhattan and the 
East River for the first time. 


Map of Manhattan and the East River created by 
Cornelius Hendrickson during the Block Expedition. The 
red arrows were added later to indicate locations of 
Native Tribe villages. 

Information and image source: Bell B. Another Early 17 Century 
Map By Cornelius Hendrickson Referencing Siwanoys. In: Historic 


Pelham. www.historicpelhamblogspot.com. August 13, 2018. 
Accessed: 6/10/2024. 


When exploring Long Island, the Tyger was often anchoring off shore for days at a time so 
Hendrickson could travel inland with guides from one of the 13 Native Tribes on the island, all 
subsets of the Algonquin Nation. He mapped inlets and small rivers, sketched the terrain and 
interviewed natives about their lifestyle. At first, he used translators and later in the journey, 
conducted the conversations himself, given his capacity for picking up languages and dialects. 
Hendrickson drew portraits of individuals he interviewed, which were received “with great 
glee” by tribesmen, and compensated them for their time with articles of European clothing 
including hats and European style bedroom slippers, which were “excessively sought after.” He 
was allowed access to and sketched more than 20 tribal villages, including the interiors of 
communal great lodges (main meeting halls of villages). While Hendrickson did his cartography 
and ethnographic investigations, Block and ship’s crew hunted and trapped, and approached 
tribal leaders about fur trading possibilities. After obtaining several trade agreements, and 
exploring and mapping Manhattan and Long Island, the explorers returned to New Netherland 
in March 1613. (Stapler, 2011)

During what was planned to be a brief respite to unload furs, the Tyger mysteriously caught fire 
and sank while moored adjacent to the future site of the World Trade Towers in lower 
Manhattan. There has been conjecture about the source of the fire over the years, including 
sabotage by a competing fur trading company, or sabotage by Block’s own crew, who briefly 


190 


staged a mutiny over inequities in profit sharing from beaver pelt sales. Whatever the cause, a 
new boat had to be constructed for the mission to continue. Just four months later, the result 
of this effort was the construction of the Onrust (Restless), which was according to Block’s 
expedition log: “a small yacht of 45 feet in length, with a beam of 11.5 feet and a 38 foot keel, 
capable of 8 lasts” (i.e., 16 tons of cargo). The Onrust is believed to the first ship, other than 
small skiffs, built in North America. (Rittner D. Adriaen Block and the Onrust: Setting the Stage 
for the Dutch Colonization of North America. 2016. Available via Amazon Prime. 


www.amazon.com) 


A scale replica of the Onrust built for New York State’s 
Quadricentennial (1609-2009) by volunteer craftsman who 
used 17" century boat building equipment and materials. The 
replica is held together by 4000 handmade wooden nails 
(trunnels) and iron rivets cast in a 17% century forge near 
Albany, NY. The Onrust replica is now located at the 
Connecticut River Museum in Essex, CT.

At some point during the spring or summer of 1613, Cornelius’ wife Sennetje Rutger and five of 
their 12 children arrived in New Netherland (re-named New Amsterdam in 1624), which was no 
more than a crude trading post at the time with a population of less than 100. Sennetje was 
probably one of the first females to reside at the post and her children were possibly the first 
youngsters in the fledgling community, although records about ship arrivals and passengers in 
the formative years of the colony are sketchy as described in the side note below. The 
remaining seven children of Cornelius and Sonnetje were teenagers ensconced at boarding 
schools or married adults living independently in Holland. Sennetje and the children resided in 
one of the first framed houses constructed in the fledgling colony. In the front room of the 
home, Sennetje conducted a school for her five children, eventually joined by several other 
children of other early arrivals to New Netherland. 


A side note: /n 1821, the state of New York elected to “sell all books, documents and papers of 
every kind, belonging to the old East and West India Companies, of a date prior to 1700 at 
public auctions” apparently in a fund raising effort and to rid government file rooms of what 
was considered to be waste paper. (Sypher FJ. The First Families: News From New Netherland. 
New Amsterdam History Center. www.newamsterdamhistorycenter.org. February 10, 2016. 
Accessed: June 8, 2023) As a consequence, knowledge of early arrivals to the New Netherland 
and events in this trading compound have had to be assembled from myriad other sources, 
producing a rather fragmentary history of the early years of New Netherland. It is known from 
Dutch maritime sources that two or three Dutch trading ships arrived annually in the spring and 
summer from approximately 1611 to 1624. Crews of these ships and unknown numbers of 
passengers often wintered in New Netherland before returning to Holland in the spring. Most of 
the travelers on these ships were likely traders and other businessmen who hoped to strike up 


191 


agreements with local tribes, and then return to Holland. However, as in the case of Sennetje 
Rutger and her children, some passengers evidently elected to remain in New Netherland each 
year, slowly building up the non-trader population, and creating the foundation for subsequent 
Dutch colonization. Beginning in 1624 with the arrival of the Eendracht (English: Unity) and Niue 
Nederland, each laden with an estimated 25-30 families per ship, the Dutch government 
commenced a dedicated effort to populate the colony in an effort to stave off potential 
encroachments and land claims by other European nations. (Macy H. 375"" Anniversary of the 
Eendracht and Nieu Nederland. NYG&B Newsletter. 1999; 10(1): 3-5). As an FYI, the intended 
destination of the Mayflower in 1620 was the mouth of the Hudson River (i.e., New York Bay), 
which, if achieved, would have certainly brought them into contact with the residents of New 
Netherland. North Atlantic winds and shoddy navigation led the Mayflower to the vicinity of 
Cape Cod in present day Massachusetts. 


Sennetge’s school was likely the second in North America for European children, following a 
school started in 1609 at the English colony in Jamestown, Virginia. Sennetje had teaching 
experience in Holland, working as a tutor for wealthy families and also teaching in an 
elementary school run by the University of Utrecht. Children could attend this school if their 
parents donated money to the University. Sennetje was admitted as a student to the University 
of Utrecht during the years she taught at the school, an exceedingly rare accomplishment for a 
17" century female. It is not clear if or when she graduated, or if she was the first female 
Utrecht student as some historians claim. Another female student, Anna Marie van Shurman, 
was certified as proficient in 14 languages and admitted to Utrecht in 1636 where she attended 
classes behind a screen so male students could not view her and thus be distracted from 
lectures. (Utrecht University Website: Noted Alumni. www.uu.nl. Accessed: May 28, 2024) 


Frustrated by the delay and fearing further crew mutiny, Block and Christiaensen were eager to 
return to Holland with their cargo of pelts. They wanted to collect the substantial cash rewards 
offered by the Dutch States General for trade agreements with Native Peoples and for maps of 
charted waters and lands. Most importantly, Block and Christiaensen sought an exclusive 
charter to monopolize the pelt trading business with North American tribes within the mapped 
lands. The States General was sufficiently impressed with the maps and agreements to grant a 
trading charter to Block, with Christiaensen as his principle partner. However, Block never 
activated the terms of the charter because he elected to return to his privateering career, 
working for a private Dutch company, Noordsche Compagnie, that was attempting to break-up 
Norway’s control of the North Sea whaling industry. 

While in New Netherland awaiting completion of the new boat, Hendrickson received his next 
assignment, endorsed by both the States General and the DEIC: “traverse and map entirety of 
the coastline south of New Netherland harbor to the Poutaxat Inlet (i.e., later called Delaware 
Bay after an English Lord de la Warr who purchased land on both shores of the Bay), find the 
sources of the Bay and follow the main source until no longer navigable, while searching for 
ideal locations for construction of stockades (i.e., forts) and trading posts.” Upon completion of 
the task and submission of documentation and a report, Hendrickson was promised by the 
States General, a “substantial remuneration to be promptly remitted.” (O’Callaghan, 1848) 


192 


Block, Christiaensen and Hendrickson decided to travel up the coast of New England in the 
Onrust to reach Cape Cod where the cargo ship, Fortuyn, awaited for the return to Holland. 
After off-loading, pelts, maps, tribal agreements, supplies and most of the crew to the Fortuyn, 
Hendrickson would return to New Netherland in the Onrust with a skeleton crew, and 
commence planning for his exploration of the New Jersey coastline and Delaware Bay. 


Block decided to attempt a new and potentially faster route to reach Cape Cod. From 
exploration on a small sloop, Hendrickson had learned that the river east of New Amsterdam 
led to a body of open water between the north shore of Long Island and the coast of New 
England, which provided a more direct path to Cape Cod than sailing around the south side of 
Long Island. Based on this information, the crew of the Onrust navigated a treacherous strait of 
what is now known as the East River separating present day Queens and Manhattan (although 
vastly narrower in 1613), which had swirling tidal currents. Block named this dangerous 
passage, Hellegadt (Hell Gate). After being spun around in whirlpools caused by the clashing 
tides of New Netherland harbor and Long Island Sound, and bouncing off rocks along the 
shoreline, the crew of the Onrust eventually emerged into the open waters of Long Island 
Sound, the first Europeans to do so. Block, Christiaensen and Hendrickson spent the next six 
months fur trapping, seeking trading agreements with local tribes, exploring the north side of 
Long Island and navigating several rivers that flowed into Long Island Sound including what are 
now known today as the Housatonic and Connecticut Rivers. The crew of the Onrust sailed 
more than 60 miles north on the Connecticut River. (Varekamp JC. Adriaen Block, the Discovery 
of Long Island Sound and the New Netherlands Colony. Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University 
Publication. 2011. Accessed June 2, 2024 via www.savethesound.org) 


A side note: As Susan and | drive to the Bradley Airport after visiting our grandchildren in 
Connecticut, we approach Hartford from the south on Interstate 91. Many times, we have 
driven by a sign along the Connecticut River that reads: Adriaen’s Landing, but never stopped to 
investigate. We will the next time. The marker identifies the estimated spot where Block 
anchored the Onrust near present-day Hartford to allow Hendrickson and others to explore 
inland, the first Europeans to reach the area. Today, Adriaen’s Landing is also the name of an 
river front development in Hartford that includes the Connecticut Convention Center, 
Connecticut Science Center and a retail-residential complex. 


A few days after arrival in the Hartford area, Block, Hendrickson and several crew used a 
shallow bottomed skiff to reach the area of present-day Enfield, Connecticut where sandbars 
prevented further progress. In Connecticut as in Long Island, Hendrickson interviewed and 
sketched Native Peoples, which he described as Siwanoy after hearing tribesmen use this term 
to refer to other people in villages. In reality, the term is derived from “siwan”, which refers to 
the wampum that northeastern tribes used as currency for trading and also for recognition of 
achievements, and “oy”, which refers to the artisans who made wampum from clam and oyster 
shells. Hendrickson used Siwanoy on maps of Connecticut, New Jersey and Delaware to indicate 
Native villages, and the term was used by subsequent mapmakers. In actuality, Siwanoy did not 
refer to a specific tribe, but instead was a slang word used to describe tribal artisans who 
designed wampum, with a negative connotation as in “they're Siwanoy; they just sit around and 
make wampum all day.” (Buckland JH. The First Traders on Wall Street: The Wiechquaeskeck 
Tribe of Southwestern Connecticut. Westminster: Heritage Books. 2009) 


193 


During the later phase of this coastline exploration, the Onrust crew came upon a small island 
off the coast of Rhode Island that Block admired so much that he named it after himself — Block 
Island. Block is also credited by some historians for the name of Rhode Island when he, or more 
likely Hendrickson, who maintained the topographical journals, labeled present day Rhode 
Island as Roodt Eylant (anglicized to Rhode Island by English settlers) after noting the red clay 
shores. (Rittner D. 2016) Finally reaching Cape Cod and the awaiting Fortuyn, Block turned the 
Onrust over to Hendrickson who quickly departed for New Netherland to reunite with Sennetje 
and the children. Block sailed for Holland on Christiansen’s ship with his pelts, trade 
agreements with several Native tribes and geographic sketches that later would be turned into 
polished maps. The bulk of the cartography sketches and accompanying notes were created by 
Hendrickson, and quite likely, a few were drafted by Christiaensen. However, Block claimed 
them as captain of the expedition, and Hendrickson acquiesced, perhaps to make sure he got 
control of the Onrust, or perhaps because of a pre-existing agreement. About a hundred years 
later, the Royal Dutch Geographic Society re-labeled many of the maps to indicate either 
Hendrickson or Christiaensen as primary authors. (O’Callaghan, 1848; Varekamp, 2011) 


Notes on Wampum: Wampum was small cylindrical beads meticulously carved from specific 
types of oyster and clamshells. Wampum was used for multiple purposes: decoration, 
indication of status, recognition of achievement, and as decorations to be worn at special 
events. As clothing accessories, finely carved shells were strung together as necklaces or made 
into belts worn laterally across the chest. Wampum belts told a story based on the design and 
color of beads. Gifting of wampum belts commemorated treaties among tribes and with 
Europeans. Later, European colonists started to mass-produce Wampum to use as currency in 
trading with Native Peoples, which deflated its value, and led to declining use among 
northeastern tribes. (Dubin LS. North American Indian Jewelry and Adornment: From Prehistory 
to the Present. New York: Harry N. Abrams Inc. 1999) 


Example of beaded Algonquin wampum belt from the 1700s. Beads 
were carved from oyster and clamshells selected for color and 
texture.

Hendrickson’s 1614-1616 Expedition 

Back in New Netherland in the spring of 1614, Hendrickson decided he needed a “second 
smaller but still substantial craft with shallow draft and clear observation lines” for the 
upcoming voyage, and commissioned the same craftsmen who constructed the Onrust to build 
the ship. While the new ship was being assembled, Hendrickson recruited a crew of 22 
including 12 seaman, four militia men, “handy with musket” for protection/show of force, and 
three male and female pairs (i.e., spouses) who served multiple functions as scouts, trackers, 
translators and Native ways advisors (i.e., 17" century cultural consultants). In two of the pairs, 
both spouses were mixed race (i.e., Native American-European) and capable of communicating 
adequately in several prominent tribal languages of the East Coast. The mixed race population 
was substantial in the early days of New Netherland for the same reasons that the Metis 
population grew in the Washington and Oregon Territories in the 18" and 19" centuries. The 
third couple was European, but had lived for a decade among the Mohawks, and had developed 
facility with Native languages. Their capacity to read and write Dutch allowed the scouts to help 
Cornelius with map labeling and the trip log. When observing tribal life in Long Island and 
Connecticut, Hendrickson noted that the political, hunting and warfare leaders were all males, 
but for day to day village operations, female priests (spiritual guides), healers and elders made 
the decisions. Accordingly, he believed that female guides and linguists might make village 
leaders more comfortable and willing to communicate, a theory that was proven correct 
throughout the journey. 


To conduct a shakedown cruise on the Onrust with his new crew, Hendrickson explored the 
area known today as Staten Island, circling and charting it by water and exploring inland on foot 
with his guides / language specialists. He then moved on to the large Raritan Bay (named for 
the Raritan sect of the Lenape tribe) that feeds water into New York Bay. Hendrickson mapped 
the contours of Raritan Bay for the first time, found the source (i.e., Raritan River), and followed 
it north to the Wachung Hills, the highest point in New Jersey, the first European to reach the 
area. Along the way, he engaged in his usual interactions, sketching and note taking with Native 
Peoples, and picked up a 23 crew member, an unusually tall teenage Raritan boy who was 
persistent in his request to join Hendrickson. Because of his height, the young man eventually 
came to be known among the crew as Groot Schop (Big Kick), apparently referencing his height 
and his tribal name of Pennakick. 


The light green area is Raritan Bay, explored to its source in 
central New Jersey for the first time by Cornelius Hendrickson 
in 1614. Monmouth County, NJ, south of Raritan Bay, would 
eventually become home to many descendants of Cornelius 
Hendrickson and other Hendrickson lines. 

Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 8/9/2024. 


When Hendrickson and the Onrust crew, with the addition of Groot Schop, returned to New 
Netherland in August 1614, the new companion ship was ready to sail. Named the Liseren 


195 


Varcken (Iron Hog) for unknown reasons (perhaps its appearance), the vessel’s construction 
may have suffered from Hendricson’s absence. It was squat and ungainly looking, shorter but 
much wider than the Onrust, rode low in the water, but had a “deeply upturned bow with over 
laying of metal to allow close approaching of shallows and rocky shorelines.” The Onrust, Iron 
Hog and six trailing skiffs (three attached to each main ship) departed for the New Jersey coast 
on the last day of September 1614. The charting expedition made good progress during 
October. But as the Lenape villages became aware of the little flotilla that frequently stopped to 
allow crew to come ashore, more and more Natives walked to the shoreline to see the 
spectacle, especially women, teenagers and young children. The presence of a tall, apparently 
handsome, Raritan teenager among the crew was duly noted by the villagers and led to “much 
enthusiasm among the Lenape youth” when he came ashore. Soon villagers started to bring 
food and other gifts to beach campsites where members of the crew waited for Hendrickson 
and the guides to return from their dry land exploration. The crew accepted the gifts and 
exchanged clothing, tobacco and cooking utensils with the Lenape. Often, the food and gift 
exchanges evolved into social events, lasting deep into the evening. After numerous of these 
beach parties, Hendrickson’s crew was distracted, the ships were overloaded with food, and the 
expedition’s inventory of gifts for potentially less friendly tribes was depleted. Hendrickson 
decided to put a stop to the celebrations. Via one of his scout teams, he identified an influential 
Lenape leader, and convinced him to constrain the villages from gift giving, promising a 
“wonderful demonstration” and onboard tours of the /ron Pig when the expedition reached the 
mouth of Delaware Bay. 


With the beachfront social events curtailed, Hendrickson and crew made better progress 
southward, reaching present day Cape May at the mouth of Delaware Bay in January 1615. A 
large crowd of Lenapes had gathered for the promised event. The militia men obliged by firing a 
small cannon mounted on the /ron Hog into the ocean several times, shooting their loud and 
smoky blunderbusses into the air, and lighting flares (gunpowder in tubes). A musket and pistol 
shooting demonstration also occurred. The noise and smoke from these volleys thrilled the 
children, but may have unnerved some of the adults who stopped to ponder the implications of 
these weapons. Village groups were invited to nominate three people for portraits, and 
Hendrickson obliged by tirelessly sketching the selected individuals throughout the day. In 
groups of eight, Natives were rowed around the Onrust on the skiffs and out to the /ron Hog, 
where they could walk around on deck for a few minutes. Finally, just before nightfall, a final 
round of cannon fire, flares and blunderbuss volleys lit up the sky. Both ships and the trailing 
skiffs then sailed away into the mouth of the Bay where they anchored for the night. 


The next morning, Hendrickson and his men found that the initial stretch of the Bay was 
treacherous to navigate, especially for the Onrust, which had a much deeper draw than the /ron 
Hog. In his log, Hendrickson noted that: 


“The bay within is full of sandbars, shoals and swirly tides in and amongst these bars, and even 
though there are many kills and channels by which we discovered navigation trails through it, 
one should not come in the bay with a deep drawn ship, and not come in unless he is familiar 
with these moving shoals and bars, for it is a dangerous bay.” (O’Callaghan, 1848)
