Accessed: 8/4/2024. 


In addition to the tricky navigation due to the shallow water and sand bars, the journey 
northward through the Delaware Bay also was far less social than along the Jersey coast. On the 
western side of the Bay, Mohawks were the principle tribe, and they only interacted with 
Hendrickson to request trades for weapons, which he repeatedly declined. On the eastern side 
of the Bay, the Lenape were less evident, choosing to follow the progress of the ships from the 
forests, but rarely attempting to interact. Perhaps the firepower show at the mouth of the Bay 
dampened their enthusiasm, or perhaps Hendrickson and his ships were no longer new news. 
The expedition had almost reached the neck of the Bay near present-day Pea Patch Island when 
eight Mohawk warriors emerged from the scrub brush one evening. The Mohawks approached 
the crew’s campsite, where several crewmembers were waiting for Hendrickson to return from 
an exploration. The Mohawks requested to speak with the four militia who, unusually, 
happened to be ashore at the same time, likely a protocol breach. The “men with weaponry” 
were offered an incredible reward if they would accompany the Mohawk band on a raid of a 
Susquehanna village to retrieve a kidnapped mother and child. The Mohawks then produced a 
large satchel full of Dutch Florins (historians remain puzzled as to the source of the coinage), 
which they promised to give to the four militia upon completion of the mission. For unknown 
reasons, perhaps boredom, desire for adventure, or simply greed, the expedition’s military 
crew gathered up their weapons and abruptly departed with the Mohawks in spite of their 
shipmates attempts to stop them. 


The cannon on the /ron Hog was fired twice in succession, a pre-arranged signal for 
Hendrickson to return to camp, which he did by nightfall. There is debate among historians 
about Hendrickson’s actions after reaching camp, but it was ultimately decided that walking 
into the high brush and trees in search of the militia men and Mohawks could lead to an 
ambush. Hendrickson ordered the two ships to cast off and anchor at Pea Patch Island in the 
middle of the Bay to preempt an attack during the night. After heated conversation between 
Hendricson and the crew, the decision was made to push ahead without the militia as they 
“cast their lot, we will endure without their participation”. The next morning, Hendrickson and 
crew continued their voyage, entering the narrower body of water that today is known as the 
Delaware River. 


198 


Meanwhile, the four militia and the eight Mohawks approached the Susquehanna village, 
probably near present day Christiana, Delaware, where the captives were supposedly held. The 
12 men swooped into the village with substantial musket firing, hoping to terrify the 
inhabitants, only to find the camp largely deserted. Within moments, a large number of 
Susquehanna men rose up out of the brush and unleashed a torrent of arrows, then rushed in 
with spears and clubs. Three of the four men from Hendrickson’s crew were struck by arrows 
and wounded, although none fatally. The fourth crewmember, a man named Kleynties, snuck 
away during in the melee, and headed toward the river. Two of the eight Mohawks were killed, 
and the others managed to flea, abandoning the wounded militiamen, but not before grabbing 
their muskets. Afterward, the Susquehanna decided this campsite was unsafe, gathered their 
belongings and headed north, taking the three wounded Europeans with them. 


Kleynties reached the river by the next day, and in a turn of good fortune, he rushed out of the 
grasses lining the muddy river bank at the exact instant that the /ron Hog, with Hendrickson 
aboard, slowly coasted along the shoreline. Hendrickson’s first instinct was to administer the 
customary lashes for insubordination, but the crew objected and he deferred the punishment 
“until and upon further consideration when NN port (New Netherland) is reached”. Instead, 
Hendrickson decided that pursuit of the three captive crewmen was now warranted. He 
organized a pursuit party comprised of himself, four of the guides/linguists, the Raritan 
teenager, and two of the crew with familiarity with muskets. After directing the crew to take 
the /ron Hog back to Pea Patch Island for safety, the rescue team headed north, pulling a hastily 
constructed sled loaded with gifts. 


Because an entire village of Susquehanna were trekking north with three wounded captives, 
progress was slow, and it did not take long for Hendrickson’s group to identify their trail and 
catch up. The Susquehanna were well aware of the approaching Europeans and what they 
wanted. Halting their advance, three Susquehanna envoys were sent to discuss the situation 
with Hendrickson and his men. Impressed by the language facility of the Europeans, the Raritan 
lad’s inclusion in the group, and also wanting to rid themselves of the three wounded men, the 
Susquehanna and Hendrickson quickly reached an agreement for release of the crewmembers. 
The tribe received the entire contents of the sled, which included much sought after bedroom 
slippers, European breeches (pants), shirts, metal cooking kettles, a sketch book and pencils, , 
and a keg of salt-preserved meat. 


A side note: The journey to intercept the Susquehanna led Hendrickson and colleagues into the 
land that would ultimately become Pennsylvania. They were the first Europeans to set foot in 
the geographic region that would evolve into William Penn’s Grand Commonwealth 70 years 
later. 


After the rescue party returned to the shoreline and rendezvoused with the rest of the crew, 
the little flotilla proceeded east on the Delaware River toward present-day Philadelphia. The 
wounded men recovered sufficiently to resume normal routine by the time of the return trip. 
For abandoning their posts, they were punished with 25% reduction in compensation. As the 
Delaware River narrowed and became considerably shallower, most of the exploration was 
conducted from the Iron Hog with the Onrust anchored in the middle of the river and used as a 
supply station. During this phase of the operation, Hendrickson sailed the /ron Hog up the 


199 


Schuylkill River through the land that would become Philadelphia to the area of Reading, PA, 
where he ran into several Susquehanna wearing clothing exchanged to the tribe several weeks 
previously. During the final months, Hendrickson’s crew had limited contact with Native 
Peoples and concluded their journey when they reached a series of five foot waterfalls in the 
river near present day Trenton, NJ, about 40 miles east of Philadelphia. 


Sensing the fatigue of the crew, Hendrickson decided to immediately commence the return to 
New Netherland, but a major decision had to be made. In spite of its perceived ugliness, the 
Iron Hog had proven its worth on the final leg of the exploration, navigating the many shallows 
of the river and facilitating shoreline charting. However, it was slow moving and difficult to 
maneuver on the open sea, leading Hendrickson to beach the little ship, toss the cannon into 
the River and load everyone onto the Onrust for the journey home. Sticking to the middle of the 
Bay, traveling the deepest depths available at full sail, and limiting shore time on the New 
Jersey coast as much as feasible, the Onrust reached New Netherland harbor in early August 
1616, nearly two years after departure. All 23 crew who departed with Hendrickson in 
September 1614 returned alive. After off loading most of the crew and briefly reuniting with his 
family, Hendrickson and a skeleton crew returned Groot Schop to the Wachung Hills and 
dropped him off with a satchel of clothing and other gifts. After two years with Hendrickson 
and the crew, the lanky teen was now fluent in Dutch and also had picked up considerable 
English from the guides. Approximately five years later, Groot Schop, who now used the name 
Andreas, settled on Staten Island with a group of Raritan tribesman who desired to establish 
trade relationships with the Dutch. Andreas acted as their translator during negotiations. 
Although the venture was only mildly successful, Dutch traders eventually hired Andreas for 
translation and negotiation jobs. Over the next 20 years, Andreas travelled up and down the 
Hudson, and along the New England and Long Island coastlines on Dutch trading boats. He 
disappeared from New Netherland ship logs around 1640, and his fate is unknown. 


At some point during the 1614-1616 expedition, the three teenage sons of Cornelius and 
Sonnetje had traveled to New Netherlands to join their mother and five younger siblings. The 
family, after reuniting, deliberated the pros and cons of remaining in the Americas. Ultimately, 
it was decided that the Hendrickson’s would return to Holland so that Cornelius could file his 
report to the States General and the DEIC supported by his maps, notebooks and sketches to 
obtain the promised financial reward for his efforts, and the family could resume a more 
civilized life in Utrecht. 


The States General response to Hendrickson’s report was notably tepid. According to 
O'Callaghan, rather than focusing on potential sites for Dutch fortifications and trading posts in 
Delaware Bay, Hendrickson’s report concentrated on his personal interests, which included 
wildlife (unique animals, fowl and fish not seen in Europe), trees, plants and vegitation, and 
Native attire, customs, language and architecture. Perhaps Hendrickson assumed that his maps 
and cartography notes indicated good sites for military and commercial sites and he did not 
need extensive narrative to amplify. However, O’Callaghan observed that the States General 
was distracted by other political and military events at the time of Hendrickson’s report, and 
they did reward him “rather handsomely” even though his report was tabled and not dealt with 
for five years. The DEIC also tabled Hendrickson’s report for several years before follow-up 
action was initiated. Ultimately, his exploration of the Delaware Bay region led to the 


200 


establishment of a Dutch fort and trading post in 1633 at the confluence of the Schuylkill and 
Delaware Rivers, and another fortification near present day Philadelphia. (O’Callaghan, 1848). 


A side note: Hendrickson’s entire report to the States General, dated August 28, 1616, and 
apparently written while he was at sea traveling back to Holland with his family, appears 
verbatim in “The Dutch and Swedes on the Delaware 1609-1664” by Christopher Ward. 
(Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press. 1930; accessed June 2, 2024 via 
www.archivesfiles.delaware.gov). 


Before the Hendrickson’s departed for Holland, Cornelius sold the Onrust to another Dutch 
explorer, Cornelius Jacobsen Mey, who commonly signed his name as “May” after settling in 
New Netherland to become its first Director. Although May conducted further explorations of 
the Delaware Bay (Cape May is named after him), he did not use the Onrust. The sale of the 
Onrust to May is the last historical record of the ship. Its fate is unknown. (New York State 
Library. New Netherland Institute and Research Center. Cornelius Jacobsen Mey, Director of 
New Netherland. www.nysl.nysed.gov. March, 2011. Accessed: June 25, 2023) 


After his return to Holland, Cornelius accepted an administrative position with the DEIC and 
never again participated in a charting expedition, although he continued to produce maps for 
public display based on information provided by others. He and Sonnetje played an important 
role years later when they took in their grandchildren, Hendrick and Ida Ede Hendriksz, after 
the death of the children’s parents. Cornelius and Sonnetje co-parented their grandchildren for 
five years until her death, after which Cornelius cared for the children for many more years 
until literally a few days prior to his death. As described on page 37 on Chapter II, Cornelius 
made arrangements prior to his death for continuation of Hendrick’s high school and college 
education, and for Ida Ede’s employment. 


For historical accuracy, it is important to note that a Dutch sailor by the name Jan Jacobsz Bens 
and three companions claimed, in a document written in 1620, to have traveled up Delaware 
Bay to the mouth of the Delaware River in 1611, three years before Cornelius Hendrickson. 
Bens claimed that they used a yacht known as the Liseren Varcken (Iron Hog). The one page 
document was actually an oral testimony transcribed into the notarial archives of the 
Gemeentearchief Amsterdam (Amsterdam Municipal Nautical Archives). Jacobsz Bens worked 
for a well-established Rotterdam merchant, Hendrick Eelkens, who according to the testimony, 
allowed Jacobsz Bens to pursue a rumor about the existence of a “wondrous bay at the south.” 
Since New Netherland records clearly identify August 1614 as the launch date for Hendrickson’s 
Iron Hog, historians have tended to discounted the Jacobsz Bens’ testimony, but also noted that 
it is likely that other Europeans may have entered the bay prior to Hendrickson, although none 
did any charting or produced maps. After all, Hendrickson’s superiors at DEIC knew about the 
bay and tasked him with exploring it. It is known that Henry Hudson in 1609 anchored his ship, 
Halve Maen (Half Moon), at the mouth of Delaware Bay near present day Cape May, and sent 
one of his subordinates to investigate the bay in a skiff. Based on his subordinate’s description 
of the shallowness of the bay and its numerous sandbars, Hudson concluded that this waterway 
was not likely a passage to the Pacific. Hudson remained at the mouth of the bay only three 
days before continuing north to his main destination, which was body of water that bears his 
name, the Hudson River. Hudson’s accounts of this journey, including his brief layover at Cape 


201 


May, were widely publicized in Europe. Hendrickson almost certainly studied these reports, 
including Hudson’s description of the entrance to Delaware Bay. (Morgan M. Henry Hudson 
Visits Delaware Bay In Quest For Route to the Pacific. Delmarva Now Magazine. 
www.delmarva.now. September 18, 2021. Accessed June 10, 2024) 


Notes on Initial Encounters of European Colonists and Native Americans: Many histories of 
the exploration of North America by Europeans portray both Native Peoples and European 
immigrants as experiencing mutual culture shock and inability to communicate when they first 
encountered each other in the early 1600s. In reality, and as well understood at that time by 
Cornelius Hendrickson, Adriaen Block and other explorers, Europeans from various nations had 
been wandering around the eastern seaboard of the U.S. and Canada for decades prior to the 
establishment of New Netherland. Most of these early arrivals were fishermen. Irish, Bretons 
from northwest France, Portuguese, and especially Bosque’s from the northern region of Spain 
had fished the Grand Banks adjacent to Nova Scotia and along the upper coast of New England 
since approximately 1520, nearly 100 years before New Netherland was established. As we will 
see later, Christopher Columbus learned about North America from these fishermen. By 1520, 
the Bosque operated a fishing fleet of 200 boats and several thousand men in these waters. 
(Axtell J. At the Water's Edge. Trading in the 16" Century. Essays in the Ethnohistory of North 
America. New York and Oxford: Oxford University Press. 1988) Bosque fishermen sometimes 
wintered in coastal camps and routinely interacted with Native Peoples. 


Fishermen’s tales of abundant wildlife near to shore stimulated trappers and hunters from 
North Sea nations to make the trip to Canada and New England. As a consequence, by the time 
Block and Hendrickson started their explorations, the Native Peoples they encountered had 
picked up elements of European languages, wore articles of European clothing received in 
trade, gave their children biblical names (Peter, Paul and Elizabeth were popular), integrated 
mixed race children fathered by Europeans into their villages, and were relatively familiar with 
European ways. At first meeting, there may have been culture shock, but it was mostly on the 
European side. Early European settlers were aware of the indigenous peoples of North America 
before they landed, but had stereotypical views based on staged encounters on the European 
side of the Atlantic. (Savor CO. Sixteenth Century North America. The Land and The People As 
Seen by the Europeans. Berkley: University of California Press. 1971) 


Historians estimate that at least 300 Native Americans, mostly men, were taken back to Europe 
by early explorers, including Adriaen Block who transported four to six Natives to Holland every 
time he returned home. Some of the reverse-travelling Natives were lured by stories of 
European life, others were tricked with promises of lavish gifts, but most were kidnapped and 
forced into the journey. By the time the Pilgrims waded ashore at Plymouth in 1620, sightings 
of North American Peoples were common in European cities. Explorers displayed Native 
“specimens” during meetings with the investors who they hoped to entice to fund their 
explorations. Native Americans also were exhibited in theatres or circus-like performances for 
the general public who paid admission to see “amerikan aboriginals in their fearsome 
demeanors and natural forest regalia.” Effort was made to incorporate a few female Natives 
into Dutch or English society, dressing them in European clothing and teaching them domestic 
skills. A few others, most prominently Matoaka (i.e., Pocahontas) who was married to Virginia 


202 


colonist John Rolfe, were brought to England to demonstrate that a female Native could be a 
suitable bride for a gentleman. 


A side note: Pocahontas was a nickname derived from Matoaka’s playful and mischievous 
nature. Rolfe preferred Pocahontas to Matoaka because it was easier to pronounce. 


After the novelty wore off or the Natives were no longer useful in fund-raising endeavors, the 
males were forced into slavery or simply abandoned to the streets. Females were often treated 
better, but many, including Pocahontas and her young son, caught European diseases and died 
before returning to their homeland. It is estimated that less than 10% of Native Peoples 
brought to England or Europe ever returned to North America.

Historian Caroline Pennock of the University of Sheffield estimated that more than 5,000 Native 
American women, who were wives of early colonists or traders, and their children traveled to 
England and Northern Europe between 1600 and 1700. These family members were better 
treated than the exhibits brought across the Atlantic by Block and other explorers. However, 
more than a few of the spouses and children who survived European diseases were discarded, 
sold into slavery or forced into prostitution. 

A side note: Beginning with Columbus in the 1490s, thousands of Caribbean and South 
American Natives were captured in battle or kidnapped by Spanish and Portuguese explorers, 
pirates and military, and brought to the Mediterranean as labor or sex trade slaves. The Spanish 
and Portuguese made no pretense of integrating New World natives into Iberian culture.

to petition the Crown concerning contentious issues, and also were treated well.

Columbus had completed a commercial voyage to England and Ireland, delivering spices, fabrics 
and Mediterranean pottery to several ports including Galway on the west coast of Ireland, the 
final stop. Columbus was intrigued by tales of an abundant land to the west of Iceland that he 
had heard from Bosque fishing boat captains, and like most educated Europeans, he was aware 
of Leif Eriksson’s journey to Vinland. (Cohen JM. The Four Voyages of Christopher Columbus: 
Being His Own Log-Book, Letters and Dispatches with Connective Narrative Drawn From the Life 
of the Admiral by His Son Hernando Colon and Other Contemporary Historians. New York: 
Penguin Books. 1969) Columbus decided to make the 800-mile trip from Galway to Iceland to 
investigate first hand. Arriving in October, Columbus spent nine months at Ingjladsholl, the site 
of Leif Eriksson’s 10" century village and the main port for the Icelandic fishing fleet in the later 
half of the 15" century. Columbus questioned fishermen about the fishing beds to the 
southwest of Iceland, and learned from village elders about Icelander’s frequent travels in prior 
centuries to a forested shoreline to retrieve lumbar that they called Markland (a wooded land; 
probably Labrador), rather than Vinland, which likely referred to Newfoundland or New 
Brunswick. (Johnson K. How Columbus’s Winter in Iceland Helped Him Get to America. European 
Conservative. March 2022) 


As described by his son Ferdinand in a biography, Columbus made two exploratory “ventures to 
the Southwest, sailing merely more than 100 leagues (roughly 310 miles) beyond Thule” 
accompanied by Bodvar Jonsson, Ingjladsholl’s priest for the local Catholic parish (side note 
below) and a crew of local sailors. (Colon F, Keen B, editor and translator. The Life of the 
Admiral Christopher Columbus by his Son Ferdinand. New Brunswick, NJ: Rutgers University 
Press. 1992). In the 15" century, European writers often used the word Thule (Latin: edge of 
known world) to describe Iceland and Greenland collectively, although Thule originally was 
associated only with Greenland during the Viking era of the 9-11" centuries. Iceland and 
Greenland were linked by an ice sheet for much of the medieval period, which may have led 
Europeans to perceive them as a single entity. The ice receded in the 15" century, allowing ship 
travel to resume between the islands. It is unclear if Columbus traveled 100 leagues to the 


204 


southwest of Iceland or 100 leagues beyond Greenland. The later would have brought 
Columbus within 300-500 miles of Labrador, depending on landing site, requiring three to four 
sailing days, leading to fascinating what ifs in the event the journey continued. Ferdinand 
Columbus did not shed light on what his father learned on these journeys. (Quinn DB. Columbus 
and the North: England, Iceland & Ireland. William and Mary Quarterly. 1992; 49(2): 278-297) 


A side note: Estimates of the speed of 15" century merchant ships indicate that, with favoring 
winds, a loaded cargo ship on open water averaged four knots (4.4 miles) per hour, or roughly 
100 miles per day. For example, Sir Francis Drake routinely noted his daily distance on voyages. 
He completed one 1100-mile journey with a loaded cargo ship from Plymouth, England Portugal 
in ten days. An empty cargo ship, such as the one Columbus sailed to Iceland, could achieve 
faster speeds, up to 7 knots per hour (7.7 mph), as much as 175 miles per day. (Casson L. Speed 
Under Sail of Ancient Ships. Transactions of the American Philosophical Association. 1951; 82(1): 
136-148. Accessed June 3, 2024 via www.penelope.uchicago.edu.) 


In addition to explorations with Jonsson, Columbus traveled to the town of Hvalfjardarer to 
confer with the Bishop of Iceland, Magnus Eyjolfsson, who spoke Italian acquired during his 
priesthood in Rome. Eyjolfsson had an interest in Markland exploration and reportedly shared 
logbooks of Icelandic expeditions to the western lands to acquire lumbar. (Moosmuller OP. 
(translated by Upton G.) Columbus’ Interview With Bishop Magnus in 1477. In: Pre-Columbian 
Discoverers of America. Chicago: A.C. McClurg Co. 1911. Digitized in 2021 by Heritage History 
(www.heritage-history.com). Accessed: March 19, 2022) It should be noted that a few historians 
have disputed accounts of Columbus’ travels to Iceland, contending that he actually sailed to 
the Faroe or Spitsbergen Islands. This seems unlikely, given Columbus’ familiarity with the 
North Atlantic and North Sea gained during commercial journeys, his famed navigation skills, 
and the fact that these islands are north of Ireland, not northwest.

A side note: Iceland converted to Christianity in 1000 and came under the jurisdiction of the 
Catholic Church, which appointed the first Icelandic Bishop in 1056. (History of the Catholic 
Church in Iceland. 2019. www.catholica.is. Accessed: March 17, 2022) The Reformation reached 
Iceland in the 16" century, leading to the demise of Catholic influence on the island and the rise 
of the Lutheran church, which is now the primary denomination.

Here There Be Witches - Mary Molly Reeve Webster (1618-1698); mother of Johanna 
Anna Webster, wife of Benjamin Goodman Sr. 

The Massachusetts witch trials were a sordid chapter in the history of the American colonies, 
revealing the worst side of religious zeal and the dangerous power of irrational mass hysteria, 
stoked by articulate fear mongers. In the Goodman family lineage table (Section II, page 91), we 
met Johanna Anna Webster (1640-1719), who was the wife of Benjamin Goodman Sr. (1639- 
1735). Anna’s mother was a woman named Mary Molly Reeve who became the catalyst for the 
witch hysteria that swept the Massachusetts colony in the late 1600s. 


A list of several prominent books on the New England witchcraft frenzy appear at the end of 
Mary Molly Reeve Webster’s story. 


Mary Molly Reeve (she preferred Molly) was born in Covington, England to poor shopkeepers. 
At the age of 12, her parents arranged a marriage to 18-year-old William Webster (1612-1688), 
the son of an affluent landed family in exchange for a tenet lease on the Webster estate. Molly 
worked as a domestic at the Webster estate for 12 years, until her marriage was annulled after 
she bore four children by William, the youngest of which was Anna Webster. The annulment 
was arranged so William could marry Sarah Waterbury (1618-1655), also from a landed family. 
Sarah, William, his parents (John and Agnes Webster) and Molly’s two oldest children 
immigrated to Connecticut in 1640 after John Webster was appointed as Governor of the 
Connecticut Colony. John Webster was a barrister who handled legal affairs and property 
management for the crown’s estates near Nottingham and Leicester. The governorship was 
apparently a reward for his legal efforts on behalf of the crown. Anna and a sister remained at 
the Webster estate to be raised by William’s grandparents. 


After William’s departure to Connecticut, Molly was separated from Anna and her other 
daughter and put out on the street. Two years later, she showed up in Sandwich, England, a 
seaport town in Kent (southeast England) where she met and married James Skiffe Jr., a ship 
captain who annually piloted a ship loaded with immigrants to Massachusetts and returned 
roughly 8 months later with a cargo of lumber and beaver pelts. James was in town often 
enough for the couple to have three children. However, in 1652, Molly and James divorced 
based on infidelity charges filed by James. Indeed, while James was away on his annual 
voyages, Molly, who by all accounts was quite social and unusually tall with green eyes and 
auburn hair, had liaisons with several men in Sandwich. After the divorce, Skiffe moved 
permanently to a coastal community in Massachusetts south of the Plymouth Colony, also 
named Sandwich, and became a pillar of the community, serving in governance roles and was a 
successful cooper who made barrels and casks from seasoned wood. He married and had nine 
children with his new wife, named Martha, who, ironically, also went by Molly. 


After the divorce, Molly Reeve with her three children by Skiffe, wandered back to central 
England by unknown means, landing in Bedfordshire around 1655, where she met an old suitor 
(more or less) — William Webster, her first husband, that she married as a literal child bride. It 
seems that William epitomized the wealthy ner-do-well stereotype, and after being divorced by 
Sarah Waterbury, was dispatched back to England by his parents to mature under the tutelage 
of a stern aunt and uncle in Bedfordshire. Molly, willing to let bygones be bygones, soon joined 
up with William again, and she reconciled with daughter Anna who was now a teenager. Molly 


207 


and William remarried and had tumultuous 33-year marriage. There is no evidence that they 
had any additional children. Molly and William were evidently both hotheaded, which led to 
two yearlong separations, but they eventually reunited after each spat. Meanwhile, daughter 
Anna married Benjamin Goodman in 1659, of the formerly wealthy Southill Manor Goodman 
family discussed in Chapter II. The closing of Southill Manor triggered Anna and Benjamin’s 
immigration to the Virginia Colony in North America. 


Molly and William, struggling financially, pleaded with Benjamin Goodman to pay their way 
across the Atlantic, and he eventually agreed, a significant financial undertaking. In 1668, the 
Goodman entourage consisting of Ben, Anna, 11 children, Molly and William traversed the 
Atlantic and landed at Port Royale on the Rappahannock River in Virginia. Dismayed by the 
crude frontier culture in rural Virginia and horrified by a slave auction they observed near 
present day Richmond, Molly and William soon departed for New England, which they hoped 
would provide a more inviting environment. 


Molly and William settled in the puritan town of Hadley, Massachusetts, north of present day 
Springfield on the Connecticut River and remained there for the rest of their lives. As in 
previous locales, William was indolent, and brought in minimal money with odd jobs. Molly 
took whatever jobs she could find in the small community as a seamstress, waitress in a tavern, 
and housekeeper but the couple often had to relay on food donations from neighbors. Her “red 
hot temper, hard opinions and feisty nature” soon got Molly into a series of disagreements with 
members of the community, earning her a reputation of being difficult and unpredictable. 
Disliked and mistrusted, neighbors began to blame Molly for various odd occurrences such as 
milk that would not churn, chickens falling down chimneys into the fire, cattle that refused to 
walk past her house, a tavern patron who became ill after a meal she served, her uncanny 
ability to cure warts with a secret paste, and having cat scratches on her arms. 


In February 1683, the Hadley City Council reported Molly as a “presumed practicer of witchery 
crafts” to the Northampton Regional Court. After examining Molly physically and verbally, the 
court decided the evidence was inconclusive, and potentially “could be otherwise explained.” 
Her case was referred to a higher tribunal in Boston. In May 1683, a panel including Governor 
Simon Bradstreet, the Deputy Governor and nine other administrative officers heard the case 
against Molly. This panel found that Molly was “likely guilty of spell making and other 
witchcrafts” and ordered a trial by peers in June. After three days of testimony at the June trial 
and another disrobed inspection, Molly was found not guilty and released. 


Rendition of the June 1683 trial of Molly 
Reeve on witchcraft charges brought by 
her Hadley neighbors. Her acquittal led to 
further harassment and_ ultimately, 
violence. 


Image source: SlideShare. www.slideshare.net. 
Accessed: 5/11/2024. 


208 


The verdict was not received well in Hadley and public harassment of Molly increased. Virtually 
any sickness of sudden onset in the town was attributed to Molly’s “black and devious arts.” In 
1685, a prominent Hadley citizen by the name of Philip Smith, who was the judge of the local 
court, and also an individual who suffered from gastrointestinal disease for much of his life, 
suddenly fell ill in the midst of a trial. Smith was confined to bed as he had been many times 
previously. This time, Smith decided to blame Molly Reeve for his ills, telling friends and his 
nursemaid that her casting of a “malicious spell” led to his suffering. Smith lapsed into delirium 
likely due to a spiked fever and cried out that he was in “anguishing pain.” His nursemaid 
claimed that bottles of his medicines disappeared, likely spirited away by the witch Reeve and 
reported seeing a giant cat in Smith’s bed chewing on his leg “as if a morsel from the spit.” 


During Smith’s illness, a gang of Hadley men drug Molly from her house after beating William, 
intending to hang her, based on the prevailing belief that if a witch’s aura is disturbed by pain 
(i.e., if she is distracted with her own anguish), her spell would be broken or weakened. They 
tied a noose around her neck and hoisted her off the ground from a limb of a large elm tree 
across the street from her house. Then they waited for at least four hours (some accounts 
indicate she hung from the tree over night). When these Puritan men finally considered her 
sufficiently close to death, or actually dead, they cut her down. Molly was indeed unconscious, 
but not dead yet. They rolled her body down a hill to a large mound of snow, buried her in it, 
and then walked away assuming that her body would not be found until a spring thaw. 
Although 67 years old, Molly was still strong and refused to die. She managed to claw her way 
out of the mound, and staggered back home to tend to her beaten husband. She did not tell 
her husband about the attack, and he only found out when a group of teenagers threatened 


Molly with another hanging as she and William walked to market several days later. 
=> . 


Hadley Puritans attempted to break Molly’s evil 
aura and release Philip Smith from a “cast spell 
of death” by inflicting great pain, so as to 
distract her concentration on evil doing. The 
plan failed and Molly lived to suffer more 
abuse. 


Image source: Smithsonian Learning Lab. 
Learninglabsi.edu. Accessed: 5/12/2024. 


The aura-breaking gambit failed to work. After several days of high fever and probably sepsis, 
Smith died. Observers of his body reported various odd deformations such as lumps and bulges 
and claimed that his body bled long after death. Smith’s death provoked hysteria among the 
citizenry. On two occasions shortly after Smith’s death, Molly was drug from her house and 
beaten with sticks, and attempts were made to burn down the tiny house, which failed due to 
rain and snow fall. Oddly, considering these events, Molly was not referred to court for a new 
examination of her witchcraft, and Molly pursued no legal action, probably assuming that no 
good would come of it. William died soon after, but Molly continued to live in Hadley for 13 
more years, residing in the same little house, living in poverty. She continued to face verbal 
abuse, but suffered no more violence. 


209 


The events in Hadley caught the attention of Cotton Mather, a Harvard educated Puritan 
clergyman (minister of Boston’s influential Congregationalist Old North Meeting House) and 
scholar, who began to write and speak in 1687 about the “stupendous spell casting witch Molly 
Reeve Webster.” Mather concluded that Molly was likely responsible for Smith’s death and 
other “dreadful and unexpected deaths and happenings” in Hadley, declaring: “Upon the 
whole, it appears without question that the witch Reeve had brought a period of torture that 
ended the life of so good a man.” Cotton Mather’s writings, along with those of his father, 
Increase Mather, a former President of Harvard College, were catalysts for the arrests of 
approximately 160 women, men and children, trials, torture, and execution of 20 women, one 
man, several female children and two dogs, for supposed witchery during 1692-1694. 


Inspection of a defendant during a Massachusetts 
witch trial in 1693. Physical deformities, markings, 
abrasions, bruises and animal claw marks were 
considered to be indicators of a practitioner of the 
dark arts. 


Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. 
Accessed: 5/11/2024. 


Beginning with his commentaries on Molly Reeve Webster, Mather’s persistent endorsement of 
witchcraft as the cause of mental illness, disease and accidents was a key factor in stoking the 
hysteria that gripped Massachusetts in the 1690s. Mather’s 1692 book, “The Wonders of the 
Invisible World: Tryals of Several Witches Lately Executed in New England”, provided an 
unfortunate sense of respectability to the trials. (Digitized and available from Google Books 
(www.books.googleusercontent.com). Accessed: May 4, 2023) 


Mather’s influential book contained sordid details from the trials of women accused of witchery 
and later executed by hanging, dunking and stoning. He included a summary of the witch trials 
and executions during the 1640s in Hartford, and offered a tribute to Mary Reeve Webster, for 
raising alertness to women who are “susceptible to impurity and unholy thoughts and 
behaviors.” This was the underlying premise for the witch hysteria: male perception that 
outspoken women, and a few men, were being influenced by the devil and his minions. 


In 1982, the Canadian author, Margaret Atwood, published a poem “Half-Hanged Mary” that 
refocused attention on this bleak period in America’s colonial history. The poem is organized 
around each of the many hours that Mary (Molly Reeve) Webster hung from the elm tree. 


The poem begins: 

7pm 

Rumor was loose in the air 
hunting for some neck to land on. 
! was milking the cow, 

the barn door open to the sunset.

| didn’t feel the aimed word hit 

and go in like a soft bullet. 

| didn’t feel the smashed flesh 

closing over it like water over a thrown stone. 


! was hanged for living alone. 

For having blue eyes and a sunburned skin, 
tattered skirts, few buttons, 

a weedy farm in my own name, 

and a surefire cure for warts. 

Oh yes, and breasts, 

and a sweet pear hidden in my body. 
Whenever there’s talk of demons 

these come in handy. 


Atwood M. Half-Hanged Mary. Poem Analysis. https://litcharts.com. 2006. Accessed: May 21, 
2023. 


Atwood took a bit of poetic license in this stanza: Molly did not live alone, and the ragged house 
was assuredly in her husband’s name given Massachusetts property law in the 17" century. 
However, the poem is an indictment of irrational hysteria and anti-feminism. In 1985, Atwood 
dedicated the first edition of her novel, The Handmaid’s Tale, to Mary Reeve Webster: 

“The Handmaid’s Tale is dedicated to Mary Reeve Webster because she is an example of a 
female person wrongly accused. But she is slightly a symbol of hope because they didn’t actually 
manage to kill her. She made it through.” (Atwood M. The Handmaidens Tale. New York and 
Toronto: McClelland and Stewart Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. 1985) 


Notes on Cotton Mather: In spite of his irrational fascination with witches and advocacy for 
their punishment, Mather was a prolific author of journal articles, pamphlets and books. He 
was considered one of the leading men of science in the colonies and advocated systemic, 
hypothesis-guided exploration of scientific questions (i.e., the scientific method). Mather 
conducted and published well-respected work on hybridization methods for crops, genetic 
traits and dominance in plants, and the revolutionary concepts, in the 17" century, of germ 
theory and vaccination against diseases spread by human contact such as smallpox and 
measles. The later was an intensely personal issue with Mather after his wife and three children 
died during a measles epidemic. He was an outspoken advocate for tobacco cessation (pipes, 
cigars and chaw) and banned smoking in North Church much to the disdain of his congregation. 
Much of Mather’s theory and research on these and other topics was published by the Royal 
Scientific Society of London, which elected him as a Fellow in 1713, the first colonist to achieve 
this honor. He also played a key role in the conversion of a small prep school in Saybrook, 
Connecticut into Yale University in New Haven. Mather never declared himself as an abolitionist 
(he briefly owned three slaves inherited in an estate dissolution) but had, for that era, open- 
minded views on the equivalency of all races, employed freed slaves at North Church and 
castigated Boston leadership for the poor housing available to the Black Freeman population. 
After a 1724 protest by Black Freeman over segregated and sordid housing, Mather defended 


211 


the protest, asking White city commissioners, “would you yourself ever reside within such 
unhealthy accommodations?” However, Mather’s engagement in the persecution of women 
accused of witchcraft sullied his reputation in the scientific community, blocked his selection as 
Harvard President, and contributed to intense resistance to his smallpox and measles 
inoculation plans for the city of Boston, especially among mothers of children. The inoculations 
were never implemented in his lifetime. 


Reverend Cotton Mather, a man of contradictions. He urged

Beaver Pelt Economics - Hendrick Willemz Hendriksz (Hendrickson) [1636-1707] 
Primary sources of information for the life of Hendrick Willemz Hendrickson included: 


Schenck AD. The Rev. William Schenck: His Ancestry and His Descendants. Washington DC: 
Rufus Darby Publisher. 1843. Re-released by Higginson Book Company (www.higginson.com) in 
2015 and also available at WorldCat Digital Library Catalog. www.searchworldcat.org. Accessed: 
December 2, 2022. 

Schenck AD. The Rev. William Schenck: His Ancestry and His Descendants. Washington DC: 
Rufus Darby Publisher. Updated in 1869 and 1883. Re-released by Higginson Book Company 
(www.higginson.com) in 2015 and also available at Google Books. (www.books.google.com). 
Accessed: November 30, 2022. 

Sinclair DA and Stakes AL. Hendrickson Genealogy in Monmouth County, New Jersey. Boston: 
New England Historic and Genealogical Society (www.americanancestors.org). 1936. Available 
via www.americanancestors.com. Accessed: December 3, 2022. 


These sources were supplemented by several books and articles on Dutch New Netherland, the 
British take-over of the colony, the beaver pelt industry and the transition of Fort Orange from 
Dutch to English control, which are listed at the end of Hendrick Hendrickson’s story. 


Hendrick Hendriksz was the grandson of Cornelius Lambert Hendrickson. | could not find a 
portrait of Hendrick, but a prior history described him as “tall and robust following more after 
Mooy Lambert than grandfather Cornelius, who albeit lanky, was slim and refined.” (Sinclair 
and Stakes, 1936) After Hendrick’s parents, Daniel Hendriksz (1604-1640) and Emma van 
Guilder (1612-1640), died in carriage accident when he was five years old, he and his sister Ida 
Ede lived with their grandparents (Cornelius and Sennetje Rutger) for 10 years. Shortly before 
his death, Cornelius arranged for the 15 year old Hendrick to complete high school at an English 
boarding school to upgrade his English, and also arranged for Hendrick’s admission to the 
University of Glasgow in Scotland. After graduation, Hendrick returned to Holland to attend the 
University of Leiden Law School where he graduated in 1660. During law school, Hendrick 
married Gisseltje Alberts (1640-1687). The young couple had a child, but the marriage did not 
work out, and they divorced in 1662. After law school, Hendrick secured a position with the 
Dutch West Indies Company (DWIC) in the contract and tariff division. Soon after, he agreed to 
undertake a three-year assignment in New Netherland to investigate beaver pelt smuggling, 
which was rampant and a substantial source of lost tariff revenue for the DWIC. Given his 
recent divorce from Gisseltje, perhaps Hendrick was looking for a change of scenery. His sister, 
Ida Ede, had already immigrated to New Netherland so there would be at least one friendly 
face to greet him upon arrival. 


On March 24, 1663, Hendrick departed Holland on the Rooseboom (Rosetree), which turned 
out not to be a coincidence, and arrived at New Amsterdam on June 2. (Tepper M, Fellows- 
Bailey R. Immigrants to New Netherland. Lists of Passengers 1654-1664. New York Genealogical 
& Biographical Records. 1974; 94(4): 193-200) |da Ede and her new husband, living in Flatbush 
(preset-day Brooklyn) provided a room for Hendrick in their still under construction home. He 
lived with them during his first year in the colony, helping with the finishing of the house. This 


213 


led to an unfortunate injury for Hendrick. He fell off the roof while hammering shingles and 
broke his leg. The bone did not set properly, and he walked with a limp for the rest of his life. 


Shortly after arrival, Hendrick reported to Peter Stuyvesant, the Director-General of New 
Netherland to discuss his assignment for the DWIC. Stuyvesant was supportive of the young 
attorney’s plans for detecting smugglers and impressed with his legal training. Stuyvesant asked 
Hendrickson if he could complete some overdue legal work for the colony and also asked him to 
join his Council of Nine (that actually had more than 20 members), an advisory group to the 
Governor representing various constituencies in the colony. Hendrickson agreed to both 
requests. Stuyvesant had been Director-General of New Netherland since 1647, with its 
population based in New Amsterdam (lower Manhattan). The entire colony included much of 
present-day New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Delaware. Stuyvesant, who previously 
managed Dutch colonies in the Caribbean for 25 years, was transferred to the floundering 
colony to restore order after a decade of weak management by the prior Director-General. 
Stuyvesant did just that, using strong-arm tactics that earned him a tyrant reputation among 
some colonists who preferred the lax environment of the preceding administration. Thanks to 
Stuyvesant’s efforts, the colony was on solid economic footing in 1663 when Hendrick arrived. 
The population was expanding with monthly arrivals of new immigrants. (Cody MW. Peter 
Stuyvesant: Dutch Leader of New Netherland. New York: Chelsea House. 2013.) Although a 
capable administrator, Stuyvesant was also a religious extremist, committed to the supremacy 
of the Dutch Reformed Church (DRC), with no tolerance for Lutherans, Baptists, Jews and 
Quakers in particular. Only DRC members were allowed to workshop in public, and he actively 
sought to prevent organized religious activities by members of other groups. 


A 1660 portrait of Peter Stuyvesant. He had a 40-year career with 
the Dutch West India Company managing colonies in the 
Caribbean, South American and North America and was a veteran 
of numerous battles with Spanish and British privateers. In 1644, 
he lost his right leg to a cannonball in a battle to reclaim a Dutch 
colony on Saint Martin. He used a wooden leg thereafter, 
adorned with silver nails, earning the nickname: Old Silver Nails. 
As Director-General of New Netherland, the feisty Stuyvesant 
drove off a Swedish colony in present-day Delaware, claiming 
that land for Holland, and had constant squabbles with the

Hendrick, who started to use the surname Hendrickson after arrival in New Amsterdam, hired 
several informants to help investigate the pelt smuggling. Beaver pelts were the most 
important trade product of the New Netherland colony, driven by European demand for top 
hats, coats, wraps, sashes, mittens, slippers and boots made from water repellant beaver fur. 
Between 1640 and 1670, at least 25,000 pelts were shipped annually to Holland and France. 
Hendrickson soon discovered, as he suspected before he left Holland, that the Rooseboom’s 
captain, Pieter Reyersz Van der Beets, and his first mate, under the direction of the ship’s 
owners back in Holland, were key players in the smuggling enterprise. 


Like most Dutch transatlantic ships of that era, the Rooseboom carried people to the America’s 
on the westward leg, and carried beaver pelts, animal hides for leather products and lumber on 
the eastward leg back to Europe. After off-loading passengers and their baggage, the 
Rooseboom journeyed up the Hudson River (which the Dutch called the North River in the 
1660s) to Fort Orange (near present day Albany), which was the center of the beaver pelt 
industry in in North America. The pelt industry was controlled by a closely-knit, and heavily 
inter-married group of Dutch and Mohawk trappers and traders, and a powerful guild, which 
represented them. At Fort Orange, pelts and hides were loaded under the inspection of a Dutch 
tariff officer who calculated an exit tax, which was paid by the ship’s captain. Back in New 
Amsterdam, additional pelts acquired in trade from Long Island Algonquin tribes were loaded, 
inspected and exit taxed. And then the Rooseboom sailed east to Europe, or so everyone 
assumed. However, as Hendrickson’s informants (including two Rooseboom crew members) 
reported, the Rooseboom made a few stops before clearing North America. Near Montauk, and 
also along the Connecticut coastline, additional pelts, uninspected and untaxed, were loaded 
onto the ship. On the other side of the Atlantic, before landing in Amsterdam, the smuggled 
pelts were off loaded onto small sailboats (i.e., corsairs) to avoid the Dutch port of entry tax. 


In the 1660s, there was no way to text, fax or telegraph this information to Dutch authorities so 
the culprits could be nabbed on the return trip to Europe. Instead, Hendrickson reported the 
findings of his investigation to Stuyvesant and the Council, and then they waited until the 
following year, April 1664, when the Rooseboom returned to confront the captain and make 
arrests. Interrogation of Captain Reyersz Van der Beets revealed that ten ship captains and 
owners were involved in the tax evasion scheme. The order issued by Stuyvesant for New 
Amsterdam militia to board the Rooseboom to inspect for smuggling appears below. 


This document ordered Captain Pieter Reyersz Van der Beets 
to vacate the Rooseboom so militia could inspect the ship for 
evidence of smuggling. There is no record of what was found, 
but Reyersz Van der Beets and crewmembers were arrested 
and shipped back to The Netherlands. The captain was fined 
an unknown amount of money but soon after was appointed 
captain of another passenger ship. He made at least two 
more round trips between the Netherlands and New 
Amsterdam, apparently without incident. Information and image

Hendrickson’s report reached the DWIC in September 1664. He recommended tighter cargo 
monitoring including placing tariff agents on board the ships for the entire round-trip, tagging 
and numbering each pelt and more exact counting of pelts by independent auditors before 
departure from the port of New Amsterdam and after arrival in Holland. These 
recommendations were ultimately enacted, but not by the Dutch. At the same time as 
Hendrickson’s report was carried back to Holland on a returning ship, a British squadron of four 
frigates, each with 36 cannons, and two smaller sloops carrying 400 soldiers under the 
command of Richard Nicolls (1624-1672) anchored near the western end of Long Island and 
sent a surrender demand overland to Peter Stuyvesant. (Chisholm H. Nicolls, Richard. 
Encyclopedia Britannica. 11" edition: Vol. 19. Pages 663-664. London: Cambridge University 
Press. 1911. Available at www.wikisource.com. Accessed: June 26, 2023) 


Nicolls fought in the English Civil War on the royalist side and commanded on-board soldiers 
(i.e., naval marines) in the Anglo-Dutch Wars. He was hired by a consortium of wealthy English 
merchants who were concerned that England was falling behind in the race to claim lands and 
establish trade agreements in North America. Consortium members had the ear of the Duke of 
York (James) who was the brother of King Charles II, who ascended to the throne after the 
demise of Oliver Cromwell’s Protectorship in 1660. Charles, prone to grandiose promises and 
actions that rarely worked out, told his brother that he could have all of New Netherland when 
and if England captured the lands. The when and If statement was the sticking point. England 
and Holland recently had fought two naval wars to determine supremacy in shipping and access 
to North America, and the Brits lost both conflicts. The consortium pressured James, (who 
assumed the throne in 1680) to independently take control of the Dutch colony, which was 
“minimally defended and there for the taking.” James, financially indebted to several 
consortium members, agreed to hire Nicolls, a freelance military commander, pay the crew and 
hire 400 mercenary soldiers if the consortium supplied the ships. Funding for leasing of four 
frigates and two armed sloops was raised, and Nicoll’s fleet sailed for North America. The 
operation was launched without the knowledge of Charles Il or other administrators in the 
Royal Court, and only a few parliament members knew about the venture. 


Stuyvesant received Nicoll’s capitulation request and conditions on August 28, 1664. Nicoll’s 
terms were lenient — essentially, everything stays the same for New Amsterdam citizens, but 
the colony name is changed from New Netherland to New York, and | (Nicolls) replace you 
(Stuyvesant) as Director-General. New Amsterdam residents could keep their land and 
businesses, would have full rights and liberties as English citizens, would have no British soldiers 
quartered in their houses, taxes on beaver pelts and other hides would remain the same, 
religious freedom was guaranteed, all churches could continue to function as usual, all taverns 
could remain open, Dutch ships could continue to travel between the colony and Europe with 
no additional taxes, loading and dispensing cargo as before, and administrators and attorneys 
of the colony could remain as long as they desired or as performance indicated. 


With encouragement from his personal attorney, Johannes de Becker, Stuyvesant’s initial 
reaction was to resist even though he could muster 100 soldiers at best and had only a small 
supply of ammunition. However, the Council of Nine disagreed, arguing that a bombardment 
from the British ships would destroy the colony they had worked so hard to build. Several 
Council members leaked the surrender conditions to key merchants in New Amsterdam. On 


216 


September 2, 93 merchants led by Stuyvesant’s wife and his son approached the Director- 
General and urged him to accept the British terms. Over de Becker’s protests, Stuyvesant finally 
relented and directed the Council of Nine to work out final details with Nicolls and his staff. 
Nicolls was thrilled. He had no interest in attacking New Amsterdam and risk destroying a 
valuable property. In fact, he was due a sizable bonus if New Amsterdam capitulated without 
conflict. The capitulation treaty was signed on September 6, 1664 and the transition ceremony 
was held on September 8, 1664 at the fortification wall that Stuyvesant built at the south end of 
Manhattan, now the beginning of Wall Street.

One task remained for Stuyvesant before he and his wife retired to their 250-acre farm that 
occupied a large part of what is now Columbia University. The fur trapper guild at Fort Orange 
(present day Albany, New York) was not happy about the impending transition to British control 
and had threatened resistance in conjunction with their Mohawk allies. During the surrender 
negotiations, Nicolls stressed to the Council of Nine that Implementation of the lenient terms of 
the transition from Dutch to British governance was contingent upon compliance by all Dutch 
communities including Fort Orange. In spite of these warnings, an incident at a small trading 
post tested his patience and almost scuttled the negotiations. 


On September 4, the Dutch trading post at St. Alms, near present day New Castle, Delaware, 
fired upon a British detachment sent to investigate the site, eliciting British return fire, resulting 
in the deaths of a Dutch trader, a Mohawk wife of another trader and a British soldier. An angry 
Nicolls suspended talks for two days until New Alms was secured and Stuyvesant promised that 
Fort Orange would respond peacefully. Fort Orange was substantially larger than St. Alms, 
especially in the fall season when it was crowded with Mohawk and Dutch trappers who 
returned to the community with their winter and spring catch to fulfill contracts with buyers. In 
one of his last acts as Director-General, Stuyvesant dispatched Hendrick Hendrickson to Fort 
Orange to calm fears among the Dutch traders and their Mohawk business partners, and 
prepare them to peacefully greet one or more ships full of British soldiers who would soon 
descend upon Fort Orange to raise the Union Jack. 


Hendrickson sailed up the Hudson River on September 9, 1664 with Stuyvesant’s attorney, 
Johannes de Decker, two prominent New Amsterdam merchants who traded with Fort Orange 
and two members of the colonies’ militia. Probably nothing in his New Netherland experience 
prepared Hendrickson for the scene he encountered at Fort Orange, which was called 
Beverwijck (Beaver District), by its residents in reference to a village with that name behind the 
fort. The dock and piers in front of the fort were lined with trader’s boats and Mohawk canoes 
as was the shoreline for two miles north and south of the dock. Hendrickson and his 
companions had to beach their sailboat several miles north of the fort and hike along the 


217 


shoreline to reach the front gate of the compound. Once inside, they were immersed in a 
swarm of European and Mohawk trappers and traders, other merchants, and children running 
everywhere with mothers and older siblings trying to round them up — in a carnival-like 
atmosphere with musicians, puppet booths for children, food and drink stalls, displays of 
weapons, trapping and tanning equipment hawked by vendors, large tables where trappers and 
buyers negotiated, and a raised platform where wrestlers were cheered on by surrounding 
crowds. Hudson Valley historians estimate that 3,000 Mohawk and Dutch trappers and traders, 
their business partners, visitors from New England (early Hudson Valley tourists) and families of 
the trappers descended on Fort Orange during the fall trading season. 


For 9 months a year, Fort Hudson housed 
300 people. The community swelled to 
several thousand in the fall trading season 
when trappers returned to exchange pelts 
for commodities. 

Image Source: Albany Institute of History and Art. 
www.albanyinstitute.org. New Netherland Artworks 
of Len Tantillo. Accessed: 5/22/2023. 


Hendrickson’s group finally made their way through the throng and reached the main building 
at the center of the compound know as Beverwijck Hall where Dr. Johannes de la Montagne, 
the Fort Orange commandant and chair of the Trappers Guild resided and had his business 
office. Dr. de la Montagne was an interesting character. He was French but received a medical 
degree from the University of Leiden in 1636. Equal parts healer and entrepreneur, he came to 
New Amsterdam to open the largest medical practice in the community and also to manage a 
400 acre tobacco plantation in Manhattan that encompassed the northern end of present day 
Central Park and the south end of Harlem. The tobacco enterprise was successful and he 
became a confident of Peter Stuyvesant who appointed him as commander of Fort Orange and 
Director of the Trapper Guild. (Bowers BE. Johannes de la Montaigne. The Old Homestead: 
History of the Bowers and Allied Families. http://bowershomestead.com/de-la-montagne.html. 
Accessed: July 14, 2023) 


Much to Hendrickson’s surprise, de Decker forcefully urged de la Montagne to resist the British 
who were likely to sail up the river within the next two weeks. de Decker argued that the 
trappers’ Mohawk allies would rally to the defense and fend off the British, and he contended 
that because of Fort Orange’s isolation, the British would lose interest and focus their attention 
on New Amsterdam. Of course, de Decker’s position ignored the fact that the beaver pelt trade, 
centered at Fort Orange, was the primary economic engine of the New Netherland colony, and 
one of the main reasons why the British consortium backing Nicolls wanted the colony. 


No living person knows what was said during the remainder of the meeting, but the outcome is 
known. Attorney de Decker left the meeting an unhappy man. De la Montagne, although 
disconcerted about the prospects of a British take-over of his pelt trading operation, realized 
his position was untenable. Bombardment by a 36 gun British frigate would level the 
compound. He also knew that the Dutch relationship with the Mohawks, a key member of the 


218 


Iroquois Six Nation Confederacy, was tenuous, in spite of massive inter-marriage among Dutch 
traders and Mohawk women, and also among female Mohawk trappers and Dutch merchants. 
(Fenton W. The Great Law and the Longhouse. Political History of the Iroquois Confederacy. 
Norman OK: Univ of Oklahoma Press. 1998) His spies had informed him that Confederacy 
leaders had made overtures to British politicians in New England about shifting their alliance 
away from the Dutch. Indeed the Confederacy and the Mohawks would soon become the main 
tribal ally of the British in North America, a relationship that would last 125 years. (Graymont B. 
The Iroquois in the American Revolution. Syracuse NY: Syracuse University Press. 1972) 


Once de Decker relented, Hendrickson prepared the terms of capitulation and decided to 
remain at Fort Orange until a British detachment arrived. However, Hendrickson soon learned 
that de Becker was meeting independently with Mohawk leaders and influential Dutch traders 
to drum up support for overthrowing de la Montagne. Dr. de la Montaigne was informed and 
de Becker was placed under house arrest. The fall trading festival was suspended, and all but 
the most trusted trappers and merchants were sent away. A British frigate with 100 soldiers 
arrived on the morning of September 24, 1664 under command of Colonel George Cartwright. 
Hendrickson, de la Montagne and Cartwright reviewed the articles of capitulation and the later 
two signed the document that afternoon. Dr. de la Montaigne, the handful of Dutch soldiers at 
the Fort, members of Hendrickson’s original travel party and de Decker sailed back to New 
Amsterdam on the frigate while Cartwright and his soldiers took control of the site. Cartwright 
asked Hendrickson to stay at Fort Orange to coordinate meetings among the Dutch and 
Mohawk trappers, their principle buyers, the tax agents and British officers who would manage 
the Fort. In early December, Hendrickson finally left Fort Orange and sailed back to New 
Amsterdam (now New York). In New York, the new Governor Nicolls rebuked de Decker for 
inciting resistance at Fort Orange and banished him from the colony for six years. After the 
banishment, de Decker could only return to his 160-acre farm on Staten Island and not enter 
New York City. de Decker went back to Holland, devoted his time to writing two books 
criticizing Stuyvesant and de la Montaigne, and then returned to Staten Island in 1671 where he 
died from unknown causes shortly after arrival. (Clute JJ. Old Families of Staten Island. New 
York: Clearfield Printing. 2013. Accessed: June 5, 2024 via www.genealogy.com. Also available 
at Google Books. www.books.google.com) 


Hendrick Hendrickson resumed his monitoring of beaver pelt smuggling, now working for both 
the British port authority and the DWIC, which was allowed to continue commerce within the 
colony with a cut of the revenue for the Crown. Hendrickson also did legal work for Peter 
Stuyvesant involving real estate transactions, and found time to take a bride, Jane Suitgirt 
Luitgirt. Hendrick and Jane bought a house in Flatbush on the street where his sister Ida Ede 
lived. When Hendrick’s three-year anti-smuggling assignment concluded in 1666, he was 
offered a position as the Chief Tax Assessor for a Caribbean Dutch colony. Stuyvesant urged him 
to accept the job, extolling the virtues of island life, but Hendrick declined the position and 
resigned from the DWIC. Instead, he and Jane sold their house, and had their belongings 
shipped to .... surprise, Beverwijck, now renamed as Albany in honor of a royal benefactor in 
England (a Lord Albany) who was pouring money into the community on the Hudson. 


219 


In Albany, Hendrick set up a law practice, which served the Duke of Albany, local citizens, New 
York merchants, and members of the Mohawk tribe who owned property in Beverwijck in 
conjunction with their Dutch in-laws. Over the next 20 years, Hendrickson became a prominent 
citizen, serving on the commissioner’s council several times and also serving on community 
planning committees. Jane Luitgirt was appointed as town librarian in a new facility funded by 
the Duke of Albany and also was involved in placing abandoned mixed race (Mohawk-Dutch) 
children with Beverwijck families, including, possibly, their own household. Hendrickson’s 
original will, written in 1677 mentions three “taken in children” in his household. Funds were 
set aside for Jane’s nurturance of these children, but there was no further reference to these 
children in subsequent editions of the will. All four of Hendrick and Jane’s children were born in 
Albany including William Hendrickson who was Okey Hendrickson’s grandfather. 


In 1692, shortly after Jane’s death, Hendrick and his children, who were now teenagers and 
young adults, moved to Monmouth County, New Jersey for a brief period during which 
Hendrick purchased 500 acres of land that he sold three years later for a tidy profit. In 1693, 
Hendrick moved to adjoining Middlesex County where he purchased 1500 acres in five plots 
near present day New Brunswick. In his final will, dated 1706, Hendrick allocated four plots to 
his children and the fifth plot, where he lived, was identified as the family homestead for 
purchase by whichever child wanted it. Most of the 1500 acres ultimately became the campus 
of Rutgers University in New Brunswick when a Hendrickson descendant in 1766 sold four of 
the parcels to the Dutch Reform Church of New Jersey, which established Queens College on 
the site, named for the 22 year old Queen Charlotte of Great Britain and Ireland. Queens 
College was renamed Rutgers College in 1825 after Henry Rutgers, a Revolutionary War hero 
and successful New York businessman, donated substantial money to ensure the college’s 
solvency. His great-great-grandfather was the brother of Cornelius Hendrickson’s wife, Sennetje 
Rutgers. Sennetje’s brother was a faculty member and provost at Utrecht University in Holland. 
The seal, motto and charter of Rutgers University were largely based on Utrecht University. 
(McCormick RP. Rutgers: A Bicentennial History. New Brunswick, NJ: Rutgers University Press 
and Rahway, NJ: Quinn and Boden Co. 1966. Accessed from Internet Archives (www.archives.org 
on May 27, 2024) 


Hendrick apparently did not continue his law practice in New Jersey. Instead he opened a 
sundry store (i.e., a colonial convenience store) that included a tavern and roadhouse that he 
operated in collaboration with his daughter Francyntje (Francy; 1671-1750) until his death in 
1707. Hendrick and Jane’s children remained in the New Brunswick area, as did most of their 
offspring. As a consequence, Hendrickson is a common family name in central New Jersey in 
2023. Hendrick Hendrickson was the first person in our Hendricson line that elected to live 
permanently in North America. Great grandson Okey Hendrickson (1734-1830) began the 
westward movement of the family when he relocated his family to Kentucky in 1794. 


Notes on Historical Sources for Pelt Smuggling and British Capture of Fort Orange: Much of 
what is known about Hendrick Hendrickson’s interventions to minimize pelt smuggling and his 
involvement in the negotiations to effect a non-violent transfer of Fort Orange from Dutch to 
British control are based on reports he submitted to the DWIC and also to the Dutch parliament 
(States General) in 1664. As with Cornelius Hendrickson’s maps and logs, these documents are 


220 


maintained in the Amsterdam Municipal Archives, a section of the Dutch National Archives 
known as Archives of the States General, and the Archives of the Old West Indies Company at 
The Hague. Testimonial accounts of the surrender of Fort Orange and transference documents 
appear in Gehring CT (translator and editor) Fort Orange Records and Civil Minutes, 1656 — 
1678; Syracuse, NY: Syracuse University Press, 2000. Accounts of pelt smuggling strategies, and 
efforts to stop it are described in a 2012 dissertation and subsequent publication by Kimberly 
Todt of Cornell University titled: Countries Without Borders — Markets With Opportunities. 
Dutch Trading Networks in Early North America, 1624-1670. Other information sources that 
informed the description of pelt trading and the British acquisition of the Dutch colony are 
listed on page 222. 


Notes on the Beaver Pelt Industry: The Mohawk tribe, and a smaller Mahican tribe inhabited 
the Hudson River Valley for thousands of years before Dutch/English explorer Henry Hudson 
anchored his boat, the Half Moon, near present day Albany in 1609, the first European explorer 
since Giovanni da Verrazzano in 1525 to visit the river. At that time, Europe was in the grip of 
the Little Ice Age, with year-round cold temperatures and endless rain, stoking demand for 
warm and water-repellant clothing. Hudson noted that beaver were literally everywhere — “on 
the river, marshes, shores, grasses, forests.” Following Hudson’s reports, hundreds of mostly 
Dutch trappers and traders made their way to the Hudson River over the next 20 years, leading 
to the establishment of Fort Orange by the New Netherland colony in 1624. 


Sensing an economic opportunity, virtually all of the Mohawk clans required Dutch traders to 
take Mohawk wives as a means to build long-term trading partnerships. These marriage 
alliances ensured continual flow of much desired European goods into the clan, and at the same 
time, discouraged Dutch traders from establishing partnerships with other Mohawk clans or 
other tribes within the Iroquois Confederacy. It is estimated that 80% of the beaver trapping 
was accomplished by Mohawks, and a fairly extensive number of these trappers were women. 
To cement trade alliances, female Mohawk trappers were also encouraged to take husbands 
among the Dutch traders who lived in Beverwijck or with beaver pelt exporters in New 
Amsterdam who periodically traveled to Fort Orange. About 20% of the trapping was done by 
Dutch men, who preferred to do it themselves rather than relying on Mohawk trappers. These 
independent trappers made agreements to only hunt and trap in designated areas, and often 
these agreements were sealed with marriage to Mohawk or Mahican women. In addition to 
business alliances, these marriages also produced a large number of mixed race children, many 
of whom grew up to become trappers themselves if they largely remained with their tribal clan, 
or grew up to be traders if they gravitated to their father’s side of the relationship. 


Beverwijck was substantially impacted by the marriage strategy in that many of the Mohawk- 
Dutch couples elected to build or buy homes in Beverwijck, and raise their families within that 
community. Additionally, during the fall trading festival, hundreds of Mohawk and Mahican 
trappers and traders came to Beverwijck to live with their Dutch relatives. As the festival grew 
in scope, many clans found it more convenient to purchase homes, working through their Dutch 
in-laws, for use during the August — October trading season. Several hotels were built in 
Beverwijck to accommodate vendors, entertainers and merchants from New Amsterdam and 
Europe. These were likely the first hotels in North America outside of Boston. 


221 


The business of beaver pelt trading was not accomplished as often depicted in films. Trappers 
and buyers did not barter over price. Instead, trappers signed contracts with buyers during the 
fall trading festival which stipulated the number of pelts and other products, such as deer, fox 
and wolve hides, to be delivered by the following August — October using a set product to goods 
exchange rate. For example, ten pelts were typically exchanged for a four foot rifle or a set of 
European axes; eight pelts were exchanged for a set of metal cooking kettles; six pelts equaled 
a head to toe set of men’s clothing or a high quality six inch knife; four pelts equaled a full 
length mirror or a European musical instrument, etc. The negotiations that Hendrickson 
observed when he entered Fort Orange were centered on what exchange items each Mohawk 
clan wanted for the beaver pelts and other hides they agreed to deliver the following year. 
Trappers would hunt and collect pelts from November through April when fur was the thickest, 
women of the clan would scrape and prepare the skins over the summer, and then the trappers 
and their families would return to Fort Orange in the fall to collect their goods. Traders and 
export merchants traveled to Fort Orange with a huge inventory of products to be exchanged 
for the designated numbers of pelts.

The Morgan’s Go West - Morgan (1688-1767), Catherine (1692-1773) and Zack (1734- 
1795) 


The primary informational sources for the history of the Morgan family in Wales and North 
America appear on pages 154-155. Several books and articles on the Delaware Colony and the 
establishment of the state of West Virginia are listed at the end of the Morgan family story. 


As described in Chapter II, Morgan Wilm Morgan was unusually well educated considering the 
modest circumstance of his childhood in Wales. We could find no portraits of Morgan, but he 
was described as robust. Records of the “Gog Magog Games” at Cambridge, an annual sporting 
festival for college students so named because they occurred in the Gog Magog Hills near the 
campus, note Morgan’s participation in an array of Gog Magog competitions: oars (rowing), 
swimming, lawn bowling, wrestling, and football (a precursor to Rugby played on rural roads 
which involved kicking and carrying, but not passing, a large ball toward a designated goal, 
often a gate to a country estate). Morgan also was listed as a participant and winner in several 
events of the annual Cotswald Olimpick Games, a 17" and 18"" century multi-sport festival, 
originated in 1612 and sponsored for decades by a prominent attorney and businessman, 
Robert Dover. Dover graduated from Cambridge and likely was also involved in the 
establishment of the Gog Magog Games, much to the consternation of university 
administration who deplored the students’ enthusiasm for these “vain and needless” athletic 
contests and associated social events, which led to “intellectual idleness, neglect of studies, and 
divers other misdemeanors.” (Goode A. College Archivist. The Gog Magog Olympics at 
Cambridge. The Emmanuel College Blog. www.emma.cam.ac.uk. February 9, 2022. Accessed: 
June 12, 2024) 


The Cotswald Olimpick Games were conducted in central England during Spring Bank Holidays, 
which gave workers several four-day weekends in April and May each year. For these holidays, 
lenders, barter markets, horse, sheep and cattle auction houses, and other financial institutions 
of that era were closed on Friday and Monday to reduce attempts to conduct business. (Clarke 
S. Olympus in the Cotswolds: The Cotswold Games and Continuity in Popular Culture, 1612- 
1800. International Journal of the History of Sport. 1997; 14(2): 40-66.) Two amphitheaters 
were constructed near the bucolic village of Cotswald and another along a nearby lake to host 
events. Each venue was surrounded by food and entertainment booths, pop-up taverns, stages 
for theatrical performances, and large camp sites to house athletes and attendees. (Williams J. 
The Curious Mystery of the Cotswold “Olimpick” Games: Did Shakespeare Know Dover, and Does 
it Matter? Sport in History. 2009; 29(2): 150-170) Morgan participated in the Games in three 
different years between 1706 and 1711 and was recognized as an individual champion in field 
running (probably a type of cross country event; 1706 and 1708), large man wrestling (1708), 
and with Cambridge teammates, two oars (rowing) events in 1709. Winners of individual events 
received five pounds, which is approximately $400 in 2023. (Burns FDA. Heigh for Cotswold! A 
History of Robert Dover’s Olimpick Games: A New and Revised Edition. London: Robert Dover’s 
Games Society, and Harry Righton and Evesham. 1981) The Cotswold Games continued, almost 
annually, until 1852 when they were cancelled because of rowdiness within the campsites. The 
Games were re-activated in 1963 as a summer festival and continue to this day.

that William Shakespeare, an acquaintance of Robert Dover, the
