Quaker records in Delaware, Morgan’s first destination in North America, also noted his 
participation and accomplishments in swimming and rowing at the Christiana Summer Sport 
and Gaming Festival including “third finisher in the Midsummer Eve Race crossing the 
Delaware” in 1716, and “M Morgan six man crew has top spot in 10 league bay race” in 1717. 
(Jordan JW. A History of Delaware County and Adjoining Pennsylvania. Philadelphia: LH Everts 
Co. Digitized and available via Internet Archive and the Online Books Page of the University of 
Pennsylvania Digital Library (www.onlinebooks.library.upenn). Accessed: May 22, 2023) 


Morgan apparently traveled to Delaware from England in 1713 with an assignment from the 
Royal Court: investigate financial malfeasance within the administrative offices of the Colony. 
We could find no record of any report or recommendations filed by Morgan, therefore, it is 
unclear if he carried out his assignment or not. It could be that he submitted his findings but 
like many documents of that era, they were destroyed or lost over the past 300 years. We do 
know that Morgan quickly settled into the Delaware villages of Christiana, where he built a 
house, and nearby Wilmington, where he worked. Within a few years, he emerged as a leading 
citizen. With his new wife, Catherine Garretson (1692-1773), he opened a mercantile store, 
which included a tailoring shop run by Catherine. Morgan, who apparently had an interest in 
fashion, contributed to the shop by creating felt hats and beaver adorned topcoats for 
customers. Catherine also functioned as a clerk and bookkeeper in the store where local 
citizens could buy household goods and “elegant, high style clothing” shipped from Europe or 
“made here on premise to your wishes.” 


Morgan functioned as a middleman in the beaver pelt industry, working with the Lenape tribe 
in New Jersey to arrange sales with European buyers. In 1719, he was appointed as the chief 
coroner for the Colony, and in 1721 was appointed as a judge on the highest court in Delaware. 
Additional, he was sufficiently connected to become the personal attorney for Governor and 
Lieutenant Governor of Pennsylvania, handling real estate transactions, deeds and wills, and 
also handling commonwealth litigation, mostly foreclosures and boundary disputes. By all 
accounts, Morgan and Catherine were doing well in their new Delaware home. The Morgans 
had sufficient wealth to pay the fare for numerous relatives to journey across the Atlantic to 
North America including Morgan’s uncle and family, who were Quakers and settled in Berks 
County, Pennsylvania. This sponsored family including Sarah Morgan (1698 — 1770) who was 


224 


Daniel Boone’s mother. (Faragher JM. Daniel Boone: The Life and Legend of an American 
Pioneer. New York: Holt. 1992; Spraker HA. A Genealogical History of the Descendants of George 
and Mary Boone Who Came to America in 1717. Rutland, VT: The Tuttle Company Publishers. 
1922. Digitized edition produced in 2018 available from Amazon Book Clubs) 


Morgan and Catherine adopted four children who were orphans of fellow colonists and also a 
mixed race child of a female Lenape trapper and an English trader. Morgan family histories 
contend that this child was David Morgan, who would become a famous frontiersman and tutor 
of George Washington as described in Chapter II. No evidence of this adoption could be found, 
although descriptions of David in prior Morgan family histories used code words for Native 
ancestry: “ruddy, inscrutable, severe black hair.” If true, David Morgan would have been 
among thousands of mixed race children who blended into families of early colonists. 


It also appears that Morgan and Catherine were engaged with the Wilmington Friends Meeting 
House for the bulk of their time in Delaware, somewhat surprisingly considered Morgan’s 
Church of England training. Catherine was more engaged on a day-to-day basis, but Morgan 
was noted in Meeting House records as a frequent benefactor, contributing funds to pay for 
building expansion and for member travel to regional Quaker meetings. Much of what we know 
about the Morgans and their activities in Delaware is based on Quaker records from the 
Wilmington Meeting House, which, as usual, were quite thorough. (History of Wilmington 
Friends Meetings. Wilmington Monthly Meeting of the Religious Society of Friends. 
www.wilmingtondefriendsmeeting.org. Accessed: August 7, 2023) 


In spite of their success, Morgan and Catherine decided in 1730 to leave Delaware. Apparently 
it was a rather abrupt decision. The mercantile and pelt businesses were hastily sold to 
Catherine’s brother and a family friend respectively, and Morgan resigned his three other jobs 
(coroner, judge and Pennsylvania Commonwealth legal counsel) on the same day: February 11, 
1730. What was the attraction? In 1730, the General Assembly of the Virginia Commonwealth 
enacted a land parcel act to promote movement of people into the northwestern region of the 
state now know as West Virginia (WVA). The act handsomely compensated real estate 
developers for every family unit they attracted to the newly opened “Western Virginia Colony”. 
Family units (defined as husband, wife, and at least three children) who selected an available 
plot of five to ten acres and improved it for three years were eligible to receive a deed for up to 
1000 acres. A real estate development company headed by Alexander Ross and Bryon Grant 
were awarded a contract by the General Assembly to spearhead the population effort. The 
contract stipulated that Ross and Grant would receive the 2023 equivalent of 1.5 million dollars 
if they settled 100 families in the new colony by 1735. Ross and Grant focused their recruitment 
efforts on English, Dutch and Swedish residents in the Delaware Colony (Reminder: Sweden 
originally established the Delaware settlement, but Peter Stuyvesant merged it into New 
Netherland, and then the British took over in 1664). It appears that Ross and Grant were 
convincing salesmen. Morgan and Catherine were among several Delaware families who 
decided this opportunity was too good to pass up. Within weeks of resigning his jobs, Morgan 
and several friends were on their way to the newly opened territory to scout potential acreage. 
(Rice O, Brown S. West Virginia: A History (2" ed.). Lexington: University of Kentucky Press. 
1994) 


225 


The map on page 61 in Chapter II indicates the area of land available for settlement in the 
northeast panhandle of present day West Virginia. Morgan’s explorations in the spring of 1730 
led him to select a nine-acre parcel on Mill Creek, a rapidly flowing tributary of the Opequon 
River suitable for a gristmill and navigable all the way to Winchester, Virginia, a major trading 
center in that era. He soon after submitted his claim to the Ross and Grant WVA Land 
Development Consortium. Mill Creek runs through the present day community of Bunker Hill, 
West Virginia (WVA), which Morgan and Catherine founded when they moved with seven of 
their children to that location in March 1731. 


Morgan and Catherine were the first settlers to submit their provisional claim to the Ross and 
Grant Consortium, and also the first to be approved by the Land Development Office of the 
Commonwealth of Virginia. This claim is the historical basis for the assertion found in many 
textbooks that Morgan and Catherine were the first European settlers in West Virginia. 
However, unrelated to the Virginia Commonwealth program, several families of German- 
speaking immigrants had settled in an area of West Virginia along the Potomac River in 1717 
known as Potomke among local tribes. It was originally renamed New Meckenlinburg by these 
German settlers. The settlement was not permanent; families came and went, and the small 
village was unoccupied by Europeans from 1729-1735 until a group of Scottish settlers arrived 
and stayed. The Scottish families later changed the name of the community to Shepherdstown. 
Thus, the Morgan settlement that became Bunker Hill technically was not the first West Virginia 
settlement, but it was the first continuously occupied community in the new territory. 


In 1734, after building a cabin, barn, stables, cattle pen and a rudimentary grist mill on the 
provisional property, which Morgan and Catherine named Rockdale Spring Farm, the Morgans 
were granted a permanent deed to 1,000 acres adjacent to their original homestead. 


This cabin was constructed by Morgan and Catherine Morgan in 
1731 in the community of Bunker Hill in Berkeley County, WVA. 
The cabin was destroyed during a 1756 battle in the French and 
Indian War, but re-built by Zack Morgan in 1758 using wood 
from the original structure. The nine-acre Morgan property is a 
WVA state park with hiking trails, a historical exhibit, and a 
park alongside Mill Creek with monuments commemorating 
Morgan family contributions to West Virginia. Image source: 
Library of Congress. www.loc.gov. Title: The Morgan Cabin, home of WVA's 
first known permanent white settler in the Torytown area of Berkeley 
County. Accessed: 6/18/2023. 


Nothing in their background suggests that Morgan and Catherine had the skills to establish and 
manage a 1000-acre farm on the frontier, but they gave it a go for the next 20 years. As best as 
can be determined, the farm was a middling success, and did not develop to full potential until 
Morgan deeded the entire property to son Zackquill (Zack) in 1758. Zack purchased additional 
land adjacent to Rockdale Spring Farm that was more suitable for agriculture. Zack enhanced 
crop volume and variety, constructed a better gristmill, purchased two boats to increase 
produce shipment to Winchester and other markets, and as a result, substantially increased the 
operation’s profitability during the next several decades. Morgan and Catherine continued to 


226 


live in the re-built Bunker Hill cabin. Zack built a more elaborate two-story home for his own 
family at Rockdale Spring Farm. 


The blue structure is Zack Morgan’s original house 
built in 1760 after he assumed control of the farm. 
The brick expansion was added in 1783 after he 
returned from the Revolutionary War. 

Image source: WikiMedia Commons. 
www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 6/20/2023. 


Although Morgan and Catherine’s farming venture produced marginal outcomes, they were 
successful in other activities. Morgan held a number of magistrate positions in the rapidly 
developing Western Virginia Territory including serving for ten years on a circulating judge 
panel that moved from community to community to hear cases. Morgan opened a tavern in 
Bunker Hill in 1739 and obtained the first liquor license in WVA history. He threw himself into 
local county and territory politics, winning and losing elections for a variety of positions during 
the 35 years he lived in Bunker Hill. Although Morgan appears to have had no military training 
or experience, he managed to create and then get himself appointed the captain of a local 
militia unit that was established in 1746 and convinced his wife to make uniforms for the corps 
of 17 men. Catherine stitched the name Mountain Men over the breast pocket of each militia 
shirt and also created several flags for the unit with the words Mountain Men stitched under an 
outline of a mountain. During George Washington’s time as an surveyor apprentice for David 
Morgan (1749-1752), they would often journey to Bunker Hill to finalize maps and re-provision. 
Several Washington biographies mention his enjoyment of watching Bunker Hill Mountain Men 
militia during Sunday afternoon marching drills and marksmanship exhibitions, and the “levity 
of the following musical promenade where militia would shed arms for fiddle, drum and fife for 
the enjoyment of all on the green.” (Hofstra WR. George Washington and the Virginia 
Backcountry. Madison, Wis: Madison House Pub. 1998.) 


Perhaps inspired by the uniform production, Catherine resumed her tailoring business, working 
out of a room in the tavern, and she also served on a commission that oversaw the primary 
school in the village. Foretelling a current trend, Catherine annually made two sets of school 
uniforms for each child (for warm and cold weather) so no child would be embarrassed about 
their tattered or grimy attire. Catherine and Morgan were both involved in the establishment of 
the Christ Episcopal Church near Bunker Hill, considered to be the first church in WVA, a fairly 
large spiritual leap from Quakerism, but perhaps represented a return to the theological 
training that Morgan completed in London. One of Morgan and Catherine’s sons, Morgan 
Morgan II, completed Episcopalian training in England, Virginia and Maryland, and returned to 
become the lead minister of the Bunker Hill congregation, a position he held for over 30 years. 
In total, Morgan and Catherine had ten children, six of their own including Zackquill (Zack) 
Morgan (1734-1797) and four adopted, likely including the aforementioned David Morgan 
(1721-1813). Along with his parents, Zack is considered as the principle founder of WVA. 


227 


Zack Morgan (1734-1795) 
Zack was the only child of Morgan and Catherine to be born in West Virginia. He was sent east 
for his “proper upper education.” At age 13, Zack arrived at the Academy of Philadelphia, and 
returned to WVA six years later at age 19. The Academy was re-chartered as the College of 
Philadelphia in 1754, one year after Zack’s departure, and became the University of 
Pennsylvania in 1791. Benjamin Franklin was the President of the Academy during the last three 
years of Zack’s time at the school. It is not clear if they ever met. Zack and his older brother 
David both served in the Bunker Hill militia established by his father, which provided the 
pathway for their participation in several battles during the French and Indian Wars of the 
1750s. These military experiences included the ill-fated campaign to capture Fort Duquesne, 
near present day Pittsburgh, from the French (i.e., Braddock’s Defeat) that is summarized in 
Chapter II (see page 60). Five of the 17 Bunker Hill militia who served under Braddock in that 
campaign were killed and two were captured and later ransomed for rifles. 


Morgan family histories contend that after returning from the Braddock Campaign, Zack had a 
long relationship with an unnamed mixed race women who traveled with a Miami clan in Ohio 
and Indiana. Zack met this women on a hunting trip in Ohio when his party sought refuge in her 
Miami village during a snowstorm. Zack apparently visited this women, whom he described as 
his common law wife, several times annually for ten years until the relationship dissolved for 
unknown reasons. These histories contend that this relationship produced two children and 
lasted until just before Zack married Drusilla Springer (1740-1796) in 1765. | found no evidence 
of this relationship, but acknowledge that is unlikely that documentation would exist for 
common law marriages, which were frequent on the frontier. 


Unlike Morgan Morgan’s wife, Catherine Garretson, | were not able to uncover much 
information about Drusilla Springer. We do know that Drusilla was originally from New Jersey, 
moved to WVA with her family as an adolescent, and came from a family with a long line of 
ministers (one of her nephew’s was the family minister for Abraham Lincoln and Mary Todd). 
Zack and Drusilla’s household grew to 13 children including James Morgan, who became a 
leading abolitionist and free state proponent for West Virginia who was assassinated for his 
beliefs, and the famous frontiersmen Levi Morgan (see pages 62-63). 


While managing the Rockdale Spring Farm, Zack continued to serve in the Bunker Hill militia, 
and was elected as its captain on multiple occasions. At the onset of the Revolutionary War in 
1776, the now 24 member Bunker Hill militia was integrated into a newly constituted qi" 
Virginia Regiment, comprised of 400 frontiersman with combat experience in the French and 
Indian War, and other conflicts with Native Peoples, and their use of rifled rather than 
smoothbore muskets that allowed accuracy at much greater distances. Most of the unit’s 
members, including Zack and David, were middle-aged or older men, 40 to 60 years old. This 
Colonial army regiment was commanded by the then Colonel Daniel Morgan (yes - that guy 
from the other Morgan family), and the unit was sometimes referred to as “Morgan’s Rifles.” 
Zack, with 20 years of militia experience, was appointed as a company commander within the 
regiment. The Riflemen fought in many skirmishes against the British in Pennsylvania and New 
Jersey in 1776 and the spring of 1777, earning notoriety for long distance marksmanship. 
(Higginbotham D. Daniel Morgan: Revolutionary Rifleman. Chapel Hill, NC: Univ of North 
Carolina Press. 1961) 


228 


In June 1777, the Virginia Riflemen were sent to northern New York as part of an colonial army 
commanded by Generals Horatio Gates and Benedict Arnold (before his defection to the British 
side) to stop a British invasion from Canada. Near Saratoga, New York, Colonel Daniel Morgan 
and his Riflemen Regiment were instrumental in defeating the British over the course of an 18- 
day battle fought in and around the hilly forests of upstate New York. This terrain particularly 
suited Zack, David and the other frontiersmen. Taking the lead in the conflict, however, 
wreaked a heavy toll on the Rifleman: fifty percent of Zack’s company were killed or wounded 
in the battle. Zack miraculously survived several gunshots, one of which clipped off the top of 
an earlobe and another tore through his hat, but only grazed the top of his head. 


Depiction of the famed Virginia Riflemen, heading to

In his post-action report to Washington and the Continental Congress, Gates wrote: “too much 
praise cannot be given to the Virginia Riflemen Regiment commanded by Colonel Morgan.” The 
British surrender at Saratoga is generally considered to be a turning point in the war, convincing 
the French and other European governments that the Colonists were actually capable of 
defeating the British, leading to a dramatic increase in European funding for the war effort and 
direct French military involvement. (Mintz MM. The Generals of Saratoga: John Burgoyne and 
Horatio Gates. New Haven: Yale University Press. 1990) 


This painting by John Trumbull depicts the British 
surrender at Saratoga. The figure in white buckskin to 
the right of General Horatio Gates represents Colonel 
Daniel Morgan, leader of the Virginia Riflemen. 

Image source: WikiMedia Commons. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. 
Accessed: 6/22/2023. 


After Saratoga, Zack Morgan continued to serve with the Riflemen under Colonel Morgan for 
two more years through dozens of battles and skirmishes in New York, Pennsylvania and New 
Jersey. In December 1779, the Riflemen Regiment was decommissioned after the British 
barricaded their Northern Army in a defensive position within New York City, and Colonel 
Daniel Morgan transferred to the Colonial Army of the South. Zack and ten other surviving 
members of the 24 Bunker Hill militia returned to the West Virginia Territory to resume their 
lives. His brother David elected to re-enlist and followed the newly promoted General Morgan 
to the south. David did not return to WVA until 1782. 


229 


Back in Bunker Hill, Zack was awarded a 1200 acre tract, “of his prudent selection” by the 
Virginia Commonwealth for his service during the War for Independence. He commenced 
scouting for suitable tracts in 1781 and soon settled on land adjacent to a picturesque bend in 
the Monongahela River that comprises present day Morgantown, West Virginia. He filed a claim 
with the Commonwealth Land Development office in May 1781 and the following September 
was deeded 1200 acres and purchased an additional 750 acres with his own funds. Part of this 
acreage would soon grow into the bustling community of Morgantown. Zack and Drusilla 
opened a boarding house, an “ordinary,” (i.e., a tavern) and a necessity store in Morgantown in 
1783, believed to be the first commercial enterprises in the community. The building housing 
the ordinary also was designated as the county courthouse and jail by the Virginia General 
Assembly until Zack could arrange construction of a facility suitable to serve as the legal and 
administrative office for the region, which he did three years later. In 1785, Zack presented a 
proposal to the Virginia General Assembly that called for the municipal incorporation of 
Morgantown as a city of the Commonwealth. After an endorsement letter from George 
Washington, Zack’s friend since the Braddock Campaign, was read to the Assembly, the 
proposal was approved unanimously on October 17, 1785. Zack was delegated authority to plan 
the community, which was named Morgan’s Township in the General Assembly’s establishment 
ordinance, but which Zack modified to Morgantown a year later in a follow-up ordinance that 
was approved by the Assembly. The second ordinance also allowed Zack to sell portions of his 
acreage in % acre units to individuals desiring to settle in Morgantown at “obtainable pricing by 
incomers.” In spite of selling these units at charitable prices, he became a wealthy man from 
this endeavor. George Washington traveled to Morgantown in 1784 and 1785 to help Zack lay 
out streets within the new city and to plan roads between Morgantown and other towns. 


Zack’s land transactions during the establishment of Morgantown financed the construction of 
a three-story home on a substantial tract of land in Morgantown. Drusilla devoted herself to 
their brood of children and managed the family’s hotel/tavern/store after Zack’s health 
declined. Zack’s final will (1793) designated Drusilla as the sole owner of the business and 
estate upon his death based on “long history of engagement with the minute details of these 
entities.” The terms of the will violated Virginia Commonwealth law at that time, which barred 
women from enterprise or property ownership. In an amended will, Zack named two of his 
sons, James and Levi, as business and estate co-owners, with Drusilla named as the property 
manager. Unfortunately, she died a few months later during an influenza outbreak and Zack 
died on New Year’s Day, 1795. James Morgan continued to manage the hotel, tavern and store 
in Morgantown in addition to his own businesses in Bunker Hill, but had no interest in farming, 
and began to sell off the family’s agricultural property. By 1820, most of the original Morgan 
farmlands in West Virginia were owned by entities outside of the family.

Okey and Friends - Okey Hendrickson (1734-1830) 


The primary informational sources for the history of the Hendrickson family in Europe and 
North America appear on pages 145-147. Several books and articles on Kentucky history are 
listed at the end of the Okey Hendrickson’s story. 


Okey, also listed via incorrect spelling on tax rolls, military records and census ledgers as Ouke, 
Okie or Okay, was Hendrick Hendrickson’s great grandson. | could not find a portrait of Okey 
that was reliably documented. His step-mother, Ida Wyckoff (1710-1784), a diligent diarist like 
many people in that era, described the teenage Okey as “gangly and all legs, a head higher than 
his fellows, with a bright, inviting smile.” Like his father, Daniel Hendrickson, and his 
grandfather, William Hendrickson, Okey lived the majority of his life in Middlesex County, New 
Jersey along branches of the Raritan River that Cornelius Hendrickson explored and mapped 
more than 100 years earlier. Okey had a diverse work career, comprising several occupations, 
perhaps reflective of his experiences growing up in a household where his father, Daniel 
Hendrickson (1709-1779) had multiple occupations, and his step-mother, Ida Wyckoff, was 
often in the public eye, sometimes controversially, advocating for public education in NJ and 
women’s right to own property in their own name. Ida also was an ardent abolitionist, not a 
popular viewpoint in 18" century New Jersey, a colony which derived considerable income 
from numerous slave auction houses where Africans, American born Blacks, and Caribbeans 
were sold as laborers, cooks, domestics, drivers, nannies, breeders and prostitutes. (Hodges GR. 
Slavery and Freedom in the Rural North: African Americans in Monmouth County, New Jersey, 
1665-1865. Madison, WI: Madison House Publishers. 1997) 


Okey’s father started out as a miller, operating a water wheel powered gristmill, which grinds 
grain, known as grist in Europe and among early colonists, into flour. The mill was located on a 
section of the Millstone River known locally as Six Mile Run. The mill was originally built by 
Okey’s grandfather (William Hendrickson) in 1690. Okey’s father added a second mill down 
stream and converted a farmhouse into a traveler stop (i.e., an 18'" century motel) on Old York 
Road, a heavily traveled route between New Brunswick and Philadelphia. Okey’s industrious 
dad also purchased a fleet of heavy-duty wagons and operated a freight hauling business, 
transporting loads from Philadelphia to New Brunswick, which had a dock on the Raritan River 
where cargo boats could be loaded, and also to Perth Amboy, which had several docks on the 
lower New York harbor. 


Re-creation of the original Six Mile Run Grist Mill, first constructed 
by William Hendrickson in 1690, and upgraded by Daniel 
Hendrickson and Okey Hendrickson. The structure was hit by 
lightning and burned in 1799, and was re-built by descendants of 
Okey in the early 1800’s. The grinding equipment, including a 200 
year-old milling stone, still function. The mill is now a historical site 
in a state park. Image source: Six Mile Run Historic District. 
www.visitsomersetnj.org. New Jersey Department of Travel and Tourism. 
Accessed: 6/29/2023. 


232 


The grain grinding process: river water 
turns the wheel, which via gear teeth, 
engages with and turns a circular millstone 
with a hole in the middle. The milling stone 
lies on another flat and circular stone 
known as the base stone. Raw cereal grain 
(grist) is poured into the millstone hole and 
filters between the base stone and the 
turning millstone. The grain is pulverized 
into flour and pours into a catch container. 
Image source: Water Mill Diagram. Ehive. 
www.ehive.com. Accessed: 6/3/2023. 


Okey’s father decided to acquire medical training after several of his freight employees (i.e., 
drivers, loaders, horsemen) broke bones and suffered head injuries in wagon accidents on the 
rutted and rocky roads of that era, which were especially treacherous when iced-over or snow 
packed in the winter. He could find no one to manage severe orthopedic injuries, so he decided 
to learn those skills himself. In 1747, at the age of 38, Daniel Hendrickson began his medical 
education via the curriculum of that era — an apprenticeship with a veteran physician. (Slawson 
RG. Medical Training in the United States Prior to the Civil War. J Evidence-based, 
Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2012; 17(1): 11-27) His apprenticeship activities 
occurred mostly on Saturday nights, Sundays (the one non-work day of that era), and weekday 
evenings. After five years of on-the-job training, his mentor declared Okey’s father ready for 
independent practice and he soon after received a diploma in the mail from a physioanatomy 
and medicine academy in Philadelphia. That academy evolved into the Philadelphia College of 
Medicine around 1760. Daniel opened a “generalized medical needs” practice in 1752 with 
offices in Middlesex and Somerset Counties of NJ, which he rotated between, and was referred 
to as Dr. Hendrickson for the last 25 years of his life. 


Aself-portrait of Daniel Hendrickson, drawn around 1750. 
Image Source: Monmouth County, New Jersey Historical Association. 
Freehold, NJ. www.monmouthhistory.org. Accessed: 6/4/2023. 


A unique facet of Daniel Hendrickson’s medical training was that he frequently brought his two 
oldest sons, Okey and John Cornelius (1738-1834), with him during apprenticeship activities. 
This mirrored his approach with the boys for his other endeavors. From a relatively young age, 
they worked at the mill, loaded and unloaded freight and tended the horses for the hauling 
business, and pulled regular cleanup shifts at the travel stop. As a teenager, Cornelius (his 
preferred first name) gravitated toward a medical career while Okey showed more interest in 
the other family businesses. At age 19, Cornelius went to Philadelphia to apprentice for two 


233 


Quaker brothers who were physicians, and after three years, he enrolled in the recently opened 
Philadelphia College of Medicine. Upon completion of the 18-month anatomy-focused 
curriculum, Cornelius apprenticed for one additional year with a rural physician in Franklin 
County (Chambersburg). He then opened his own practice in Somerset County, just north of 
West Virginia, where he and his wife remained for the rest of their lives. Cornelius was a county 
doctor and a gentleman farmer for 60 years, working until he was 90. 


Back in New Brunswick, as Daniel Hendrickson’s medical practice grew, Okey gradually assumed 
more responsibility for the grist mills, hauling business and, with his step mother, for the travel 
stop, which now had expanded to three sites along the recently opened Kings Highway (See the 
subsequent note on the Kings Highway, pages 254-255). When his father decided to delve into 
county and state politics around 1760 (primarily to improve the quality of New Jersey roads), 
Okey found himself in full control. However, he must have harbored a lingering desire to follow 
the path of his father and brother into medicine. In 1768, Okey began his own apprenticeship 
odyssey toward medical practice. A younger brother, William Hendrickson (1738-1802) largely 
took over the family hauling business, Okey’s wife, May Anne Steeps (1742-1822), handled the 
book-keeping and accounts for the grist mills, and his stepmother Ida Wyckoff managed the 
travel stops. Not much has been written about Okey’s medical training. We assume, but do not 
know for certain, that his father had a hand in orchestrating the apprenticeships. We do know 
that Okey did not spend any time at Philadelphia College of Medicine. By 1774, Okey had 
opened a medical practice in a back office of the travel stop in Hightown, a village on Old York 
Road a mile east of New Brunswick. 


Reportedly, business was slow on Old York Road. On July 3, 1776, during a momentous week in 
U.S. history, Okey (i.e., now Dr. Okey Hendrickson), hoping to expand his patient pool with a 
downtown office, signed a contract to lease a building for his medical practice on the main 
commercial street of New Brunswick. However, he was never able to complete the move. On 
the same day, the British army under the command of General William Howe, supported by 
Generals Henry Clinton and Charles Cornwallis, sailed into New York harbor and landed on 
Staten Island with nearly 30,000 troops. The Brits soon after crushed George Washington’s ill- 
prepared revolutionary army at the Battle of Long Island and several other battles near New 
York City. Taking advantage of lethargic British follow-up after victories, the remains of 
Washington’s army managed to escape New York and began a slow retreat through New Jersey 
toward Philadelphia, skirmishing frequently with British units that trailed the Americans across 
the state. However, Howe failed to cement the New York victories with a major strike against 
the tattered Colonials that would have almost certainly ended the war in the fall of 1776. 
(McCullough D. 1776. New York: Simon and Schuster. 2005.) 


Caught up in the patriotic fervor as Washington’s army retreated through the New Brunswick 
area, Okey volunteered for service in November 1776, and was assigned to the 3" Middlesex 
Militia Regiment as a surgeon and infantry private. (Stryker WS. Adjutant General, New Jersey 
Adjutant General’s Office. Official Register of the Officers and Men of New Jersey in the 
Revolutionary War. Trenton, NJ: T. Nicholson and Co. Publishing. 1872. Accessed via the New 
Jersey State Library www.nystatelib.org on June 26, 2024) After one week of training, Okey and 
the 3 Regiment joined Washington’s Continental Army that was attempting to reach and cross 
the Delaware River into Pennsylvania prior to the onset of winter (when military campaigning 


234 


stopped in the 18" century). During Washington’s retreat toward Pennsylvania, Okey 
functioned as a battlefield medic, and assisted the army’s lead surgeon, the European trained 
Dr. John Riker, a graduate of Princeton and St. George’s London Medical School, with 
amputations, wound debridement and closures, bone setting, and tooth extractions. Dental 
disease was rampant within the colonial army. Managing the symptoms and consequences of 
other diseases and conditions also occupied much of their time according to Riker’s extensive 
diary notations. These afflictions included dehydration, frostbite, syphilis and gastrointestinal 
disease, a leading cause of death during the New Jersey campaign. (McLaughlin B. The Most 
Famous Combat Surgeon of the Revolutionary War. Mountain Man Medical. July 27, 2023. 
www.Mountainmanmedical.com. Accessed: August 10, 2023) 


At the end of December 1776, with desertions mounting and morale plummeting within the 
army and within the Continental Congress, Washington decided to attempt a desperation 
Christmas attack on a combined British and Hessian (i.e., Prussian) garrison stationed on the 
Jersey side of the Delaware. This led, of course, to the famed Crossing of the Delaware and 
subsequent surprise victory at Trenton, a significant morale boosting accomplishment. (Tucker 
PT. George Washington’s Surprise Attack: A New Look at the Battle that Decided the Fate of 
America. New York: Skyhorse Publishing. 2014) 


Okey’s 3" Middlesex Regiment was one of three regiments, out of a planned five, that managed 
to cross the icy river in a snowstorm on Christmas night and routed the Trenton garrison early 
in the morning of December 26. During the battle, the Colonials suffered only five wounded and 
no fatalities, but one of the wounded was significant. It was future President James Monroe, 
who took a musket ball to his left shoulder, rupturing an artery. Okey came upon the fallen 
Monroe and packed the wound with bandages to assuage the profuse flow of blood until Dr. 
Riker could arrive. Probing the wound in the dark (it was 5:00am), Riker was able to find and 
clamp the artery. Okey was tasked with transporting Monroe to a barge reserved for ferrying 
the wounded back to Pennsylvania. Riker’s initial clamp worked itself loose when Monroe was 
loaded on to the barge. Okey managed to retrieve the clamp in the renewed gush of blood, and 
recrimp the severed artery. While Riker stayed in Trenton to tend to wounded Hessian officers, 
Okey directed the re-crossing of the Delaware River with the wounded and soldiers suffering 
frostbite (many Continental soldiers had no boots or shoes, just cloth wrappings on their feet). 
In the days following the Trenton battle, Okey supervised Monroe’s recovery until the future 
president was removed to a rear unit near Philadelphia. (Unger HG. The Last Founding Father: 
James Monroe and a Nation’s Call to Greatness. New York: Da Capo Press. 2009) 


Emanuel Leutze’s painting of Washington 
Crossing the Delaware. The victory 
increased enlistments and bolstered French 
enthusiasm for the colonists’ cause. 

Image source: Wikimedia Commons. 


www.commons.m.wikimedia.org.

235 


Two days later, the General visited the medical tent to speak to the wounded and distribute 
valor letters, recognizing heroic actions, to Drs. Riker and Hendrickson and the other medical 
staff. Following the victory at Trenton, Washington wintered his army near Morristown, New 
Jersey. Okie Hendrickson apparently was not present for periods of time during the 1776-1777 
winter camp at Morristown, although payroll and other personnel record keeping were 
notoriously inaccurate in the Colonial military. It was common 18" century protocol for officers, 
medical personnel and other camp civilians to leave winter encampments for periods of time, 
this may have occurred in Okie’s case. We do know that Riker, Hendrickson and other medical 
personnel carried out a smallpox inoculation program for the sequestered army and thousands 
of civilians residing near Morristown in the spring of 1777 to combat a major outbreak of the 
virus. (Roos D. How Crude Smallpox Inoculations Helped George Washington Win the War. 
History. www.history.com. June 20, 2023. Accessed: June 21, 2024) 


Okie was once again with Washington’s army full-time in the summer of 1777 when warfare 
resumed. In June of that year, after much hesitation, Howe and 20,000 British and Prussian 
troops began a drive toward Philadelphia, the colonial capital and seat of the Continental 
Congress, hoping to finally end the uprising by capturing the fledgling nation’s key city and its 
political leaders. The Brit’s name for this military was the Philadelphia Campaign. (Harris, MC. 
The Philadelphia Campaign, 1777. Havertown, PA: Casemate Publishers. 2023) Washington’s 
army moved out of winter camp and attempted to block the Redcoat’s rather slow advance 
toward Philadelphia. In skirmish after skirmish, and major battles near Brandywine and 
Germantown, Pennsylvania, Washington’s army performed reasonably well, but were 
eventually pushed back, allowing Howe’s army to finally enter Philadelphia at the end of 
September, 1777. In traditional 1g" century European warfare and statescraft, when an enemy 
nation’s capital was ceased, the defeated side capitulated and treaty negotiations ensued to 
create new governance, geographic boundaries and taxation. To British dismay, members of 
the Continental Congress fled, and simply set up shop elsewhere as a provisional government. 
Instead of surrendering, Washington took the remains of his beleaguered army to nearby Valley 
Forge, PA and hunkered down for a long, harsh winter where he focused on re-training his 
troops and officers. The resources that Howe expended in capturing Philadelphia severely 
hampered a parallel British campaign in northern New York, leading to the surrender of an 
entire British army at Saratoga just nine days after the capture of Philadelphia (see page 230). 


Howe’s sluggish capture of Philadelphia and the Brits’ concurrent defeat at Saratoga convinced 
the French that proactively supporting the American’s cause would be advantageous to their 
much broader, international, war with Britain concurrent with the American Revolution. A 
Treaty of Alliance was hammered out in the fall of 1777 and signed in February, 1778. Soon 
after, a large French fleet was sighted off the coast of Long Island, which sent tremors through 
the British War Ministry. The multi-faceted impact of the Treaty Of Alliance, the demoralizing 
surrender at Saratoga, the improved performance by Washington and his army during 1777, 
and the presence of a French fleet threatening New York City led British parliament and military 
high command to conclude that victory in the U.S. north was no longer feasible. Britain formed 
a new North American strategy with three foci: focus military action on the southern colonies, 
perceived in the UK, accurately, to be less committed to the concept of a new nation, reallocate 
many British troops to the Caribbean and Mediterranean theaters of the Anglo-French War, 


236 


and withdraw Howe’s army from Philadelphia into New York City to repel a potential French 
attack. The British withdrawal to NYC however was to be implemented without General Howe, 
who, under pressure from the War Ministry, resigned his Commander-in-Chief position due to 
criticism of his less than proactive efforts to defeat the colonials. Henry Clinton, not at all 
sympathetic to the revolutionary cause, was assigned the task of withdrawing back to NYC. 
(Hoffman R, Albert PJ. Diplomacy and the Revolution: The Franco-American Alliance of 1778. 
Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia. 1981) 


A side note: Prior to and during the American Revolutionary War, William Howe often, and quite 
publically, expressed his support for American independence, and believed that the various 
punitive taxations imposed on the colonies were unfair and politically dangerous. In 1774, he 
stated he would refuse an assignment to fight against the Americans, although he obviously 
changed his mind on that point. As we will see elsewhere in this family history, Howe was not 
the only high level British commander during the Revolutionary War who personally supported 
the American’s pursuit of Independence, but served out of duty to the Crown. (Smith D. 
Whispers Across the Atlantick: General William Howe and the American Revolution, London: 
Bloomsbury Press. 2017) 


In June of 1778, Clinton reluctantly commenced the withdrawal of approximately 21,000 British 
troops from Philadelphia. Although committed to implementing the orders of the British War 
Ministry, Clinton was determined to “administer one more sound thrashing” to the Colonial 
army on the 100 mile journey back to New York. He hoped that a resounding victory might 
stimulate a reconsideration of military strategy in the northern colonies, or if sufficiently 
decisive — end the war. Clinton had been stationed in North America since 1775, serving under 
Howe’s command in Boston, NYC and Philadelphia, and accordingly, was involved in numerous 
military actions to suppress the Colonials. Over the years, he had proposed many plans to Howe 
for defeating the rebels, and, in particular, for capturing or killing Washington, that were far 
more aggressive than Howe’s often-reluctant strategies. Howe and/or the War Ministry ignored 
or rejected virtually all of Clinton’s ideas for quashing the rebellion, and generally considered 
Clinton to be an annoying pest. So, by the time Clinton finally achieved command, he was 
itching to lure Washington into a direct full force battle, confident that he could smash the 
Continental Army and finally bring the colonists to their senses. (O’Shaughnessy AJ. The Men 
Who Lost America. British Leadership, the American Revolution, and the Fate of the Empire. 
New Haven, CT: Yale University Press. 2014) 


Washington had his own agenda in the summer of 1778. Through information provided by his 
sophisticated spy network, which had infiltrated the British high command, Washington was 
well aware of the British plans to withdraw Clinton’s army back to NYC as part of Britain’s over- 
arching plan to de-emphasize the northern colonies in its global war with France. From a purely 
military perspective, Washington was content to let the Redcoats sequester themselves within 
NYC with a diminished force, but with an eye to national and international political optics, he 
also wanted to appear proactive in ”chasing the enemy across New Jersey” inflicting hit and run 
damage where feasible, but avoiding a full-on confrontation. (Chernow R. Washington, A Life. 
London: Allen Lane Pub. 2010) 


237 


The trudge across New Jersey ensued with Clinton’s army camping often, hoping to entice the 
Colonials into an attack. Washington’s 15,000-man army, including Hendrickson and the 3% 
Middlesex Regiment, shadowed the Brits and launched small assaults on supply wagons and 
rear guard units. To further entice Washington into a major attack, Clinton divided his army into 
two sections: most of the combat troops and artillery were in one column, and the second unit 
was composed of a 1500 wagon supply train protected by a small retinue of infantry. Both 
armies camped near Monmouth, New Jersey on the night of June 27, 1778. Sensing an 
opportunity for a low risk attack with high likelihood of an outcome he could claim as a victory, 
Washington ordered Marque de Lafayette to attack the rear guard of the wagon train the 
following morning, a Sunday, with 4,000 troops. That attack never reaching it’s target because 
de Lafayette urged his men to march too quickly in the morning humidity, and with men and 
horses exhausted, the column ground to a halt. Washington next tabbed General Charles Lee to 
attach the Brit wagon train with several thousand recently arrived and largely untrained 
soldiers. Lee’s initial attack on the wagon train column was a chaotic disaster, in part due to his 
overly cautious approach, which alerted the British to an imminent attack, and in part due to 
the uncoordinated movement of the raw troops. Factors that he could not fully control also 
were in play including free-lancing by his unit commanders, and the rapid arrival of a counter- 
attacking force of 8,000 men, much larger than expected, led by General Charles Cornwallis. 


Clinton had anticipated the Colonial attack on the wagon train and was ready to pounce. Lee 
dithered at first, stunned by the abrupt reversal of fortune. But he regrouped, gathered most of 
his commanders and quickly conceived a plan for a defensive retreat. The Americans repelled 
several British counter attacks as they attempted to march toward Washington’s main army, 
but the retreat eventually became disorderly, with some units breaking and running. After 
receiving word that Lee’s attack had been bungled, Washington raced ahead of his main army 
with a small contingent of aides to find Lee trying to restore order. Outraged at the chaos and 
what he considered a premature retreat, Washington confronted Lee on horseback as 
hundreds of soldiers watched and sent him to the rear, taking command himself around noon. 
Although this brief conversation was one of the most famous moments of the Revolutionary 
War, no one knows exactly what was said, but it is clear that Lee took the reprimand poorly. In 
later years, both Washington and Lee were evasive about this brief meeting on horseback. 
(Ecelberger G. Did Charles Lee Disobey George Washington’s Attack Order at Monmouth? 
Journal of the American Revolution Online. www..allthingsliberty.com. March 7, 2024. Accessed:

Within an hour, Washington managed to re-assemble the soldiers into several defensive lines 
that held off attacks by Cornwallis until the main component of the Continental Army arrived, 
and de Lafayette moved his now rested troops into the defensive line. Washington, Lafayette 
and Mad Anthony Wayne quickly arranged the army into a strong defensive position on the 
only high ground, in a generally flat terrain, near a cluster of farmhouses and other buildings, 
including most prominently, the Courthouse of Monmouth County. (Bluhm RK. Battle of 
Monmouth, American Revolution (1778). Britannica. www.britannica.com. June 22, 2024. 
Accessed: June 25, 2024) 


By 2:00pm, Clinton’s main cohort of troops re-joined with those of Cornwallis, bringing his 
21,000 soldiers face to face on an open battlefield with Washington’s smaller force of 15,000 — 
just what Clinton wanted! But the situation was not ideal. First and foremost, it was exceedingly 
hot, humid and hazy. Field reports by British and American military scribes and contemporary 
newspaper articles all assert that it was nearly 100 degrees with “monstrous humidity and a 
gray hazy sky obscuring the sun.” Anyone who has spent a summer in the Mid Atlantic states 
certainly recognizes that description. A large portion of Clinton’s army had already fought a 
battle in the morning, then quick marched to this position and now were faced with mounting a 
second assault. Secondly, Washington’s army had efficiently reformed from the chaos of the 
morning and moved into position much faster than Clinton expected. By the time Cornwallis 
and Clinton united, the Americans were ready and waiting. This was a day of surprises for 
Clinton. (Morrisey, B. Monmouth Courthouse 1778: The Last Great Battle in the North. Oxford, 
UK: Osprey Publishing. 2004)

In spite of these factors, Clinton, perhaps assuming, or hoping, that the Americans were still 
disorganized from the morning’s events, launched several assaults across the field that were 
repulsed. Around 3:00pm, Clinton directed his artillery to open fire, which would allow his 
infantry to rest and hydrate, and perhaps would rattle the Colonial troops who had a history of 
scattering under bombardment. To his dismay, after both sides fired opening salvos, the 
American’s rolled at least 15 heavy artillery carriages into place atop the highest ridge on the 
field to supplement another group of cannons on the other side of their line. This new battery 
had excellent positioning to fire directly into the main British artillery group. The American 
batteries unleashed a massive barrage of well-aimed ordinance from both positions, firing by 
many estimates three times the number of rounds as the Brits. Clinton was forced to move 
much of his artillery out of harm’s way, placing these cannons nearly beyond their range to aim 
accurately, diminishing their effectiveness. Clinton’s unit commanders, without orders, started 


239 


moving their infantrymen backward to get out of the zone of Colonial artillery bombardment, 
giving the impression to observers on site that the British were retreating. (Morrisey, 2004) 


A side note: The Battle at Monmouth Courthouse was fought near a substantial population 
center. Many local residents and camp followers (i.e., spouses and families of soldiers, 
prostitutes, merchants, cooks, water providers, seamstresses, elderly men looking for 
excitement, and widows of deceased soldiers) came out to observe and assist American soldiers 
participating in the conflict, an action that led to the mythology of Molly Pitcher. For major 1g" 
century wars, an army of 15,000 soldiers could have as many as 3,000 camp followers who 
interacted extensively with soldiers as they marched, during evening camps and even amidst 
battles. Military leaders relied on these followers for food, water, entertainment, cleaning and 
repairing of uniforms and equipment, medical care, transport of dead and wounded, and 
baggage hauling. The British Army of the North under Howe and then Clinton also had a 
substantial number of camp followers including Tory supporters of the Brits, prostitutes, 
merchants (i.e., food and clothing vendors) and wives of officers and soldiers. It has been 
estimated that approximately 5,000 British spouses followed their soldier husbands to North 
America during the Revolutionary War. Most remained in the relative comfort afforded by 
colonial NYC, but 1,000-2,000 followed the army in its various campaigns against the rebels. 
Thus, at Monmouth, both sides undoubtedly had camp followers playing support roles during 
the battle. (Blumenthal W. Women Camp Followers of the American Revolution Philadelphia: GS 
McManus Press. 1952. Accessed via WorldCat www.search.worldcat.org on June 23, 2024) 


Clinton at first exhorted his units to return to the front lines, but eventually realized the 
situation was dire. in contrast to Washington who almost always remained behind the arena of 
conflict (except on this day), Clinton led from the front and was actually in the midst of the 
bombardment himself, experiencing close calls. The artillery exchange cast a dense smoky layer 
that hovered five to ten feet off the ground between the two armies on this sultry and windless 
day. Because of the smoke, coupled with the humidity laden haze, Clinton and his troops likely 
could not see the Americans at the top of the incline even though they were but a few hundred 
yards away. 


Around 5:00pm, the artillery barrage from both sides ceased. Neither side had an endless 
supply of ordinance, and the intense heat had disabled so many gunners that cannons could no 
longer be operated. In the quiet that followed the last cannon report, Clinton sized up his 
options. Attempt another ground assault late in the day with exhausted and rattled troops, or 
execute a strategic repositioning to separate his army from the Americans? Although furious at 
the missed opportunity, Clinton went with the later option, ordering a withdrawal. Because of 
the haze and smoke, Washington did not at first realize that the Brits were leaving the field. 
Once he determined what was happening, Washington saw another “political optics” 
opportunity: send small units of soldiers to attack the rearguard of Clinton’s army with the goal 
of hurrying the Redcoats’ flight from the field. Between 5:00pm and nightfall, Washington’s 
commando-like attacks on the withdrawing British columns inflicted considerable damage, and 
sped up the pace of withdrawal, thus enhancing the perception of a British retreat. That night, 
both sides camped less than a mile from each other. Sometime after midnight, the Brits quietly 
marched away toward awaiting ships at Sandy Hook on the Jersey coast that ferried Clinton and 
his army to Manhattan. Although a point of considerable debate among Revolutionary War 


240 


historians, it appears that Washington was most likely aware of the British departure, or at 
least anticipated it would occur. He likely had already decided not to press his luck by giving 
chase. He had already achieved his military and political goals. 


The Redcoat army evacuated to a defensive position within NYC where they remained until 
October, 1781. More than 10,000 of the 20,000 British troops sequestered in New York were 
diverted to the southern colonies or to other sites internationally in the broader Anglo-French 
war of 1778-1783. An excellent book by Lender and Stone, Bloody Sunday: George Washington, 
the Monmouth Campaign and the Politics of Battle (Norman, OK: University of Oklahoma Press. 
2016. Volume 54 of the Campaigns and Commanders Series) summarizes the political and 
military ramifications of the battle that had an inconclusive outcome at nightfall, but which 
came to be perceived as an important American victory in the weeks afterward. The events of 
that day also changed the public’s perception of George Washington’s ability as a military 
leader, and many political leaders in the U.S. and Europe began to see him as a potential civilian 
head of a new North American nation.

Notes on the Battle of Monmouth and the Molly Pitcher Legend: From Washington’s action 
reports to Congress for June 28, 1778 (side note below), it is known that Dr. Okey Hendrickson 
served as a field medic, helping wounded and otherwise impaired soldiers on the battlefield 
that afternoon (the 3™ Middlesex Regiment remained with Washington’s main army and did 
not participate in Lee’s morning raid). With other surgeons, Okey moved to a rear surgery area 
following the conclusion of action to attend to the wounded. Monmouth was a notable 
engagement for many reasons, including the fact that Washington’s Continental Army “held the 
field” for the first time in an open battle against a full force British army comprised of more 
than 20,000 well trained English and Prussian regulars. However, in the centuries since the two 
armies clashed on that stifling hot Sunday, the battle came to be at least as well known as the 
inspiration for the Molly Pitcher legend (Griffith WR. Molly Pitcher and the Battle of Monmouth. 
American Battlefield Trust. www.battlefields.org. November 16, 2011. Accessed: June 7, 2023) 
In the course of his duties that day, it is possible that Okey may have crossed paths with the 
soon to be famous Molly Pitcher. | could locate no evidence of this, but given Molly’s activities 
that day in support of the artillery brigades, and the need for medical support of the 
cannoneers who were all-important to the outcome of the engagement, it seems logical to 
assume that Hendrickson, Riker and other medics probably focused their attention on the 


241 


artillery units during the Sunday afternoon cannon duel. It was essential to keep the men on 
their feet and firing away at Clinton’s army below. 


Washington’s field notes for the June 28" engagement, possibly ghost written at least in part 
by Alexander Hamilton, provided general comments on movements of the medical corps at 
Monmouth, suggesting they were sent “where needed most,” provided estimates of fatalities 
and “the quantities of men treated after-action” and offered observations about the impact of 
the weather on his men, noting that they “were beat out with heat and fatigue” by the end of 
the day, a factor in his decision not to further chase Clinton. Washington also reported that his 
own horse had died due the intolerable heat of the day. (Fitzpatrick JC. Writings of George 
Washington in the Revolutionary War From Original Manuscript Sources (39 volumes). Vol 7: 
General George Washington Recounts the Battle of Monmouth Court House. Washington DC: 
U.S. Government Printing Office. 1931-1944. Curated by HathiTrust (www.hathitrust.org). 
Accessed at New Jersey State Library. www.njstatelib.org on June 26, 2024) 


Aside note: Washington was extremely dedicated to the task of preserving his communications, 
both personal and professional, throughout his life, and in particular during the Revolutionary 
War Period. In May, 1781, Washington formed a special unit of “scribes, clerks and librarians” 
headed by Colonel Richard Varick to retrieve, organize, label and copy all of his letters to 
politicians, civil officials and other military personnel (including “enemy officers and British 
subjects”), daily reports, field action summaries after clashes with the British, proposals, 
budgets and other letters sent to the Continental Congress, military orders and plans, and the 
agenda and minutes of War Council Meetings (i.e., meetings with his top field commanders). 
Over four years (1781-1785), working from an office in Poughkeepsie, New York, Varick and his 
team assembled 44 bound volumes, each with more than a thousand pages, of Washington’s 
war-related documents from 1775 to 1785. The Varick Papers are a prized and heavily accessed 
collection at the Library of Congress, serving as perhaps “THE” fundamental research source for 
Revolutionary historians because they are able to extract dense, first hand, detail from this 
collection. For example, Washington’s interactions with Molly Pitcher on the day of and the day 
after the Battle of Monmouth are described from his perspective within the section labeled: Civil 
Officials and Private Citizens. (Library of Congress. www.loc.org. Collection: George Washington 
Papers. Series 3, Varick Transcripts, 1775-1785)

A side note: The writers and producers of Animal House, Chris Miller, Harold Ramis, and Ivan 
Reitman, contended at the time of the film’s release that it was based on their collective 
collegiate experiences at Dartmouth College (Miller), Washington University (Ramis) and 
McMaster University (Reitman). However, they eventually allowed that well-known events at 
other colleges may have played a role in shaping the script. References to Dickinson in the 
dialogue, the climatic Halloween Parade, Bud Rubendall’s “depraved” statement (repeated 
nearly verbatim by Dean Wormer in the director’s cut of the film), use of Carlisle musicians who 
often played Dickinson frat parties to portray Otis Day and the Knights in the roadhouse scene, 
and Dickinson ROTC events that were eerily identical to those portrayed in the film, have made 
decades of alumni suspicious, although the College Board of Trustees and administration almost 
certainly desire to bury the Animal House rumors, which divert attention from the college’s long- 
standing tradition of high academic standards and highly selective admission criterion. In 2024, 
Dickinson was ranked # 46 out of 221 highly selective national liberal arts colleges and # 36 for

best undergraduate educational experience / teaching. (U.S. News and World Report 2024 Best 
Colleges Report. www.usnews.com. Accessed: August 19, 2024) 


Molly was born in Trenton, New Jersey as Mary Ludwig, but she acquired the nickname of Molly 
in childhood and it stuck. She moved to Carlisle after she married William Hays in 1777, so her 
name at the time of the Monmouth battle was Molly Hays. William was a native of Carlisle, and 
had been active in protests against British taxation for a number of years before the war for 
independence. Soon after their marriage, William joined the 4° Pennsylvania Artillery Brigade, 
which was formed in Carlisle. Like many childless wives of Colonial soldiers, Mary became a 
camp follower. Mary spent the winter of 1777-78 at the Valley Forge winter camp with William, 
and joined a Women’s Camp Brigade led by Martha Washington that washed soldiers’ clothes 
and helped the medical staff with sick soldiers. During the army’s training at Valley Forge and 
throughout the ensuing New Jersey Campaign of 1778, Molly and numerous other women 
formed a carrier battalion that transported water to quench the thirst of artillerymen and the 
horses pulling cannon carriages, and to swab and cool cannon muzzles. Therefore, by the time 
Molly arrived at the Monmouth camp the evening prior to the June 23" engagement, she had 
gained battlefield experience during preceding skirmishes with Clinton’s army. (Bohrer ML. 
Glory, Passion and Principle: The Story of Eight Remarkable Women at the Core of the American 
Revolution. New York: Simon and Schuster 2007) 


Washington’s own reports compiled in the Varick Transcripts, indicate he was well aware of 
Molly and her water conveying colleagues by the time of the fight at Monmouth. During the 
battle on that intensely hot afternoon, Molly and several other women raced back and forth 
between a bubbling spring that fed a small stream and the front lines carrying water in large 
blue glass pitchers as well as buckets. When a group of soldiers needed water, they would wave 
a kerchief and yell, “Molly — Pitcher,” and thus the legendary name was born. When the artillery 
fight dominated the battlefield for several hours, Molly concentrated her efforts on the position 
of William’s 4" Pennsylvania Brigade, which was part of the artillery group occupying a high 
ridge, overlooking the battlefield. 


Sensing that their efforts were carrying the day, William and colleagues loaded and fired 
furiously, but at a price — the heat and humidity dropped many gunners to the ground from 
heatstroke (dehydration), including William. Many versions of the Molly Pitcher legend, and 
paintings of the scene, imply that William Hays died at Molly’s feet, but this was inaccurate. He 
recovered from likely exhaustion and dehydration and continued service with Washington’s 
army. With William and other men out of action, Molly apparently did drop her pitcher, and 
stepped up to help her husband’s gun team. In the diary of a soldier on the battlefield that day 
(Joseph Plumb Martin) a women is described hoisting the sponge rod to clean cannon barrels of 
residue from previous firings. Near the conclusion of the artillery duel, Plumb Martin describes 
how this women tossed cannon balls down the barrel herself and rammed them down with the 
other end of the sponge rod, as depicted in the painting below. (Martin JK. Ordinary Courage: 
The Revolutionary War Adventures of Private Joseph Plumb Martin. New York: Wiley-Blackwell 
Publishing. 1993) The Plumb Martin diary has served as a principle resource for many 
Revolutionary War historians and is considered one of the best representations of the lives and 
battle experiences of Colonial soldiers.

At some point, a British cannonball flew between her legs and tore away a substantial part of 
her skirt and petticoat, but she continued with her duties. According to legend, and at least 
partially substantiated in Washington’s after-action comments in the Varick Transcripts, 
Washington asked Molly about her shredded clothing shortly after the battle, to which she 
replied: “I suppose it could have been worse. A little higher and the ball would have carried 
away more than my petty coat.” The next day, Washington decorated Molly and her water 
carrying colleagues in front of a large number of troops. Molly was presented with a gold coin 
of unknown denomination and a scroll proclaiming her as a non-commissioned officer of the 
Continental Army at the rank of Sergeant. From that point on, Sergeant Molly became her 
nickname. During the ceremony, Washington again asked about the tattered dress, and Molly 
remarked that she “felt but a cooling breeze beneath, welcome on such a miserable day.” She 
apparently had a way with words. 


Of course, with any legend, there are doubters and controversy. Because other camp following 
women served in similar capacities as Molly Hay at Monmouth and other engagements, some 
historians have questioned whether or not the Molly Pitcher story reflects the collective efforts 
of several women. For example, Joseph Plum Martin did not specifically name the cannon- 
ramming female in his diary, and Washington’s after-action notes refer to a Molly Pitcher, not 
to Molly Hay. (Teipe EJ. Will the Real Molly Pitcher Please Stand up? Prologue. 1999; 31(2). 
Accessed via Internet Archive www.archive.com on June 24, 2024) However, given that William 
Hay was a known entity and Molly was with the 4" Pennsylvania Artillery unit during the final 
hours of the battle, it seems likely that her actions are, at least in part, based in fact. Molly and 
William returned to Carlisle after the war. William died in 1789 and Molly soon after married 


After Monmouth, Okey administered minor medical aid to Washington on several occasions 
during the remainder of the New Jersey campaign, including treatment of lingering knee pain 
that afflicted the general throughout the war (likely arthritis) and his famously ill fitting ivory 
dentures, for which Okey had no answer except to order several sets of dentures in different 
configurations hoping that one would fit comfortably (they did not). 

Washington and other Continental Army senior staff made New Brunswick their command post 
for several weeks after the battle, in part to attend the court marshal of General Charles Lee 
who was accused of disobeying orders during the botched attack on the British rear guard, and 


245 


perhaps the larger social intelligence error of writing ill-tempered letters to Washington, and to 
other military men and politicians, complaining about Washington’s lack of competence. Dr. 
Okey Hendrickson and George Washington by now were well acquainted, and Washington 
accepted Okey’s offer of lodging at his Hightown home on the outskirts of New Brunswick. 
During dinners, Okey and May Anne encouraged Washington to have the trial held at his 
family’s travel lodge, one of the larger buildings in the area. However, the mayor of New 
Brunswick, who owned the largest tavern (White Horse Tavern, which still stands) prevailed. 
After an acrimonious month long trial, Lee was suspended from the army for one year, but 
never returned to duty after further alienating members of the Continental Congress with a 
stream of vindictive letters. (Papas P. Renegade Revolutionary: The Life of General Charles Lee. 
New York: NYU Press. 2014) 


With the British hunkered down within New York City, the conflict in New Jersey essentially 
ceased. Okey Hendrickson was discharged from his three-year term of service in July 1779 and 
returned to his multiple business interests including his medical practice, which he operated 
out of its original site on Old York Road. With endorsements and letters of recognition from 
General Washington, Dr. Riker and other Continental Army notables adorning the office walls, 
Dr. Okey’s medical clientele increased, and he strove to revitalize the gristmill and hauling 
enterprises. One of the travel lodges now had a tavern, modeled after the White Horse, and 
business improved as people returned to the area with the decline in hostilities. 


In August of 1781, Washington planned a fake attack on New York City to disguise the 
movement of the bulk of his troops to Virginia to entrap the British Southern Army at Yorktown. 
Washington created a bogus set of battle orders and allowed them to be stolen by a known 
Tory spy. Roughly 2,000 troops were quite visibly marched into Monmouth County, New Jersey 
and positioned near the shoreline, easily discernable by British ships in New York harbor. A 
large camp, suitable for 10,000 troops was set up with rows and rows of tents, weapon 
stockpiles, large bread ovens, and big campfires at night. During the initial days of the camp 
setup, Washington and his entourage rode over to New Brunswick to visit Okey Hendrickson. 
The objective of the visit was two-fold: first to ask Okey to divert most of his freight wagons to 
make fake deliveries to the Monmouth encampment, and second, to request Okey to re-enlist 
for six months to serve as a camp medic. Even without combat, medical services would be 
needed for 2,000 soldiers, and Washington could not be certain that the British wouldn’t probe 
camp strength with raids, or even shell the camp from the harbor. (Stewart LS. Deception and 
the Battle of Yorktown. U.S. Army Intelligence Center of Excellence. Fort Huachuca, AZ. October 
18, 2022. www.army.mil.>USAICoE. Accessed: July 22, 2023) 


Okey agreed to both requests, and then he and Washington toured the Hendrickson’s newest 
gristmill on a branch of the Raritan, which gave Okey, ever on the outlook for business 
opportunity, an opening to talk Washington into a contract to deliver Hendrickson-milled flour 
to the camp bakery, as well as spirits from his tavern to the officer’s mess tent. Accounts vary as 
to how long Washington remained with the Hendrickson’s before returning to his headquarters 
— probably three or four nights. The bogus camp remained in place until the end of September, 
1781 when the British command in New York finally discerned that Washington and his army, 
along with Lafayette’s French troops, were bearing down on Cornwallis who was holed up in 
Yorktown, Virginia at the end of a skinny indefensible peninsula. 


246 


Washington visited Okey and Mary Anne again in the fall of 1783 while on his way to a 
Continental Congress meeting in Princeton, New Jersey. On this trip, Washington was making a 
show of traveling along the King’s Highway, which passed through New Brunswick, to 
encourage colonial governments to invest more money into road maintenance. He spent 
several evenings at the Hendrickson house and conducting meetings with aides in town, again 
at the White Horse Tavern, mostly working on a speech he was scheduled to present to the 
Congress, and a proposal for more spending on the Kings Highway, which was tabled and not 
addressed by the Congress. 


After the war, Okey and his family settled into a routine for several years, maintaining a 
relatively affluent and seemingly comfortable life. Around 1790, Okey grew restless with his 
varied businesses in New Jersey, and according to previous Hendrickson family histories, 
became a fervent opponent of a religious movement sweeping the colonies known as the 
Second Great Awakening. (Mathews DG. The Second Great Awakening as an Organizing 
Process, 1780-1830. American Quarterly. Baltimore MD: The Johns Hopkins University Press. 
1969; 21(1): 23-43) This period of religious revival essentially pitted individuals who believed in 
the traditional doctrines, rituals, sermons and hymns associated with the major denominations 
in Colonial America, against a new wave of intensely evangelical believers who advocated a 
personal approach to religion, similar to Quaker beliefs, with appeals for incorporating 
spirituality into daily life, strict morality, high levels of piety, increased freedom for women, and 
a more proactive role for ministers. 


Supporters of the “Awakened Faith” (or “new Faith”) argued for a theatrical (i.e., performance) 
model of preaching in contrast to the traditional passive model where ministers read bible 
passages verbatim, selected hymns and led prayers. It was argued that awakened ministers, 
and their followers, should be aggressively evangelical, seeking to inspire morality through fiery 
hell and brimstone rhetoric, and preaching damnation for those perceived to be sinners, with 
particular focus on alcoholism and slave ownership. It was also argued that congregations could 
be organized outside of the main denominations, and could meet outdoors, in tents, or in 
member’s homes, a threat to established church infrastructure. This threat was not taken 
lightly; Catholic and Protestant church establishment harshly criticized the Awakened Faith 
movement and sought legal injunctions to close Tent Revivals. (Kidd T. The Great Awakening: 
Roots of Evangelical Christianity in Colonial America. New Haven: Yale University Press. 2007.) 


The Awakened Faith movement was strong in New Jersey and New York leading to generational 
divisiveness in society. Traditionalists tended to be older and male and new faith followers 
tended to be younger and female. Additionally, Awakened Faith followers were urged by their 
ministers to actively seek out non-church goers and bring them into the fold. (McLoughlin WG. 
Revivals, Awakenings and Reform: An Essay on Religion and Social Change on America, 1607- 
1977. Chicago, ILL: University of Chicago Press)

Nothing in the historical record suggests that Okey or Mary Anne were particularly religious and 
no record of church membership was found, which was unusual in that era, especially for 
prominent citizens of an affluent community like New Brunswick. | uncovered no evidence that 
they were slave owners, but slave ownership was so casual and socially entrenched that | 
cannot rule out that a deeper historical dig might produce records of slave holdings by the 
Hendricksons. Perhaps Okey and his wife were too aggressively pursued to join a new faith 
congregation, or were caught up in theological debates within their family or with friends. We 
don’t know why, but it is apparent that Okey was sufficiently troubled by the Great Awakening 
to ponder leaving New Jersey. 


In August 1790, Okey, traveling with one of his sons, Daniel Elbridge Hendrickson (1768-1863), 
met up with his brother Cornelius in Somerset, PA, and the party journeyed to Kentucky to 
meet with a land agent who had been recommended to them — Daniel Boone (1734-1820). 
Boone, a long-time Kentucky frontiersman, was already famous in the eastern colonies for his 
explorations leading to European settlement of Kentucky and parts of West Virginia, the 
opening of the Cumberland Trail across the Appalachian Mountains and his adventures with 
Native tribes and Anglo frontier bandits. (Lofaro M. Daniel Boone: An American Life. Lexington 
KY: University Press of Kentucky. 2012) 


Boone turned to surveying and real estate later in life to pay off large debts that he owed to 
investors and land speculators. Boone was a notoriously inept businessman who had been 
swindled in a number of too good to be true property acquisitions and had lost thousands of 
dollars on dubious commercial ventures including a ginseng root farm, making and selling 
maple sugar, operating a restaurant and a race track with an adjoining “continental-style casino 
for games of wit and cunning.” Gaming casinos were declared illegal by the newly formed 
legislature when Kentucky achieved statehood, which sank that business venture. Boone and 
his wife, Rebecca Bryan (1739-1813), then opened a clothing store in the rural community of 
Marysville, Kentucky, along the Ohio River. Although Marysville was one of the larger 
communities in the region, it had only 500 residents. The store attempted to sell high end 
European fashion from London and Paris, which Rebecca ordered at considerable cost. 
Surprisingly, Daniel and Rebecca were able to attract a substantial investment to underwrite 
this venture. Not surprisingly, high-end fashion was a low priority for rural Kentucky residents, 
and that business also failed, leaving Daniel and Rebecca with even more debt. Next, the 
Boone’s turned to horse breeding. To finance this business, the Boone’s sold most of their 
property and scoured Kentucky, Virginia and North Carolina to purchase a stable of 
thoroughbreds. Boone corralled the costly herd near a tavern he owned in Maysville, but failed 


248 


to post a guard one evening, leading to the inevitable — the entire herd of 20 high priced horses 
were let out of the pen and likely were quickly swept up by local tribesmen or Anglo bandits. 


A side note: Although the traditional characterization of Boone’s faulty business acumen is 
largely accurate, recent studies of Boone’s entrepreneurial endeavors argue that he and 
Rebecca were no more or less successful than the majority of business owners on the 
hardscrabble frontier. They had a couple of enterprises, including their Marysville tavern, which 
provided reliable sources of income. (Hammon N, Harris J. Daniel Boone the Businessman: 
Revising the Myth of Failure. Register of the Kentucky Historical Society. 2014; 112(1): 5-50) 


Additionally, Daniel and Rebecca were both the subjects of popular paperback novels that were 
best sellers in the eastern colonies and in England, but they failed to secure literary 
representation, and received no income from these numerous publications. 


One of two portraits of Daniel Boone created by James
