An avid letter writer, Rebecca Bryan Boone shared stories of 
frontier life with friends in her native North Carolina, some of 
which made it into regional newspapers. A newspaper in Richmond 
invited Rebecca to submit stories for publication, which she did, 
and these articles were picked up by other East Coast papers. 
Eastern writers, eager to tap into public demand for frontier 
novels, produced 11 books based on these stories, telling 
embellished accounts of Rebecca’s adventures in “Kentuck”. The 
books were popular, but Rebecca received no compensation for her 
stories. Citation and image source: Bohlen M. Rebecca Bryan Boone 
Remembered. Wilkesboro, NC: Wilkes Journal Patriot. January 3, 2023. 
www.JournalPatriot.com. Accessed: 8/29/2023. 


Boone proved to be a diligent real estate agent for Okey Hendrickson. After two months of 
searching available properties, the group identified an eight-acre parcel on the Cabin Creek in 
what would eventually become Lewis County after Kentucky statehood was conferred. The site 
was near the Ohio River and the border with the Ohio Territory. First time settlers in Kentucky, 
then a single county of Virginia, were allowed eight acres without cost if they built an entry 
road and a living structure within three years of the first claim. Boone indicated that Cabin 
Creek had good flow year-round for a gristmill and that the land was fertile and tillable with few 


249 


rocks, all of which turned out to be true. Collecting his fee from Okey, Boone headed off to 
Frankfort, the territorial capital, to file Okey’s claim, and Cornelius caught the monthly Ohio 
River Ferry which took him east toward his home in Western PA. Okey and Daniel rowed and 
floated a six oar skiff, donated by Boone, to Maysville, KY, about 60 miles away, to order 
supplies for a rudimentary house, which they constructed by Christmas 1790 with the 
assistance of local craftsmen recommended by Boone. It was the first house built in Lewis 
County, Kentucky. After hiring one of the locals to stay in the house and supervise construction 
of the access road, Okey and Daniel made their way home to New Brunswick, arriving during a 
January snowstorm.

Between 1790 and 1794, Okey journeyed on his own or with son Daniel to Cabin Creek several 
times to check on progress and start improvements on additional property that Boone 
identified for them. Supported by endorsement letters from George Washington, Okey 
convinced the territorial governor to cede him 350 acres in 1791 in recognition of his 
Revolutionary War service, and 1500 acres in 1794 for starting three businesses in Cabin Creek 
(a print shop / post office, a sundry store and a blacksmith) and luring several other families to 
the area. Even though he had owned land in Kentucky for barely a year, Okey was appointed by 
the Governor in 1791 to represent the region of Kentucky that included Cabin Creek in the 
Virginia General Assembly (prior to statehood, Kentucky was a single county within the state of 
Virginia). Daniel Boone was appointed representative for the central region of Kentucky. 
Hendrickson and Boone traveled to Richmond together for the start of the Virginia General 
Assembly on October 1, 1791 and roomed together in a boarding house during the session. 
Both argued in front of the Assembly in support of a statehood bill for Kentucky that failed by 
one vote in 1791, but passed in the spring 1792 Assembly session. 


After closing his medical practice, the travel lodges and the tavern, Okey, Mary Ann and four of 
their younger children departed New Jersey in the summer of 1794 for frontier life in Cabin 
Creek. The gristmills and freight hauling businesses were taken over by two adult sons who 
elected to remain in New Jersey. Although Okey and Mary Ann had a large tract of land in 
Kentucky, there is no evidence that they actively farmed this property. They allowed Boone and 
others to use the land for guided hunting excursions, and allowed logging to occur in a forested 
section of the acreage. In 1797, they also traded a section of creek front property for an 


250 


adjoining wooded parcel, described as “many hundreds of hardwood oak forests” in a loca 
Maysville newspaper, which they leased for hunting excursions to Boone and other local guides. 


Okey apparently did not resume his medical practice and instead devoted himself to county and 
state politics. He was elected Lewis County Commissioner three times, held a statewide 
position as the Roadwork and Ferry Commissioner for nine years and also secured Justice of the 
Peace positions in Lewis and two adjacent counties. He was granted a liquor license in 1808 and 
opened two taverns, one in Cabin Creek and another in the village of Poplar Flat a few miles 
away, where Okey and Mary Ann purchased additional property, built a second house, and 
gradually made it their primary residence. 


Okey lobbied hard with the state legislature and the Governor to make Poplar Flat the seat o' 
Lewis County, offering in various proposals from 25 to 50 acres of his own land to build a 
county courthouse, other governance offices and a county park. These proposals were rejected 
by the legislature in favor of larger communities. In his Roadwork and Ferry Commissioner role, 
Okey often chaired statewide transportation committees appointed by the legislature. He 
served on several of these committees with Levi Morgan. Hendrickson, Morgan and severa 
County Commissioners once went on a shoreline inspection tour of the Ohio River near 
present-day Cincinnati looking for a site to build a ferry system across the river. The site 
selection tour concluded with a hunting trip in southern Ohio, led by Morgan. When Morgan 
offered all of the Commissioners half price registration for one of his future Hunting Safaris, al 
accepted the offer, but it does not appear that Okey ever participated. Prior Hendricson family 
histories noted that Okey was not an outdoorsman, and disliked hunting and fishing. 


Levi Morgan and Okie appear to have had a contentious professional relationship, often finding 
themselves on opposing sides of transportation and land development issues. Morgan typically 
opposed infrastructure development projects, preferring that “Kentuck” retain its frontier 
ethos, and stated in newspaper articles that the fledgling state should focus on tourism (the 
source of his livelihood), trade networks with Native Peoples and small, independent farming. 
Okey advocated development of highways, building bridges over creeks and rivers, (he 
particularly favored all weather covered bridges, which were common in his native New Jersey) 
expansion of the logging industry, and creation of towns on the Ohio River with docks to 
transport wood to rapidly expanding eastern cities. Based on public statements printed in 
newspapers, both men were uncomfortable with slavery and did not own slaves, but were 
resigned to the expansion of the institution in Kentucky. 


A side note: Okey and Levi’s beliefs about the inevitable spread of slavery and slave-powered, 
plantation style, agriculture in Kentucky were accurate. The territory was ultimately admitted 
into the Union in 1792 with an economy and a social culture heavily dominated by the state’s 
planter class slave owners who raised tobacco, hemp and livestock on large estates, primarily 
located in the Bluegrass Region of north central Kentucky. Plantation owners actually imported 
too many slaves from Virginia and North Carolina as new agricultural operations were rapidly 
established in the 1780s and 1790s. As a consequence, Louisville became a major market for 
auctioning off excess slaves and a departure point for ships transporting sold slaves to the Deep 
South. The slave trade industry was a substantial catalyst in the development of Louisville. 
However, by the time of the pre-Civil War Antebellum Period (roughly 1845-1860), the state’s 


251 


population had divided into two camps: slavery supporters in the Bluegrass Region, and 
Unionists and abolitionists in other areas of the state that were largely populated by free 
workforce, small plot farmers who were decidedly less affluent. During the Civil War, Kentucky 
was a border state, along with Delaware, Maryland, Missouri and West Virginia (see map 
below), with a declared policy of neutrality. Kentucky never formally joined the Confederacy, 
even though several Bluegrass counties formed a shadow Confederate Government based in 
Bowling Green. The shadow government and a contingent of Kentucky militia loyal to the 
Confederacy were expelled from the state by Union troops in 1862, and played no meaningful 
role in the state thereafter. (Klotter JC, Thompson-Friend C. A New History of Kentucky (2" ed) 
Lexington, KY: University Press of Kentucky. 2019)

Okey and Levi were linked by several Hendrickson — Morgan marriages, and thus were in each 
other’s company from time to time. During one interaction widely reported in local 
newspapers, Hendrickson and Morgan, their spouses, several children and even a few 
grandchildren attended a wedding on a celebration barge floating down the Ohio River on a hot 
summer evening in 1807. Marriages, anniversary’s and other celebrations on decorated 
riverboats were popular on the Ohio River in the ig" century. At one point during the steamy 
evening, Morgan decided that everyone should cool off with a swim, starting with the young 
grandchildren who were probably getting restless as the party wore on, and perhaps getting on 
his nerves. Levi grabbed one of Okey’s grandchildren, and carried her to the edge of the barge. 
Okey rushed over to wrest the child from Levi’s grasp, and in the tussle, toppled all three of 
them into the water. Others jumped in to rescue the floundering threesome while the barge 
pilot struggled to slow the downriver float. With some degree of struggle, all of the soaking 
wedding guests were hauled back on the barge with Okey and Levi bellowing at each other until 
their respective spouses finally “drug the dripping belligerents to opposite ends of the craft.” 
(Poplar Flat Trader; July 15, 1807 In: Churchman CR. Kentucky Descendants of Colonel Morgan 
Morgan. Louisville, KY: University of Louisville Library Document Service. 1994). 


252 


A side note: By the time little communities on the frontier, such as Cabin Creek and Poplar Flat, 
reached a population mass of 100 or so, virtually all had recruited a printer and equipment to 
publish at least a weekly newspaper, primarily devoted to business advertising: announcements 
of crops coming in, logging or tilling tracts for sale, dates of guided hunting expeditions, slave 
auctions, cargo barge and ferry schedules, equipment for sale, mail arrival and “goings on” 
including new settlers in the area and social events. The first business that Okey started in Cabin 
Creek was a printer/postal shop, which was typical for frontier communities. These print/post 
shops were also distribution centers for the monthly editions of eastern newspapers that were 
shipped to frontier towns and avidly consumed by the population. A popular Sunday afternoon 
activity was newspaper reading, in which a literate family member, often a child/adolescent, 
read the news aloud to a gathering of family members, with breaks for discussion of events. 
(Copeland DA. Colonial American Newspapers: Character and Content. Newark, NJ: University of 
Delaware Press. 1997. Accessed June 27, 2024 via The Printing Museum 
www.printingmuseum.org.) 


Both of the Hendrickson brothers who moved west, Cornelius and Okey, lived to the age of 96. 
Although Cornelius Hendrickson was a full-time country doctor until he was 90 years old, Okey’s 
quality of life appears to have declined during his final 20 years. His pal Daniel Boone, 
perpetually pursued by debt collectors, including Okey himself (see below), grew discontented 
with Kentucky and moved his family to Missouri in the early 1800s. He only returned 
periodically to try to settle debts that were not forgiven. Mary Anne lived to the age of 80 but 
died many years before Okey, and most of their children married (including two Hendrickson — 
Morgan marriages) and moved their families to Indiana or Illinois. Only son Daniel remained 
and he was occupied with several businesses of his own and a very large family. Exhibiting signs 
of what we would now call dementia, Okey moved to an isolated cabin at the back of his 
property that Boone had built years before as an overnighter for his hunting tours. Daniel 
routinely checked on his dad and brought him food. On a visit in December 1830, Daniel found 
Okey lying dead in the fireplace. He had apparently tumbled out of his rocking chair into the fire 
and burned to death. Okey’s burial site is unknown, but he is remembered in Kentucky as one 
of the leading pioneers of that state. For our Hendricson family line, Okey started the westward 
migration that ultimately led to the family’s residence in Walla Walla, Washington. Few people 
in that era could say that they were friends with both George Washington and Daniel Boone. 


One final Okey Hendrickson — Daniel Boone story, which appears in two of the preceding family 
histories, and which | heard my father, Harold Hendricson, tell on several occasions. | cannot 
verify the accuracy of this event, but the circumstances and reactions of the participants seem 
to fit what is known about both men. Boone was perpetually in debt to others. Based on his 
reputation, cheerful demeanor and perpetual optimism, people were endlessly willing to loan 
him money for business schemes, where Boone promised a great return on their investment. 
Most of these investments did not pan out as intended and he struggled to pay back his 
investors. A couple of years before Boone left Kentucky, Okey loaned $500 to his friend and 
dedicated a shoreline tract on Cabin Creek to start an 18" century equivalent of a dude ranch 
for eastern tourists. Several years went by, the ranch was never developed, and Boone never 
mentioned returning the money. Soon after, Boone departed the state, in part to avoid a 


253 


particularly angry New York investor who convinced a local sheriff to issue an arrest warrant for 
Boone with a sizable bounty attached. 


Years later, on one of his settle-up visits to Kentucky, Boone dropped by to visit Okey and Mary 
Anne. Inviting the Hendrickson’s outside, Boone proudly displayed a wagon full of dead 
squirrels and other larger animals including a badger. “There you go,” said Boone, “dinners for 
500 days; we’re square up now.” Okey, pleased to see his friend again, but less impressed with 
the settlement offer, reached into the wagon, grabbed a dead squirrel by the tail, spun around 
and clubbed Boone in the head with the rodent, knocking the aging frontiersman to the ground 
(he was at least 75 years old at the time, as was Okey). Standing over Boone, Okey wagged the 
squirrel in his face and retorted, “these dray (i.e., colonial term for a bunch of squirrels) won't 
never be greenbanks, so we won't be squared, until you get up and help me and May Anne 
cook that badger for a proper dinner.” According to the legend, the old friends proceeded to 
have a fine meal, regaling each other with stories, before Boone said good-bye to the 
Hendrickson’s for the final time. 


Notes on the Kings Highway: King Charles Il of England desired to improve transportation 
among the American colonies and improve intra-colony commerce. He ordered the colonial 
governors to collaborate with his engineers on construction of a “wide and well graded highway 
to run continuously between the southernmost and northernmost reaches of the colonies.” 
Construction began in 1650 in southern Maine, and 85 years later, in 1735, the highway 
reached Charleston, South Carolina. The crown initially paid for highway development, but as 
decades passed, much of the construction and maintenance costs were transferred to colonial 
citizens via turnpike fees, and to colonial governments via increased highway taxes. In doing so, 
these imposed usage and upkeep assessments became part of the ever-increasing package of 
colonial grievances about unfair taxations. 


The Kings Highway was designed to pass through 20 commercial 
centers in the colonies to expand north-south commerce, 
encourage people to travel between colonies, and promote re- 
location from more populated northern colonies to under 
populated southern colonies. Much of present-day U.S. Route 1, 
which begins in Maine and ends in Key West, Florida, traverses 
the original Kings Highway. Citation and image source: Kristen B. The 
Oldest Road in America, the King’s Highway, Passes Right Through New 
Jersey. www.onlyinyourstate.com. April 27, 2023. Accessed: 8/3/2023. 


Although originally well constructed using cutting edge 17" century highway technology, many 
colonies neglected maintenance. Colonial and British troop movement on the highway caused 
considerable damage during the Revolutionary War. As President, Washington encouraged 
states to budget roadway repairs with mixed results. New Jersey, Pennsylvania, New York and 
Massachusetts periodically funded highway maintenance, but not enough to consistently 
maintain the roads, and the southern colonies largely ignored road maintenance. 


254 


The King’s Highway roadbed was constructed along the 1,300-mile course in four phases. A 12- 
foot wide roadbed was scraped into the ground with hoes to a depth of 4 feet below the 
surface. Slaves in both northern and southern states did the construction work. Next, large flat 
stones were laid as the bedrock. Then a layer of mixed dirt, sand and pebbles was poured over 
the stones and tromped down by slaves walking back and forth on it. Finally a layer of pea 
gravel was poured as the top layer. The roadway was slightly crested to encourage water 
drainage. Around 1800, several states began to cover over deteriorated sections of the King’s 
Highway with a wood plank roadbed. This worked adequately until freight wagons and 
stagecoaches with iron-rimmed wheels destroyed much of the plank roads. After the Civil War, 
concrete mixing became more sophisticated and asphalt was introduced in the U.S. for the first 
time. Pennsylvania Avenue in front of the White House became the first asphalt-paved street in 
1871. Plank roads largely disappeared by 1890, replaced by asphalt or crushed stone. 


When the original stone roadbed fell into disrepair, long 
stretches of the King’s Highway were covered with wood 
planking during 1800 to 1860. During his time as New Jersey 
highway commissioner Dr. Daniel Hendrickson, Okey’s father, 
lobbied the state legislature for road enhancement funding with 
minimal success. He did secure funds for an experimental plank 
road one mile in length near Trenton, which attracted public 
curiosity, but no additional funding to expand the project.

www.fs.usda.gov. Accessed: 6/19/2024.

Dining With Cornwallis - Eleanor Lindley Maris (1749-1783) and George Maris (1743- 
1782) 

The primary information source for the history of the Maris family in North America is: Maris GL 
and Pinkerton Maris A. The Maris Family in the U.S. A Record of the Descendants of George and 
Alice Maris, 1683-1885. West Chester, PA: FS Hickman Printing. 1885. This book was digitized by 
HathiTrust in 2013 and is available from several sites including the University of Pennsylvania 
Online Library (www.onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu) and Amazon Books. Several books and 
articles on the Quaker experience in North Carolina and the Revolutionary War in that state are 
listed at the end of George and Eleanor’s story. 


George and Eleanor (Ellie) were devout Quakers who both suffered considerably during the 
Revolutionary War as described on page 70 in Chapter Il. George was discharged from the 
Continental Army after losing an eye during a skirmish with the British in June 1778 and 
returned home to Chester, PA. He found that Ellie and their children were still suffering the 
effects of the British ransack of their home. Without their horses, wagon and farm tools stolen 
by the marauding British, and slowly recovering from her facial injuries incurred when she 
attempted to fend off the Redcoats, Ellie was struggling to provide for her children, relying on 
food and clothing contributions by the Chester Friends Meeting House. Shortly after reuniting 
in July 1778, George and Ellie decided to pack up what remained of their belongings and move 
to Orange County, North Carolina (site of present day Chapel Hill) where George’s parents (John 
Maris Sr. and Kathryn Bound Heiden) had periodically resided, and were instrumental in 
establishing several Friends Meeting Houses. George’s father had owned a successful 
blacksmith shop in a village known as Carrboro (adjacent to Chapel Hill), which he sold when he 
and Kathryn decided to reside permanently in Chester PA. To assist his son and daughter-in-law, 
John Maris re-purchased the blacksmith business and deeded it over to George. 


For the initial 18 months in Carrboro, all was well with George, Ellie and their children, with the 
exception discussed in the following paragraph, as the family settled into their new community. 
George expanded the business to include silversmith work and Ellie became active in the local 
Friends Meeting House, helping to set up a new Quaker settlement in an area known at that 
time as South Alamance. In February 1780, finding that his monocular eyesight was not 
sufficient for high quality silversmith work, George hired a black freeman, born in England, only 
known as Jonas, to function as his silversmith. The community was heavily Quaker and 
accepting of Jonas who had high-level expertise, and was in constant demand. However, there 
were substantial numbers of Tories (colonists who were British supporters, opposed to the 
Revolution and supportive of slavery) in the county who were not accepting. Three Tory 
attempts to torch George’s blacksmith building finally succeeded in destroying the structure. 
Jonas was injured when attempting to douse the blaze and nearly captured by the Tory gang. 
Not surprisingly, Jonas elected to leave NC for Canada via a Revolutionary War era 
Underground Railroad (a string of safe houses reached by clandestine night travel) primarily 
operated by Quaker groups. This early version of the Underground Railroad laid the 
groundwork for a more sophisticated operation in the 19" century. (Carey B, Plank G. Quakers 
and Abolition. Urbana, Illinois: University of Illinois Press. 2011) 


256 


Although Ellie’s initial time in Carrboro was generally pleasant, one notable event led to 
anguish. As described in Chapter II, Ellie’s brother was the notorious British loyalist and Tory 
militia leader James Lindley. (Bamberg R. Captain James L. Lindley. 
www.ncpedia.org/biography/lindley-James. 2013. Accessed: June 19, 2023) In 1779, shortly 
after Ellie and George arrived in Carrboro, James Lindley was captured during a battle with a 
Continental army brigade near Laurens, South Carolina, tried, and sentenced to be hanged, 
along with his teenage son, William, who was apprehended with him. To discourage other 
colonial families from considering the Tory path, the Continental army commander in the 
south, General Nathaniel Greene, ordered Lindley’s wife, Mary Cox, to be rounded up and 
transported to Laurens to observe the execution of her husband and son. Hearing of her sister- 
in-law’s impending extraction, Ellie traveled to Mary’s home in Reaburn Creek, South Carolina 
(a 150 mile round trip) to see her and offer comfort. However, when Ellie arrived, Mary Lindley 
refused to see her, sending a message via a servant that Ellie and George’s abolitionist beliefs 
and her other brother Thomas Lindley (a Continental army officer who commanded a regiment 
from Ellie’s hometown of Chester, PA throughout the war) were to blame for family’s troubles. 
After Mary rejected several appeals to speak, Ellie headed back to Carrboro. As described in 
Chapter II, Mary’s son William was exempted from execution, and General Daniel Morgan (yes 
— that Daniel Morgan once again, from the semi-related Morgan branch) put a stop to the plan 
to bring Mary Lindley to the execution. Mary Lindley and several of her younger children moved 
to North Carolina after her husband’s death, living 20 miles from Ellie and George, but 
continued to refuse their requests to meet.

Unsettled by Tory harassment in Carrboro, George and Ellie moved to the nearby village of 
Hillsborough, NC, also with a strong Quaker presence, and opened another blacksmith shop. 
Apparently dedicated to his convictions, George hired two brothers of Caribbean descent who 
were former domestic workers at a nearby plantation, and freed in the disposition of the 
landowner’s will. Several weeks later, a group of local Tory militia rode past George and Ellie’s 
home several times and sprayed it with gunfire on each pass. Two of George and Ellie’s children 
were wounded in the attack. At the same time, another band of Tories dragged the Caribbean 
brothers from the backroom of the blacksmith shop where they lived, intent on hanging them, 
but a group of Quakers and the town constable intervened. After an altercation, one of the 
Tories was dragged from his horse and incarcerated and the others escaped, leaving the 


257 


brothers unharmed. Following this incident, George and Ellie pleaded with community leaders 
to provide better protection and commence a search for the Tories. The mayor refused, fearing 
reprisals and likely because some of the Tories were village residents. Instead, the mayor 
encouraged the Maris family to leave town, taking the Caribbean brothers with them. 


In October 1780, the Maris family moved yet again, this time to an isolated community in a hilly 
section of North Carolina between Greensboro and Durham where Ellie had previously helped 
to create a Friends Meeting House. An original resident of the area and leader of the Quakers, 
Simon Dixon, took in the Maris family, and converted a barn into a residence for the new 
arrivals. Once again, George opened a blacksmith shop, but without the Caribbean brothers 
who apparently decided that North Carolina was not an optimal residence. Ellie continued to 
engage in Friends outreach efforts, helping develop Meeting groups in nearby villages. 
Seemingly, this hilltop village provided George and Ellie with the environment they sought. 


However, in March 1781, the quiet community and the lives of George and Ellie were disrupted 
once again by the Revolutionary War. On March 15, 1781, British troops under the command of 
General Charles Cornwallis (1738-1805) won a costly victory against the Colonials at the Battle 
of Guilford Courthouse, near Greensboro. Although the Redcoats technically won the day, 30% 
of their forces were killed or captured and 25% were wounded. Over 50% of the British officer 
corps were killed. (Babbits LE, Howard JB. Long, Obstinate, and Bloody: The Battle of Guilford 
Courthouse. Chapel Hill NC: University of North Carolina Press. 2009) 
3 og 4 c

After barely managing to repulse the Colonial attack, Cornwallis decided to declare victory 
while he still had the opportunity, and quickly repositioned his army before the Colonials re- 
grouped and attacked again. In the hasty departure from the field, Cornwallis swung his horse 
around and ran smack into tree branch, knocking him to the ground, likely separating his 
shoulder. Collecting himself, Cornwallis recognized that he and his army needed an isolated 
location for recuperation and to wait for reinforcements. His scouts recommended a hilltop 
Quaker village accessible only by one winding road, which could be easily defended. During the 
British march to their recuperation site, a late winter snowstorm swept through the area 
dropping a foot of snow on the village and the single road into town. By the time Cornwallis, his 
aching shoulder and the remains of his tattered British army trudged up the hill and into the 
village, nobody was in a good mood. Cornwallis immediately directed his troops to evict all 
residents from their homes so his troops could have shelter, slaughter cattle to provision his 
hungry army, and tear apart wagons and furniture for firewood, which must have been eerily 
familiar for Ellie, who survived the same ransacking in Chester, PA. Surveying the scene, 
Cornwallis described the Quaker village as “our egregious little Snow Camp.” The term Snow 
Camp stuck after the Redcoats departure, and the community was eventually incorporated by 
the state of North Carolina as Snow Camp. 


258 


Simon Dixon was evicted from his house, the largest in town, so Cornwallis and his surviving 
officers could use it for their residence. George, Ellie and their children were evicted from the 
reconstituted barn so it could be used as an infirmary and quarters for troops. All others in the 
village soon found themselves on the street in the midst of the blizzard. The Snow Camp 
residents were herded to the Friends Meeting House and restricted to the vicinity of the 
building, under the watch of guards. The Meeting House was only large enough to shelter a few 
families. Everyone else huddled under blankets and canvas attached to the Meeting House 
walls. Several days of intense cold followed the snowstorm, contributing to a pneumonia-like 
illness in several elders and a child. Appeals to Redcoat troops for canopies that could be made 
into tents were ignored. Finally, Simon Dixon was able to arrange an “audience” with General 
Cornwallis. To demonstrate British cordiality, Dixon was allowed to invite four Snow Camp 
residents to accompany him to the meeting. Dixon selected Ellie Maris, known for her articulate 
communication, one of the elderly Snow Camp residents with pneumonia, and two of Ellie’s 
children for effect. One of the children was Adam Samuel Maris, who, as an adult, was the first 
Maris to begin the westward trek across the continent. 


Friends Meeting House at Snow Camp, NC. During the 
British occupation in March 1781, residents were evicted 
from their homes, and restricted to the Meeting House or 
other crude structures in the vicinity. 


Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. 
Accessed: 6/28/2024. 


After a sumptuous meal served by two junior British officers, Dixon, Ellie and the others were 
ushered in to see the General. Dixon outlined their complaints and requested survival materials 
such as tents, blankets, lanterns, barrels of fresh water, secluded latrines for males and 
females, care in the infirmary for ill residents and access to their homes to retrieve clothing, 
which Cornwallis agreed to provide, although home entry and latrine use would be under 
guard. After directing one of his aides to take the sick elderly resident to the infirmary, 
Cornwallis, surprisingly, launched into a lengthy and animated discussion of the cultural and 
historical wonders of his hoped for next assignment — India. Sensing the children were getting 
antsy, he ordered more food and a dessert for them and sent them away to the kitchen. 


Apparently lonely, or at least in need of non-military discussion, Cornwallis resumed the 
conversation with Dixon and Ellie by lamenting the devastating loss of his wife, Jemima, in 
1779, which “sent him far adrift and is the reason | am here | suppose.” This led Ellie to ask 
how he (Cornwallis) could abide the “devastation wreaked upon villages such as ours and the 
despondency of all therein,” given his own grief. Cornwallis responded: “I see it as my duty to 
achieve the military goals set for me, nothing else. It is my assignment and | pursue it until 
directed to desist”, although quickly adding that he found “this particular conflict to be 
muddled and afflicts me with torturous tensions.” Switching to less personal topics, Cornwallis 
peppered the villagers with questions about life in the Americas, and during the discussion 
revealed his distaste for the British attempts to excessively tax the colonies, and to militarily 
suppress the revolt. As a Parliament member (PM) during 1765-1775, Cornwallis was one of five 


259 


PMs to vote against all taxation bills aimed at the colonies, and proposed bills to implement 
gradual independence for the colonies over a transitional period. To the amazement of his 
guests, Cornwallis rifled through a satchel and pulled out a PM-sponsored assent bill that called 
for institution of nationhood for the American Colonies by 1800. An assent bill was a proposed 
parliamentary act for debate, amendment and approval in both houses, followed by submission 
for royal endorsement. He read parts of it aloud to Dixon and Ellie, showed them his signature 
on the sponsor line, complained about PM colleagues who failed to support the bill, and told 
them that the document was background material for a book he was writing during winter 
encampments. (Saberton |. The Cornwallis Papers. The Campaigns of 1780 and 1781 in the 
Southern Theatre of the American Revolution. London: The Naval and Military Press. 2010) 


Ultimately, the conversation got around to the merits of Quakerism, which Cornwallis viewed 
skeptically, blaming the Friends Movement for social unrest in England, and which Dixon and 
Ellie defended with vigor, which startled Cornwallis. Ellie described the elevated sense of 
purpose she experienced as a Quaker women and praised the expanded role in public discourse 
for women in Friends Societies. Ellie’s comments struck a note with the General, leading him to 
discuss Jemima’s desire to be “more in the public sphere, and less stored away in the home.” 
Finally, the conversation found its way the inevitable dissection of slavery. Cornwallis agreed 
with Ellie and Dixon that slavery was deplorable, but disagreed on the timetable for abolition, 
saying “the despicable practice is the only way to power agriculture until contraptions 
(machines) are built to take the place of man’s muscles.” Ellie and Dixon argued for immediate 
abolition, but struggled to answer the General’s questions about how that could be 
implemented. Cornwallis became a vocal abolition proponent later in his government career. 


As the evening drew to a close, Cornwallis gathered the children and showed them a collection 
of sabers and pistols, which probably horrified Ellie and Dixon, and escorted the Snow Camp 
group to the door, informing them that he intended to depart in two weeks, and hoped that 
“his disagreeable time in the Americas will end soon.” A summary of the Snow Camp meeting 
by Cornwallis appears in lan Saberton’s publication of the general’s war correspondence (see 
preceding citation) and is described in other accounts of his activities during the Colonial War 
listed on page 261. Using these materials as sources, two Snow Camp residents and brothers, 
James and Bobby Wilson, wrote a play depicting the British stay at Snow Camp, with focus on 
the Cornwallis audience with Dixon and Ellie. The play title, Sword of Peace, refers to the 
Quaker’s dedication to resolving disputes peacefully. The play is presented annually at the 
Snow Camp Summer Theatre and other summer stock theatres in the Carolinas. 


Charles Cornwallis commanded British armies in the northern and 
southern theatres of the American Revolutionary War, winning 
notable victories, but also suffering significant defeats, including 
the disastrous sequestering of his army at Yorktown. In spite of his 
mixed military record, Cornwallis received high-level assignments 
after the colonial war, including tenures as the Governor-Generals 
of India and Ireland. Image source: The American Revolution. 
www.ouramericanrevolution.org. Accessed: 6/9/2024. 


260 


Even though he received no reinforcements, Cornwallis and the remnants of his army departed 
Snow Camp two weeks later and began a disastrous campaign north into Virginia. The goal was 
to attract Tory militia to replenish his army, build up a new military unit out of the thousands of 
escaped slaves who fled to British camps, meet up with another British army marching south 
from New York and draw Washington’s Continental Army of the North into a final, decisive 
battle. The plan to attract Tory militia failed, the British army stationed in New York decided not 
to venture south, and a series of questionable tactical decisions by British high command led 
Cornwallis to station his army at Yorktown, Virginia. Cornwallis’s hopes for a British infantry 
division composed of freed slaves who agreed to enlist in the Redcoat army also failed to 
materialize. (Carpenter S. Southern Gambit: Cornwallis and the British March to Yorktown. 
Norman, OK: University of Oklahoma Press. 2019) 

George and Ellie Maris both died during the winter of 1782-1783. While building an addition to 
their house in Snow Camp in the fall of 1782, George shredded his hand with a saw, which 
became infected. After lingering several weeks with a high fever, he died on Christmas Eve at 
the age of 39. Ellie died at age 34 several days after childbirth in January 1783. We do not know 
the complications that led to her demise, although the child survived. The Snow Camp 
community took in George and Ellie’s seven children and raised them, in a collective enterprise, 
over the next 15 years. All of the children grew to adulthood, married and raised children. Some 
of the siblings remained in North Carolina, while others returned to Pennsylvania. Adam Samuel 
Maris, the sibling linked to the Hendricson-Lienau line (see Maris generations 7-11 on pages 70- 
73), moved his family west and settled in Indiana. 

In addition to publications cited in this section, these sources were used to explore the lives 
of George and Ellie Maris, North Carolina Quakerism, and the Snow Camp occupation.

One Foggy Morning - Johann (John) Lienau Sr. (1808-1876) 


More than any other recent ancestor, | had to dig deep into many online genealogical data 
bases, as well as employment records, point-of-entry immigration records, and data gleaned 
from census reports, newspaper articles and obituaries to piece together the details of John 
Lienau’s life. Consequently, blanks remain to be filled-in, and | relied upon “reasonable 
speculation” to discuss possible motives or incentives for decisions made as he progressed in 
his chosen career. 


John Lienau had a nearly 50 year career at sea beginning in his native Germany where he rose 
to the position of harbor pilot at one of the largest North Sea seaports, which was followed by a 
seven years working for the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company after he immigrated to England. 
By the 1850s, this company was the largest shipping line in the world and as the name implies, 
delivered mail, travelers, and household items worldwide, but with a particular focus on Latin 
America. By 1854 John had risen to the position of Chief Mate on a Royal Mail ship, the Trent, 
with a Southampton, England to Nicaragua route and intermediate stops in Barbados, Cuba, 
Puerto Rico, and Jamaica. This position carried supervisory and training responsibilities for the 
non-officer crew of the Trent, and he was a member of the Captain’s Council that dealt with 
administrative issues. With a residence in San Juan, Puerto Rico, a new wife, the mysterious 
Ellen or Ella Lienau (see the Notes on Ellen on pages 276-277), and a young son, John had 
ambition to immigrate to the U.S. The impending transfer of the Trent to Turkey to serve as a 
troop transport during the Crimean War may have had a role in this decision. (United Kingdom 
Merchant Navy Seaman Records, 1835-1941. Database and Images. Findmypast. 
http://findmypast.com. The National Archives of the UK. Kew, Surrey. 2023) 


In March 1854, John resigned his crew position with The Royal Mail Steam Packet Company and 
the Trent, walked across the street into the San Juan office of the U.S. Mail Steamship 
Company, and accepted an advertised position. He was promptly assigned to the flagship of the 
company’s 17-vessel fleet, the Star of the West, the world’s largest steamship in the 1850s, 
which was previously described in Chapter Ill. The Star just happened to anchored in the San 
Juan harbor on the day John signed his U.S. Mail contract. A week later, John was in the 
Caribbean on the Star heading for Panama, and then a return trip to New York. 


HMS Trent, left, was the nautical home of John Lienau Sr. for 
seven years. The ship was in the Royal Mail Packet Steam 
Company fleet until the Crimean War, when it was re-fitted 
as a troop transport. Lienau departed the ship in 1854 and 
joined a steamer company delivering U.S. mail in the 
Caribbean. In November 1861 after the start of the Civil War, 
the Trent, back in the Caribbean, was boarded by Union 
soldiers from the San Jacinto, right, to remove Confederate 
envoys to England. This led to a standoff between the Lincoln 
administration and English Parliament known as the Trent

Threat of Anglo-American Conflict. Canadian Journal of History. 
2012; 47(1). Accessed: June 1, 2024. 

Image: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 6/6/2024. 


262 


However, instead of a promotion or lateral transfer, John accepted a basic seaman (i.e., deck 
hand) position at the bottom of the crew hierarchy. He was 46 in 1854 and the vast majority of 
deckhands were teens or early 20s with a few older seamen busted down for various 
transgressions. The route of the Star of the West was probably the main attraction for John: 
New York to Panama with stops in Charleston, Havana, New Orleans, San Juan, Caracas, 
Venezuela and Nicaragua. John initially registered with the U.S. Immigration Service and rented 
an apartment in Brooklyn in September 1854 at the conclusion of his first cruise on the Star. 
(New York Passenger List, 1820-1891. Database of Port of Entry Logs. FamilySearch. 
https://FamilySearch.org. Citing NARA Microfilm Publication M237. Washington D.C. National 
Archives and Records Administration. Accessed February 24, 2023) Soon after, Ella and son John 
Jr. arrived in New York and joined John at his Brooklyn residence. The family remained 
permanently in the New York area thereafter, residing at several different rentals until 
purchasing an upscale brownstone in 1868 located at 192 Concord Street in Brooklyn. A 
contemporary image of that location appears below. 


192 Concord Street (red door) in 2019. It is a 3300 sq. foot condo 
located between Park Avenue and Flatbush Avenue, 15 blocks from 
the Brooklyn Bridge. The original building at this site was constructed 
in 1865, purchased by John Lienau in 1868, re-modeled in 1915, and 
periodically updated over ensuing decades. 

Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 6/30/2024. 


U.S. Mail Steamship Company had a similar mission as the Royal Mall Steam Packet Company: 
transport mail, packages, newspapers and passengers between New York and Panama. The 
influx of two million people into California during the Gold Rush and the large number that 
remained in the state afterward stimulated demand for mail service that was enhanced by the 
rapidly expanding population in Oregon. To meet this need, the U.S. Mail Steamship Company 
delivered mail and parcels to Panama, where it was off-loaded to a mail-processing center built 
by William Henry Aspinwall, who also built the Trans-Panama Railroad that opened in 1852. 
Mail destined for California and Oregon was sorted in the center, sent to the Pacific side of 
Panama by train and loaded onto steamships of the Pacific Mail Service Company for delivery at 
west coast destinations. These ships picked up west coast mail destined for New York, which in 
turn, was loaded onto the Star of the West for return to the East Coast. The Star made 7-8 
round-trips annually, also carrying passengers in each direction. For individuals who could 
afford the 800 bedding compartments or the 200 staterooms, the Star provided a comfortable 
alternative to the wagon train for reaching California and Oregon. 


The Aspinwal Mail Center in Panama employed 300 
people who sorted and distributed mail for the U.S. west 
coast and Central American nations. Obituary: William 
Aspinwall. New York Times. January 19, 1875. 


www.nytimes.com/archives. Accessed: July 20, 2023. 
Image: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 6/17/2023. 


263 


John served on the Star of the West for seven years, apparently working diligently and was 
rewarded with incremental promotions from deckhand to Seaman First Class, Clerk (managing 
Passengers and cargo), Paymaster (ship’s finances, payroll and supply purchasing), Chief Mate, 
Pilot and by 1861, on his final voyage on the Star, he was Second Mate (second officer to the 
Captain). In 1860, the U.S. War Department, anticipating the advent of the Civil War, leased the 
Star from the U.S. Mail Steamship Service for $1,250 a day for use as a troop and supply 
transport. The Star’s first mission for the War Department was important: transporting 200 
Union soldiers and two months of provisions to Fort Sumter in the harbor of Charleston, South 
Carolina. The Fort and its 75 soldiers and officers, plus a substantial cohort of family members 
and pro-Union laborers, had been informally besieged since December 20, 1860 when South 
Carolina seceded from the Union, and had not been re-supplied since October. Buying food and 
other supplies from local markets was no longer a reliable option as the governor of the new 
Confederate state of South Carolina slowly clamped down on access to provisions for the Union 
garrison, even though he allowed Sumter commanding officers Major Richard Anderson and 
Captain Abner Doubleday (yes — THAT Abner Doubleday; more about him later) to exchange 
mail and telegrams with the Union army commanders in Washington D.C. 


On December 26, 1860, a supply ship with provisions and 60 soldiers was turned away near the 
harbor entrance by three guard steamers loaded with South Carolina militia from Fort Moultrie 
on the north side of the Bay. After this failure, the War Department, more as a point of national 
hubris and pride, given the recent secession of South Carolina, than pure necessity, was 
determined to re-provision and expand the Fort Sumter garrison in spite of the fact that 
Anderson had informed the War Department that he had sufficient supplies to hold out for 4-5 
months, and did not need a large influx of additional soldiers to house and feed within the 
largely unfinished shell of Fort Sumter. Anderson was a former slave owner from Kentucky who 
was openly sympathetic to the southern cause in spite of his devotion to defending the Union, a 
dilemma that exacted a deep emotional toll on the career army officer. He was convinced that 
the newly formed and novice Confederate government was simply saber rattling and would not 
attack Sumter. His second-in-command, Doubleday, held a total opposite view, and was itching 
to take pre-emptive action against the South Carolinians, who were vile traitors from his 
perspective. (Larson E. The Demon of Unrest. New York: Random House. 2024) 


A portrait of Robert Anderson, commander of the Union garrison 
at Fort Sumter in 1860-1861. Anderson was reluctant to take any 
action that might rile the South Carolina militia, knowing full well 
the fort was not defensible. He received almost no clear military 
orders or political guidance from the outgoing President, James 
Buchanan, who was desperate to avoid the inevitable start of the 
civil war on his watch, or from the new Lincoln administration, 
which was equally inept and passive in March and April of 1861. 
Image source: Library of Congress. www.loc.gov. Accessed: 7/10/2024. 


The Captain of the Star was John McGowan, at age 52, one year younger than Lienau, with 30 
years experience at the helm of sail and steamships, including numerous stops in Charleston 


264 


Harbor. Prior to taking command of the Star, McGowen was an officer and boat captain in the 
U.S. Revenue Marine Service, a forerunner of the Coast Guard, with combat experience in the 
Mexican-American War of the 1840s and many years chasing pirates and contraband (black 
market) ships along the Florida coastline. (Captain John McGowan, USRMS, Elizabeth City, New 
Jersey. New York Times Obituaries. January 18, 1891. www.nytimes.com/archives. Accessed: 
September 3, 2023) John Lienau was second-in-command as Second Mate and Andrew Brewer, 
younger but also with considerable experience, was the Lead Pilot. Lienau’s role on this voyage 
was diverse including serving as Relief Pilot (presumably during bathroom breaks, meals and 
rest periods), Flag Officer in charge of signaling, Bursar and Crew Chief. It is important to note 
that ship’s officers and crew were unarmed civilians working as contractors for the War 
Department. 


Aside note: The New York Times printed two front page headline articles on January 14, 1861 in 
the morning and evening editions that included detailed descriptions of the Star’s journey to 
Fort Sumter, peppered with commentary from the civilian crew and the army officers on board. 
The morning edition also printed Captain McGowen’s trip report verbatim. The evening article 
presented a lengthy synopsis of the entire journey with focus on the action within Charleston 
Harbor, amplified with quotes from Captain McGowan. Our description of the events of January 
9, 1861, from the perspectives of the ship’s crew, is largely drawn from these first hand reports 
published in the NY Times. The citations for these articles and other sources, not cited in the 
following text, are listed on page 277. 


The Star departed its New York dock at night on January 5, 1861, stopping shortly thereafter at 
Governor’s Island in the harbor to pick up 200 soldiers fresh out of training, their rifles and 
munitions, three young Union officers (Lts. Charles Wood, William Webb and Charles Thomas), 
a surgeon, PGS Ten Broeck, and provisions including food, bedding, medical supplies and 
baseballs, bats, gloves and bases — more about this later. Lt. Wood was the commanding officer 
for this 200-man unit, although he played a minimal role in the events that were about to 
unfold. Lienau supervised the onboarding process, which occurred prior to dawn on January 6. 
Heading south, the Star reached the mouth of Charleston Harbor at 1:30am on January 9, 1861. 
Based on his past experiences in the harbor, McGowan could tell that daybreak would be hazy 
with limited visibility. Charleston Harbor in 1861 had a notoriously treacherous entrance due to 
shallow depth and swirling sandbars. Typically, lanterns were hung on buoys to mark the safe 
entry channel and the rampart torches on Fort Sumter were lit all night to guide ships. But on 
this night, there were no guiding channel lights, the harbor lighthouses were dark, navigational 
buoys had been removed and Fort Sumter could not be seen. Using look-outs on both sides of 
the ship and depth soundings, Brewer slowly guided the Star through the sand bars and into 
the mouth of the Bay until the ship coasted to a stop at 4:00am, still unable to see the night 
torches of Fort Sumter. All lights on the Star were doused to avoid attracting attention from 
South Carolina militia stationed at the mouth of the Bay, and the soldiers and their officers 
were sent below deck. The Star was flying a standard U.S. maritime flag, typically used by 
commercial vessels in this era. 


A side note: A brief comment about harbor size is appropriate to help understand the events on 
the morning of January 9, 1861. Susan and | have driven the Charleston Harbor shoreline by car 
and also taken a boat tour of the Bay to Fort Sumter, which is on a tiny island roughly a half- 


265 


mile from the north and south shorelines. An important take-away: the harbor is not wide near 
the mouth where the fort is located. A ship the size of the Star of the West, suddenly emerging 
from the morning fog would look immense from either shore. Maneuvering the ship, especially 
turning it around, inside the Bay must have been challenging for McGowan and his pilot. 


Around 4:30am, for reasons that are murky, oversized versions of the 33 star Union military 
garrison flags were hoisted up flagpoles at the bow and stern of the Star. It is unclear who gave 
the order but it would have been Lienau’s responsibility as Signal Officer, although it seems 
unlikely that he would not have first consulted McGowan. Another steamship, further into the 
harbor, dimly became visible in the pre-dawn haze and then suddenly fired red rockets (i.e. 
flares) into air and lit read and blue deck torches. This steamer was most likely a harbor guard 
ship manned by South Carolina militia posted near the sand bars to detect and announce the 
arrival of incoming ships, but historians still debate the accuracy of this assumption (Larsen, 
2024). The flares and illumination from the preceding ship roused ten cadets on night duty in a 
shoreline battery at the South Carolina Military Academy (now the Citadel) located on the 
southern lip of the harbor entrance. The young cadets scurried to the wall overlooking the Bay 
to observe the commotion. The flares continued from the lead ship for several minutes, and 
then, trailing by less than a half mile, the outline of the Star began to emerge out of the haze. 
The cadets were astounded at the sight of a giant paddlewheeler seemingly just a stone’s throw 
away and flying very large and easily discernable Union military flags. 


The 33 star military garrison flag of the United States flown 
by the Star of the West on January 9, 1861. 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 7/1/2024. 


ly 


The cadet squad was led by 21-year old senior George Edward Haynesworth, who ran up a 
small incline to a barracks where the cadet’s faculty supervisor, a Major P.F. Stevens, was 
sleeping (it was 4:30am after all). After rousing Stevens from his slumber, the cadet told him a 
Union warship was entering the harbor. Stephens, probably still groggy from his abrupt 
awakening, went outside to take a look. Even through the haze, he could see that the Star was 
a merchant ship without any visible deck guns, but it was indeed, flying Union military flags, 
which was puzzling. After berating Haynesworth for confusing a warship with a merchant 
paddlewheeler, Stevens ruminated about the possible reasons for the ship’s appearance in the 
harbor, concluding that it might be in distress or possibly even lost. He added, “probably we 
should warn the ship before the boys on the north shore (the militia on the opposite side of the 
harbor) decide to fire on it.” That was all Cadet Haynesworth needed to hear. He ran back to his 
squad and told them to unstraddle the cannon (i.e., remove a covering tarp) and prepare to fire 
warning shots in front of the steamship’s bow. Haynesworth did not wait for Major Stephens to 
make his way down the hill to the shoreline battery to supervise the cadets’ actions. Around 
4:45am, at literally point blank range, Haynesworth lit the fuse on a 12-pound cannon leveled 
nearly parallel to the ground and sent the first ball roaring toward the Star. (Baker G. Cadets in 


266 


Gray. The Story of the Cadets of the South Carolina Military Academy and the Cadet Rangers in 
the Civil War. Lexington South Carolina: Palmetto Books. 1989)

firing “first shots of the Civil War’ on

in Harpers Weekly and was reprinted in 
Southern newspapers with wildly

Instead of plunking into the bay ahead of the steamship, the first ball clipped the front mast at 
about 15 feet above deck level, knocking off a tall ladder, which crashed through the pilot- 
house roof, barely missing Brewer. The second ball flew pass the pilothouse window so close 
that McGowan and Lienau both swore they could see creases in the ordinance. The third shot 
was like a low line drive in baseball (i.e., a daisy cutter), that apparently skipped several times 
on the water, fortunately slowing its rotation, and thudded sharply against the hull, knocking 
some the ship’s external paneling loose, springing a small leak, and profoundly alarming the 
soldiers in the hold. So much for military student marksmanship! The soldiers in the hull of the 
Star clamored to the staircases, demanded to be allowed topside, and banged their rifle butts 
on the hatch door and hull. 


McGowan realized that the appearance of 200 armed Union soldiers on the deck would 
enflame the situation. Lienau was dispatched to calm down the troops below deck and settle 
the young officers, a task that he apparently accomplished, although Lt. Wood was allowed to 
stay above deck, and observed the shelling. The cannon fire from the south bank alerted the 
shoreline batteries at Fort Moultrie on Sullivan Island to the north of Fort Sumter. Accounts 
vary, including McGowan’s own action report, but anywhere from nine to 23 shots were fired 
by state militia from nine pounders at Moultrie. Again, good fortune held for the Star and her 
crew. The militia, who actually were trying to hit the Star, managed to misfire on most of their 
shots, but some damage was sustained. From McGowan’s post-action report: “One shot passed 
just clear of the pilot-house, another ball passed between the smokestack and walking beams of 
the engine (the long arms that connected the engine to the paddlewheel), another struck the 
ship just abaft of the fore-rigging and stove in the planking, while another shot came within an 
ace of carrying away our rudder. Still another shot came bounding across the water at its 
surface and struck us about two feet above the water line, just below where our man was taking 
depth soundings.” (Larsen, 2024) Lt. Wood reported that one ball clipped the front mast, 
sending shards of wood raining down on the deck, rattling the soldiers even more, and another 
shot thudded off the hull, leaving a dent, but no significant damage. 


Even though the batteries north and south of the Star were observed by Lt. Wood to be “firing 
wildly with little calculation of aim,” McGowan decided that an attempt to land at Fort Sumter 
would surely throw the Star into greater danger as a stationary target parked along the island’s 
pier, and he also was perplexed by the lack of communication from Sumter. While under fire, 
he ordered the ship’s flags to be raised and lowered several times to attract Sumter’s attention, 


267 


but received no response. After concurrence from Lienau, McGowan ordered Brewer to 
navigate out of the harbor as “expeditiously as required”. This decision was reinforced soon 
after when the bow spotter identified two small steamships launched from Fort Moultrie, each 
pulling skiffs loaded with soldiers. Fortunately, the little steamers were just as slow as the Star, 
and floundered in the choppy water. McGowan directed Lienau to signal Sumter that the 
landing was aborted. Anderson and Doubleday, who had no idea that the Star had been 
dispatched to Charleston with reinforcements, watched the shelling of the steamer from the 
island fort’s ramparts. However, Anderson feared that returning fire on the South Carolina 
militia would be perceived as a hostile move and might evolve into an attack on the fort itself, 
much to Doubleday’s consternation. The garrison at Sumter failed to do any signaling back to 
the Star, because the fort’s flags were tangled in a snarled ball around the base of the flagpole 
(much like tangled necklaces) and could not be extracted for communication with the ship. 
(Moore F. The Rebellion Record: Diary of American Events, with Documents, Narratives and 
Illustrative Incidents. The Firing on the Star of the West and Captain McGowan’s Report. In: 
January 26, 1861 Harper’s Weekly. New York: GP Putnam. 1861)

By 7:30am, Brewer had navigated the shoals north of Fort Sumter albeit with a few concerning 
scrapes of the paddlewheel, and the Star was out to sea. Both militia steamers gave up the 
chase after a swell flipped one of the skiffs, tossing soldiers into the bay. By the time the 
soldiers were hauled back into the boat, it was evident that the Star had passed through the 
sandbars, and further pursuit was pointless. Once clear of the harbor, Lienau let the troops and 
officers up on deck, and McGowan explained the events of the past three hours. The trip north 
to New York was uneventful, with the Star tying up to its dock on January 13, 1861.

In South Carolina and across the south, newspaper headlines announced that a “brazen Yankee 
violation of sovereign and independent territory” had been repulsed, lauding the role of the 
military academy cadets in “firing the bold first shots for our independence”. The majority of 
the newspaper accounts of the incident were distorted as illustrated by a January 10, 1861 
article in a Charleston newspaper paper, displayed below, claiming that the Star of the West 
had been sunk, but the crew and soldiers were rescued by a passing ship.

Six more southern states succeeded by February 1° sparked by the Fort Sumter incident and 
other perceived Northern insults. In New York, McGowen’s accounts of the incident in the NY 
Times enflamed animosity toward the “traitorous Carolinians and slavers” and sparked several 
large public demonstrations calling for reprisal. Lienau, Brewer and McGowan appeared 
together on January 18, 1861 at a hearing commissioned by the NYC Steamship Association. 
McGowan did most of the talking and praised Brewer for skillful navigation under treacherous 
circumstances, and Lienau for calm management of the tension below deck. 


John Lienau lived in NYC for the rest of his life. He listed Steamship Captain and Steamship 
Master (the later suggests ship ownership) on NYC and federal census reports, evidence that he 
continued to advance in his profession. He was a member of the New York German Club and 
was an officer in an organization comprised of New York based steamship captains. He also 
entered the insurance industry in the 1860’s, serving as a director of companies that sold life 
insurance and, befitting his career, marine insurance. For the Germania Life Insurance 
Company, which targeted the German-American community in NYC, Lienau was one of 21 
original investors who met at Delmonico’s restaurant in the early 1860s to each pledge $10,000 
($240,00 in 2023) toward the $200,000 capitalization required by NYC for company formation. 
(Guardian’s History: Guardian Life Insurance Company of America (formerly: Germania Life 
Insurance of New York). www.guardianlife.com. Accessed: June 19, 2023) A NYC death 
certificate indicates that he suffered a fatal “apoplexy event” (i.e., stroke) in 1876.

financial portfolio that allowed him to invest large sums of money in these life insurance 
companies, which he did shortly after his adventure in Charleston harbor on the Star of the 
West. A career at sea as a crewmember, then as now, is rarely associated with accumulation of 
wealth. A related question is what happened to John’s apparent wealth. His son and grandson 
seemingly lived in rather austere circumstances in the following decades. 

Aftermath of the Star’s Voyage to Fort Sumter 

Fort Sumter: After the Star of the West incident, the South Carolina militia seized all federal 
(Union) property in Charleston, and repeatedly made demands for evacuation of Union troops 
from Fort Sumter, which were rejected by the lame duck outgoing U.S. President James 
Buchanan, and after March 15, by the newly inaugurated President, Abraham Lincoln. The 
Confederate States of America (CSA) sent its first appointed general, PGT Beauregard, to 
Charleston to begin siege operations. After Lincoln threatened to reinforce the little fort by 
force if necessary and then sent a poorly organized fleet of six small ships to attempt a far- 
fetched evacuation mission that never occurred, Beauregard issued a final evacuation demand, 
which Anderson reluctantly refused. The South Carolina Militia launched an artillery barrage on 
April 12, 1861, effectively starting the Civil War. Although the CSA bombardment from four 
different positions north and south of Fort Sumter did little meaningful damage to the 
compound, Anderson and Doubleday surrendered the next day when a fire broke out near a 
storage area where munitions were housed. 


The only casualties occurred during the surrender ceremony when a cannon exploded in the 
midst of a 100-gun salute, requested by Anderson and approved by Beauregard (who were 
close friends), to commemorate the lowering of the Union flag. On the i firing, a soldier by 
the name of Daniel Hough, apparently misloaded a firing cartridge into his cannon, which 
exploded when he lit the fuse, tearing off both of his arms and killing him instantly. Flames from 
the blast ignited other firing cartridges lying on the ground nearby, leading to a secondary 
explosion that injured six other Union soldiers, one of whom died several days later in a 
Charleston hospital. The cannon salute was halted after Hough’s accident, so that Confederate 
and Union soldiers could jointly build a casket, construct a cross and dig a grave for Hough in 
the rocky soil of the Sumter parade grounds. Then soldiers from both sides stood at attention 
while three more cannon blasts were fired as his wooden casket was lowered into the ground. 
And, thus, the Civil War commenced. The South Carolina militia facilitated the evacuation of 


270 


Anderson’s garrison on Sunday, April 14, 1861 by sending two small sloops, the Catawba and 
the Isabel, to transport officers, soldiers and a small number of laborers to one of the three 
Union ships waiting outside the harbor sandbars. (Swanberg WA. First Blood: The Story of Fort 
Sumter. New York: Charles Scribner Books. 1957. Accessed via Google Books. 
www.books.google.com on June 7, 2023) 


Daniel Hough was the first of approximately 360,00 Union fatalities during the Civil War. Like 
Pvt. Hough, 67% died from non-combat causes including accidents. (National Park Service. The 
Civil War — Facts. www.nps.gov. October 27, 2021. Accessed July 15, 2024) The first confederate 
fatality was a 23-year old CSA chaplain by the name of Noble Leslie Devotie who drowned late 
at night on February 12, 1861 when he fell off a gangway to a boat he was boarding at Fort 
Morgan, Alabama. Devotie was a graduate of the University of Alabama, where he was 
instrumental in founding a fraternity, Sigma Alpha Epsilon (SAE), my fraternity at Dickinson, and 
the only fraternity founded in the Antebellum South (i.e., before the Civil War). Prior to joining 
the Confederate army as a chaplain, Devotie was an ordained Baptist minister, and led a large 
congregation in Selma, Alabama. According to SAE lore and a boisterous drinking song penned 
in his honor, Noble was not immune to the appeal of liquor, and possibly was under the 
influence on the night of his dockside missteps. (Myhre EL. The History of Sigma Alpha Epsilon: 
Part One, 1856-1865. Pullman, WA: Washington State University Press. 2007) Devotie was the 
first of approximately 260,00 Confederate fatalities during the Civil War, and similar to Union 
mortality, 2/3s of these deaths occurred in non-combat situations. (National Park Service, 2021)

Star of the West: McGowan, Brewer and Lienau never served again on the Star after the Fort 
Sumter voyage. The Union Army continued to use the Star as a troop transport. Shortly after 
the surrender of Fort Sumter, Confederate forces captured the Star in Matagorda Bay, Texas 
after the ship picked up Union troops from a garrison stationed at Indianola, Texas. (Holmes 
JDL. The End of the Star. Texas State Historical Association. www.tshaonline.org. Accessed: June 
15, 2023) The Confederates changed the name of the ship to the CSS St. Philip, and used it as a 
medical ship and training center for Confederate seamen. In 1862, the St. Philip was moved up 
the Mississippi River and served as a supply and medical ship supporting Confederate troops 
besieged at Vicksburg. To foil a Union naval assault on Vicksburg in April 1863, the St. Philip was 
sunk broadside in the Tallahatchie River where its great size completely blocked the river and 
prevented the attack. The Star/St. Philip remained in the river for years. Local residents 
scavenged wood, pipes, furniture, and machinery from the carcass until what was left of the 


271 


vessel was towed into the main body of the Mississippi River and burned in 1871. (Scharf JT. 
History of the Confederate States Navy: From its Organization to the Surrender of the Last 
Vessel. Fairfax, VA: The Fairfax Press. 1977) 


John McGowen: Captain John McGowen served in the Civil War as a captain of a “Mosquito 
Fleet” of small Union ships blockading the entrance to Chesapeake Bay. After the war, he 
returned to the U.S. Revenue Marine Service and was instrumental in creating ocean rescue 
units at 12-15 mile intervals along the entire New Jersey coastline. 


Abner Doubleday: Doubleday rose to the rank of General during the Civil War, and was 
considered to be one of the most effective commanders in the Union army. His brigade played 
a pivotal role in the Union victory at Gettysburg. After the war he was a successful businessman 
with focus on modernizing transportation. One of his major entrepreneurial accomplishments 
was establishing the cable car system in San Francisco. However, he may be most remembered 
today for his association with the game of baseball. (Barthel T. Abner Doubleday: A Civil War 
Biography. Jefferson, NC: McFarland and Company. 2010)

to be the face of the new game. Doubleday fit the role perfectly. As part of marketing efforts, a 
mythology was created surrounding the origins of the game with Doubleday as a central figure. 


In actuality, the game primarily evolved from the popular English game of rounders, which 
immigrants brought to North America. Rounders has been played in England for centuries. 
(Block D. Baseball Before We Knew It: A Search for the Roots of the Game. Lincoln, Neb: 
University of Nebraska Press. 2006) Sir Francis Drake was a rounders devotee, and was in the 
midst of a tournament in Plymouth when the Spanish Armada was first sighted. When his aides 
excitedly informed him of the Armada, he told them to settle down, noting “No point spoiling a 
good match just because the bloody Spanish finally arrived. I'll have ample time to dispatch 
them after last pitch.” Johnson B. The Spanish Armada. Historic UK. The History and Heritage 
Accommodation Guide. www.historic-uk.com. June 2016. Accessed: July 17, 2023) Rounders 
involved a batter, a bowler who threw underhand as in softball, five fielders and three bases in 
the original form, later expanded to four bases. Until the start of the 19" century, players took 
turns batting, attempted to hit the pitch and round the bases before a fielder could hit the 
batter with the ball. Reaching the final base without being pegged by the ball was a run. After 
six rounds of at-bats, the player with the most runs was the victor. Rounders evolved into a 
team competition with various numbers of players per team by approximately 1800. 


The traditional English game of rounders was informally 
known as base-ball, or ball as far back as the 1500s. 
Brought to North America by immigrants, rounders was 
slowly molded into the game we now recognize as 
American baseball. The illustration at the left appeared in

Between 1835 and 1865 in the U.S., there was constant tinkering with the rounders format, 
rules, equipment and playing field. Therefore, it is difficult to pinpoint a single person as the 
creator of American baseball. It certainly was not Abner Doubleday although he helped to 
spread awareness of the game. By the end of the Civil War, a reasonably well-accepted set of 
guidelines for the game, known as the New York Rules, began to be used in leagues across the 
country. An individual named Alexander Cartwright who was a Manhattan bank clerk and a 
fireman is credited with the final version of the New York Rules. Cartwright built the first ball 
field with bleachers and organized the first touring professional team, the New York 
Knickerbockers, where players received a share of the gate receipts from crowds.
