George Edward Haynesworth: There is no record of whether or not George, who preferred his 
nickname “Tuck”, was reprimanded for his impetuous decision to fire on the Star of the West. 
Considering the notoriety that the incident brought to the South Carolina Military Academy — 
probably not. After graduation in June 1861, newly commissioned Lt. Tuck Haynesworth served 
in a coastal artillery unit in South Carolina for the duration of the Civil War, occasionally firing 
on Union blockade or supply ships that cruised too close to shore. In addition to firing what 
many consider the “first shot” of the war, Tuck also likely fired one of the last shots. In May 
1865, more than a month after Lee’s surrender, Union General William Tecumseh Sherman’s 
army marched into South Carolina to disarm rogue CSA units. When Sherman’s cavalry reached 
Haynesworth’s coastal battery, Tuck ordered his men to fire on the approaching Union 
horsemen, claiming later that he was unaware of the ceasefire. His men did fire, but only 
managed to excite the horses and anger the Union cavalry who took Tuck into custody for six 
weeks before releasing him. After the war, Haynesworth graduated from law school and 
practiced near Charleston, taking on more pro bono cases than his budget could tolerate. He 
was one of the few attorneys in the Palmetto State willing to represent Black freemen during 
Reconstruction, which earned him the antipathy of many in the community. To help with 
finances he also worked as a magistrate in a petty crimes court. In December 1887, while 
hearing a case involving a property dispute between two families with longstanding grievances, 
a gunfight broke out in the courtroom and Haynesworth was killed by a stray bullet at the age 
of 46. (Obituary: George E. Haynesworth. January 12, 1888. The Calhoun Times. Calhoun- 
Gordon County Obituaries Project. Digital Library of Georgia (www.dlg.usg.edu). Georgia Public 
Library Service. University System of Georgia. Accessed September 21, 2023) 


GE “Tuck” Haynesworth in 1863, two years after “Firing the Shot that 
Ignited the War for Southern Independence” per a Charleston, South 
Carolina newspaper. 


Image source: Wikimedia Commons. www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. Accessed: 
7/16/2024. 


Notes on the Star of the West’s Supply Mission to Fort Sumter: And now for the rest of the 
story! Under pressure from the Secretary of War, outgoing President James Buchanan, alas a 
Dickinson College graduate, and running neck and neck with Harding and Trump as the worst 
U.S. president, decided on December 28, 1860 to send the Brooklyn, the second largest U.S. 


274 


warship, to Charleston Bay to re-supply Fort Sumter. Two days later, fearing that a warship 
would inflame the already tense political situation in Charleston and receiving advisement that 
the Brooklyn was too large to enter the shallow bay, Buchanan changed his mind and ordered 
the Secretary of War to find a suitable civilian ship for the mission. The search led to the Star, 
which was directed to make a secret trip to Charleston, including loading supplies and soldiers 
at night and running without an American flag when entering Charleston harbor. After the Star 
launched in darkness on January 5 in a futile effort to avoid detection by New York city 
newspapers and Confederate spies, Buchanan changed his mind again, reaching the conclusion 
that the unarmed Star might be in danger, or, more likely, the action would enflame South 
Carolinian passions, leading to an assault on Fort Sumter. This was the last thing Buchanan 
wanted - he was desperate to get out of office before the war began. He directed the War 
Department to dispatch the Brooklyn to catch up to the already departed Star, and order 
Captain McGowan to turn back. As we know, the Brooklyn was not able to overtake the Star. 
The Brooklyn reached the Charleston on the afternoon of January 9" after the Star had already 
exited the harbor and was on its way back to New York. The big warship followed the Star 
home. (Chatelain NP. Repurposing Captured Vessels. Star of the West. Emerging Civil War. 
www.emergingcivilwar.com. October 20, 2022. Accessed: September 20, 2023) 


In spite of the efforts of the Union Secretary of War and the President to keep the Star’s 
mission a secret, the South Carolina Governor, South Carolinian militia commanders and several 
large newspapers in southern states including the Charleston Mercury were well aware that a 
steamship loaded with troops and supplies was headed south from New York harbor almost 
from the moment the ship hoisted anchor. Reporters of the New York Tribune assigned to 
monitor comings and goings in the harbor filed an article about the Star departing under the 
“cloak of darkness amid a fog of mystery, likely to convey troops to Sumter” that was published 
in the morning edition on January 6, 1861, and soon, by the new technological marvel of the 
telegram, this report was relayed to newspapers in South Carolina. Additionally, Buchanan’s 
cabinet and support staff were riddled with southern sympathizers, many of whom attended 
meetings where the re-supply mission was discussed. Various political and military leaders in 
Charleston received telegrams from these sympathizers prior to the Star’s departure that 
conveyed details about the mission. Oddly, the War Department decided to communicate with 
Anderson about the mission by sending him a letter via registered mail, which finally reached 
him several days after the Star had arrived and departed. (Larsen, 2024) 


A side note: The lead-up to the Civil War in the late 1850s and the ensuing four-year struggle 
was the first event in U.S. history, and basically in world history with the exception of sporadic 
reports during the Crimean War (1853-1856), where the public received almost instantaneous 
reports on political and military events via the magic of telegraphy. Large crowds in the North 
and South gathered at telegraphy stations, where readers shouted telegram text, or, somewhat 
slower but still “same day”, the decrypted text was re-typed and posted on bulletin boards. 
Newspapers in major cities generally could report relatively detailed accounts of war events 
within a day of a battle or an important meeting. In the 1860s, major cities were heavily strung 
with telegraph wires swaying from pole to pole, and major telegraph trunk lines were hung in 
the countryside between cities. During the war, the Union army made much more effective use 
of the technology for planning and battlefield coordination than the CSA because of the 


275 


northern states’ huge investment in telegraph lines and the building of hundreds of connection 
and decoding stations. The CSA had a much smaller telegraph network in 1861 and made little 
effort to expand the system, or use what existed for military operations. The Star of the West 
was not recalled because telegraph communication was not used land to sea or between ships 
at sea until the 1890s. (Hochfelder D. The Telegraph in America, 1832-1920. Baltimore, MD: The 
Johns Hopkins University Press. 2012) 


Historians do not agree on the question of why the ship, which had apparently entered 
Charleston Bay ahead of the Star, suddenly fired flares and illuminated deck torches. In the 
immediate decades after the Civil War, the prevailing contention was that the ship was Cuban, 
flying a Spanish flag, and aimed to alert the shore batteries to the presence of the Star of the 
West out of Spain’s sympathy for the Confederate cause. If true, how the Cuban ship 
determined, in dense fog, that the Star was a U.S. vessel remains an unknown. As an alternative 
theory, some 20" century historians contended that the lead ship, in spite of the dense fog, 
discerned that a large vessel was closing on them and simply wanted to alert the Star to its 
position to avoid a fog bound collision, a frequent occurrence in that era, not an unreasonable 
scenario. As described in the preceding narrative of John Lienau’s adventures in Charleston Bay, 
a currently prevailing theory is that the Star was detected by one or more harbor guard ships 
(probably smallish steamboats, but often not described as such) manned by South Carolina 
militia as the big paddlewheeler slowly groped its way through the sandbars. This theory is 
consistent with the fact that political and military leaders in Charleston knew that the Star was 
on its way to Fort Sumter. 


The question of who ordered the raising of the U.S. military garrison flags on the Star, in 
contradiction of the War Department directive, also has been debated. In spite of the fact that 
McGowen took responsibility in his voyage report and during hearings, some historians believe 
that he was covering for Lienau, or possibly lower level crewmembers that independently 
decided to hoist these flags. CSA participants in the incident reported that the aft Stars and 
Stripes flag was the biggest flag they had ever seen, "trailing for several yards out into the 
steamer’s wake.” (Crawford SW. The Genesis of the Civil War: The Story of Sumter, 1860-61. 
London: Forgotten Books. 2018. Originally published in 1887 by Charles L. Webster Publishing in 
New York City, a company owned and managed by Mark Twain. Accessed from the Library of 
Congress www.loc.gov on July 12, 2024) 


Notes on the Mysterious Ellen (Ella) Lienau: In spite of all the genealogical research tools 
available today, a key person in the family lineage simply remains a mystery. We know Ellen 
(Ella) Lienau existed and know rudimentary facts about her life, but all efforts to fill out her 
story came up empty. The surname Lienau is the subject of only a few family histories. One of 
these sites suggested that Ella may have been born in Germany and travelled with John Lienau 
from Germany to England, and then to the Caribbean, and finally to the U.S. as a girl friend 
and/or co-worker. (Lienau R. Pictures and Figures From My Life. Berlin: Lichterfelde Archive. 
1949. Digitized 2019 by Internet Archive. Accessed from Internet Archive on April 11, 2023) The 
Royal Mail Steam Packet Company employed females on transatlantic ships as cabin maids and 
laundry workers, as did the U.S. Mail Steamship Mail Packet Company, so that theory is 
plausible. However, the fact that Ella lived in Havana while John lived in San Juan until 1854 


276 


casts doubt on this theory. It is conceivable that Ella got to Havana by some other means, or, 
maybe she was born there (nothing is known about her race / ethnicity). John may have met 
Ella while on one of the many shore leaves in Havana that he undoubtedly enjoyed during his 
Caribbean years with the British and U.S. Mail Services.

Oregon or Bust - William Firman Hendricson (1823-1908) 


William Firman Hendricson, great grandson of Okey Hendrickson, was known as Firm or WF by 
friends, coworkers and family. He is notable for a variety of reasons. He was the person who 
formally changed the family surname from Hendrickson to Hendricson when he wrote 
“Hendricson without K” on the sign-up form for a wagon train journey to Oregon in 1845 and 
on documents he filed with the Oregon Provisional Government between 1845 and 1850 to 
submit claims for land parcels. The spelling change was made official on subsequent voter 
registration cards, U.S. census forms, birth certificates for his children and his death certificate. 
WF crossed the plains from the Midwest to the west coast four times between 1845 and 1852, 
which must be some type of record. He was the first of the midwestern Hendricson’s, across a 
multitude of families that were offspring of Okey Hendricson and his many children and 
grandchildren to make an employment and social class jump from itinerant farm laborer to 
successful farm and business owner. WF established himself as a prominent citizen in Albany, 
Oregon, firmly planting the Hendricson family on the west coast and building a degree of 
inherited wealth for his children. Like his ancestors, Cornelius, Hendrick and Okey, WF had an 
adventurous early life including a stint as a 49er in California striving to strike it rich in the gold 
rush, several ocean journeys from the Pacific to Atlantic sides of the continent and many 
overland trips by wagon train to the West Coast. Perhaps most impressively, WF overcame the 
early deaths of both parents, which left him to fend for himself from age 11 onward, with 
virtually no formal education. 


WF is also unique in that he is the first descendant among the nine families to leave a record of 
his life largely in his own words. Around the year 1900, WF and many other early settlers in the 
Willamette Valley of Oregon were interviewed about their lives before and after their wagon 
train journey to the west by a particularly active genealogical society based in Portland, Oregon. 
Reports published by this society in the pre World War | era captured the stories of these 
pioneers in considerable detail, providing readers with unique perspectives on the wagon train 
ife and the early years of settlement in the Willamette Valley. The annual publication of this 
genealogical group was titled Portrait and Bibliographical Record of the Willamette Valley Early 
Settlers Beginning in 1844. \t was printed in Chicago by the Chapman Publishing House yearly 
rom 1904 through 1913, and provided detailed information on the lives of pre-Civil War 
emigrants to the Oregon Territory including WF Hendricson, enriched by first person 
descriptions of events. WF was also interviewed and contributed historical documents (diaries, 
letters, bills of sale) for the 1885 publication, History of the Willamette Valley and Personal 
Reminiscences of Its Early Pioneers by Henry Lang. A book by Weldon W. Rau titled, Surviving 
The Oregon Trail — 1852. As Told by Mary Ann and Willis Boatman and Augmented With 
Accounts by Other Overland Travelers, provided information on the daily routine and challenges 
‘aced by wagon train participants with anecdotes provided by WF Hendricson. The monograph, 
Abner Hackleman’s 1845 Trip to Oregon by Glenn Harrison (2013; Columbia Gorge Interpretive 
Museum Publications) provided details of WF’s first trip to Oregon and anecdotes about his role 
and experiences during that caravan. Pioneer Stories of Linn County, Oregon by Lloyd Haskins 
(1984; Early Pioneer Press) also provided accounts of WF’s roles on subsequent wagon train 
journeys. The following story of WF’s life and his extensive wagon train experience is largely 
drawn from these sources, supplemented by preceding Hendricson family histories listed on 


278 


pages 145-147, sources cited in the following text, and a number of general Oregon Trail and 
Oregon Territory resources indicated at the conclusion of WF’s story. 


William Firman Hendricson was described by others on wagon trains as a man of medium 
height and very trim as befit a man who from age 11 worked as a laborer, and a man who made 
four trips from the Midwest to the west coast, largely by walking. However, despite his many 
adventures and success in later life, | was not able to locate a picture of WF that | could verify 
with 100% confidence. A photo that is “most likely” his wife Sarah at age 35 appears later in 
WFP’s story. 


WF was born in Poplar Flat, Kentucky in December 1823. His parents, John F. Hendrickson 
(1794-1824) and Nancy Wilson Hendrickson (1798-1834) moved 150 miles north to Ohio while 
Nancy was pregnant with WF, seeking better farm employment opportunities. After WF’s dad 
was killed in a grain silo accident on New Year’s Day 1834, Nancy, WF and two siblings lived 
part-time with her parents in Highland, Ohio, 50 miles from Cincinnati, and also spent time in 
Popular Flat with WF’s paternal grandparents, Daniel and Sarah Herbert Hendrickson. Nancy’s 
movement back and forth between Ohio and Kentucky continued for ten years until she died 
from unknown causes in a hotel room during one of these trips in the little community o’ 
Chillicothe, Ohio. She was just 36 years old. 


At age 11, WF found himself stranded in unfamiliar surroundings, suddenly in charge of two 
younger sisters and with a deceased mother. Remarkably, he communicated with the loca 
sheriff about the circumstances of his mother’s death, arranged for coroner services, and made 
arrangements to have his mother’s remains transported to his grandparent’s house in Highland, 
paying for the transport wagon with the small amount of money remaining in his mother’s 
purse. Taking pity, the hotel proprietor allowed WF and his sisters to stay in the hotel and fed 
them until the church pastor in Chillicothe could drive WF and his siblings to Highland in his 
carriage. Upon reaching Highland, WF found his mother’s parents to be understandable 
distraught, and soon after found himself without adult guardians when his grandparents 
decided they could only care for the two younger children. His grandparents assigned WF to a 
neighboring farmer who promised “board, bunk and bath” for the young lad if he did his work. 
Daniel Hendrickson back in Kentucky was either never contacted about taking in young WF, or 
also decided that he could not handle the responsibility. 


After being cast out by his Ohio grandparents, WF began a ten year journey into adulthood that 
carried him from place to place in Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin, Michigan and lowa where 
he landed a series of jobs on the low end of the employment hierarchy, working according to 
his own words, as a “muck boy brooming out barns and slopping out horse stalls, stable boy 
tending pigs, cattle, mules and horses, laborer repairing barn roofs, corrals and fences, field 
hand picking crops, a plowman, tilling fields behind a mule, and crewing an ore hauler in Lake 
Superior (Upper Peninsula of Michigan), making more money in a month than | made for six 
months on farms.” Finally, in lowa at the age of 21, WF reached top hand status on a small farm 
specializing in corn and pigs, and was charged with “teaching three callow boys how to do a full 
day’s worth of work,” coming full circle so to speak. 


WF was rarely enrolled in a school at any point in his life and claimed to have learned reading, 
writing and calculating from other farm hands and shipmates older than him as he moved from 


279 


job to job seeking higher pay. However, he did make an effort to attend church wherever he 
landed, which is how he met his future wife, Sarah Agnes Jackson (1828-1891) at a church in 
Pleasant Grove, lowa in 1844. Sarah, although just 16 years old, was the church organist, also 
played guitar and sang in the choir. WF, who also enjoyed singing, joined the choir, and struck 
up a relationship with Sarah. She was the daughter of a local wheat farmer, Onias Augustus 
Jackson (1802-1862). Based on correspondence and documents that he signed, Sarah’s father 
often referred to himself as OA rather than Onias. He was born in South Carolina and after 
moving as a teenager with his parents to Indiana, he married Daraxa Laughlin in 1827. The 
couple had two daughters, Alcestis and Sarah, and relocated to lowa in 1840, seeking better 
fortune after numerous years of poor harvests in Indiana. However, Onias also struggled in 
lowa to make ends meet with too little land to produce sufficient volume for meaningful profit 
and too many agricultural competitors. As a consequence, he often worked as a hired hand at 
other farms to bring in extra money. Sarah’s father met WF during one of these extra jobs and 
took a liking to the serious and motivated young man, who was courting his daughter. 


A side note: The historic record is unclear about the nature and ultimate fate of Onias and 
Daraxa’s marriage. Daraxa did not participate in Sarah’s and her father’s eventual relocation to 
Oregon via wagon train — the story of which is told in the following pages. It is not known if 
Daraxa and her husband “lived apart,” which was not unusual in an era where divorce was 
frowned upon, were legally separated or were officially divorced. Daraxa lived a long life, well 
into her 90s, and mostly resided in Rush County, Indiana until her death in 1896. 


The big news in lowa and other midwestern states in 1844 was the opening of the Oregon 
Territory to settlement, and the successful arrival of the first wagon trains of settlers into that 
territory, attracted by an abundance of fertile land in a temperate climate, especially near the 
Pacific Coast in the Willamette Valley. As previously described in the Notes on the Oregon Land 
Donation Act of 1850, the U.S. congress would eventually, in 1850, approve substantial free 
land donations to Oregon emigrants if they met stipulations for developing the property and 
permanently settling on it. Until 1850, there was plenty of land for the taking for white 
emigrants to Oregon, if a person could just get there, stake a claim, and squat on the land (i.e., 
build a shelter and keep others from claiming the land), and, foremost, all Native Americans 
had been driven off their ancestral homelands (see the previous Notes on Manifest Destiny, 
page 55). In 1843 and 1844, six wagon trains each comprised of 150-200 wagons and nearly 
1,000 people had traversed the 2,000-mile route, soon to be known as the Oregon Trail, to the 
Pacific Northwest. For WF, and thousands of other midwestern farm workers and their families, 
this seemed like the opportunity of a lifetime. 


As a Christmas 1844 gift to himself, WF ordered a copy of Emigrants’ Guide to Oregon and 
California — A Guide for the Westward Traveler. (1" ed.; Hastings L. St. Louis, MO: Charless 
Printers. 1843; reprinted in 1994 by Applewood Books) This was one of many such handbooks 
for prospective travelers to the west coast that provided recommendations for food, clothing 
and equipment, wagon design criteria, and tips for surviving the trip. Inspired by the guide, WF 
attended a “Western Settler Symposia” in January 1845 at a Des Moines hotel. The symposium 
was sponsored by Dr. Abner Hackleman, a physician and already a veteran leader of Oregon 
Trail round trips. (Harrison G. Abner Hackleman’s 1845 Trip to Oregon. Columbia Gorge 
Interpretive Museum Publications. www.columbiagorge.com. 2013. Accessed: March 5, 2023) 


280 


Hackleman and his New London Emigrating Company (named for his Connecticut-born 
parents), were recruiting a new caravan to depart in 1845. Hackelman used stunning hand 
painted lantern-slides (cutting edge 1840s media) depicting the majestic Rocky Mountains, the 
Columbia River Basin, and the lush Willamette Valley, supported by a 20-piece orchestra, which 
enraptured the audience who marveled at the scenery and the projection technology. 


WF came away from the Hackleman Symposium convinced that Oregon was his future, and a 
way to end his itinerant existence. On the final day of the symposia, he placed a $20 deposit 
and signed a pledge sheet indicating he would do his utmost to join the 1845 Hackleman 
“Oregon or Bust” caravan that was scheduled to head west from Saint Joseph on the Missouri 
River 50 miles north of present-day Kansas City. St. Joe was the most prominent departure 
point for settler caravans (as they were called then) heading west to California, Utah or Oregon. 


Stereographic lantern-slide projection, often called 
“Magic Lanterns,” captivated 1840s and 1850s 
audiences. In major cities, audiences viewed 
illuminated stories, accompanied by music and 
narrators. Hackleman’s presentation likely was a 
new experience for WF and other audience 
members.

Now engaged to Sarah, WF next had the task of convincing his finance that their future was in 
Oregon, and not in dry, dusty lowa with its bitterly cold winters. Sarah, perhaps with teenage 
enthusiasm, readily agreed before WF could finish his “well rehearsed Oregon argument” as did 
her father Onias, who loaned WF $50 for journey provisions. When WF returned, hopefully in 
1846 with a property claim in hand, he and Sarah would marry, join another wagon train and 
start their life together as they traveled across the continent to their new home in Oregon. 
Sarah’s father hoped to join them in Oregon by 1850. WF soon after talked an older farm hand, 
Thomas Morgan (1795-1886; yet another Morgan, but not a relative), into travelling with him to 
share the expenses of outfitting a canopied wagon, and buying oxen to pull the wagon. Thomas 
Morgan was born in Wales (of course!) and grew up in Sussex, England, coming to the U.S. at 
the age of 13 with an older brother. Thomas married as a teenager, but his young wife perished 
in a boating accident on the Ohio River. After that tragedy, Thomas drifted from one farm job to 
another but for much longer than WF, 25 years. At age 50, he was ready to turn his life around. 
In March 1845, WF and Thomas traveled in their tarp covered wagon with four oxen to Saint 
Joseph, Missouri to meet up with Hackleman and the other Oregon or Bust caravan members. 
When WF and Thomas reached St. Joe, they found the town teaming with people, wagons, 
oxen, mules and horses, and they could not locate the Hackleman caravan. Finally, they 
received a tip that the Hackleman group had set-up camp south of town.

When WF and Thomas approached the Hackleman camp and drove their wagon under a large 
banner announcing the New London Emigrating Company, they saw an odd sight. Dozens of 
people were walking in a large circle around the central camp where the wagons were parked 
and horses, mules, cattle and oxen idly grazed. Some wanderers were carrying small children. 
WF recognized Hackleman, approached and inquired: “what are these people doing?” The 
response: “what you'll be doing tomorrow, practicing endless, boring walking.” Hackleman 
explained that one of the lessons learned from previous caravans was that most of the 
travelers, even though they led hard lives on farms, in mines, logging and other lines of outdoor 
labor, were not fit to walk 15 miles a day, day after day, which was his daily goal for the 
journey. He explained that if a would-be traveler could not walk his one mile loop around the 
wagons 15 times for three straight days, carrying children if necessary (children had to walk the 
same miles as adults), he would bar them from the caravan and return their deposits. Everyone 
in a family had to pass the test, young and elderly. 


A side note: As will be discussed in the Notes on Wagon Train at the end of the WF Hendricson 
story, wagons were not for hauling people. Instead, they were for hauling food, water kegs, 
cooking utensils, medical and hygiene supplies, clothing, bedding, barrels for bathing and 
washing clothes, lanterns, wagon repair tools, spare wagon parts including axle trees, yokes, 
connecting poles, ropes, harnesses and wheel rims, axes, shovels, saws, wrenches and hammers, 
weapons, ammunition, and entertainment, such as books, bibles, decks of cards, checker and 
chess boards, fiddles and slate boards for the children.

On April 16, 1845, the Oregon or Bust Caravan consisting of 39 covered wagons, and one large 
camp provision wagon, under Hackleman’s control (a Conestoga Wagon eight feet longer than 
the typical settler wagon), crossed the Missouri River at a shallow point suitable for fording. 
After all wagons rolled up on the uncivilized side of the Missouri, Hackelman’s group 
commenced an anticipated five-month journey to Oregon. Hackleman’s wagon train consisted 
of 303 people. There were 38 family units comprised of 256 adults and children. The train also 
included 47 men traveling single. The single men included WF, Thomas and Hackleman’s six- 
man command team including himself as Wagon Master, and five multi-purpose scouts, 
hunters, herders and rule-enforcers. 


A Conestoga wagon was much larger than a 
settler wagon. It was called the provision wagon, 
camp wagon or captain’s wagon depending on 
the Wagon Master’s preferences. The Conestoga 
hauled replacement equipment, extra food, 
medical supplies, weapons, and commodities for 
trade with Native tribes. 

Image source: Wikimedia Commons. 
www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. Accessed: 3/7/2023. 


A herd of 150 oxen, mules and horses accompanied the train to serve as replacements for 
animals that died on the trail. The herd also included 100 head of cattle for use in Oregon, or as 
a potential food source if hunting was unproductive. The herd were tended by two or three 
riders, often supported by Native horsemen hired for this task along the trail. The herders and 
several herd dogs kept the livestock about a hundred yards away from the train to reduce dust. 


Before departure, Hackleman dismissed two families who were unprepared, and two days after 
the Missouri crossing, a third family, with five young children, dropped out and headed back, 
the parents apparently concluding that they were not cut out for five months on foot, herding a 
gaggle of children.

The photograph above depicts the John Switzler family on Hackleman’s wagon train, probably 
in Wyoming based on the mountains in the background and the browned faces, indicative of 
months under the sun. This photo by an unknown photographer is one of the first ever taken of 
a family on the Oregon Trail, and appears in many books, articles and internet sites on the early 
wagon trains to Oregon, including The West: An Illustrated History for Children (Duncan D.

could afford to outfit and travel with two wagons. Many Oregon-bound family units were multi-

WF and Thomas arrived at the Hackleman termination campsite near present-day Portland on 
September 23, 1845, about five months after departure. Along the way 11 travellers lost their 
lives (11/303; 3.6%), much lower than the average ten percent mortality rate along the Oregon 
Trail during the early years of westward emigration. During the first month, while still in the 
Kansas prairie, an entire family of six was afflicted with a gastrointestinal disease, probably 
dysentery. Their wagon was separated by one mile from the rest of the group and they were 
not allowed to enter night camp (e.g., when wagons were circled) to minimize chances of 
disease spread. Ultimately, the mother and two children died of the disorder. After their burial 
near the trail, the father and surviving children ultimately recovered, rejoined the main train 
and reached Oregon. When crossing the long dusty plains of Nebraska during the second 
month of the trip, two elderly travelers passed away in their sleep at night of unknown causes, 
and were buried the next morning. The train soon departed, with Hackleman telling the 
assembled travelers that “lingering here will benefit no one presently, and will only endanger us 
to poor weather later in our crossing. We must gather ourselves and move ahead.” 


During July in Wyoming, one of the single men rode away one evening and did not return, 
violating Hackleman’s rule of no lone riders away from the train at any time. WF and Thomas 
joined search parties the next day, but no sign of their travel companion was found by 
sundown. Anxious to continue forward movement, Hackleman selected a panel of three older 
men, including Thomas Morgan, to decide what to do with the man’s oxen, wagon and 
possessions. The panel voted to assign the wagon and oxen to a large family of eight struggling 
with an undersized wagon pulled by scrawny horses, and the man’s possessions were added to 
Hackelman’s camp provision wagon for doling out to needy travelers during the later stages of 
the trail. Five of the deaths occurred near the end of the journey. As was the norm for wagon 
trains before 1850, the Hackleman train attempted to travel the final 100 miles on the 
Columbia River via crudely constructed rafts. The river float started at a sweeping bend in the 
river marked by a striking rock formation known as Pulpit Rock near the present day town of 
The Dalles. Just past the Pulpit Rock entry point, the raft fleet entered the picturesque but 
dangerous Columbia Gorge known for gusty winds, swirling eddies and unpredictable rapids. 
During a windy and rainy passage through the gorge on a day with particularly choppy current, 
three rafts flipped, throwing wagons, supplies, and travelers into the river and two other rafts 
crashed into each other, damaging wagons, but miraculously did not sink. Three children and 
two adults could not be rescued and were swept away. Oregon Trail historians estimated that 
nearly 200 overland travelers drown on the Columbia stretch of the trail before it was 


285 


abandoned in the 1850s. (Unruh JD. The Plains Across: The Overland Emigrants and the Trans- 
Mississippi West: 1840-1860. Urbana: University of Illinois Press. 1993) 


Pulpit Rock near the first Christian mission established in Oregon 
was near the entry point for wagon trains attempting to float the 
Columbia River to Oregon City. 

Image source: Columbia Gorge Discovery Center Photo Archive. Accessed via 
Oregon Digital www.oregondigital.org on 3/9/2023.

and crossings were treacherous, a principle

As was typical with wagon trains crossing to Oregon, WF and Thomas often saw small bands of 
Natives on horseback. These bands were primarily Sioux, Kiowa and Pawnee, and largely were 
content to parallel the train a mile or so away as it crawled across the plains. With increasing 
frequency as the trip progressed, several tribesmen would approach the wagon train during 
evening camp and offer to trade commodities. The tribes typically offered food (mule deer, elk 
and bison meat), blankets, and services (hunting, guiding, assistance with river crossing, cattle 
herding) to the travelers. Deals were almost always struck so the tribal traders would not ride 
away displeased, and frankly, the trains often needed assistance. There was only one instance 
where there was tension between the travelers and Natives during WF’s 1845 crossing. 
Hackleman periodically sent out small hunting parties, to augment the food in the provision 


286 


wagon, led by one of his scouts and comprised of several male travelers handy with rifles. WF 
reported that he never was invited on a hunt trip, but Thomas Morgan often participated. 


In western Nebraska, a hunt party from the Hackleman train came upon a pack of pronghorn 
deer in a ravine. Dismounted and creeping forward in the high grass, the group reached the lip 
of the ravine, and stood to fire. To their astonishment, a half dozen well armed natives, likely 
Sioux, rose from the grass even closer to the pronghorns, and turned to face the startled wagon 
train men. After a few tense moments, Hackleman’s men backed away to their horses, and 
carefully made their way back to camp. That evening, two elderly tribal members approached 
the camp, and made it clear they wanted to meet with the Wagon Master. After the meeting, 
Hackleman gathered the men in the camp and told them, “no more hunting until we clear over 
the North Platte. The Sioux will bring us game if we tell them that we are hungry, but this is 
their range and we are to stay clear.” 


Arriving at the trail termination camp known as Oregon City along the Willamette River a few 
miles west of present-day Portland, WF was surprised to see that it was teaming with “many 
dozens and dozens of families and so many single men, probably husbands with family back 
east.” All of these people were from Hackleman’s prior caravans and those of a competing 
wagon train organizer, Lindsay Applegate. In his interviews, WF estimated to the Genealogical 
Society that “there surely was a town’s worth of people there — maybe a thousand.” The 
families had set up tents or lean-to’s attached to their wagons for shelter, and were still looking 
for property that met their needs a year after arrival. Many were discouraged, and not happy to 
see more arrivals, also searching for land. WF soon learned that scouting for available land was 
time-consuming, he would have many competitors, and that there was a hodge-podge of 
largely informal and conflicting rules governing how tracts of property were to be surveyed and 
claimed. He was especially warned to be alert for unscrupulous land agents, many of them 
British, seeking to be paid upfront by settlers to find property, or seeking to sell acreage for 
which they falsely claimed to have a deed. 


At this point, WF and Thomas divided up. WF was intent on exploring the Willamette Valley to 
the south of camp, while Thomas Morgan sought land closer to the Columbia River. Early in 
October 1845, Thomas left the camp with a wagon he purchased from an 1844 traveler and 
headed north. We do not know if WF and Thomas ever saw each other again. We do know that 
Thomas Morgan eventually settled in Portland, married again, had several children, became a 
businessman instead of a farmer, operating a hardware store / lumber yard, and passed away 
in 1886 at the age of 91 after finding the success in Oregon that eluded him in the midwest. 


WF soon deduced that many of the White settlers struggled with the task of searching for land 
because they attempted to explore by themselves with no knowledge of the region, or were led 
by land agents who also were dimly aware of the region’s geography. To the pragmatic 
Hendricson, this was foolhardy. He avoided the land agents prowling Oregon City and instead 
approached a nearby Chinookan camp to hire scouts (WF had read about the tribe in accounts 
of Lewis and Clark’s journey to the region). By Christmas, 1845, with the assistance of two 
Chinookan tribesmen (brothers) who served as his guides and enforcers, in situations of conflict 
with other “land grubbers like me”, WF had identified a 500-acre parcel of land. The land was 
located on a branch of the Willamette River, which his guides called the Santiam River, 25 miles 


287 


from present day Salem, Oregon. He documented his survey of the Santiam land and riverbank 
with his own detailed notes and sketches. Then he hired an experienced Metis surveyor (see 
pages 82-84) to verify his calculations and prepare an independent survey. On January 3, 1846, 
WF submitted a land claim with both surveys attached at the provisional government office in 
Oregon City, and provided the $25 claim holding fee, which emptied his pockets. 


A side note: The Oregon Provisional Government was created in 1843 by three early settlers 
who were elected to commissioner positions at a meeting of roughly 150 White males in Oregon 
City. Many Oregon city residents were excluded from the 1843 Oregon Governance Meeting: at 
least 50 White women residing in the encampment, nearly 100 Metis trappers and traders who 
were long-time residents of the area, approximately 60 British settlers who had lived in the area 
since the 1830s, and a dozen families of Pacific Islanders who, somehow, had made their way to 
the area. The two stated goals of the Provisional Government were to establish procedures for 
wresting land away from the control of Native Peoples who lived on the Pacific side of Oregon 
including the Kalapuyan, Chinookan and Molallan peoples, and initiating a political campaign, 
with paid lobbyists in Washington DC, for Oregon to be formally designated as a U.S. territory, 
which occurred in 1846, and as a state, which occurred in 1859. (Johansen DO. Empire of the 
Columbia. A History of the Pacific Northwest (27 ed.) New York: Harper Collins. 1967) 


However, the Oregon Provisional Government actually devoted much of their energies during 
1844 to 1847 to evicting British settlers from Oregon. The British citizens were mostly former 
trappers that had turned to real estate acquisition. The British were trying to obtain tribal 
support for a British Oregon Province, and were buying tracts of land directly from these tribes. 
At this time, the U.S. and Britain were engaged in a sabre rattling diplomatic feud over the lands 
comprising modern day British Columbia, Washington and Oregon. This dispute would not be 
inally settled until 1847 when the U.S. obtained rights to present-day Washington and Oregon. 
After the treaty, most of the Oregon Brits moved north to British Columbia but some applied 
or U.S. citizenship. lohansen, 1967) 


With his land search completed and paper work submitted, WF turned his attention to 
returning to lowa and to his finance, Sarah. Hackleman had announced that he was departing 
or a return trip to St. Joe in March 1846. WF and 30 other “Husbands of the Midwest” plus two 
disgruntled families and several Hackleman employees, signed up for the reverse trip back to 
Missouri. However, a serious glitch changed those plans. Dr. Abner Hackleman died of typhoid 
ever before the journey commenced. Upon hearing the news, the ever-resourceful Hendricson 
hustled over to the office of Hackleman’s primary competitor, Lindsay Applegate (1808-1892), 
who was also planning a return trip for men traveling single and a group of his employees. 
(Allen C. The Applegates. Portland, OR: Oregon Historical Society; Oregon History Project. 
www.oregonhistoryproject.org. 2003) WF found that Applegate’s office was a large and well- 
urnished Chinookan lodge that he rented from the tribe. Applegate agreed to take on 
Hendricson but for a $30 fee due in one month, “because of the lateness of his application and 
the accommodations that will need to be made.” WF did not have the money but quickly 
rounded up several camp jobs, including doing surveying for other prospective settlers, and 
generated the funds by Applegate’s deadline. 


288 


After loss of a son and other travelers when attempting to raft 
his 1843 wagon train down the Columbia to Oregon City, 
Lindsay Applegate scouted and established a safer route. 
Known as the Applegate Trail, the new route approached the 
Willamette Valley from the south. After Oregon achieved 
statehood, Applegate served in the legislature for many years 
and was Tribal Agent representing the Klamath and Modoc 
Peoples in negotiations with Oregon and U.S. government. He 
had the prevailing biases of the era, but ran afoul of the 
governor for arguing vigorously on behalf of tribal interests. 
(Allen, 2003) 


Image source: Wikimedia Commons. www.commons.m.wikimedia.org. 
Accessed: 3/12/2023. 


Like Hackleman, Lindsay Applegate had already led several trains to Oregon from Missouri, and 
made return trips to the Midwest to form new caravans. On the second journey in 1843, his 
train experienced a calamitous raft accident on the Columbia River. Applegate’s nine-year son 
and another youngster were swept way and drowned, along with a man who tried to rescue 
them. In Applegate’s own words: “Whirlpools looking like deep basins in the river, the lapping, 
splashing, and rolling of waves ... presently there was a wall of anguish, a shriek, and a scene of 
confusion in our boat that no language can describe. The boat we were watching disappeared 
before our eyes, and we saw men and our dear boys struggling in the water. Elisha and Warren 
[Applegate’s son] were drowned. We resolved if we remained in this country, to find a better 
way for others who might wish to emigrate.” (Applegate L. Notes and Reminiscences of Laying 
Out the Old Emigrant Road into Southern Oregon in the Year 1846. Oregon Historical Quarterly. 
1921; 22: 12-34. www.ohs.org. Accessed April 2, 2023) 


Unbeknownst to WF and other travelers that signed-up for the return journey to the east, 
Applegate intended to use an alternate route through southern Oregon and Nevada. Applegate, 
his brother Jesse and 13 of his employees had scouted the route during the winter of 1845-46. 
Applegate concluded the trail was viable in spite of encountering hostility from the Paiute tribe, 
leading to deaths of two Applegate men in a skirmish, and enduring a snowstorm that trapped 
the entourage in a cave for a week with almost no food. The Applegate Route, as it originally 
was known, also allowed travelers to take a brief side trip to view the magnificent Crater Lake 
and to see the entirety of the Willamette Valley as they trekked through it from south to north. 
By 1850, Applegate’s southern approach became the most travelled route to Oregon City. 
Ironically, it came to be known as the Barlow Road, after a subsequent wagon master, Samuel 
Barlow, found a couple of short alternative paths in central Oregon that reduced travel time by 
two days and also bypassed a few miles of tribal lands. 


Despite a tense exchange with WF and the other Husbands on the day before departure when 
Applegate informed the group that he planned to use a newly discovered route, all of the 
returning midwesterners showed up the next morning, wagons loaded and oxen or mules 
hitched, ready to depart. Applegate’s group of 38 men (30 Husbands and eight employees) 
proceeded without incident along the new route during March 1846 until they reached the area 
of Klamath Lake in southern Oregon where a large band of Paiute tribesmen appeared one 
evening and camped several hundred yards away. Even with guards posted, Paiute braves after 


289 


nightfall managed to sneak into a makeshift corral and grab four horses. As the horses were 
being led away, one of the guards (a Husband) caught sight of movement in the dark, and fired 
off a round from his pistol to alert Applegate’s group. Others in the wagon train ran toward the 
sound of the gunshot, further unnerving the guard who, apparently confusing onrushers for 
tribesman, fired another shot, striking and seriously wounding Applegate’s most trusted scout 
in the left shoulder. At the sound of the second gunshot, additional gunfire occurred, leading to 
one Husband, standing next to WF, losing part of an ear, and greatly frayed nerves among the 
whole group. (Applegate L. Oregon Historical Quarterly. 1921; 22: 12-34. www.ohs.org. 
Accessed: April 2, 2023) 


After sending his scouts out to make sure the Paiute band had departed the area, Applegate 
turned his attention to the badly injured scout, Moses Black Harris, who was one of the very 
few Black frontiersman, and one of the most famous explorers and guides of the 1820s and 
1830s. In his time, Moses Harris was as well known as Mountain Men Jedediah Smith, Jim 
Fitzpatrick, John Coulter, Hugh Glass, and Jim Bridger. (Utley RM. After Lewis and Clark: 
Mountain Men and the Path to the Pacific. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press. 2004) In 1836, 
Harris guided the wagon train led by the missionary Marcus Whitman to the vicinity of Walla 
Walla, Washington. in 1837, he was instrumental in building Fort Laramie in eastern Wyoming, 
one of the most famous of the western trading posts and later a military base. In 1838, he 
guided a wagon train led by August Sutter (of the 49er gold rush at Sutter’s Mill fame) to 
California, and in 1844 was the chief guide for the largest wagon train ever to cross the 
continent to Oregon, comprised of 450 wagons and 1400 pioneers. With WF and another 
Husband holding Moses down, Applegate extracted the round from his shoulder and sewed up 
the wound as best as he could with twine. 


An image of Moses Black Harris, by the Western artist 
Alfred Jacob Miller. Moses was born a slave in South 
Carolina and freed as a teenager. He made his way west 
in the 1820s, learned Native dialects, and lived with a 
Shoshone band for ten years. He turned to scouting and 
guiding White settlers to California, Oregon and 
Washington. Moses Black Harris was one of organizers of 
the Mountain Men Rendezvous that occurred annually 
from 1824 to 1843 on the Green River in Wyoming.

Harris. Portland: Oregon Historical Society; Oregon History Project.

It was WF’s first experience with the damage inflicted by gunfire and it left him shaken. “But for 
a few feet, it could have been me felled by a shot” he said in his genealogical interview. WF 
also described the recriminations that followed the incident with Applegate’s employees 
demanding banishment of the Husband who wounded Moses Harris. To calm the hostility, 
Applegate placed the blame on himself for not posting his own experienced men as guards and 
Moses expressed no anger toward the shooter, saying it “was just bum luck that he got shot.” 
Yet tensions within the wagon train population remained high. The Paiutes continued to follow 


290 


for several days, further adding to the stress level with WF remembering, “not one in our bunch 
got hardly an hour’s sleep until we crossed over from that piece of land.” 


When the wagon train rejoined the main Oregon Trail at Fort Hall in Idaho, Applegate left 
Moses Harris to recuperate and assigned the most outraged employee to stay behind and look 
after Moses at the trading post until the next westbound wagon train arrived. This move 
alleviated the atmosphere of animosity within the travel party, although the evening social 
hour around the campfire was far less entertaining without Moses telling stories about his 
exploring and tracking exploits over the past 30 years. The tallest tale, hotly debated by 
western historians, was Moses’ account of his journey to the Yellowstone area with Daniel 
Boone in 1812, who was 78 years old that year. According to Moses, he and Boone met up with 
Mountain Man John Coulter, the first European to see the Teton Range and the sulpheric hot 
springs of the Yellowstone region. Most historians now believe that this journey likely did occur, 
although some of the details may have been embellished by Harris and other western 
storytellers. (Belue TF. Daniel Boone’s Yellowstone Hunt. True West Magazine. March 31, 2022. 
www.truewestmagazine.com. Accessed: April 4, 2023) Moses Harris would have had a 
substantial role in the film, The Revenant, if the story of Hugh Glass’s 250 mile trek through the 
wilderness to reach Fort Kiowa, South Dakota, after being attacked by Arikara warriors and 
mauled by a bear, had been depicted accurately. Harris led a rescue party sent out by the fur 
trading company that employed Glass. Harris soon found the mountain man as he was trudging 
the final few miles toward the fort. Harris then traveled with Glass on his search for John 
Fitzgerald, a trapper who left him to die after the bear attack and stole his rifle. (Coleman JT. 
Here Lies Hugh Glass. A Mountain Man, A Bear, and the Rise of the American Nation. New York: 
Hill and Wang Books. 2012) 


WF especially lamented the departure of Moses Harris; he was learning the basics of the 
Shoshoni language from the Mountain Man, which was a base language understood well 
enough by other tribes to allow communication. Moses was also mentoring him in tribal social 
and communication norms, especially how to interpret Native behavior when they were in the 
presence of Europeans (i.e., ig" century emotional intelligence). 


A side note: Moses Harris recovered but only after an infection in his left arm and shoulder left 
him impaired on that side for the rest of his life. In spite of this limitation, Moses found success 
locating property for settlers in Oregon and Washington. Eventually he was able to purchase his 
own land near Vancouver, Washington where he lived with his Metis wife. In 1855 at the age of 
76, Moses reluctantly accepted “just one more” job for Applegate, which involved guiding a 
wagon train largely populated by eastern investors back to Missouri. A cholera outbreak during 
the final days of the return journey took his life less than 50 miles from St. Joseph, Missouri. 


To compensate for the loss of two men, Applegate assigned WF to manage the provision wagon 
and one other Husband with good rifle skills to serve as a hunter. One of the roles of the 
provision manager was to negotiate with tribal bands that approached the train seeking to 
trade. To accommodate the trading and avoid irritating the tribesman, Applegate had 
scrounged through Oregon City and a nearby Metis camp before they departed to stock the 
provision wagon with hand mirrors, hair brushes, combs, metal kettles, hammers, wood saws, 
old pistols, tins of tobacco, pipes, footwear, coats with buttons and other desired items. 


291 


Applegate handled the trading until the train reached Nebraska with WF assisting and then WF 
took the lead as the train progressed toward St. Joseph. In his genealogy interviews, WF shared 
how much he enjoyed the bartering role, describing several lengthy trade meetings running late 
into the night with Sioux elders, who enjoyed haggling with settlers as a form of entertainment. 
In one notable negotiation that WF considered a win for the wagon train, he swapping a set of 
kitchen kettles, a box of discarded hats and two “used-up” oxen in exchange for a Sioux led 
bison hunting trip that yielded meat for the entire wagon train for weeks. 


WF reached St. Joe, Missouri in early August 1846 and was home in Pleasant Grove, lowa by the 
end of the month, anticipating marriage to Sarah and preparation to return to Oregon the 
following spring. However, those plans did not play out. During WF’s 17-month absence, Onias 
Jackson and Sarah struggled. Two years of lean crops led to a bank foreclosure on his small farm 
for mortgage payment failure. Onias was now unhappily working on the farm as an employee 
for a trustee named by the bank, trying to pay down the note with meager monthly earnings. 
Sarah was waiting tables in a roadhouse on the trail to Des Moines to bring in extra cash. 
Remembering his prior employment on cargo ships hauling iron ore across the Great Lakes, and 
sizing up the Jackson’s situation as hopeless, WF proposed that he, Onias and Sarah leave lowa 
and head for Northern Michigan (i.e., the Upper Peninsula) where an iron ore mining company 
was aggressively recruiting employees at unheard of high salaries. Initially flabbergasted, Sarah 
and her father came around after WF reviewed the financial advantages of defaulting on the 
loan, simply walking away, and heading north to Michigan. 


Six weeks later the threesome were in Marquette, Michigan. WF landed a crew position on a 
iron ore freighter shipping between Marquette and a steel mill in Sault Ste. Marie in Ontario, 
Canada. Likely assisted by WFs persuasiveness, Onias found himself in a desk job in the mining 
company office and Sarah obtained work in a boarding house/restaurant. The three rented a 
house on a hill with a view of Lake Superior, and spent the next two years making money with a 
goal to raise enough funds for Sarah and WF to get married. With success in Michigan, planning 
for Oregon took a backseat to their life in Marquette. In the summer of 1847, more than a year 
after he departed Oregon City, WF received word from the newly installed Territory of Oregon 
that his 1845 claim was invalid due to non-activity, which ended further contemplation of a 
move to Oregon. In the spring of 1848, WF and the Jacksons returned to Rush, Indiana where 
Sarah was born so that WF and Sarah could marry in the same church where her parents 
exchanged their vows. At that point, it looked like Marquette, Michigan would become their 
permanent home and talk focused on whether to buy an older home or build a new one, with 
room for father-in-law Onias. However ... one Sunday morning in the fall of 1848, WF picked up 
the Marquette newspaper on the front porch, opened it and read headlines about a Gold Rush 
in California. WF and Sarah’s lives were about to change once again. 


| would like to have been a fly on the wall when WF introduced the idea to Sarah and her father 
of yet another trip to the west coast, this time to the gold fields of California. Even though they 
collectively had three steady incomes, were planning to build a home, and apparently enjoyed 
living in Marquette, WF’s argument in favor of a try at striking it rich ultimately won over his 
wife and father-in-law. In early March 1849, WF said good-bye to his now pregnant wife, and 
soon was on the trail west, a member of a wagon train comprised of 170 men with 
approximately 50 ox drawn wagons. The Wagon Master was Peter Burnett, who, the year 


292 


before, had scouted and established a trail from Fort Hall, Idaho to the southernmost of the 
two California gold rush fields near Sutter’s Mill where the first nuggets were discovered.

In his remembrances, WF made only a few comments about his Forty Niner (49er) venture. He 
suggested that his time panning was limited to a few months (he arrived in the gold fields near 
Coloma, about 30 miles from Sacramento, in July, 1849) observing, “more steady money was 
made providing than panning.” In spite of that comment, it appears that WF had early luck in 
his stream panning and decided to cash out. We know that WF traveled to San Francisco in 
November of 1849 to open an account and make a deposit at the one and only bank in 
California in 1849, the Naglee Bank and Repository. Subsequent to that deposit, WF never again 
appeared to be financially challenged for the remainder of his time in California, his return trip 
to New York by steamship, during his two subsequent overland journeys to Oregon, or while 
establishing his farm near Albany, Oregon. We can only conjecture about his apparent profits 
from a few months of gold mining, but they must have been reasonably substantial. 


A side note: /n contrast to the popular perception of 49ers’ fruitless panning efforts that led to 
financial ruin, the majority of gold rush participants made money on the venture, and 5-10% 
accumulated generational wealth. Overall, the panhandlers profits from sale of gold nuggets 
infused at least 40 billion dollars (in 2023 value) into the U.S. economy, injecting extensive 


293 


amounts of newly minted currency into people’s pockets, and helping to create a cash economy 
to replace an outdated barter system (Hine RV, Faragher JM. The American West: A New 
Interpretive History. New Haven: Yale University Press. 2000). However, the Gold Rush era had 
devastating effect on California’s indigenous Native Americans, who were aggressively forced 
off their ancestral tribal lands, leading to a severe population decline and widespread poverty. 
(Madley B. An American Genocide: The United States and the California Indian Catastrophe, 
1846-1873. New Haven: Yale University Press. 2016) 


49ers working a slew along the American River, searching 
for gold nuggets. Living conditions in makeshift mining 
camps with bars, brothels, taverns, jails and flophouse inns 
were as WF described in a letter to Sarah and Omar — 
squalid. It’s not surprising that the prim WF disengaged 
from this environment as quickly as feasible.

3/14/2023. 


After completing his banking, WF returned to Sacramento and took a job as a traveling sales 
clerk for Samuel Brannan Mercantile, selling mining equipment, tents, cots, boots and blankets 
in camps along the American River, where more than 100,000 people huddled in flap cities (i.e., 
tents), largely unprepared for the winter weather. Consistent with WF’s cryptic observation 
about providing versus panning, Sam Brannon was the first millionaire to emerge from the Gold 
Rush, using profits from his supply stores to buy huge amounts of real estate in California, 
which he lost in a divorce settlement following various nefarious business and political actions. 
(Bagley W. Scoundrel’s Tale: The Samuel Brannon Papers. Spokane WA: Arthur H. Clark 
Publishing and Utah State University Press. 1999) While in Sacramento working for Brannon, 
WF received a letter from Sarah, mailed three months earlier, indicating that Onias had lost his 
job with the Marquette iron ore company. They had moved back to their hometown in Rush 
County, Indiana, where both were having a hard time finding work. The letter may have pushed 
up WF’s departure timeline, although it seems like he was already planning to leave California. 


In April 1850, WF purchased a ticket for a San Francisco to New York passage via steamship 
connecting by mule caravan through the Panama Isthmus to the Atlantic side. The total cost 
was $450. He departed San Francisco on the SS Oregon, one of 17 steam paddle wheelers 
owned by the Pacific Mail Company, simultaneously a collaborator and a competitor with the 
U.S. Mail Steamship Company where John Lienau worked beginning in 1854. WF arrived in 
Panama 16 days after departure, spent a night in Panama City on the Pacific side, and on the 
next day commenced the pack trip with mules to the Caribbean side (the Aspinwall railroad was 
not built until 1852). We know that WF carried his gold with him on the homebound trip 
because he reported in his interviews that his first action in New York after clearing the ship 
was to walk to the Bank of New York, now operating as BNY Mellon, where he cashed in 
virtually all of his gold. Historians have found that with no other transport options that were 
considered safe or reliable, most 49ers carried their nuggets with them on their return trip 
home. Not surprisingly, the Panama jungle crossing was infamous for banditry. It has been 
estimated that least three billion dollars (2023 valuation) of gold and currency were stolen 


294 


during this hazardous trek, or on the connecting steamships, during the peak gold rush years. 
(Brands WH. The Age of Gold: the California Gold Rush and the New American Dream. New 
York: Anchor Books. 2002) However, WF apparently passed through Panama without incident 
and boarded the SS Falcon steamship on the Caribbean coast at the port of Colon on the 
Chagres River where the Aspinwal Mailing Processing Center was located (see page 263). 


Back in New York in early June 1850, the enterprising Hendricson purchased a freight wagon, 
went to the busy docks, and shortly after picked up a cargo shipment to transport to Cleveland. 
At this point in time, the New York harbor was receiving vastly more European, Caribbean and 
South American shipments than the poorly organized and under resourced teamster industry 
could handle. It was common practice to use independent teamsters to haul freight under a 
“paid when delivered” system. Hendricson unloaded his wagon at a Lake Erie dock, collected his 
fee, and shortly arrived back in Rush, Indiana to re-unite with Sarah, his infant daughter Leona 
and his father-in-law. He found them at a boarding house for farm workers where Onias was 
functioning as the property manager and Sarah was a housekeeper. We speculate that the 
reunion was not particularly cheerful in spite of WFs good fortune in California. At some point 
shortly after arrival, WF unveiled his latest scheme, which once again involved Oregon. 


While WF was traveling home from California, Congress passed the Oregon Land Donation Act 
of 1850 that provided settling families (i.e., husbands and wives) with up to 640 acres of 
donated (i.e., free) land to entice settlement. (Robbins WG. Oregon Donation Land Law. Oregon 
Encyclopedia. Project of the Oregon Historical Society. 2021. www.oregonencyclopedia.org. 
Accessed: April 7, 2023) WF later referenced the “storm that brewed in Rush” after he proposed 
an almost immediate departure for Oregon City to avoid missing out on good land. Sarah, 
understandably upset at being left behind twice while WF trekked west, only agreed to the 
venture if she accompanied WF this time, but she did not want to take her infant daughter until 
she was older. Sarah also was not comfortable living 2,000 miles from her father. Ultimately, a 
compromise was reached. Sarah and WF would travel to Oregon in 1850, acquire property and 
get settled, and then WF, by steamship and the Panama isthmus, would return to pick up Onias 
and Leona and travel with them to Oregon in 1852. Onias and Leona would move in with 
Onias’s sister in a nearby town until WF returned. This elaborate plan was feasible because the 
Pacific Steamship Company now operated passenger paddle wheelers up to the Columbia River 
to accommodate the rapidly growing population. We do not know why Sarah and WF did not 
elect to travel to Oregon by steamship, which was much faster and more comfortable. This 
decision is especially perplexing as it appears that Sarah may have recognized that she was 
pregnant with their second child even before the wagon train began its journey. 


On August 15, 1850, a late starting date for an Oregon Trail journey, WF and Sarah departed in 
a wagon train led by Wagon Master Seth Leweling from Council Bluffs, lowa on his second trip 
to the west coast. There were 42 wagons and approximately 160 adults and children in the 
train, mostly from lowa and Illinois. WF would later comment that this train was less organized 
than others he experienced, and barely averaged ten miles a day for the first month, not a 
sufficient pace to cross the mountain passes in Wyoming and Idaho before snow season set in. 
Two faster moving trains passed Leweling’s caravan during September, and three wagons in his 
group, apparently annoyed at the slow pace, pulled out of line and joined one of the speedier 
trains. A week later, three families in the Leweling train dropped out and headed back to 


295 


Council Bluffs after a series of accidents with their wagons, which slowed the entire group 
considerably (i.e., all wagons waited while damaged wagons were repaired). Soon after WF and 
Sarah witnessed the spectacle of a 300 wagon “go-back caravan” with over a thousand people 
plodding east, the victim of poor food resourcing and a very dry year that provided inadequate 
grazing for the hundreds of animals in that train. The go-back wagon train apparently made an 
impression on Leweling. He quickened the train’s pace to the normal 15 miles a day. 


Wagon accidents were common and a 
principle source of slow pace. Wagon train 
historians estimate that 20% of all wagons 
were forced to abandon the trip, and 
became “go-backs.” 

Image source: Slideshare. www.slideshare.net

Leweling at first was standoffish around WF, perhaps intimidated (I’m guessing here) by WF’s 
considerable wagon train experience, and his knowledge of “Indian Ways”. But, as the journey 
proceeded, Leweling increasingly turned to WF for route and general trip management advise 
and by Wyoming had asked WF to take the lead for trading negotiations with Native Peoples. 


After a dry and dusty, but not snowy, traverse of the Oregon Trail, Sarah and WF reached 
Oregon City by means of the southern Applegate (now Barrows) Route in mid December. 
During the journey, they managed to isolate themselves from a cholera outbreak that took 11 
lives, the bulk of two families. Three other travelers died from accidents (falls and a shooting 
during a hunting excursion), and an elder person, traveling with her daughter and son-in-law 
died from unknown causes. The fatigue and mental exhaustion of the seemingly endless trudge 
across the continent is evident in diary entries by the deceased woman’s daughter: 


Sunday, October 29 — Mother taken worse yesterday morning, lingered through the day and 
died about 9am this morning. We are now about 30 miles below Salmon Falls on the north side 
of Snake River. 


Monday, October 30 — Mother buried about 10 o’clock this morning under stones about 200 
yards above the crossing of the river. After crossing, we traveled eight miles to a spring to 
refresh the stock. 


Source: Flora SF. Emigrants to Oregon: Words of Oregon Trail Travelers. Chapter 6: The Diary of 
Eliza Richey. www.oregonpioneers.com. 2009. 

Sarah and WF lost of two of their four oxen on the trip, but fortunately had purchased two 
other animals in Council Bluffs to bring along in the wagon train’s supplemental herd. On the 
positive side there were two births near the end of the trail and both infants survived, which 
must have been comforting to Sarah who by the final stretch of the Trail was at least six months 
pregnant. After settling in the termination camp adjacent to Oregon City, which WF noted was 
looking more like an actual town, they immediately commenced their search for acreage. 
Without the aid of the Chinookan brothers who helped in 1845 (they had been run off by the 
territorial militia like most of the other Natives in the region), WF and Sarah scouted on their 


296 


own, and in February 1851 filed a claim for two adjacent 320 acre tracts, per the stipulations of 
the 1850 Land Donation Act, located six miles southwest of an emerging village in the middle of 
the Willamette Valley called New Albany.

The tracts were located adjacent to a small river named after the Calapooia tribe (also spelled 
Kalapuya) that historically resided in the area. The Calapooia River is an 80-mile tributary of the 
Willamette River. The Hendricson’s acquired 60 yards of direct riverfront access. Unlike many 
other rivers in Oregon, the Calapooia name remains to this day. There were two ponds on the 
land fed by snowmelt run off and underground springs. Mildred and Harold Hendricson, in their 
genealogical notebook, indicated that the homestead is located just south of the 
Albany/Corvallis KOA campground on Oregon State Highway 34. (Palmer T. Field Guide to 
Oregon Rivers. Corvallis: Oregon State University Press. 2014) Sarah gave birth to her second 
child, Lavinia, in March 1851 on this property. Lavinia was the first Hendricson born in the 
Pacific Northwest. After Lavinia, five subsequent children, including Omar Pasha Hendricson, 
who would extend our Hendricson family line, were born at this farm. 


Although the land in WF’s mind was not nearly as fertile as his lost 1845 claim on the Santiam, 
(he wrote many letters to the territory governor protesting the “jumped land”) the new tract 
turned out to be a solid choice. He and Sarah would live on this rural property for nearly 40 
years, engaging in farming with diverse, almost year-round crop rotation, stock raising and 
breeding, gradually expanding the farm to more than 2,500 acres with a main house, two 
smaller homes for children and grandchildren, a crew house for employees and three barns. 
Within the next year, Sarah and WF had acquired neighbors on each side of their property and 
others directly across the trail leading to New Albany. 


In May of 1851, WF fulfilled his pledge to return to Rush, Indiana to pick up daughter Leona, 
and his father-in-law. WF made it back to Rush in August of that year via Pacific and Atlantic 
steamships, the Panama Isthmus crossing and yet another freight hauling gig, this time to 
Chicago. WF continued his freight hauling locally in Indiana until the 1852 spring travel season 
arrived. Meanwhile back in Oregon, Sarah, who appears to have been a confident and capable 
young woman, and new daughter Lavinia lived alone on their farm, but with assistance from a 
nanny and a 60 year old man named Newton Henton hired by WF to supervise labor crews. 
Working together, Newton and Sarah supervising land clearing and tilling, fall seeding of grain 
crops, and construction of the first barn. Sarah also involved herself in the formation of a new 
Methodist Episcopal Church in New Albany, which would become a cornerstone of Hendricson 


297 


family life for decades, and, was a founding member of the Apollo Club, a musician’s group that 
eventually evolved into the Albany Philharmonic Society in the 1880s. 


In March 1852, WF, Onias, Leona, and a new travel partner, Onias’s recently widowed sister, 
arrived in Council Bluffs to await the departure of a wagon train that they had arranged to join. 
Once again, it is not clear why the quicker, safer and more comfortable steamship option was 
not selected. During his genealogical interviews, WF apparently was not asked about his 
preference for overland travel versus steamships, and did not offer any observations about 
mode of transportation. Since his 49er days, WF appears to have been on solid financial ground, 
and almost certainly could have afforded cabin space on a steamship. Yellow Fever, a life- 
threatening virus transmitted by mosquitoes, was rampant in the Caribbean in the 1850s, 
causing thousands of deaths annually. We conjecture that avoidance of Yellow Fever may have 
been a consideration for WFs westward trips, especially for the third journey with a pregnant 
wife, and the final trip with his young daughter and two older travel companions. For whatever 
reason, overland travel selected for WF’s final wagon train trip to Oregon. 


The four-person Hendricson-Jackson group, supported on this crossing with two covered 
wagons, joined a train headed by Wagon Master Jacob Jones at Council Bluffs, lowa. They 
crossed the Missouri River on March 23, 1852. The Jones train was comprised of 49 families and 
38 wagons plus the usual herd of replacement livestock, oxen and mules. Forty-two of the 
families were relatives of Jacob Jones and all were affiliated with a third generation Great 
Awakening Revivalist Congregation (see page 247) intent on establishing a less doctrinaire 
spiritual community in Oregon. Jacob Jones was the congregation’s spiritual leader. 


A_ side note: There were three phases, or generations, of the Great Awakening Movement in 
North America. Okey Hendricson experienced the first generation in the late 18" century in New 
Jersey. A second generation emerged around 1820, stimulated by urbanization and perceived 
de-personalization of human existence in cities. The third generation in the 1850s focused on 
social justice (slavery abolition and better relationship with Native Peoples) and enhancing 
Christian behavior among men. For example, the YMCA movement was started during the third 
generation of the Great Awakening. (Kidd, 2007) 


The other seven families on this trip represented a mixed bag of travelers, unique in that four o 
the adults within the group (WF, two men and a women) had previously completed the Oregon 
Trail. As WF and his family soon learned, the New Awakening families planned to implement 
their non-traditional religious experience during the crossing to Oregon, with nightly reviva 
gatherings. Additionally, Jacob Jones had never led a group across the Oregon Trail before. His 
Wagon Master experience consisted of guiding the 42 Jones families from Milwaukee to Council 
Bluffs, a pedestrian journey over established roads. As evidence of his inexperience, Jacob 
failed to outfit a provision wagon for the convoy, which decidedly hampered the journey. 


Similar to Wagon Master Seth Leweling in 1850, Jacob Jones initially was not receptive to 
suggestions from Hendricson or the three other experienced Oregon Trail travelers. Instead o' 
plodding along like Leweling’s group, Jones set a rapid pace, aiming for 20 miles a day (versus 
the conventional 15 miles), rousing the travelers at 3:30am in order to be on the road by 5:00 
am, and not stopping until 5:00 or 6:00pm. Within a month, three Wisconsin families peeled of 
at the first of several trading posts that had recently popped up on the Nebraska plains, saying 


298 


that they were fatigued and would latch-on to a subsequent train. Shortly after the first peel- 
off, three families, consisting of 19 people, self-assessed that cholera was running amuck within 
their group, and per expectation, isolated themselves a mile behind the main train. Nine deaths 
occurred and the survivors in these families turned around and headed back to Council Bluffs. 
The appearance of Cholera ignited panic within the train’s population, leading to agitation to 
stop and determine whether to continue. At this point, two more families made that decision 
for themselves, deciding that Milwaukee looked pretty good after all and opted to go-back east. 


The train was halfway across Nebraska at this point, pragmatically at a point of no return, and 
had lost eight families already. Wagon Master Jones, apparently in a bit of panic himself, finally 
held a meeting with WF and other experienced Oregon Trailers to assess the situation. The 
experienced travelers all recommended pushing ahead, telling Jones that fatalities will occur 
but the train had to maintain a forward schedule, no matter what tragedy befell them. They 
also recommended a more reasonable pace. Jones followed this advice, changing the morning 
rouse to 4:30am and making night camp no later than 4:00pm. Like Leweling, he also turned 
more and more to WF for guidance and once again assigned him to be the point person for 
tribal communication and negotiations, although without a store of tradable goods for 
bartering. To prepare for trading meetings, WF had to scrounge utensils, clothing, tools and 
tobacco from the wagon train population, and bought many items at a trading post.
