Tribal interactions were more difficult on this journey than on prior trips. Instead of requesting 
trading sessions, tribal spokespersons often approached WF with complaints, usually related to 
overgrazing by the wagon train’s livestock, which in the drought conditions of the 1850s, 
reduced grass and other vegetation available to animals. Tribes also complained about over- 
hunting by wagon trains, depleting the mule deer, bison and elk herds, and they complained 
that the clattering noise of hundreds of iron-rimmed wheels and the ever present dust cloud 
frightened away smaller game animals including antelope, badgers and foxes. In 1852, tribal 
complaints were usually not accompanied by demands or threats, that would come later, but 
WF spent considerable time soothing the frayed nerves of tribal leaders, who were starting to 
recognize the implications of the endless stream of wagon trains crossing their territories. 


WF’s main annoyance on this journey, shared by his non-Wisconsin travel partners, was the 
nightly spiritual revival meetings led by Wagon Master Jones himself, a devotee of the fire and 
brimstone, hell and damnation style of preaching. Rather than relaxing, reading and getting to 
bed early, the majority of the travelers spent the evening “hollering, bellowing, stomping and 


299 


singing” deep into the night, which made the herd restless, elicited noise complaints from tribal 
spokesman, and contributed to a sleepy-eyed, laconic start to the next day. Eventually, the 
seven non-Wisconsin families separated their wagons from the main circle in the evenings, 
which cut down the noise enough so that they could converse within their own group, although 
getting to sleep at an early hour remained problematic. However, by the time the train reached 
the mountains of Wyoming, the fatigue of the journey had ground down the Wisconsinites to 
such an extent that they hit the hay almost immediately after supper. 


On a positive side, WF learned that his father-in-law was a dedicated artist. Onias had a 
sketchpad in his hands at all times and a pencil stuck behind his ear, even when walking or 
herding livestock. WF reported that Onias “rendered countless sketches, often doodling whilst 
walking”. During the evenings, he brought out a set of colored pencils as well as fine point 
charcoal tipped artist pens to produce a large collection of landscapes and other scenes of trail 
life. After reaching the Willamette Valley, he donated his notepads to libraries established by 
Willamette Valley communities in the 1850s. None of his illustrations appear to have made it 
into collections of Oregon Trail memorabilia (see side note on pages 303-304). William Henry 
Jackson, the western photographer and artist, produced dozens of Oregon Trail paintings 
between 1880-1900. In his autobiography, Jackson reported that he based his paintings on 
original sketches drawn by wagon train travelers because he did not personally witness any of 
the Oregon Trail caravans, which ceased in the 1870s. (Jackson WH. Time Exposure: The 
Autobiography of William Henry Jackson (3 edition; original 1933). St. Louis, MO: Patrice Press. 
1994). Several of WH Jackson’s Oregon Trail paintings appear below. They depict scenery that 
Onias likely witnessed first hand and probably sketched himself. Source for the three Jackson 
images below: Wyoming Tales and Trails. www.wyomingtalesnandtrals.com. The Oregon Trail. 
Accessed: March 26, 2023.

The Jacob Jones train entered the south end of the Willamette Valley in September 1852, and 
the Hendricson-Jackson wagons peeled off from the others on September 19 when the train 
passed three miles east of WF and Sarah’s land on the Calapooia. After a massive amount of 
cross — continent travel between 1845 and 1852, WF never again left the Pacific Northwest. WF 
and Sarah became wealthy from their agricultural endeavors, and they engaged in many social 
and educational organizations in Linn County, where Albany is located, and also in nearby 
Corvallis. In 1865, the Hendricson’s donated an unknown amount of money to support the 
expansion of Corvallis College, which evolved into Oregon State University (OSU) by the 1880s. 
They made annual contributions to the school’s endowment fund, and hosted fund-raising 
events at their Calapooia farm. The Hendricson’s donations may have been substantial as WF 
was appointed by the Governor to the commission that selected the first OSU President, 
William A. Finley, and later served on other commissions and committees pertinent to the 
university. (Landis L. Oregon State University. Oregon Encyclopedia. Project of the Oregon 
Historical Society. 2020. www.oregonencyclopedia.org. Accessed: April 11, 2023)

The Hendricson’s annually paid $10,000-11,000 in property taxes in the 1890s, roughly 19 times 
higher than the average property tax paid by 2,800 other residents (average: $580) listed on the 
Linn County tax rolls in that period. The 2024 valuation of $11,000 is approximately $330,000.

Assessor. Linn County Oregon Genealogy Trails. Genealogy Trails History Group. 2022. 
www.genealogytrails.com. Accessed: April 14, 2023) Review of Linn County tax rolls from 1882- 
1892 and the Oregon census reports indicate that the Hendricson’s owned multiple rural 
properties in the county in addition to the Calapooia homestead, owned residential tracts 
within Albany and also owned residential and commercial property in Corvallis. WF owned or 


301 


co-owned a variety of businesses in the 1880s and 90s including a grocery store, a crockery and 
dishware store, a steam powered sawmill, and a freight hauling enterprise, which also sold, 
leased and repaired farm equipment. With business partner Terry Conn, WF was an a major 
economic force in Albany and Corvallis over the final 30 years of his life. WF’s son Omar 
apparently managed the grocery store for a few years before transitioning to farm equipment 
sales. | could find no information as to the disposition of these businesses after WF passed 
away in 1908. In his will, only disposition of property in Albany, Corvallis and Portland is 
mentioned. 


In 1888, with Sarah struggling with cancer, WF leased the Calapooia farm to several tenants in a 
profit-sharing partnership and purchased an in-town home at 490 Broadalbin Street in Albany 
so Sarah could be closer to her doctors and home care nurses. After Sarah’s death in 1892, WF 
re-married in 1894 to Mary Fronk who also traveled to the west coast in a wagon train at age 
14. Mary’s parents acquired considerable wealth in the neophyte west coast hospitality 
industry, ultimately owning a chain of hotels in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Portland and 
Seattle. WF became a deacon in his church, held trustee positions in two local banks, and was 
Chairman of the Western Oregon Republican Party Coordinating Committee for ten years.

WF was a supporter of Theodore Roosevelt, particularly admiring Roosevelt’s push for a 
national park system. WF sent Vice President and then President Roosevelt numerous 
invitations to visit Western Oregon, which finally paid-off. On May 22, 1903, WF Hendricson 
and three other Republican officials had a ten-minute audience with Roosevelt in his train car 
lounge when the President stopped in Portland in the midst of a 25 state railroad tour.

A side note: Many wagon train travelers, especially women, wrote trip diaries to record their 
experiences and observations of life on the Oregon Trail. Many of these diaries have been 
preserved in various collections housed in Oregon museums and libraries, and also by 
genealogical societies. The publication, Across the Plains, Mountains and Deserts: A 
Bibliography of the Oregon-California Trail (2014), edited by William Bagley, a historian for the 
National Park Service, describes 4500 documents produced by wagon train travelers. These 
documents include diaries, maps, legal documents, short stories, and artwork. The Bagley 
bibliography lists a diary written by Sarah A. Jackson Hendricson, but the indicated website is 
now inactive. Perhaps future family historians can do a more exhaustive search and locate 
Sarah’s account of her Oregon journey, as well as examples of Onias Jackson’s artwork. 


A side note: Onias Jackson elected to return to Rush, Indiana in 1862. We could find no 
information about the catalyst for his trip back east or his mode of transportation. We 
conjecture that he may have desired to see his other daughter, Alcestis, again, or possibly re- 
connect with Daraxa. Onias died shortly after returning to Indiana. 


Notes on Wagon Trains: Primarily due to motion pictures and television shows in the 1950s and 
60s, most notably the popular series Wagon Train starring Ward Bond, a number of myths 
about wagon train structure and travel procedure have endured. These notes address three of 
these myths. Principle sources of information for this myth busting were: Unruh JD, 1993 (Cited 
previously) and Pingenot BE. The Great Wagon Expedition of 1850. Southwestern History 
Quarterly. 1994; 98: 183-225. 


Ward Bond, left on horse, starred in the TV series 
Wagon Train, based on his prior show, Wagon Master, 
one of the first westerns made for network television, 
and which focused on a Mormon wagon train. Both 
series were hits, but included inaccuracies about the 
wagon train experience, such as families riding in their 
wagons, the single-file line-up of wagons and the 
frequency of Native American hostility. 


Image source: The Movie Data Base. www.themoviedb.org. 
Accessed: 4/21/2023. 


Travel formation. In paintings, films and on TV, wagon trains have been depicted as traveling in 
a long single-file column of several hundred wagons, winding through hills and valleys. The 
early caravans proceeded in this manner, but this formation posed many problems. 
Communication between sections of a long, single-file train of wagons was challenging. One or 
more wagons at the end of the train could experience breakdowns or accidents, and it would 
take considerable time for the Wagon Master to even become aware of the situation. Long 
single file columns also required hiring additional trail riders (assistants to the Wagon Master) 
to ride up and down the column to identify problems, and convey messages back to the leader, 
driving up personnel costs. Early caravans found that rounding a long single-file column into an 
encirclement camp at night was difficult to accomplish in an orderly and time-efficient manner. 
An immense amount of dust and debris was kicked up by a wagon train, the bulk of which 
enveloped the wagons and walkers at the back of the column, making an already dreadful 


303 


experience even worse. A long single-file column was easy prey, particularly the rear section, in 
the instance of an attack by a band of tribesman or Anglo bandits. It was virtually impossible to 
quickly move into any type of defensive position. 


By 1850, It was determined that wagon trains composed of 40-50 wagons were optimal for 
communication and management versus giant trains with hundreds of wagons and more than 
1,000 travelers. Except when traversing narrow mountain passes, the basic wagon train 
configuration evolved into a side-by-side, multiple column formation as shown on the next 
page. Each column or compartment of eight to ten wagons and roughly 40-50 people, elected a 
Captain to serve as the leader of their group. The Wagon Master and his assistants met nightly 
with the Captains to resolve problems, assess and manage resources, and plan the upcoming 
days in the journey. Dust was reduced, and wagons in each column could rotate front to back, 
allowing a couple of days every week in front of the dust, rocks and manure being thrown 
backward as the train progressed. Five or six side-by-side columns (essentially a moving box 
formation) provided a stronger defensive posture. With each column moving their own wagons 
into a small circle in the evening, this task was accomplished more efficiently so human walkers 
and wagon pullers (mules, oxen and occasionally horses) could have more time to rest. 


A side note: The wagons were circled at night to sequester livestock and prevent them from 
wandering off. Protection from tribal attack was a consideration, but not the primary reason for 
the circling the wagons. 


Image source: Equine Heritage Institute. 
www.equinineheritageinstitute.com. Accessed: 4/24/2023. 


Attack by Native Tribes. Western emigration historian John Unruh reported 362 deaths among 
wagon train travelers due to violence by Native Peoples on the Oregon Trail from 1843 
(crossing of first major Oregon-bound wagon train) to 1868, the final year before trans- 
continental travel by locomotive was possible. He also documented a roughly similar number of 
Native deaths from these encounters. For context, the overall number of wagon train deaths 
during this timeframe has been calculated in several studies as 25,000 to 30,000. The number 
of emigrants who traveled overland to Oregon, or to California (using the Oregon Trail for 2/3s 
of their journey) was approximately 400,000, for a trip fatality rate of 7%. The annual trip 
mortality, from all causes, from 1843 to 1850 was 10%, but declined to 5% after 1850 as travel 
protocols were better established, river crossing techniques were improved and personal 


304 


hygiene regulations were more aggressively enforced. Less than one-tenth of one percent of 
Oregon Trail mortality was due to violent confrontations with Native Peoples. 


The main causes of emigrant death were bacterial infections of the gastrointestinal tract, 
primarily Cholera and Typhoid Fever, caused by poor personal sanitation and ensuing bacterial 
infection of food and water, drowning’s, injuries from handling livestock, wagon accidents 
including tip-overs from wind gusts, children falling beneath wagon wheels, hunting accidents, 
dehydration, snakebites, and malnourishment. Virtually every wagon train also had occurrences 
of people wandering off who were never seen again and presumed dead. Outside of Cholera 
and other gastrointestinal diseases that often wiped out an entire family within a couple of 
weeks, the majority of deaths occurred among the elderly and children. 


In Circle the Wagons!, Greg and Susan Michno explored violent interactions between Native 
Peoples and wagon train travelers and other western emigration myths. They found that hostile 
confrontations between wagon train travelers and Native tribesmen almost never occurred as 
depicted in the classic Hollywood movie scene of whooping warriors racing around circled 
wagons firing arrows or rifles from gymnastic positions on horseback. Most migratory tribal 
bands were small and had only a few young warriors who were far too valuable to lose in a 
futile attack on a well-armed wagon train. Wagon Master’s typically required each wagon to 
have at least two rifles and/or shotguns, vastly more firepower than Native tribes. 


Greg and Susan Michno explored the mythology of Native 
American attacks on wagon trains, and examined other false 
narratives about western emigration. For example, they found 
evidence of just 31 tribal attacks on wagon trains between 1843 
and 1868. During this period, 1,700 wagon trains journeyed from 
the Midwest to Oregon, Utah or California. However, several 
attacks resulting in high mortality among settlers and tribesmen 
were extensively reported in the eastern press, feeding a 
perception of tribal hostility. Michno GF, Michno SJ. Circle the 
Wagons! Attacks on Wagon Trains in History and in Hollywood 
Films. Chicago: McFarland Press. 2008. 


Unruh estimated that the majority of pioneer fatalities associated with tribal encounters 
occurred away from the wagon train during hunting excursions when travelers and Natives 
surprised each other while traversing the same grounds. In panic or confusion, guns were fired, 
spears were thrown, knives flashed and there were deaths on both sides. 


Tribal-traveler violence increased in the 1860s when a substantial cohort of hunters starting 
using wagon trains as a means to reach bison herds. Perceived over-hunting of bison triggered 
tribal reprisal, often in the form of ambushes set for hunters or night assaults on specific 
wagons know to include hunters. Unruh reported that many of the 362 wagon train deaths 
attributable to Native Peoples occurred after 1860. By that time, the plains tribes, especially the 
Comanche’s and their Kiowa allies, realized that “white man was never to leave our lands.” 
While their parents in the 1840s and 1850s tolerated the White travelers and used them as 
trading partners, the new generation of 1860s tribal leaders was less accepting, led by the 
Kiowa War Chief, Big Bow, who advocated tribal cooperation and preemptive action. Violence 


305 


boiled over when locomotives started barreling through ancestral hunting and grazing lands 
after 1868. When a large component of the post Civil War Union army moved across the 
Missouri into Western territories in 1869, organized resistance intensified. 


The Kiowa were the most likely to act aggressively 
against wagon trains after 1860. These Kiowa were 
photographed at a Kansas trading post in 1861. Upper 
right is Big Bow (1833-1900), a Kiowa Nation War 
Chief who pushed for aggressive resistance. Less well 
known to the Anglo world than other tribal leaders,

Traveler’s Preparation. Another myth about wagon trains is that travelers experienced a high 
death rate because they were poorly prepared for the arduous journey. In reality, the main 
problem was inexperienced Wagon Masters. The requirements imposed by experienced Wagon 
Masters (i.e., employed by a travel company or by the Oregon Territory to lead caravans) 
ensured that pre-trip planning was methodical for professionally led groups. Unfortunately, 
many of the Wagon Masters were not experienced. WF Hendricson’s numerous journeys 
demonstrate the diversity in train leadership. Hackleman and Applegate each had made 
multiple round trips. Seth Leweling had only one previous trip under his belt and Jonas Jones of 
Wisconsin had none. Wagon train groups were often led by inexperienced Wagon Masters who 
were selected by travelers based on status: a church congregation leader such as Jonas Jones, 
an older family patriarch, which was the case in Drusilla and Amanda Morgan’s trip to Oregon, 
or a prominent person. The wagon train that transported Ira Goodman’s family was led by the 
mayor of the town where the family lived, who was a banker by trade. 


When done thoroughly, accumulation of required supplies and acquisition of a covered wagon 
that met specifications cost $1,000 - $2,000 in the 1850s ($38,000 - $76,000 in 2024 valuation). 
Since most of the westward traveling families were not wealthy, it often took several years to 
pull together that level of funding. The wagons were packed with supplies intended to get the 
family through a five-month journey. A family of six was expected to depart with 2500 pounds 
of food, water, cooking utensils and equipment (shovels, hammers, saws, wrenches, files, 
augers, carving knives, wagon replacement parts, buckets of spare nails, bolts, nuts, and hinges, 
weapons and ammunition). Food supplies represented 50% of the weight: 500 pounds of flour, 
200 pounds of lard, 200 pounds of bacon, 200 pounds of beans, 100 pounds of coffee and 50 
pounds of salt. Travelers used these ingredients to prepare morning and evening meals in iron 
skillets and kettles, with the menu heavy on biscuits and flapjacks, occasionally enhanced with 
bacon. Meat was obtained from cattle in the wagon train’s herd and from hunting expeditions. 


In well-managed caravans, wagons were inspected by the Wagon Master or his trail riders 
when they arrived in the departure camp for sturdiness, state of repair and capacity to haul an 
initial load of 2500 pounds. In the U.S., the evolution of scales for weighing large objects, such 
as wagons, was accelerated by the desire of experienced Wagon Masters to weigh wagons prior 


306 


to departure. St Joseph and Independence Missouri were two of the first cities outside of New 
York to have large commercial scales. 


By 1850, sanitation and personal hygiene were recognized as essential for the maintenance of 
health during the journey. To minimize Cholera and Typhoid Fever outbreaks, most Wagon 
Masters instituted requirements for each traveler to have a personal hygiene bag that included 
towels and wash cloths, multiple tooth brushes, one pound of baking powder (for tooth 
brushing and treating wounds) a roll of binding tape (bandage), one pound of bathing soap, 
three pounds of lye soap for washing clothes including undergarments at least weekly, and 25 
rolls of toilet paper (a relatively new invention in North America). Regulations for placing latrine 
areas one hundred feet downhill from the wagons were instituted after 1850. 


When professional Wagon Masters were not on the trail, they often toured cities in the East 
and Midwest to conduct seminars about the Oregon Trail, similar to the Hackleman symposium 
that WF Hendricson attended in Des Moines. At these meetings and by mail order, prospective 
travelers could purchase a wide variety of guidebooks on travel by wagon train. Some Wagon 
Masters required their travelers to purchase a designated travel manual. Professional Wagon 
Masters, employed by travel companies promoting Oregon emigration or by the Oregon 
Territory, were paid a 2024 equivalent salary of $150,000 annually for the Western journey, a 
return trip, orientation symposia, and managing the departure camp along the Missouri River. 
Other Wagon Masters such as Seth Leweling and Jonas Jones essentially received tips from 
travelers, much like a 2024 tour guide might be tipped at the end of a trip.

Bright Lights of the Big City - Theodore Stefano Girault (1873-1943) and Bessie 
McAnespy Girault (1874-1946) 


Chapters II and Ill described the journey of Theodore Stefano Girault from turned-out street 
urchin bounced among orphanages in 19" century London, to a teenager on the cusp of being 
tossed into the British penal system for theft and attempted escape from a reform school, and 
inally, to a participant in a child labor program (British Home Child Service; BHCS) working on 
an isolated farm in rural Canada. Fourteen years later, Theodore (Theo) was a well-respected 
‘oreman (manager) of three farms and a new husband, married to the sister of the man who 
procured his labor from the BHCS. Quite a journey. But there is more of the story. 


To explore Theo and Bessie’s life together, | primarily relied on Susan’s recollections of family 
history, a large trove of Girault family photographs dating back to the 1890s, many of which 
were annotated on the back side with names and event descriptions, two Girault genealogical 
websites, BHCS immigration records (www.Britishhomechildren.weebly.com), census reports, 
newspaper articles, wedding announcements, diaries and obituaries. A synopsis of Theo’s life 
rom 1880 to 1920 at www.surname.rootschat.com, derived largely from BHCS data, was also 
helpful. 


After Theodore and new bride Bessie McAnespy were wed in 1901 near the farm in Portage 
Vale, New Brunswick where they met 14 years earlier, the newlyweds left rural life behind and 
headed for the, even then, bright lights of New York City (NYC). Without any qualifications 
other than eagerness to learn, Theo quickly landed a job with the investment-banking firm 
Edward B. Smith, a Philadelphia-based financial services company, which had just opened their 
irst office in NYC. With on-the-job training, Theo became an order clerk for stock, bond and 
other investment transactions working with a brand-new telegraphic system for communicating 
orders to the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). As best as | could tell from company records 
and U.S. census reports, Theo worked his way up to supervising a room full of telegraphic 
exchange clerks by 1910, and by 1920, he was functioning as a stock broker and doing financial 
advising for clients of Edward B. Smith. 


Theodore, left, and his best men for his wedding ceremony with 
Bessie. The young man at the top right is Theo’s comrade-in-arms 
from the Barton Regis Rural Work Farm in England, Henry 
Mitchell. As 13 year olds, Theo, Henry and George Harvey, who 
earlier moved to Manitoba and out of Theo’s life, were shipped 
to Canada on the same boat as part of the British Home Child 
Service. Henry Mitchell had a long career in the Royal Canadian 
Navy. /mage source: Girault family photo. 


By the Roaring 20s, the Edward B. Smith Company was one of the two largest investment firms 
in New York. The company was originally founded during the Gilded Age of the 1880s to take 
advantage of two new phenomenon in America: (1) a substantial number of people had 
discretionary money they could afford to invest in wealth building ventures, and (2) fast 


309 


growing cities and the initial vestiges of suburbia needed funding for infrastructure: roads, 
bridges, schools, hospitals, electrification, sewers and government buildings. Consequently, the 
financial underwriting industry and the bond market boomed, especially, the new municipal 
bond strategy. 


After purchasing a seat on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in 1898, Edward B. Smith 
expanded rapidly and hired a substantial number of employees, mostly young and eager like 
Theo Girault. Smith’s biggest competitor when Theo was hired in 1901 was the Charles Barney 
Company, also started in Philadelphia, which was more of a financial center than New York until 
1900. Charles Barney was the son-in-law and one time protégé of the financier Jay Cooke, who 
sold treasury bonds to finance the Union cause during the Civil War. A series of investment 
misadventures and miscalculations caused Jay Cook to declare bankruptcy in 1873, triggered a 
severe market sell-off and an ensuing recession. Charles Barney saw an opportunity to take 
advantage of depressed prices (i.e., buy low and sell high) and started his own firm in 1873, 
which gradually grew until he had the resources to buy a NYSE seat, also in 1898. Shifting 
primary operations to New York, the Charles Barney Company experienced steady success for 
the next 30 years until the Great Stock Market Crash of 1929. (Smith Barney Inc. Company 
History. Funding Universe: Company Profiles. 2021. www.fundinguniverse.com/companies- 
histories/. Accessed: March 13, 2023) 


In the aftermath of the 1929 meltdown, 75% of the investment firms based in New York 
dramatically scaled back operations or folded. By 1931, the Smith and Barney Companies were 
the two most vibrant firms still functioning, thanks to conservative lending and investment 
practices in the 1920s. Both companies benefitted from the financial sector chaos. They 
absorbed clients and picked-up quality employees from failed competitors. So, what did Smith 
and Barney do? They merged into what was known for decades as Smith Barney Investments. 
Smith, where Theo worked, focused on underwriting and investment banking, while the Barney 
arm of the new corporation focused on brokered stocks and bonds. (Smith Barney: The Early 
Years. Ten Decades of Continuity and Change. Smith Barney Forum. May-June 1973. In: 
International Directory of Company Histories. Vol. 15. St. James, MO: St. James Press. 1996) 


And how did these developments impact Theo Girault? Theo was working his way up the 
corporate ladder within Edward B. Smith and had reached mid-management by the time of the 
1929 crash. When the Smith and Barney merged, it seems that Theo was one of the big 
winners, promoted upward to one of the new firm’s 27 general partner positions. The almost 
immediate good fortune of the newly integrated Smith Barney was also Theo’s good fortune. 
Theo and Bessie moved out of NYC to the affluent suburb of Hastings on the Hudson, where 
they purchased a substantial house. Their daughter, Laura, married Charles Lienau in 1935 on 
the terrace of their house. A photo on page 121 shows the Girault home. 


Bessie was also industrious. Despite having three children between 1902 and 1908, Bessie was 
employed until 1920, and perhaps beyond, as a telephone switchboard operator. Like Theo, she 
rose to a managerial role. The 1920 U.S. Census indicates that a nanny, Abigail Maerten, resided 
in the Girault household, which may explain Bessie’s capacity to work outside the home. 


310

Unlike many recent immigrants to the U.S., Theo and Bessie were eager to demonstrate their 
patriotism prior to and during World War | (WWI); 1914-1918. For example, as early as 1914, 
Theo and Bessie’s names appeared on planning committees for the Progressive Preparedness 
Society (PPS), a component of the controversial American Defense Society (ADS; see Notes on 
this organization on pages 316-317). The PPS believed that American involvement in the 
European war was inevitable, “and therefore... we better be prepared.” From the start of the 
“Great European War,” the PPS ardently supported the British-French-Russian side of the 
conflict. (Franz M. Preparedness Revisited: Civilian Societies and the Campaign for American 
Defense, 1914-1920. Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era. 2018; 17(4): 663-676) 


However, throughout the nation as a whole, there was deep division within the largely 
immigrant U.S. population concerning who to support among the WWI combatants. Nearly 70% 
of all families residing in the U.S. in 1915 had immigrated during the past 60 years from other 
countries. The huge population of Irish immigrants was universally disdainful of Great Britain. 
German support for Irish rebels in the 1916 Rebellion against the British led many Irish- 
Americans to look favorably upon Germany. The substantial population of German immigrants 
tended to be affluent and politically influential, and either favored their motherland or argued 
for neutrality. Members of the huge Italian immigration wave that started around 1900 
supported the German-Austrian axis, which was the position of the Italian government 
although that nation managed to avoid combat roles. The increasing number of Asian 
immigrants to the west coast had deep antipathy toward Russia because of the 1905 Russo- 
Japanese War and thus tended to favor the German-Austrian side. There was powerful 
opposition to U.S. entry into the conflict among rural Whites and their congressional 
representatives due to a strong Nativist (i.e., isolationist) orientation among this segment of the 
population. Woodrow Wilson ran for re-election in 1916 and won using the slogan “He Kept Us 
Out of the War”, which likely reflected the nation’s prevailing beliefs at that time. (Leary WM. 
Woodrow Wilson, Irish Americans and the Election of 1916. The Journal of American History. 
1967; 54(1): 57-72) 

Several events turned most of the population against Germany-Austria between November 
1916 and April 1917: German U-boats increasingly attacked U.S. shipping in the North Atlantic 
and sank dozens of cargo ships, with extensive loss of life (the U.S. was supplying munitions and 
food to Britain to break the German blockade); German use of mustard gas, beginning in 1916, 
was considered barbaric; German bombing of cities from airplanes, also seen as an atrocity, was 
widely publicized in the U.S. newspapers and shown in newsreels before motion pictures, 


310 


stirring up public outrage; appealing to the nations’ White supremacist population, Germany’s 
use of soldiers from Africa was widely publicized even though the majority of these conscripted 
soldiers fought the British in the Middle East, North Africa and East Africa and not in Europe 
(see Notes on pages 315-316); public outrage over the German campaign of espionage and 
sabotage in the U.S. was galvanized by newspaper coverage of deadly munitions depot 
bombings in California and New York; and finally, the “Zimmermann Affair” became the 
ultimate tipping point. A coded cable message sent by German Foreign Minister Arthur 
Zimmermann in January 1917 to the German Ambassador to Mexico was intercepted and 
decoded by the forerunner of the British Secret Service, and sent to the U.S. State Department. 
From this telegram, it was learned and massively publicized in the U.S. that Germany was 
encouraging Mexico to invade Texas, New Mexico and Arizona to divert U.S. military resources 
from Europe. If the Alliance won the war, Mexico was promised control of lands in these states. 
Although Mexico had no intention or capacity to act on this proposal, the intercepted cable 
enraged Congress and the general public, which increased pressure on Wilson to drop his 
neutral stance. The first book of the famed historian, Barbara Tuchman, describes the origins, 
transmission, discovery, decoding and ramifications of the Zimmermann Telegram. (Tuchman B. 
The Zimmermann Telegram. New York: Ballantine Books. 1958) 


The Zimmermann Telegram, comprised of 171 sets of numbers, 
was intercepted and deciphered by cryptographers in Britain’s 
famous Room 40 intelligence Unit that decrypted 15,000 
German communications during WWI. Room 40 was the 
predecessor to the British Secret Service Andrew C. Her 
Majesty’s Secret Service: The Making of the British Intelligence 
Community. New York: Viking Press. 1986. 

Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 4/30/2023. 


By the time President Wilson sent a war declaration to Congress on April 2, 1917, much of the 
U.S. population had been stirred into a patriotic, anti-German fervor, a huge shift from just the 
year before. Draft Board and 1920 census records indicate that Theo attempted to enlist three 
times, once with each service branch, army, navy and marines, but was rejected because of 
astigmatism, and his age. Not deterred, he joined a Civilian Shore Patrol brigade. These 
volunteer civilian groups in the NYC area were formed in 1916 by the American Defense Society 
(ADS) in loose coordination with the newly established U.S. Coast Guard (until 1915, the U.S. 
Water Life Saving Service) and the bomb squad of the NYC Police Department, although neither 
agency was enthusiastic about this ADS-supported activity. (Blum H. Dark Invasion. 1915 - 
Germany’s Secret War and the Hunt for the First Terrorist Cell in America. New York: Crown 
Publishing Group / Harper Brothers Inc. 2014) The principle catalyst for civilian patrolling was a 
saboteur attack in New York harbor where a small band of German agents blew up a vast 
munitions depot on Black Tom Island near the Statue of Liberty, killing seven people, and 


312 


destroying unknown billions of dollars of ammunition and weapons intended for shipment to 
the Russian army (see Notes on Black Tom Island Explosion on pages 317-318). The civilian 
patrols watched New York Harbor and the Long Island shoreline to detect attempts to smuggle 
saboteurs ashore from German U-boats. Although NYC units patrolled nightly for two years, 
they never encountered a U-boat or a saboteur. (Jaffe SH. New York at War. Four Centuries of 
Combat, Fear and Intrigue in Gotham. New York: Basic Books. 2012) The Germans did attempt 
to off load spies and paramilitary personnel along the coasts of New England, North Carolina, 
Florida, California, Oregon and Washington. These efforts were scuttled by bad weather, 
equipment failures and alert Coast Guard or state police patrols. 


Bess was a participant in a Victory Garden Program to home grow vegetables in playgrounds, 
parks, church courtyards and on rooftop raised gardens so that farm produce could be directed 
to the war effort. Bess joined a Women’s War Workers (WWW) organization (also known as the 
Women’s Land Army) to produce blankets, caps, socks and gloves for soldiers, and led a WWW 
campaign to get every housewife in her neighborhood to sign a pledge card from the U.S. 
National War Gardens Commission stating that she would: “carry out the instructions of the 
U.S. War Effort Food Administrator in the conduct of my household to can food for future use, 
grow vegetables in the backyard or other convenient space, limit consumption of meat to three 
times a week for all family members, reduce as much as possible the use of fats and wheat in 
meal preparation., and above all, bolster the morale of their families at home and loved ones 
overseas.” (Schumm L. America’s Patriotic Victory Gardens. History. www.history.com. 
September 1, 2018. Accessed: April 17, 2023) Bess also was involved in Boots for Troops rallies 
where people came to hear patriotic speeches, war updates and patriotic music from the NYC 
Fire Department Band, and donated boots, gloves, sweaters and knit caps for soldiers. One 
such Program at Ebbets Field in Brooklyn (home of the Brooklyn Dodgers) drew 35,000 people. 
Bess Girault was listed as a donations coordinator on the agenda. 


The Victory Garden Program during WWI was wildly popular, at least 
partially due to the largest and most aggressive advertising campaign 
ever attempted by the federal government to that point in U.S. history. 
Gowdy-Wygant. Cultivating Victory: The Women’s Land Army and the 
Victory Garden Movement in Britain and the U.S. Pittsburgh: University of 
Pittsburgh Press. 2013. 

Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 4/29/2023. 


We know little about the personal lives of Theo and Bessie. From photographs, | concluded that 
they returned often to New Brunswick for summer vacations, and their children, Theo Jr. Evelyn 
and Laura, grew up in a home in Brooklyn that had a substantial backyard, with trees and what 
appears to be a vegetable garden. Bessie was evidently fond of collecting autographs 
throughout her life. We found several of her autograph books among the Girault’s extensive 
photo collection. A couple of autograph excerpts appear below. 


313 


Face page of one of Bessie’s autograph books, and an entry by her daughter, Laura in 1917: “ Dear 
Mother, May your life be long and sunny, and Daddy, grow fat and funny. Your daughter Laura.” 


Two autograph book entries written in 1900 when Bessie still lived in New Brunswick. The entry on 
the right is presumably some type of joke among friends. 


Theodore Stefano Girault had a truly remarkable rags to riches life — basically the epitome of 
the American Dream that drew 19th century immigrants to the U.S.A. But, mysteries remain to 
be explored. There must be more to the story of Theo’s abandonment by his affluent father, 
but no details were uncovered. He apparently had no contact with his older brother and sister 
although he was in the British child welfare system for 11 years before being sent to Canada 
and spent 13 years in the British Home Child Service. His sister, Emily Alexandrine Girault (1860- 
1947), claimed that she was prevented from contacting Theo, but it does not seem like it would 
have been difficult to locate him prior to or even after his BHCS relocation to Canada. We do 
not know why Alexandrine or her older brother, both relatively affluent in their own right, did 
not strive to locate and contact Theo. We also have no idea of what, if any, schooling he 
received during his journey through the English orphanage system. Interestingly, without any 
knowledge of his father’s or grandfather’s involvement in the financial industry, Theo also 
elected to pursue the financial sector for his career. 


Theo passed away on March 17, 1943 at their home in Hastings on the Hudson. Bessie 
remained at their residence until her death in 1946. Theo and Bessie are buried in the same 
plot in the Portage Vale Baptist Cemetery, less than five miles from the New Brunswick farm 
where they first met in 1887.

Notes on African and African-American Soldier’s Participation in World War I: In keeping with 
the times, WWI messaging campaigns by the U.S. government to the public played on racial 
fears. An intense propaganda campaign was implemented to build support for U.S. engagement 
in the European conflict based on Germany’s conscription of 80,000 equatorial Africans for 
combat roles in the conflict. Posters, film newsreels and press releases printed in newspapers 
proclaimed that this action violated rules of decency and war etiquette. However, the French 
army included more than 100,000 Black and mixed race French citizens, as did the British army. 
More than 700,000 Black Americans registered to enlist, 300,000 were selected, 120,000 were 
sent to Europe and 40,000 experienced frontline combat with 800 deaths and 3,000 wounded. 


Conscripts from Rwanda, Tanzania and 
Mozambique fought for Germany in WWI, primarily 
in the forgotten “second front” (Middle East, North 
Africa, East Africa) where colonial powers Britain 
and Germany fought to expand territory. 50,000 
soldiers died in the conflict. Strachen H. The First 
World War in Africa. New York: Oxford Univ. Press. 2004.

A 1917 U.S. Army recruitment poster that appeared in popular 
news magazines. Note the less than subtle “Cultur” on the ape’s 
club. Many commentators suggested that this poster was based on 
the King Kong legend. However, the screenplay for the original King 
Kong movie was not written until 1932. More likely, the movie 
drew concepts from posters like this created by Harry Ryles Hopps,

During combat missions, Black American units were paired with French units, because American 
commander General John J. Pershing refused to integrate them into White brigades. (Maloney 
W. WWI African American Soldiers Battle More than Enemy Forces. Library of Congress Blogs: 
Timeless Stories from the Library of Congress. www.blog.loc.org. February 23, 2018. Accessed: 
April 7, 2023) Black soldiers were treated the same as other soldiers within the French 
commands, which were racially diverse. After the ceasefire, when U.S. troops were pulled back 
from front lines and gathered in French and Belgium communities for re-deployment, Black 
American soldiers were well received by the citizenry, who did not distinguish between White 
and Black troops when lavishing praise on victorious soldiers. Black American soldiers found 
that they could walk and eat where they wanted, attend movies with other people, and shop 
where they wanted. Shopkeepers were just as happy to take their money as that of the White 
soldiers. When 100,000 Black American soldiers returned to the U.S., many expected that their 


315 


participation in the War would change perceptions. As we know, the Black American soldiers 
were wrong. The 1919 Red Summer of White Supremacist racial terrorism was, in part, 
triggered by the supposed “superior attitude” of returning Black soldiers. Several triggering 
events in the Red Summer were attacks on uniformed Black soldiers who entered restaurants, 
bars and hotels in White areas of cities. (Goldenberg R. African American Troops Fought to Fight 
in World War I. History Website of the U.S. Department of Defense. www.defense.org. February 
1, 2018. Accessed: April 20, 2023) 


Notes of the American Defense Society (ADS): The ADS was formed in 1915 to advocate for 
U.S. intervention into WWI on the side of the British, French and Russians. The first ADS 
Director was Teddy Roosevelt. (Handbook of the American Defense Society: Serve at the Front 
or Serve at Home. New York: ADS National Headquarters. 1918. Available via Internet Archive. 
www.internetarchive. Accessed: April 16, 2023) At first, the ADS focused on raising public 
awareness of German lobbyists (influencers), spies and saboteurs, urging private citizens to 
watch for and report suspicious activity to the police or the military. The ADS also organized 
supply-raising campaigns for shipment to the allies fighting the German-Austrian axis. After the 
Black Tom Island explosion, the ADS organized civilian patrols to look for German agents and 
after war was declared in 1917, veered into overt political activism pressuring Congress to 
promptly send a “full-strength overwhelming force” to Europe and campaigned aggressively for 
enactment of strenuous sedition laws that would allow arrest and internment of enemy (i.e., 
German and Austrian) aliens and sympathizers. The ADS particularly focused on identifying 
teachers who supposedly spread “anti-American” ideas in classrooms and encouraged students 
and parents to report teachers who were not sufficiently patriotic. Across the nation, but 
particularly in NYC, teachers were accused of seditious activity, reputations were ruined, many 
were fired and numerous others resigned. (Mann M. The Home Room Front. The ADS and the 
Battle for Teacher Loyalty During WWI. New York Historical Society Museum and Library. June 2, 
2023. www.nyhistory.org. Accessed: November 7, 2023) By the end of war, the ADS was 
advocating for the abolition of the German language and German culture in the U.S. and had 
aligned itself with other nationalistic organizations in a “100 percent Americanism” movement 
that was strongly anti-immigrant and laced with racism. The influence of the ADS faded in the 
1920s. There is no indication that the Theo and Bess were involved in any ADS-supported 
activity other than patrolling shorelines and supply raising.

Notes on the Black Tom Island Munitions Explosion: Black Tom Island was located in New York 
harbor near Liberty Island where the Statue of Liberty stands. The island was constructed from 
landfill from NYC and New Jersey trash dumps that was poured around a large rock said to 
resemble a black tomcat. The man-made island was connected to the mainland by railroad 
tracks on a causeway. In the early 1900s, a mile long warehouse and train depot were 
constructed on the island. During WWI, munition company’s stored vast amounts of weapons, 
small arms ammunition, artillery shells, TNT and detonators in the Black Tom warehouse for 
distribution to Britain, France and Russia. On July 16, 1916, two million tons of ammunition and 
250,000 pounds of TNT and detonators in train boxcars and barges at Black Tom were waiting 
for loading onto ships for transport to Russia. Shortly after midnight on the 16th, two German 
saboteurs reached the island by rowboat and a third walked along the train causeway to reach 
the fundamentally unguarded island. The trio set fires in at least four boxcars loaded with tons 
of TNT, and placed several bombs with timing fuses on ammunition-laden barges and near the 
doors of warehouses. The saboteurs (Michael Kristoff, Kurt Jahnke and possibly Lothar Witzke — 
involvement not firmly established) then climbed back into the boat and rowed away. At 
2:15am, a gigantic explosion rocked the NYC region, decimated Black Tom island, badly 
damaged the Statue of Liberty and blew out a million windows in Manhattan including all of the 
stained glass windows in St. Patrick’s Cathedral. The explosion was felt as far away as Rhode 
Island and Maryland, and is considered the largest explosion ever to occur in North America, 
equaling the simultaneous detonation of several atomic bombs. (Witcover J. Sabotage at Black 
Tom: Imperial Germany’s Secret War in America, 1914-1917. Chapel Hill, NC: Algonquin Books 
of Chapel Hill. 1989) 


A disorganized manhunt ensued that was alternately led by the Interstate Commerce 
Commission, the Directorate of Naval Intelligence, and a member of the NYC Police Department 
Bomb Squad named Tom Tunney. No centralized national intelligence agency existed in 1916, 
and the nation had no sabotage and terrorism laws or established punishment guidelines. 
Eventually, a network of German agents, directed by a debonair Manhattan socialite with 
connections to the German Foreign Office, were linked to the explosion. The three purported 
saboteurs were finally identified by 1920. Kristoff’s participation was well established and he 
was jailed. Due to shoddy police work and legal bungling, he was not convicted and released. 


317 


He was imprisoned shortly afterward for unrelated crimes, and died of tuberculosis in 1928 
shortly after prison discharge. Witzke was also apprehended and admitted involvement in other 
sabotage activities in the U.S. including a munitions depot explosion at Mare Island, California, 
but his direct participation in the Black Tom bombing was never established. However, he was 
implicated as a participant in the yearlong planning that preceded the attack. Witzke was 
eventually sentenced to death in the U.S. but was pardoned in 1923 after he heroically 
prevented a prison boiler explosion, saving many lives. He returned to Germany where he 
eventually became a German parliament member after WWII. Jahnke was never apprehended, 
returned to Germany and served as a Nazi intelligence agent in WWII, but was captured and 
executed in 1945 by the Russians. (Witcover, 1989) Howard Blum’s novel, Dark Invasion, 
describes the German espionage and sabotage network in the U.S. during WWI, and the 
haphazard, although sometimes successful, efforts to thwart this secret war.

Harold and Mildred Go To War 

Harold and Mildred were casual friends who had started to date in Walla Walla before World 
War II disrupted their relationship in its early stages. They did not see each other from spring 
1942 until spring 1946, yet managed to sustain a relationship during their extended wartime 
separation, although the connection by correspondence was bumpy and, ironically, came to an 
abrupt halt during their one and only wartime phone conversation in the summer of 1945. This 
phone call triggering a relationship hiatus that lasted several months after both returned to 
civilian life. They eventually resolved their differences and married in November 1946. 


A primary mechanism for their wartime communication was a postal innovation known as V- 
Mail, short for Victory Mail. It was implemented by the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to provide a 
mail service to and from U.S. soldiers stationed overseas. The official name for the service was: 
Army Micro Photographic Mail Service. The V-Mail goal was to reduce the physical bulk of the 
millions of letters being sent to soldiers, airmen and sailors, and thereby save space on cargo 
planes and ships for valuable war materials. Based on data collected in the early months of 
1942 and the British experience fighting Germany and Japan in 1940-1941, the USPS 
determined that approximately 600,000 letters would be mailed by servicemen or their 
significant others PER DAY when U.S. forces were fully deployed in Europe and the Pacific. One 
day’s worth of letters on traditional stationary sent by regular-sized stamped envelopes would 
fill 150 mailbags, each weighing roughly 70 pounds for a total weight of more than 10,000 
pounds (five tons). The USPS estimated that the same 600,000 letters distributed via the V-mail 
process would require only four small mailbags, weighing 40 pounds each. Instead of a mail 
loading process requiring a substantial crew of men and forklifts to lift heavy pallets of mail 
onto trucks for delivery to distribution sites, with V-Mail, one man and a jeep could handle the 
entire process. These estimates and predictions by the USPS proved to be accurate during the 
course of the war. However, the system had one major glitch as we will see shortly. 


Notes on V-Mail During WWII: The USPS copied an existing British system created for soldiers 
and sailors stationed in the Middle East in the 1930s that transmitted microfilm images of 
letters written on proscribed small stationary. In June 1942, the USPS unveiled a one-page 
standardized V-Mail stationary form, with a fold-over flap to create an envelope, which was 
seven by nine inches. An aggressive nationwide campaign was implemented to encourage 
spouses, families and friends, and soldiers overseas, to use these forms. A letter written on V- 
Mail stationary was first examined by mail censors, who could block delivery or blackout 
sections. Once approved, the V-Mail was then photographed to create a microfilm negative. 
Military postal centers overseas (i.e., APOs - Army/Air Force Post Offices or FPOs (Fleet Post 
Offices for Navy personnel) and V-Mail centers in the U.S. received the microfilm spools, which 
each contained roughly 2000 letters. At the V-Mail centers, dozens of civilians or members of 
the Women’s Army Corp (WACs) printed the negatives that were then sorted by location and 
distributed to designated APOs and FPOs overseas and hometown post offices in the U.S. The 
resulting V-Mail print was 4 % by 5 % inches, representing 55% of the original stationary.

From spring 1942 to fall 1945, more than one billion V-Mails were sent. Roughly 60% were from 
the U.S. to servicemen overseas and the other 40% were mailed in the reverse direction. In 
spite of calls to patriotism and extensive advertisement of the V-Mail system, these one billion 
pieces of V-Mail represented only 20% of the total mail between servicemen and significant 
others in the U.S. Approximately 70% of letters and other small parcels were sent by regular 
mail through the USPS, and about 10% were delivered to recipients via other means — most 
typically, through the postal system of other friendly or neutral nations and by servicemen 
traveling to war zones or back home who often carried dozens of letters to distribute upon 
arrival. One of the primary barriers to V-Mail usage was the widespread impression that they 
were difficult to read, either because the writer’s cursive was tiny in order to cram in extra 
information, and/or the microfilm photography was flawed. The USPS collaborated with several 
companies to manufacture and market V-Mail reading glasses (i.e., magnifiers) but this effort 
failed to entice additional users. My experience in attempting to read Harold’s V-Mail 
communications verified the readability issue.

found the format challenging to use. As the war progressed, most of 
the V-Mails were sent by servicemen overseas, who often had no 
other option, while family and friends at home primarily relied on 
regular USPS mail delivery to overseas APOs and FPOs.

Mildred Hendricson saved 41 V-Mail and regular USPS letters that Harold Hendricson wrote to 
her between 1942 and 1945 when he served in combat zones in North Africa, Sicily, and Italy. 
Thirty-two of the letters were V-Mails and nine were sent by regular USPS mail. Harold wrote 
several of the USPS letters when he was hospitalized recovering from wounds. Only one letter 
from Mildred to Harold survives, which is not surprising since he was almost continuously in 
front line combat zones. Harold also sent at least two letters (one V-Mail and one USPS) to 
Mildred’s parents, Archie and Maude Dennis, and based on comments in his letters to Mildred, 
also sent V-Mails to his parents, Mabel Hendricson and William F. Hendricson, but these 
communications no longer exist. 


Based on the content of the letters (i.e., references to discussions not included in surviving 
letters), it appears that some correspondence is missing, but | have the sense that these 41 
letters represent the majority of Harold’s communication to Mildred during WWII. Because all 
but one letter is from Harold to Mildred, reading them is similar to hearing only one side of a 
telephone conversation, or being able to read only one person’s contributions to a long string 
of text messages among several people. Yet, certain themes are evident because Harold’s 
comments tended to be triggered by statements or inquiries made by Mildred in her letters. 


One recurrent theme is the amount of text, considering the limited V-Mail format, they devoted 
to coy flittering with each other, or probing for indications of commitment. Harold and Mildred 
were in their early 20s during the war and were obviously curious about each other’s 
interactions with members of the opposite sex. Based on Harold’s responses to Mildred’s 
letters, and her letters to her parents, which are excerpted in the next section, it’s apparent 
that there was considerable socializing at her stateside stations and travel in mixed gender 
groups to cities for shopping, dining, dancing and shows. He often countered with descriptions 
of dances, dinners, and USO shows that he attended in the company of WACs as well as social 
events attended by young women from the local community. All of this banter about social 


321 


activity was communicated in a light-hearted manner, but the underlying intent seems clear — 
do we have a future or not? The question was not addressed head-on until they finally talked 
by phone in August of 1945. 


Another theme was Mildred’s frequent expressions of discontent, or discomfort, about her 
relatively undemanding stateside assignments that provided ample opportunity for sight seeing 
and entertainment, and Harold’s attempts to re-assure her that the WACs were “doing their 
part,” by freeing up more men to serve in combat roles. I’m not sure that is what she wanted to 
hear, but that was his recurrent response. He did write in one V-Mail that “there is plenty of 
sight seeing going on over here in down times” and in another letter commented that “we just 
requested more and better cameras to photo all the amazing things we see almost everyday.” 


A third theme is the downward spiral of Harold’s estimation of surviving the war, which he 
often discussed openly in the letters (surprisingly this got through the censors), and the de- 
humanizing effects of incessant violence, also discussed in blunt detail. Harold’s V-Mails near 
the end of the war often included reflections about his capacity to re-join society considering all 
the death and mayhem he had experienced, and statements that he was considering 
volunteering for Pacific duty as the European war wound down. Harold was evidently deeply 
conflicted about his plans after discharge as was Mildred. As discussed later in this section, 
Mildred applied for at least two positions that would have led to a career in the regular Army, 
with a multi-year commitment, rather than post-war demobilization. 


Excerpts from Harold’s WWII Letters to Mildred, 1942 to 1945 
Clarifying comments appear after some of the letter excerpts. 


Fall, 1942 (not dated) Possibly written in Ireland where Harold’s 1 Army Division was training 
for the North Africa invasion. USPS regular mail. Three excerpts from a four-page letter. 


“| imagine the city of Kalama is quite a place. Perhaps the place where the new blushing 
schoolmarm marries the son of the leading lawyer or rancher. | have been thinking that 
marriage is quite an up to date proposition” Comment: Mildred Dennis was high school teacher 
in the small town of Kalama in western Washington at the time of this letter. 

“It’s going to be quite a satisfaction to find out if one is really a man. But enough about that. 
Perhaps you are wondering what is going to happen to us. All | have been informed at present, 
as of 1500 today, is that mail is to be sent to an address of APO 3340, Postmaster New York, 
N.Y. By reading between the lines, you can ferret out my meaning.” Comment: APO 3340 was 
well known during WWII to be North Africa. Servicemen were not allowed to discuss geographic 
locations, but APOs were used as indicators. Oddly, censors did not blackout such remarks. 

“To make your civilian life, with all of its shortages and rations bearable, | will get you a fine 
shawl from the finest shop in Cairo, or perhaps some intricate African necklace. For my self, |!am 
going to get a bottle of the finest champagne the Deutchers haven’t yet consumed.” 

May 14, 1943. North Africa. V-Mail 

“Well at last | again get time to write. Sorry for the long delay, however, have been quite busy. | 
am now in the hospital, having had an accident. | lasted through the last push that brought us 
thru to a victory here in Africa. | was lucky and my injury this time was light as was the first one. 
| hope my luck does not run out and let me down in the next theatre.” 


322 


Comment: Soldiers were told not to discuss the type, location or severity of their wounds and 
injuries, and directed to not to use phrases such as “was wounded, was shot, or was burned” in 
their letters. Harold was wounded at least twice in North Africa, both leading to 
hospitalizations, and also suffered a mysterious accident on one of his first days in North Africa, 
or perhaps during training in Ireland, which was severe enough that he was evacuated to 
England for a week, and then promptly returned to his unit. 


June 3, 1943. North Africa. USPS letter 

“Please excuse my penmanship because | am writing this from the top of the hospital building 
where | have been taken for a sun bath, and the wind up here is quite strong, causing the papers 
and my self to shake around. Shortly before dinner today, my first sergeant came to see me. My 
outfit was moving positions and passed quite near to the city in which | am confined. He brought 
me what little of my equipment that was not burned (Harold’s tank had taken a direct hit from 
German artillery, and exploded; he jumped to safety but suffered burns and wounds from flying 
debris). Also, the sergeant managed to bring some of the souvenirs | had collected, which the 
later days of the campaign produced profusely (i.e., German and Italian pistols, binoculars, 
gloves and sunglasses). / was glad to hear how my company had mostly survived the last four 
days of fighting after | was injured, and luckily the bulk of the resistance had crumbled that day. 
My company’s casualties were exceedingly low. It is hard you know, when you realize that in 
your hands lay the lives of many, many men; men who live and love and want to go home again, 
to see them killed or mangled, and perhaps know that you in part were responsible.” 

June 6, 1943. North Africa. USPS letter 

“lam getting quite a kick out of a French girl that is running around on the roof of a villa not far 
away. She is wearing a halter-top in order to get a suntan | suppose. Accidently | picked her up 
in my field glasses as | looked out to sea to view all the ships, and she saw me looking. Every 
time | looked her way, she stamped her feet, yelled something in French that | could not 
understand, and waved at me in that age-old gesture of thumb to nose. | am just ornery enough 
to keep making her angry.” 

June 15, 1943. North Africa. V-Mail 

“Now that Africa is a zone of containment (i.e., a ceasefire is in place after the German 
surrender), | hope to get a chance to see some sights and take pictures after being at the front 
line the entire time | have been over here. Perhaps | can now erase a few of those pictures from 
my mind that give me nightmares and awaken me at night by my shaking. A few bottles of 
cognac, plenty of sunshine and good food for a change will help.” 

August 28, 1943. Sicily. V-Mail 

“Some of the WACs who are stationed nearby appeared in our neck of the woods a short time 
ago. They are more G.I. than our soldiers; very by-the-book. | am supposed to meet a WAC 2 
Lt. next week and go to a dance and dinner with her set up by USO for men and women officers. 
Hope to get the women officers’ slant on fighting a war.” 

September 12, 1943. Salerno, Italy. V-Mail 


“My letters in the near future will probably be far apart out of necessity. | only hope that I don’t 
lose the capacity to write altogether. | don’t feel as lucky as | used to, but am glad that | hada 


323 


chance to do a small bit in bringing this war to an end in a short time. | imagine that a lot of 
amazing news will appear in the U.S.A. in a few days that will make everyone happy. Well, gal — 
keep having a good time in the army. You should send me a snapshot so | could appreciate what 
a U.S. WAC looks like. Pardon the scribbling, but !am minus my fourth finger.” 


A side note: Although this V-Mail was dated September 12, 1943, it was written previously. The 
amazing news that Harold mentioned was the allied invasion of the boot of Italy south of 
Naples, the first allied incursion onto Nazi-controlled mainland Europe, which occurred on 
September 3 and 9, 1943 in two separate landings. An invasion force of British and Canadian 
troops invaded the toe of Italy on September 3. Hendricson and thousands of other Americans in 
the Fifth Army landed at Salerno, south of Naples, on September 9. After these landings, which 
were initially successful, the fascist Italian government, that had recently deposed and arrested 
Benito Mussolini, surrendered to the Allies. However, several days later, Nazi paratroopers freed 
Mussolini from confinement and installed him as the leader of a new fascist Italian government, 
based in Northern Italy, aligned with Nazi Germany. Harold’s participation in the Salerno 
landing may account for his ambiguous comment about a missing finger, likely an attempt at 
humor in reference to a hand injury. British, Canadian, and American troops faced stiff German 
opposition after the invasion, and the campaign ground to a halt far south of their target, 
Rome, in the fall of 1943 with heavy casualties. (Holland J. The Savage Storm: The Battle for 
Italy 1943. London: Transworld Publishing. 2023) Comment: In Savage Storm, Holland explains 
the chaotic political maneuvering in Italy during WWII. Various pro fascist groups contended for 
power while underground anti-fascist resistance groups tried to aid the Allies and topple the 
fascist leadership, hoping to restore a democratic government not aligned with Germany. 


This map depicts the Allies invasion routes in September, 1943. 
The plan evolved from complex political negotiations among the 
British, French, Soviets, Italian resistance and Americans. 
Churchill and Stalin were adamant about opening a second front 
to divert German resources from Russia and Northern European. 
American leaders Marshall and Eisenhower were skeptical, 
accurately, that an Italian invasion would weaken the Nazi and 
feared, also accurately, that a brutal campaign north through 
Italy would produce few strategic victories, but would result in
