December 15, 1943. Unknown location in Italy. USPS Mail. Three excerpts from a four-page 
letter. 

“Today | received your letter with the pictures. You look swell to me and | sure enjoyed the 
letter. | imagine Eagle Pass, Texas is quite a dreary place as far as the gay life is concerned. 
Eagle Pass sounds like some of these small Italian villages, only no ancient Roman ruins. | wish | 
was able to take pictures of my present battle steed (i.e., his tank) and its crew. | have a very 
sentimental attachment for this one because | feel if | lose it, | shall not get another. Several, 
unfortunately, were, ah ... disposed of in recent weeks! Every member of my crew is over six 
feet. It’s really an ace crew, all with a lot of battle experience. Had one of them in a position 


324 


where his head was outside all the time, and had to put him in another spot because his hair is 
so vividly red, and attracted a lot of attention, so to speak (if you get my meaning).” 


“| was never too sentimental as far as the beauties of nature and also other beauties too, but | 
certainly will be glad to see the U.S.A, ... if ever. All this time overseas is gradually wearing me 
down, and | stop to think of the U.S.A. only once in a while. Now | am afraid of getting into the 
mood where | will hate to go west, and miss all the good things in life, and forget all the good 
things that life has already given to me (an apparent reference to staying on the East Coast 
after the war rather than returning to Walla Walla). Guess that’s silly; but enough of that. How 
about this: | heard a “Moron” joke today. It’s about the football player who flooded the field 
with water so the coach could send him in for a sub.” 


“When | saw the picture of you in the G.I. mess kitchen it made me so hungry that | popped open 
a can of rations. Of course, it had to be cold but | just closed my eyes and dreamed that it was 
Eagle Pass Turkey. Well gal, take care of yourself. See you for sure in 44! Hal” 


December 29, 1943. Unknown location in Italy. V-Mail 


“| wear that medal you sent me, and not long ago, an Italian women tried to drag me off to 
mass. Nearly got religion, didn’t |.” 


February 11, 1944. Anzio Beach, Italy. V-Mail 

“We got a barrel of beer brewed in Italy by an American brewmaster. It was a welcome change 
after such a long dry period here in the beachhead. Also, we got a shipment of fresh eggs, the 
first we’ve had. Had quite a feast for a whole day. | hope it does not pertain to the old saying, 
like — the condemned man ate a hearty last meal. We get quite a kick out of listening to Axis 
Sally each night on the radio. Contrary to German opinion, she really raises our morale and 
plays way better music than any of the American stations (i.e., Armed Forces Network; AFN). 
Well, gal, keep your fingers crossed for us and hope for the best. Love, Hal.” 


A side note: /n an effort to make an end run around (i.e. outflank) the stout German defenses 
south of Rome, known to U.S. Gls as the “Gustav Line” that had stalled the Allied advance 
northward, the U.S. Fifth Army and the British 15" Army Group, collectively comprising 36,000 
troops, made a surprise amphibious landing on January 22, 1944, at a sandy beach and marsh 
area known as Anzio, 80 miles north of the Gustav Line. The initial landing caught the Germans 
and their fascist Italian cohorts off guard, but dithering and ill-advised decisions such as 
hunkering down on the beach versus immediately pressing inland against the initially thin 
German/ltalian defense; and targeting Rome, a meaningless objective versus attacking the 
Gustav line from the rear by British and American command staff allowed the entire invasion 
force to be pinned down on the beachhead for several months thereafter, during which the 
Germans launched several major offensives aimed at shoving the allies off the beach. The 
February 11, 1944 V-Mail was written while Lt. Hendricson and the rest of the U.S. Fifth Army 
were trapped at Anzio. During that month, the Germans bombarded the Allies daily with 
artillery fire, launched a massive assault on the beach perimeter on February 18, and destroyed 
the pumps draining the Anzio marsh fields, in a partially successful effort to flood the beach with 
salt water. After changes in command structure, the Allies finally landed over 100,000 
reinforcements, which provided the force needed to break through the German defensive ring at 
the end of May, 1944. (Atkinson, R. The Day of Battle: The War in Sicily and Italy; 1943-1944. 


325 


The Liberation Trilogy. New York: Henry Holt and Company. 2007) Comment: The 
commendation for Harold’s first Silver Star included this narrative. “For gallantry in action on 18 
February, 1944 near Carraceto, Italy. On this date, during the heaviest German assaults on the 
Anzio beachhead, 1st Lt. Hendricson, in complete disregard for his own safety, forced his tank 
into the enemy positions, and, although under direct and close fire from a number of Mark VI 
tanks, fired his entire basic load of ammunition into a wadi containing several companies of 
German infantry. He killed or wounded four hundred of them before his tank was hit and 
burned. This action by Lt. Hendricson broke up the German attack for which the Germans had 
massed major numbers of troops and slowed the German offensive in this sector, a potent 
factor in holding the beachhead during this critical period.” Note: A “wadi” is a ravine or 
channel that is dry except in rainy season. 


An article in the local Walla Walla newspaper, the Union-Bulletin, included a more colorful 
quote from Harold, apparently extracted from a letter written to his parents: “The German’s 
looked like they were all dressed up and lined up for a parade, and then they started trying to 
climb up the side of the ravine. It was like shooting ducks at a carnival stall.” The article went on 
the report that “two enemy companies were almost completely liquidated” and Hendrickson’s 
tank, named Spare Parts, also destroyed an anti-tank gun concealed inside a windmill and 
“bagged a Mark IV tank hiding under a haystack, before being hit by an armor piercing shell. 
Hendrickson and crew jumped to safety and made it back to American lines, taking a German 
prisoner along the way.” Oddly, the Walla” newspaper spelled Hendrickson with a “K”. (Walla 
Walla Union-Bulletin Archives, 1944. www.wallawallaunionbulletin.newspaperarchives.com. 
Accessed October 2, 2024) 

April 11, 1944. Anzio Beach, Italy. V-Mail 

“Well another day and still healthy, but not wise. Wish somebody would win this war; I’m 
getting as bored as the devil with this place. Guess it’s because there is nothing to do except 
fight and nobody to see except other soldiers and Germans. Had a stroke of bad luck and broke 
my only pair of good sunglasses. Now | have to sweat out someone getting killed so | can inherit 
his. Wish | was there (Bradley Field, CT apparently) to do a little real partying myself. When | 
finally get into Rome, I’m going hog wild for sure. Don’t let any of those warriors in the soft jobs 
snow you back there. Love, Hal” 


September 17, 1944. Central Italy. USPS Mail. Three excerpts from a five-page letter. 


“Lam sorry that | have not written for so long. | got quite a kick out of your last letter. You sound 
more like one of the soldiers who have been overseas for three years than ones who haven’t. 
Your references to stuffed-shirt officers tickle me. Almost everyone here is now hopeful for a 
quick end of the war with Germany, however, some of them are too optimistic. We may have 
quite a lot of stiff fighting yet here in Italy.” Comment: This letter was written three months 
after the D-Day landings in Normandy. The U.S. and U.K. media assumed that the Allies’ quick 
advance toward Germany after the invasion would continue unabated. Overly optimistic 
predictions of German surrender were commonplace in newspapers and radio broadcasts. 


“As for myself, | don’t know how I'll ever endure a peaceful life again (providing of course!). 
Seems as if my very being was born and raised with gunfire and dust and mud and blood and 
the dead. | was thinking the other day how hard it would be to stay out of trouble and readjust 


326 


myself as | have absolutely no compunction about killing sex or race or whatever. Well, | must 
stop being so morbid. Don't know why | am because | sure don't have a hangover. I’m going to 
be a hard man to hold for some time if | ever get back to the States. When and if | do, | don’t 
think Walla’ is the best place. | want to go someplace where no one knows me and start from 
the bottom rung. Probably stay on that rung too.” 

“You seem to always apologize for sight seeing so much. What do you suppose the boys over 
here do when they get a chance? Keep their eyes shut? Well soldier, keep your shoulders back 
and keep em coming. Love, Harold.” Comment: The September 17, 1944 letter was written 
after eight months of incessant combat, with high Allied casualties as the U.S. and British 
armies broke out of Anzio and started a slow slog north through mountainous central Italy 
against an aggressive German defense. 

By Mildred Dennis. September 27, 1944. Windsor Locks, Connecticut. USPS Mail The only 
surviving WWII letter from Mildred Dennis to Harold Hendricson, in which she responds to his 
September 17 letter. Two excerpts from a five-page letter. 


“Returning to a peaceful and quiet life will have its problems no doubt. Somehow, | feel it won’t 
be as much of a readjustment as your are anticipating. Men who have been discharged from the 
service and are now back from overseas are making very good civilians. With your intelligence 
and good judgment, | expect you to do the same. Seems it's a human faculty for forgetting or at 
least letting time dim the unpleasant details of life.” 


“Wish you were here at Bradley tonight (i.e. the USAF air base at Bradley Field; Mildred was 
assigned to the Women’s Army Air Corp). Being a brazen hussy, | took it for granted that | 
would be the one to show you sights around Bradley (if you were ever up here). Frankly, we 
don’t have many in the immediate vicinity that you would be interested in. However, New York 
has anything one might want to find as you probably know. That would be the place for you to 
celebrate your return. | might come down to see that no one tries to hold you down too much. 
Please don’t enjoy the belle signoras too much over there. Remember that not all brunettes are 
in Italy. Love, Mildred” 

October 24, 1944. Central Italy. V-Mail 

“Had a proud moment yesterday when two of my original boys were given battlefield 
commissions by General Clark (Commanding General of the U.S. Fifth Army). Makes me feel 
swell to see fellows | have trained and fought with really go to town. About those nightspots you 
mentioned in your last letter, I’d really like you to show them to me. !’Il bet with everyone in the 
U.S. believing in a very near end to the war, there is a lot of celebrations back there. Well pal, 
keep your chin up. Love, Harold.” 


February 22, 1945. Santa Lucia, a suburb of Rome. USPS Mail. Two excerpts from a four-page 
letter. 


“Don’t be too surprised at receiving an actual letter from me instead of those lousy V-Mails. | 
am spending some R & R time (i.e., Rest and Relaxation days behind the frontlines) in a nice 
little town by the name of “Lucia” where | saw a show of “Panama Hattie” last night. It was 
fairly good even with a mediocre cast. Have just finished listening to the AFN news. Sounds as if 
with the advent of good weather, we can finish the European campaign off pretty soon. Hope | 


327 


get a chance to come home to the States after it is over, although it might be interesting to try 
out the quality of those Japs.” 


“Not so long ago, we had a Brigade Officers Dance with the local crop of Guinea Girls as guests. 
They can’t dance very well, and when the snack bar opened, the dancing part of their evening 
was complete. Food was a greater enticement than us soldiers.” Comment: In WWII, the phrase 
“Guinea Girls” was used by Brits and Americans to refer to women from southern Italy who had 
a darker complexion, i.e., more Mediterranean in appearance, than women from northern Italy. 
Today, as then, the phrase is considered to be demeaning. 

March 6, 1945. Northern Italy. V-Mail 

“This country and the war gets quite rugged at times. What | would really enjoy would be a 
bottle of whiskey. Not that | have turned into a heavy imbiber, but it chases away my bad 
dreams sometimes. One of the officers in the Company received a bottle that was packed neatly 
away in newspapers, to avoid detection, and we drank it last night. The occasion was the return 
of a buddy who had been listed as missing for some time, but was actually injured, lost some of 
his memory and was being cared for in an Italian village. Well gal, don’t slay those Northerners 
with your Texas drawl and take care of yourself. Love, Hal” 


March 30, 1945. Northern Italy. V-Mail 

“| have been regularly receiving your letters and packages of cigs. | really get a boost of morale 
from both. It makes me ashamed at your faithfulness in writing. | solemnly swear to endeavor to 
write more often. From all indications we should end the European campaign in a short time. | 
have been talking to some of the men in my Company who have returned from furloughs in the 
States, and they say it is a wonderful place. | wonder. Love, Harold” 


June 30, 1945. North Italy near the Switzerland border. USPS Mail. The final WWII letter from 
Harold to Mildred that survived the war. Two excerpts from a five-page letter. 

“Sorry to not have written more often. Cannot say | have been working too hard the last few 
weeks, but have been playing quite hard. There is lots of good beer over in Switzerland and quite 
a few parties and dances over there too. Was very glad to see the end of the war as | was very 
tired of sending friends of mine out on jobs where | knew that some would not come back. One 
day near the end, every officer | had was killed. Some | had known for three years.” 

“Two days ago, they declared certain of us as essential post-war personnel and will move us to 
Germany where we are forming a new Administrative Division, called an Occupation Army. | 
suppose | will remain there for some time, running the government for those damn Germans. 
Hope that you are having a good time now that the Euro war is behind us. | sure would like to 
return to the States. Guess | haven’t much chance in going back however. Perhaps they think 
I’ve got too many points to be a proper citizen. Well, gal — don't let them send you to the Army 
of Occupation. Love, Harold” 

Comment: Harold Hendricson was appointed provisional mayor of the town of Ulm, Germany, 
located in the German state of Bavaria, shortly after this letter was written. He and a staff of 
other U.S. officers were assigned to the city during the post-war transition period until suitable 
(i.e., non-Nazi affiliated) German administrators could be identified. As discussed in the Notes 
below on the U.S. Army Point System for determining post-war activity, Harold’s options at the 
end of the European War were most likely: (1) assignment to the Army of Occupation, or, as an 


328 


experienced and well decorated officer, (2) re-deployment to the Pacific to prepare for the 
invasion of Japan, anticipated to occur in 1946. 


Notes on the U.S. Army Point System at the end of WWII. Near the end of the European war in 
the spring of 1945, the U.S. Army developed a point system, known as the Adjusted Service 
Rating Score, to determine, along with unit-level criteria, which of the six million servicemen in 
Europe would be: (1) demobilized and transported back to the States on hundreds of military 
and civilian conscripted ships in a program named Operation Magic Carpet, (2) assigned to an 
Army of Occupation based in Germany, or (3) transferred to the Pacific to participate in the 
invasion of Japan. As late as June 1945, U.S. military leaders, for the most part unaware of the 
Manhattan Project, planned to transfer 800,000 officers and soldiers from Europe to the Pacific, 
anticipating that the Japanese could not be defeated until late in 1946. Soldiers received points 
for months of service (total and overseas), numbers of named campaigns, medals, promotions, 
nominations and other recognitions including Purple Hearts for combat wounds and injuries, 
and number of dependent children. Initially, 85 points were needed for rotation to the U.S., but 
this number was considered unattainable by many soldiers and their stateside families, and 
large protests broke out in the U.S. and overseas. Late in 1945, the threshold number was 
reduced to 50. On the other hand, a very high point total might lead to a different, and 
potentially less desirable outcome. | remember that my dad often claimed that he had 
accumulated 140 points by May 1945, and thus, due to this high level of combat experience, 
was a potential target for re-assignment to the Pacific. Instead, he wound up in the Army of 
Occupation as a provisional mayor, an assignment he was not excited about, but begrudgingly 
accepted after learning that he could fly to London from a nearby airbase for weekend revelry, 
which he apparently did often. WACs also had a point system; 44 points were needed for 
discharge based on criteria pertinent to women soldier’s roles and tasks. Mildred Dennis 
achieved this threshold in December 1945 and was discharged soon after, returning to Walla 
Walla early in 1946. (Gault O. Operation Magic Carpet. Chatsworth MA: Challenge Publications. 
2005; Ziemke EF. The U.S. Army in the Occupation of Germany, 1944-1946. Center for Military 
History. Washington DC: U.S. Government Printing Office. 1975; The National World War II 
Museum. www.nationalww2museum.org. Bamford T. The Points Were All That Mattered: The 
U.S. Army’s Demobilization After World War II. August 17, 2010. Accessed: August 22, 2024)

Excerpts From Mildred Dennis’ WWII Letters to Her Parents 

Mildred wrote to her parents, Archie and Maude Dennis, at least weekly for the duration of her 
nearly three years in the Women’s Army Air Corps (WACs). A total of 259 letters survived and 
were maintained in a shoebox by her mother, Maude Dennis. Review of the surviving letters 
indicates that Mildred likely mailed other letters, but they did not make it into Maude’s 
collection. In this letters, Mildred often commented on her correspondence with Harold. Many 
of her letters were lengthy, six or more pages, thus the following excerpts provide only small 
slices of Mildred’s total volume of communication with her parents, who also appear to have 
sent letters and packages of food and other supplies to her almost weekly. None of her parents’ 
letters appear to have survived the war. All of Mildred’s correspondence with her parents was 
by regular USPS mail, including the new service in the continental U.S. — Air Mail. Mildred and 
her parents also talked with some regularity by telephone, especially in the later years of the 
war as transcontinental phone service improved to support the war effort. It is evident from her 
letters that Mildred routinely communicated with a number of servicemen in addition to 
Harold, some of whom appear to be childhood friends or high school classmates, while her 
relationship with others is not known. Mildred’s surviving letters begin after she completed the 
six-week basic training phase at Fort Des Moines, lowa, the centralized WAC training site for the 
entire U.S. 


Several themes are evident in the letters: Mildred’s ambition to do useful work that helped the 
war effort, a goal which she only intermittently achieved from her perspective, her personal 
ambition to receive promotions in military rank, also a frustrating pursuit; her concerns for 
Harold’s welfare and dismay at receiving only sporadic communication from him, and her desire 
to take full advantage of the social and cultural opportunities near the bases where she was 
stationed, especially in New England during 1944 and 1945. Overall, Mildred’s letters to her 
parents provide perspectives on the stateside war experienced by hundreds of thousands of 
service men and women who did not go overseas. 

July 5, 1943. Fort Des Moines, lowa 

“| really like this army life, even though we are always on the run. | really like all the drilling (i.e., 
marching in close quarters). It’s fun being able to do all the eyes right, eyes left and different 
types of drilling and different pacings. We just fell out (i.e., dismissed from the classroom), and 
had an intensive hour of drill as we have our first parade this afternoon.” 

July 12, 1943. Fort Des Moines, lowa 

“Don’t worry about me at night. Any man who tries anything on this post would be a fool. There 
are hundreds of women here, and plenty of military police. Did you know that Fort Des Moines is 
called the Women’s West Point?” 


August 4, 1943, Fort Des Moines, lowa. Two excerpts from a five page letter. 

“Well, now | am officially Private Mildred M. Dennis. Finally! We were sworn in at a mass 
ceremony at 8:30am this morning. It was broadcast over NBC (Radio), but it would be so early 
out there in Lowden that you probably didn’t hear it. NBC also made a film of it, so | imagine 
that it will be shown soon in theaters before the real movie comes on. If you see the film, there 
were a few girls in the center of the film with white uniforms on. I’m standing about 6 people to 
the right of them on the first line of those with white uniforms.” Comment: WACs were a new 


330 


and not universally accepted concept in WWII. Mildred was in the second cohort to graduate 
from WAC basic training. She and other WACs were called “auxiliaries” until completion of basic 
training and not given a U.S. army rank until their third month of service, in part because many 
military leaders assumed, incorrectly, that the majority would drop out during basic training. 
(Ziobro M. “Skirted Soldiers.” The Women’s Army Corp and Gender Integration of the U.S. Army 
During World War Two. Army Historical Association. www.armyhistory.org. Accessed: August 
30, 2024) 

“| was called into the base dentist office yesterday, and he filled one tooth. He filled two more 
teeth today, and I'll finish up Friday with another filling, and then have them cleaned. He’s a 
nice young doctor, and seems to be very good. | wore my cook’s uniform yesterday, so now he 
calls me “Cookie.” Nothing like a little teasing to make me feel right at home.” Comment: After 
completion of basic training, Mildred was assigned to the Cooks and Bakers School for two 
months to prepare her for duty as a line cook or supervisor of cooks at WAC or regular army 
mess halls stateside or, potentially, overseas. Training focused on preparing, cooking, serving, 
transporting and storing mass quantities of food.

Mildred’s note on the back of this photo indicates that

“| told Mother on the phone yesterday that | would have news September 7. By that, | mean | 
will know what | will be doing for the next few weeks. | will either stay here and go to 
Dehydration, Butchers and Mess Sergeants School, or | might be sent to some post in the field. 
The latter is what | want of course, but chances are that | will have to stay here, darn it! 
Although everyone tries to tell us the living conditions here are so much better than anywhere 
else. But | still like the excitement of getting to move around and seeing new places.” 

“Mother also said | had a letter from Harold that was sent to your address. That was certainly 
welcome news. | rather felt he would write when it was over in Sicily, but | didn’t think it would 
arrive so soon. Coming to you thru San Francisco seems odd. Must have been a plane coming 
that way or else there was a clipper going to SF.” 


September 21, 1943. Fort Des Moines, lowa 

“We're going to Dehydration, Butchers and Mess Sergeants School starting this week. Overall, 
I’m really glad as it is a very interesting course, all about foods they send overseas and how they 
are managed. They are prepared by extracting the water, and then adding the water back when 
it is time to use the foods. The knowledge won't be as valuable for me at this time, but if |! am 
sent overseas after the war to help feed the people in the conquered countries, | will have to 


331 


know this, and how to manage delivery. This course will make 13 weeks of school, and still more 
to come after this, so | think |! am really getting my money’s worth from the Army.” 


“Harold wrote a nice letter. He had just received the 1st letter | wrote when first coming to Des 
Moines. The mail is certainly slow catching up with him. You might tell his folks that it was 
dated August 28". He said he had purchased some souvenirs he thought | would like, but had no 
way of sending them to me due to V-Mail. Oh, Harold did say there were some WACs stationed 
where he is now, and he is going to meet a WAC 2" Lt. | had thought about sending him a 
picture or snapshot of myself, but if he’s seen a WAC now, he can imagine what | look like in 
uniform. They say they let the older WACs go overseas. | hope she was 30 at least and a blond.” 
Comment: There was running dialogue throughout the letters from both Harold and Mildred, 
mostly the latter, about his preference for brunettes and disdain for blondes. 

October 17, 1943. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“| have my new assignment here in Eagle Pass. The have put me in the main office for the mess 
halls at this base. It seems my cooking days are over at least as long as | am in Eagle Pass. |am 
quite pleased as it seems like a step up in the right direction. | have just met my new boss! He 
came down to the base Saturday afternoon. His name is Lt. O’Shaughnessy. Nothing like a good 
Irishman to work in the mess office. He is very nice in a reserved sort of way. After our meeting, 
he was nice enough to give me most of the afternoon off, and he drove me to my barracks as we 
was going my way. He is an extremely nice 1° Lt. and safely married! He wants me to supervise 
the bakers and cooks here in our six mess halls, give them suggestions, make sure things get 
done properly, and to introduce new dishes into the menu when possible. Sounds pretty good, 
doesn’t it.” Comment: Mildred was transferred to Army Air Force Base in Eagle Pass after 
completion of the four week Dehydration, Butchers and Mess Sergeants School. Initially, she 
assumed an administrative role at Eagle Pass, which soon expanded to other roles. 


“There are two nice places on the other side of the Rio Grande in Mexico. In the U.S., we would 
consider them to be nightclubs. Dining and dancing with a bar in an adjoining room. They serve 
the best lime-ade | have ever tasted. Now all | need is to find me a non-commissioned officer 
who likes to dance. That’s the ones with stripes on their sleeves. We (WACs) are not allowed to 
go to Mexico with the commissioned officers here, that’s the fellows who are the bosses. For a 
while at least | am going to be so busy getting into the swing of my job with Lt. O’Shaughnessy, | 
won’t have time for much dancing and such.” 


Mildred, with a WAC colleague identified as “Ruth” shortly after 
being transferred from Fort Des Moines to the Army Air Force Base 
in Eagle Pass, Texas. Mildred had several jobs at Eagle Pass 
including supervising meal prep at six mess halls, recruiting, and 
serving as a dietician at the base hospital.

November 7, 1943. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 


“I'm listening to the “Army Hour” this afternoon. It’s a broadcast in tribute of the men serving in 
the North African area (i.e., Mediterranean). I’m listening to General Eisenhower right now. | 
hope that the European war is over by this time next year. If it progresses as it has in the last 
few weeks, it ought to pretty well over. Somehow | feel that Harold is allright. He didn’t write 
before when he was in action in Africa, and when it’s over in Italy | think he will write again. | 
know it isn’t easy for his mother to not hear, and he probably doesn’t realize how terribly 
worried she and his father are. Even here when I’m very busy, | lose touch of when | wrote last, 
so! can imagine that time passes very quickly for Harold.” 

November 17, 1943. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“Well, believe it or not, |!am on detached duty service recruiting WACs. So far, | have mostly just 
ridden around Texas and laughed at a funny Lt’s. jokes. His name is Cavello, and he is really a 
scream. | and one other WAC, a driver, this funny Lt., and our Company Commander make up 
the recruiting group. Right now we are at Camp Clark Springs near a town called Brackettville, 
which is an Army cavalry post that has been here since before the Civil War days, so it is old and 
well established. We’re recruiting some of the civilian workers here — we have eight prospects so 
far. Camp Clark is a huge post made up almost entirely of Negroes. There is a large group of 
Negro WACs stationed here as well. The camp is quite attractive: it has lots of green lawn, trees, 
alittle brook running through it and stately old stone buildings to house the troops. 


Notes on Camp Clark and the Black Seminole Indian Fighters: Camp Clark Springs was 
established in the 1850s by the U.S. federal army as a base for troops assigned to protect White 
settlers west of San Antonio from raids by Comanche, Mescalero, Kickapoo and Lipan tribes 
that operated out of the Sierra Madre Oriental Mountains of northern Mexico. The land for the 
base, originally named for the Las Moras Springs, was leased by the Army from the famed 
Maverick family who were influential in the development of the San Antonio region in the 19" 
and early 20" centuries. (Marks PM. Turn Your Eyes Toward Texas: Pioneers Sam and Mary 
Maverick. College Station, Texas: Texas A&M University Press. 1989) The Las Moras Springs are 
one of the largest group of artesian springs in Texas, discharging 12 million gallons of water 
daily from an underground aquifer. Prior to the intrusion of White homesteaders, the Las 
Moras Springs (Los Moras = the “Mulberries” in Spanish) were a recreational site for Native 
tribes in the area. 


The Confederate Army took over the fort in 1861, named it after the first Confederate Governor 
of Texas, Edward Clark, and used it for training recruits and as a hospital. After the conclusion 
of the Civil War, the U.S. Army reclaimed the facility as a training site and home base for several 
companies of Seminole-Negro Indian Scouts, a branch of the Army’s Buffalo Soldier Divisions, 
comprised almost entirely of Black soldiers. This military unit was assigned the arduous and 
dangerous task of minimizing damage from bands of raiding tribes who often swept down from 
the Sierra Madres and across the Rio Grande to attack the many isolated White and Hispanic 
settlements in South Texas. The unit also launched counterattacks into Mexico from Camp Clark 
to try to disrupt the operations of these tribes and capture their leaders. 


333 


The Seminole-Negro community, also known as the Black Seminoles, numbered in the 
thousands by the mid-19" century. This cultural group of mixed Native American and African 
racial origins, emerged when escaped Black slaves in the 18™ and early 19" centuries gravitated 
to central Florida, which was a Spanish Territory until 1821. Spain welcomed escaped slaves 
with promises of freedom if they accepted a Catholic baptism. Central Florida was also inviting 
to fleeing slaves because it was thinly populated by Whites, who were mostly struggling, 
“hardscrabble,” small plot farmers who had no use for slaves, had limited organized 
governance, and was primarily populated by several bands of Seminoles, who accepted Blacks 
within their community. (Kuiper K. Black Seminoles. Britannica. www.britannica.com. August 
11, 2015. Accessed: August 29, 2024) Over the decades, the arriving Blacks integrated into the 
larger Seminole culture. In the 1820s, affluent White land developers from Georgia urged the 
federal government to push out the Seminoles so Florida land could be opened up for 
plantation agriculture. The U.S conducted three military campaigns to defeat and relocate the 
Seminoles that concluded in 1855 and ultimately led to the forced removal of 80% of the 
surviving Seminole and Black Seminole population to a desolate reservation in Oklahoma. 


Black Seminoles who escaped the relocation fled to the Caribbean and Mexico. The government 
of Mexico, desiring to populate their northern states and also defeat Native Tribes who 
plundered settlements in this region, discouraging population growth, enticed several hundred 
Black Seminoles with land and military jobs to move to the northern states of Coahuila, Nuevo 
Leon, Sonora and Tamaulipas. Brigades of Black Seminoles in the Mexican Federal Army gained 
fame for their scouting, tracking and fierce Indian fighting skills on the south side of the Rio 
Grande in the 1850s and 1860s. In the 1870s, the U.S. recruited, with similar enticements, many 
of the Black Seminole soldiers to move north and enlist in the U.S. Army to serve in the frontier 
war against the Sierra Madre-based tribes, who had primarily turned their attention to the 
north side of the Rio Grande. (Porter KW. The Black Seminoles: History of a Freedom-Seeking 
People. Gainesville, Fl. University Press of Florida. 2013) 


Camp Clark served as the base the Black Seminole units until they were disbanded in 1914. It 
also served as the base for two regiments of Black Buffalo Soldiers, and then, in the segregated 
20" century military, for all-Black Army units, including the 4" Cavalry Brigade, which Mildred 
Dennis observed on her recruiting trips in 1943. (Haenn B. Fort Clark and Brackettville: Land of 
Heroes. Mount Pleasant, South Carolina: Arcadia Publishing. 2002) Today, Camp Clark Springs is 
a tourist attraction with camp grounds, a park containing the hot springs, a 100 yard long 
swimming pool fed by the springs, hiking trails, and the remnants of the military base.

November 28, 1943. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“Well ... this was my day to really catch up on my correspondence, but somehow all | got done 
was a letter to Harold. He’s getting to be a bit of a problem to write to. You know Daddy, you 
always said he was cynical. Well, I’m afraid the war is increasing it, or he is trying to cover up his 
real feelings with gruffness. Maybe it’s just his natural desire to argue. He answers my letters 
the day they arrive seemingly (although they often take weeks to reach him). But | can expect to 
take some going over about something in every one of them. | guess if | had been through what 
he has, | wouldn’t be so cheerful either. Then again, he seems to can’t get over the fact that | 
joined the WACs. | haven’t much to write him but about except what I’m doing in the WACs, so 
we bicker across the Atlantic about the WACS. Maybe he is just teasing — | hope so. It would be a 
real tragedy if he lost his sense of humor.” 


“That’s one thing | look for (in men) quicker than anything else. Maybe that’s why | have 
enjoyed my recruiting trips so much. Lt. Cavello has a great sense of humor and takes delight in 
teasing me about my rosy cheeks, and my two cows that | accidently mentioned one day. He 
tells everyone about them. Last week, the Captain didn’t go with us, so we really had fun. Lt. 
Cavello forgot he was a Lt. and the four of us were just a happy little family. We went up to 
Kerrville for three days and then stopped of in San Antonio for the weekend where Lt. Cavello 
treated us to a Thanksgiving dinner. Don’t think | am getting romantic ideas. He’s a little short 
fellow, and you folks know that | like them tall.”

December 19, 1943. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 


“| went to the Christmas dance last night, and had a very enjoyable time. It was given by the 
Mechanics Battalion stationed at Laredo, and they had 70 gallons of beer, dozens of sandwiches 
and a beautiful big cake. After a glass or two of beer the fact that | hadn’t danced in two years 
didn’t seem to bother me much. I’m not becoming a naughty girl, but a little cheer seems to 
loosen me up a bit. You folks always did say that | was too quiet. Anyway, | met a rather nice 
fellow from Laredo, Jack O’Neill, who wants to take me out in the near future. | also danced at 
least once with the three officers that were there, which was rather fun. One had been a civilian 
pilot for five years before the war, but was still bashful. His name is also Jack, Lt. Jack Beeson.” 
Comment: Both of the Jacks became dinner and dancing companions for Mildred during her 
Eagle Pass deployment. Mildred’s dates with an officer, a sporadically enforced WAC taboo, 
apparently caused quite a stir in the women’s barracks, based on her descriptions of outings 
with Lt. Beeson in letters to her parents.

December 29, 1943. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“Jack (Sgt. O’Neill) are going to Mexico for dinner Saturday night, that is if he gets back from 
Laredo in time. He is really stationed there but goes back and forth. He also has to go appear 
before the Officers Candidate Board for OCS School. | am going recruiting again next week to 
San Antonio, so the letters may be a bit few and far between. Don't worry about me, !’Il try to 
write better than | did on my last trip.” 


January 5, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“Well, | was out recruiting again at Crystal City and Carrizo Springs about an hour from here, 
and when | got back to the field, a good long letter from Harold was here. He’s a first Lt. now, 
and | gathered from his letter in a pretty cheerful frame of mind. The last line of the letter was - 
See you for sure in 44. That’s wonderful news for me, and I'll be home when he comes even if | 
have to go AWOL. The letter was written December 15, and posted Dec. 18. It got here in 17 
days, the quickest letter to come yet.” 


“At the last count, | still had 16 thank you letters to write [after Christmas]. Of course, | never 
have Harold’s or my Mom and Pop’s name on the letter writing list because those are two 
letters | love to write. They take preference over all others. If | don’t be careful I’ll be talking 
myself into something that doesn’t exist as far as Harold’s concerned.” 

January 12, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“You asked about Jack who | guess | mention often. Sgt. Jack O’Neill is from Mississippi, and 
don’t worry it isn't really serious. Last night, | went to Mexico for dinner, and was supposed to 
be back at the USO to meet him at 10:00 for drinks and dancing. But | was having such a good 
time with my friends, | didn’t get back until 10:45. Well, Jack wasn’t waiting around, and | didn’t 
blame him, so | came home to the barracks with the girls. | just got through with calling him and 
apologizing, and | do hate to do that. He isn’t the kind that grants my every whim, thank 
heavens.” Comment: Mildred’s relationship with Jack O’Neill was broken off after he departed 
South Texas for Officer Candidate School (OCS), although they apparently continued to 
communicate via letters for a unknown period of time. 


February 28, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“Ratings (i.e., promotion lists) came out and Helen Petty (Mildred’s best WAC friend) made Sgt. 
The medical corps hasn’t any more rankings to give out, so I’m afraid you will have to bear with 
your daughter as a Pvt. for some more time to come. Doesn't really matter, when | see how 
many boys are only Pvt. and are overseas fighting. | would like to take all the ratings away from 
the fellows stationed here and give it to those overseas.” 

March 25, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“| had a letter | wrote to Harold in July last year returned to me. | wrote it regular mail because | 
had a lot to say. Evidently, he got the last one | sent. I’ll bet he thinks the WAC is having an 
effect on me. No, | haven’t heard from him recently, but | guess I'll swallow my pride and keep 
on writing to him. His V-Mail letters may have gone astray.” Comment: The collection of 
surviving WWII correspondence between Harold and Mildred includes 12 V-Mail or USPS letters 
that Harold sent to Mildred between July 1943 and March 1944. Mildred must have belatedly 
received these V-Mails after writing this letter.

March 31, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“By the way, don’t write to Eagle Pass any more as | am leaving here soon. Can’t say exactly 
where | am going [Army regulations], but it’s out of the state of Texas. | won’t be any closer to 
home, but it won’t take me any longer to get home and | may be able to get there a bit sooner. 
Much nicer climate and close to some interesting places. Seems silly | can’t say where I’m going, 
but this is the Army! And, don’t worry about me going overseas. The air base here is slowly 
being closed and they are dibbling us WACs out to other bases. | was the only one here with the 
right qualifications, for the job | am going to next, so | was picked for the assignment.” 
Comment: Mildred was transferred to Bradley Air Field near Hartford, Connecticut to serve as a 
dietician at an Army Air Force hospital. She departed April 4 from Eagle Pass and arrived at 
Bradley Field five days later via bus and train travelling through seven states on the journey. 
She wrote at least one letter every day of the trip and mailed them along the way, describing 
the sites and cities she passed in considerable detail. 

April 4, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Eagle Pass, Texas 

“The Army has been a great opportunity for me to see the country and | am enjoying it a great 
deal. I’ve learned one other thing however — don’t become too attached to any one in the army, 
because one never knows what is going to happen. | never dreamed that | would be shipping out 
from here, although a few girls [WACs] have been going now and then for weeks. | guess | felt | 
would be the last to go, and here it is that | am practically the first. Leaving when everyone is 
telling you how much they are going to miss you makes it hard, but | would have felt bad if they 
had just said — well, so long and have a nice trip.” 


April 12, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“| like my new dietician job here at the hospital very much and think | will like it even better as 
time goes by. It isn’t going to be hard work and it’s the sort of place where everyone calls you 
Miss Dennis. | appreciate that now that | have become a dietician after being Pvt. Dennis at 
Eagle Pass. The mess officer, my boss, a captain, has outdone himself being nice. He stops me as 
| go through the office, asks me how | like my work, says he hopes that | will like the nutrition 
department, etc. He said any time | had any trouble at the hospital or with the WAC 
department, just let him know and he would do his best to fix things up. Really nice to know you 
have your boss behind you.” 


Private Mildred Dennis’ during a trip to New York while stationed 
at Bradley Field in Connecticut. 


April 19, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, CT. Two excerpts. 


“I’m sure I’m going to enjoy this part of the country. Last night, another WAC in my barracks 
and | went to Hartford. Along the way we saw houses with signs saying they were built in 1768, 


337 


1771 or 1800. You know how | like old things, so I’m really going to eat up the old brick houses, 
and the white and green colonial style houses. Hartford is a town of 170,000 and has plenty of 
interesting places to go, stage plays from New York, nice restaurants, good stores and service 
people like us WACs are well liked here. Tickets to stage plays can be obtained free for those of 
us in the military.” 


“The girl | went to Hartford with last night is Jewish. She took me to a Jewish Sadder as her 
guest. It was very interesting, and | have never seen so much food and wine in my life. We sat at 
a table with two Jewish families, seemingly wealthy and well educated. Their older children 
were in the service, but there were three younger boys at the table that were cute as bugs ears. 
They were 5 yrs, 9 yrs and 13. Those Jewish fathers fairly doted on those boys. The dinner, of 
course, had a long religious preliminary, most of which was chanted in Hebrew. Every once ina 
while you eat a bitter herb, then certain kinds of crackers, drink some wine, or eat raisins.” 

May 11, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“I’ve been debating quite awhile over telling you folks this, but | guess parents would just as 
soon take the ups and downs with their kids. I’m applying for a straight commission as a 
dietician in the Army Nurse Corps. Capt. Peachy at Eagle Pass urged me to do it under a new 
directive that has come out. | filled out my papers in Eagle Pass before | departed and took the 
physical for it, but | still have to complete some more papers up here and probably take another 
physical. | don’t know what my chances are and that’s why | haven’t told you sooner than this. 
For that reason, don’t tell anyone about it. Not even Lloyd or the Hendricsons. If | don’t make 
the grade, we will be the only ones to know. It will mean a second Lts. Commission and a 
transfer to the Army Nursing Corps. | will need my transcript from WSC [Washington State 
College], which is in the WSC folder in the top drawer of chest in my closet. Make sure to send 
transcripts for all of my WSC years including summers 1941 and 1942.” Comment: There was 
no further mention of the Army Nurse Corps, which would have been a regular Army position 
with an enlistment period of seven years. Either she did not complete the application or it was 
not accepted. In the later case, she likely communicated the outcome to her parents by 
telephone. In the spring of 1945, Mildred also applied for Admission to the Army Dietician’s 
School, another regular army commissioned position. This application was arduous involving 
interviews, physical exams, review of college transcripts, and accumulation of recommendation 
letters from military and civilian sources. However, with sooner-than-expected end of the 
Pacific war in August 1945, the Dietician School was closed until the Army determined the 
future of the WAC branch, and thus, her application was returned. 


July 7, 1944. North Platte, Nebraska. Letter written on the return to Bradley by train after a 
three-week furlough to Walla Walla 

“I’m anxious to get back to Bradley now after reading the news of the big circus fire at 
Hartford. The two Alice’s that | often talk about had tickets to go to the circus yesterday 
afternoon. | hope they couldn’t get a day off or changed their minds or something. The 
newspaper in Cheyenne was full of the circus fire story this morning. They listed it with the 
major catastrophes of the century.” 

A side note: A fire started by still unknown circumstances broke out during the July 6, 1944 
afternoon performance of the Ringling Brothers and Barnum & Bailey Circus in Hartford. Fed by 
the paraffin wax that waterproofed the tent walls and ceiling, flames within minutes engulfed 


338 


the arena and bleachers where 7,000 people, including the two Alice’s from Bradley Field, were 
in attendance. At least 168 people were killed and 700 were seriously injured by fire, smoke 
inhalation, falling debris, burning wax and the crush of the crowd fleeing the arena with many 
victims trampled in the chaos. Both of the Alice’s survived as did notable circus clown Emmett 
Kelly and the Flying Wallendas, who were performing their aerial high wire routine when the fire 
spread to the bleachers. (O’Nan S. The Circus Fire: The Story of an American Tragedy. New York: 
Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group. 2008) 


The crowd at the July 6, 1944 performance was largely 
composed on women, children and soldiers with free 
passes, including Mildred’s WAC friends. The Ringling 
Brothers and Barnum & Bailey fire is considered the 
greatest disaster in Connecticut history.

July 7, 1944 letter — continued 


“A soldier and a sailor from Washington adopted me as their special charge last night. The car 
where | was sitting was comfortable, but was full of noisy civilians and crying babies. No one in 
there seemed to be interested in keeping it clean either, so the boys took pity on me as they say, 
and found me a seat in their car. This car is all soldiers and sailors, and is the best car on the 
train, and much cleaner than any other car on the train. That’s a lot of words to say that | now 
have a very comfortable seat in a streamliner car. The soldier is a bit boring and overly 
attentive, and the sailor is interesting and married with a brotherly attitude. Mildred always 
seems to hit it that way.” 

July 15, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Some of the new girls that have just come from WAC Basic got there Pfc’s or one stripe while | 
was gone. If | wasn’t a good-natured soul. I’d probably blow off a little steam about that. No use 
feeling sorry for myself. | have plenty of company in the stripeless wonders brigade.” 

August 24, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Have another new job here. I’m doing clerical work in the office of Sergeant Major Hager of the 
Bradley Field Hospital; no more dietician work. | have a B.A. not a Doctors degree. Wish | had 
the Drs. degree, but it is still in the dim distant future. I’ve been thinking seriously of going back 
to school when this war is over. The fall of Paris was good, but somehow I’m afraid | won’t feel 
like yelling my head off when the war is over. Guess there will be plenty of people to get excited 
without me.” Comment: Related to the July 15 and August 24 letters, Mildred’s frustration at 
seeing others promoted ahead of her appeared to reach its peak in the summer of 1944. 
November 5, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“| now have yet another new job as an accountant. Thursday evening Captain Britten, the head 
of my hospital section, asked me if | could come to his office for a few minutes before | left. He 
also called Sgt. Hager in. The job of managing one of the two hospital financial accounts was 
turned over to me completely. It’s a big responsibility involving thousand and thousands of 


339 


dollars. Frankly, | am pleased as it means that the Captain is satisfied with my work. It’s a job 
that needs doing and big enough one to make me feel | am doing my part in this old war.” 
November 23, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

Comment: Many of the hundreds of letters that were not excerpted for this section on 
Mildred’s wartime correspondence included detailed descriptions of her trips with other WACs 
and servicemen to major cities and locales of the Northeast including Montreal, Boston, New 
York, the Maine shore, the Jersey shore, Rhode Island and various towns in Massachusetts. 
Mildred also made at least two trips to Berwick, Pennsylvania by bus, approximately 250 miles 
from Bradley Field, to visit relatives of her grandfather, Joseph Lloyd Dennis. The following 
excerpt is from a six page letter describing a trip to Washington DC with one of the Alice’s from 
the WAC corps at Bradley Field. It is characteristic of Mildred’s other travel reports. 

“Oh yes, something else we did Sunday night. On the way to dinner, we walked down 
Pennsylvania Avenue, which runs on the backside of the White house. It was all lit up and looked 
lovely, although not as large as | had expected. By the last day, we hadn’t been near the Capital 
and both of us were disappointed, but we found a change to our train schedule to New York that 
gave us time to visit the Capital. We were both as tickled as two kids with lollypops. We hated to 
go back to Bradley without seeing the Capital. | haven’t been thrilled about anything for a long 
time, but it was really a wonderful feeling to know that you were walking through your nation’s 
capital. The most outstanding statue in the Capital foyer was a bronze of Will Rogers, sent by 
Oklahoma. The statues from each state don't need to be statesmen, but merely people who are 
typical of the state and suggest what the state represents.” 


November 30, 1944. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 


“Heard the Army Hour yesterday afternoon and one of the broadcasts was directly from the 5h 
Army front in Italy. A Sgt. In the combat zone described the lousy weather that the troops have 
been having to contend with, and some times the sound of artillery shells bursting around his 
area would drown out the speaker’s voice. Well, anyway, | sat down a bit later and wrote Harold 
a nice letter. Just yesterday | was figuring up and | have received one letter from him since last 
May when | got all of those letters all at once. Really a terrific sucker, aren’t I?” 

January 6, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“If the first few days of the new year are any indication of the year to come, it is going to be a 
very good year for me. First, a grand letter came from Harold, then my call home was so 
successful, and then a 2™ letter from Harold with his picture in it. He look wonderful. Just as 
handsome as ever and that old charming smile. It’s the next best thing to seeing him, and that | 
know is impossible for a while. Some one that | showed the picture to, noticed what long fingers 
he has, and | was glad to see that he has all of them on his left hand. Only part of his right hand 
shows in the picture, so that must have been the fingers he lost. | hope his mother gets his 
picture soon. The first letter was written on October 24 and wasn’t postmarked until Dec. gf: 
The transportation facilities must have been bad. He mentioned two of his Sergeants receiving 
battlefield commissions, and how proud he was of them. He also sent a copy of the decoration 
that he received last February. Comment: The false assumption that Harold had lost fingers on 
one of his hands lingered on literally until he returned from Europe after the war. Although 
Harold suffered six wounds and other injuries that required medical attention or 
hospitalization, his parents, Mildred and her parents were only aware of some of them and also 


340 


received, or deduced, inaccurate information about several of these injuries, including, as we 
will see latter, that his face had been badly burned — like the missing fingers, also not true. For 
parents of WWII servicemen, the daily stress of not knowing what was actually happening to 
their sons must have been overwhelming. As in Harold’s case, receiving confusing, misleading 
or completely inaccurate tidbits of information certainly served to extenuate anxiety. Staying 
busy to divert one’s attention away from the grim realities of the war must have been a 
national pastime. From Mildred’s letters, it’s obvious that her parents took on a variety of 
wartime jobs, charitable activities, and joined organizations supporting parents of individuals in 
the armed services including a Parents of WACs chapter. 


February 5, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Your WAC is not longer a Pvt. Yesterday, the orders came out, and | am now a Private First 
Class (Pfc.), which means | will now wear a stripe, when | get around to sewing it on. The most 
important thing is that | will get $4.00 more pay a month. Please don’t put a notice in the 
newspaper. When boys are dying and getting medals for outstanding accomplishments over 
there, | don’t want an article about a Pfc. promotion.” 


March 25, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Received a V-Mail from Harold yesterday. Very happy go lucky letter. Really sounded like the 
Harold we knew at home when he was in a good mood. | asked him to send a request for 
cigarettes, and he said he could use them, and that just any old brand was good enough for him. 
| have 40 packs of cigs saved up for him, and | intend to take the box to town tomorrow to mail, 
and when I’m at the PO, add in packaged food to finish out the weight, using their scale.” 
Comment: USPS placed a weight limit on overseas packages. Partially filled boxes were taken to 
the Post Office, along with a bag of other items, which were added to the box until the weight 
limit was attained. It was then sealed and postmarked. Mildred’s parents sent her a dollar bill 
every month, which she used to buy cartons of cigarettes to ship to Harold. A carton of Camels 
was 50 cents in 1945. Families were encouraged to mail cigarettes to their servicemen, and 12 
smokes and waterproof matches were included in the daily k-ration kit starting in 1942. The 
military believed that cigarettes enhanced morale and mood, relieved boredom, and reduced 
appetite, the later a significant issue for food deprived front line soldiers. (“Smoke Em if You’ve 
Got Em.” Army Historical Foundation. www.armyhistory.org. Accessed September 9, 2024)

During WWII, brands exhorted U.S. citizens to buy their product 
and send it to servicemen. Blum A. Keep Em Smokin’. Tobacco and

May 5, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Oh yes, | read in yesterday’s newspaper where the Italian partisans [i.e., anti-fascists] turned 
over Mussolini’s widow and two children to officers of the 1°‘ Armed Division. [Harold was in the 
1" Armed Division of the U.S. Fifth Army]. That was at Como, Italy, and that is the town on the 
border with Switzerland where | thought Harold was, or is.” Comment: Rachele Mussolini, son 
Romano and daughter Anna Maria, both teen-agers, surrendered to Fifth Army representatives 
near Lake Como soon after the European ceasefire to avoid likely execution by anti-fascist mobs 
roaming northern Italian cities in the initial days after the war looking for and killing Mussolini 
collaborators. Rachele, Romano and Anna Maria were exiled for three years to the island of 
Ischia 50 miles off the coast of Naples, after which all three returned to Italy and resumed 
normal lives. Romano became an internationally recognized jazz musician and Anna Marie 
became a noted Italian radio and television personality. Two of Mussolini’s older children fled 
Italy to escape the mobs, but returned to their homeland later in life. (Information source: 
Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: September 11, 2024) 


A side note: A long-standing Hendricson family tradition, cultivated by Harold himself, is that he 
was part of a reconnaissance unit that entered Milan on April 29, 1945 to assess potential Nazi 
resistance, which turned out to be non-existent as German officers and soldiers were simply 
waiting to surrender. As they investigated the downtown area, the Recon Detail passed by the 
bodies of Benito Mussolini and his mistress, Claretta Petacci. Less than two hours before the 
Americans arrived, Mussolini and Petacci, along with four other fascists, were infamously hung 
upside down by their heels at a gas station in a central square of the city after execution by 
firing squad the previous day in a village near Lake Como. Harold stated that he witnessed the 
cutting down of these bodies. It’s one of a very few WWII incidents that he was willing to 
discuss. Numerous published accounts by U.S. military and Italian eyewitnesses indicate that the 
first arriving Americans were aghast when their tank and infantry column rolled into the square 
and observed a large, out-of-control mob throwing rocks and shooting at the bodies, among 
other desecrations. The American cleared the space around the gas station and ordered Italian 
Partisans to remove the bodies to an Allied controlled morgue. Exactly which Americans were 
involved in this action remains murky, but the event was filmed by a Stars and Stripes (the 
armed forces newspaper) photographer embedded with Harold’s reconnaissance unit as they 
entered Milan’s Piazelle Loreto, where the gas station was located, around 2:00pm on April 29. 
The Piazelle Loreto had great symbolic meaning for Italian anti-fascists. In 1944, 15 partisans 
were murdered and their bodies were dumped in the square by I] Duce’s paramilitary henchmen. 
(Luzzato S. The Body of I! Duce: Mussolini’s Corpse and the Fortunes of Italy. New York: Henry 
Holt and Company. 2014) 

May 15, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“The war being over in Europe seems pretty wonderful, but somehow | have failed to get 
excited. Either | don’t realize it really happening or | have sense enough to know that there is 
still a long stretch ahead of us in the Pacific. Everyone is filling out their points scorecard for 
getting out of the army. Practically none of the fellows here have enough points unless they are 
back from overseas. That is as it should be. | like to see the boys overseas getting a break, and 
then have the big jerks here have to sweat out going to the Pacific. | am anxious to know if 


342 


Harold will get out now. As far as points are concerned, he should be sitting pretty for a 
discharge. | hope he doesn’t get noble now, and decide to volunteer for the South Pacific.” 

May 30, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Still no letters from Harold. Guess | shouldn’t expect one yet, but | am not a patient waiter. He 
is going to get just as many letters back as he writes from now on as he can’t be any busier than 
lam. It was allright to overlook lack of letters while he was in the thick of it, but not now.” 

June 14, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Did something unusual last night that | enjoyed very much. A group of the medic boys at 
Bradley were going to a baseball game, and they asked if any of the medic WACs wanted to go 
along. | thought it would be fun for a change. Went to ballpark via a Burma Road truck, one of 
those big ones with benches on the sides and a canvas cover. There were ten medic guys and 
four of us medic WACs. That proportion would be a boost to recruiting, but some of them are 
married, and we have worked with them so long in the hospital that the romantic angle is long 
gone. Anyway, it was a good game. Williamsport, PA won over Hartford by the score of 2-1. We 
came back to base in the truck and stopped off at a nice roadside restaurant for a snack. A 
bunch of us had banana splits, which should do things to my waistline.” 

June 29, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“The New York Times yesterday reported a list of the divisions that would make up the 
Occupational Army for Germany and the 1* Armored Division [Harold’s Division] was listed. | 
guess that is better than fighting the Japs, but | should think that 3 years overseas is enough. 
Based on the article, | imagine Harold is coming home for 30 days furlough, and then will go 
back to Europe. Seems a bit stupid to shift men who fought Germans in Italy to the occupation 
of Germany. | was sorry to hear about Mrs. Hendricson being so upset. | wonder if Harold 
being home for a short time will help any? | hope Mr. H can induce her to finally see a doctor. 
There are shots and other means to counter that sort of thing. | hate to think of Harold coming 
home to any discord. He has been through a lot and his recent letters seem to have a fairly 
healthy outlook on life. Comment: In this excerpt from a June 29, 1945 letter and other letters 
not excerpted, Mildred commented on a mental health affliction that Harold’s mother 
experienced in the spring and summer of 1945, which apparently induced considerable tension 
within the household. The symptoms appear to be consistent with acute anxiety induced by an 
apparently exaggerated account of wounds her son reportedly received in the final days of the 
war. As described earlier in this book, Harold was wounded the day before the 5 Army crossed 
the Po River south of Milan, effectively ending the German resistance. However, the injury did 
not require transfer to a rear medical unit, and as described previously he was at the front of an 
armored column that entered Milan on April 29, 1945. His parents somehow received word 
that he had been burned, leaving disfiguring scars, which was false. It’s possible they 
confabulated a report of a craniofacial injury he experienced when a cement tank hatch 
slammed into his head, which happened more than a year earlier, with the wound he 
experienced the day before crossing the Po River. 


July 27, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 


“Had a letter from that Captain. [In the spring of 1945, Harold was promoted to Captain]. The 
letter was written back in June, which seems like it took a long time getting here considering it 


343 


was airmail. He seemed to be in good enough spirits, although not too happy about being 
declared as essential and getting stuck in the Army of Occupation. He did not mention any 
wounds and the scars must not be as serious as Mrs. H was led to believe. | think if they were 
permanently disfiguring he would have told me.” 

August 18, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“So, Harold is home. |’ll bet his mother is walking on air and his dad is trying to act indifferent, 
and not doing so good at that. It makes a person feel good that the army finally got around to 
bringing someone home that really deserved it. | imagine he is tired and will probably notice it 
more now that he is home and can just relax for a while. Just can’t seem to realize that the war 
is all over. Think | will go to church tomorrow as | feel as you do that church is the place to 
celebrate a victory such as this. | have been a bit disgusted with the WAC girls here as they do 
not feel that way, and many of them celebrated for three days — every night they got stupid 
drunk right here on base. Tuesday night | did not get to sleep until 4am, so | jumped at the 
chance the next day to go to New York for two nights. New York was much calmer and 
practically back to normal except the streets still had lots of parade paper on them and the food 
supply in restaurants was running low. There were about six policemen every block around 
Times Square to say nothing of lots of MPs and SPS.” Comment: As evidenced by a flurry of 
letters shortly after the August 18 letter excerpted above and, apparently, a long phone 
conversation with her parents, Mildred was quite dismayed by Harold’s sudden appearance in 
Walla? (dismay likely does not capture the extent of her emotions), and even more distraught 
about his lack of communication with her about the furlough back to the States. Little is known 
about how Harold got home so rapidly other than he arrived on a ship in Florida in early August 
and, presumably, traveled by train to Walla”. While in Florida, he apparently called his mother, 
Mabel, to let her know he was heading home. Mabel called Maude and Archie when her son 
arrived. Sensing her daughter’s distress about the situation, Maude arranged a phone call 
between Harold and Mildred on August 27, 1945. Mildred’s letters do not describe the 
conversation, other than saying that it “helped me straighten things out and brought me back 
to earth.” Subsequent to this call, which was the first time they had talked to each other in four 
years, Harold and Mildred seemingly went their separate ways for an extended period of time. 
However ... as we already know, they eventually re-engaged when both were back in the Walla? 
full time, and were married November 16, 1946, a whirlwind rekindling of the relationship. 
October 1, 1945. Army Air Force WAC Detachment, Bradley Field, Connecticut 

“Well, it's official, 1am going to Westover Field, up in Massachusetts. | will work on the same 
financial account | am managing down here at Bradley Hospital, which is what | wanted. Makes 
a person feel good that their work was good enough that another base requested me.” 
Comment: After the end of the Pacific war in August, 1945, Mildred and the other WACs at 
Bradley heard a variety of rumors concerning their relocation because Bradley Air Field and the 
base hospital were being deactivated. Most of the rumors involved bases in either Virginia or 
South Carolina, neither of which were appealing to Mildred. The assignment in Westover also 
included a promotion to Corporal. 

October 22, 1945. 112'" WAC AAF Brigade, Westover Field, Massachusetts 


“All settled in at Westover. | am writing this in my own room, which | was fortunate to get. 
Everyone here has been simply grand. The Captain who is CO of the WACs at Westover, and the 


344 


other officers | work for have gone out of their way to make me comfortable. None of the 
Captain and Major to Corporal stuff here, and my direct boss at the hospital, Major Baglia, has 
the grandest sense of humor. | have my own office in the hospital and am the only WAC working 
in the admin of this Hospital. | also will not have to do much of my own typing when doing 
account reports as there are two civilian typists available.” 

November 9, 1945. 112" WAC AAF Brigade, Westover Field, Massachusetts 

“| checked on my points at the orderly room yesterday, and as | suspected, I’m still stuck on 26. 
Unfortunately, the Army deducted the two months that | was deferred in 1943.” [Mildred was 
allowed to defer WAC boot camp by two months so she could complete the spring semester at 
the high school where she was teaching.] “My account report is due tomorrow, and | seriously 
hope I can find the $1.63 that is keeping it from balancing. | have been awfully busy getting the 
hospital account straightened out, so | know | haven’t been writing as often. Between my two 
boy friends and the accounting job, | never have a dull moment.” Comment: During the fall of 
1945, Mildred “had an Air Force fella” by the name of Leonard Hardy, also stationed at Bradley, 
that she met on a WAC sightseeing trip to Springfield, Massachusetts. Leonard was her movie 
and dinner partner on weekends, and another “fella” by the name of Jerry Summers, stationed 
at Westover, played the same role during the week. 

November 19, 1945. 112"° WAC AAF Brigade, Westover Field, Massachusetts 

“So, | gather from your recent letter that Harold made an inquiry about me via his mother. Well, 
did he. | will be home one of these days when my points allow it. When he gets home, he can 
look over what the Army has done for me. Frankly, | think it is an improvement. | have a great 
deal more self-confidence now, and | am certainly independent, and capable of taking care of 
myself, and sure have shown that | can handle a whole bunch of different kinds of work in the 
Army. Don’t be too harsh in your judgment of Harold. We will never know many of the awful 
things that happened to him, that he carries with him I’m sure, probably always will carry. And 
please, | hope you can continue to be friendly with Harold’s parents. Don’t let Harold and my 
differences change your attitude, and | hope Mr. and Mrs. Hendricson’s difficulties have been 
ironed out, now that the war is over. Comment: Harold’s six-month Army of Occupation 
assignment in Germany should have ended in December 1945, but it is unclear when he 
actually departed Europe, and arrived in Walla’. 


December 18, 1945. WAC AAF Separation Center. Fort Dix, New Jersey. Letter number 259 in 
the collection saved by her parents. 

“Well, I’m here at Fort Dix in New Jersey going through the separation process. Dix is not far 
from Philadelphia. They have taken away my extra uniform, checked that | have transportation 
home and asked me where to send my mustering out pay. It’s colder than the blazes here —1 
haven’t been warm since | got here, and the bad weather is going to continue, plus terrible 
traveling conditions. There is blizzard between here and Chicago, makes me wonder if | will 
make it home by Christmas. | am scheduled to depart Philadelphia on December 20, so it is 
doubtful. If | think it is too much of a risk of getting stuck somewhere like Chicago on the way, | 
can go back to Westover, and stay until the weather clears up. | number of my friends will be up 
there at Christmas. Actually, they asked me to stay on for a while to help the civilian who took 
over my accounts as she is scared of all the bookkeeping. Lots of WAC girls | knew at Bradley 
and Eagle Pass are here waiting like me to get out. It’s fun to see all one’s old friends.” 


345 


Comment: Bowing to pressure from parents and spouses of servicemen to reduce the discharge 
points, the U.S. Army suddenly dropped the point threshold for Gls and WACs in early 
December 1945 as a “Christmas gift to the nation.” (Bamford, 2010) Most of the one million 
men and women who benefitted from the decision were thrilled, but many, especially those 
stationed in the States, were caught off guard, and were less excited. Many Gls and WACs had 
no immediate plans for civilian life, and consequently, were looking forward to military pay, 
food, and housing for several additional months until they could solidify their next steps. We do 
not know where Mildred stood on this issue, but based on the tone of her final letters, it seems 
that she may have welcomed a few more months in the military. Mildred seemed to be 
especially enjoying her post-war assignment at Westover Field. Mildred did not get home by 
Christmas due to bad weather. She and two other Westover WACS took a bus back to their 
former base for the holidays, where she did additional work in the hospital accounting 
department, presumably on an unpaid basis. Mildred returned to Walla’ in January, 1946. She 
gained acceptance into graduate school at Washington State College (WSC) for the summer 
semester 1946 to complete coursework needed to advance her teaching salary and renew her 
teaching certificate. When Mildred and Harold reconnected, she decided to not re-enroll at 
WSC. 


Harold and Mildred’s wedding day: November 16, 1946. First 
Congregational Church, Walla Walla, Washington.
