Going to Ballgames — William Dennis Hendricson (1948 - ) 

My father, Harold Hendricson, and | shared the same birthday, November 4, which | think 
provided a reason for us to sustain a closer relationship than perhaps we would have 
otherwise, due to rather sharp differences in personality, temperament, and communication 
style. Given my Dad’s aggressiveness in pursuing career-enhancing assignments in the Army, 
and his willingness to go literally anywhere on special TDY (i.e., temporary duty) assignments, 
which often took him places where spouses and dependents could not go such as Lebanon, 
Korea, and Venezuela, he was not around much during my childhood. Additionally, the bulk of 
his career as an officer in armored (i.e., tank) divisions took place during the height of the Cold 
War with Russia. The central premise of U.S. military strategy in the 1950s and 1960s was that 
Russia would unleash a massive ground attack spearheaded by Russian tank divisions through a 
wide valley that ran from the Germany — Poland border to Frankfurt in central Germany known 
as the Fulda Gap. Consequently, he was constantly away from home during the many years we 
lived in Europe participating in weeks and months-long “War Games” at locations not even 
known to his wife, preparing to repel the invading Russian horde. (McCauley M. Russia, America 
and the Cold War, 1949-1991. Harlow, UK: Pearson Education Publishing. 2008) 


Because of this awayness, my primary childhood memories of my dad are related to the 
countless 3,000-mile coast-to-coast car trips that occurred before and after each of his 
stateside or European assignments, and also our guys-only road trips to ballgames, primarily 
when we lived in Virginia in the early 1960s. During cross country car journeys, which always 
occurred in summer or early fall, my Dad calculated routes and daily driving distances based on 
location of ballparks where major league baseball (MLB) games could be seen. Thus, a family 
car trip from New York or Virginia to the West Coast would proceed slowly at first, only 200-300 
miles a day, because of stops in D.C., Cleveland, Detroit or especially Chicago to see games. 
Once clear of Chicago, the last MLB outpost on the way to the state of Washington in the 1950s 
and 60s, the goal was to cover as many miles as possible, up to 700 per day, to make up time, 
departing at dawn and not pulling into a motor court (i.e. a motel) until well after dark, and 
only after checking the rates and inspecting the rooms at each of the 3-4 motels that might 
exist in a smallish town in the vast expanse between Chicago and Walla Walla. 


The MLB ballpark visitations on the cross-country drives were Bill and Harold ventures; my 
mom and Shirley were left to soak up the ambiance of that evening’s motor court and prepare 
and consume a meal in the room; my mom always traveled with a two burner hot plate, and 
ample grocery supplies. Cross-country routes were also modified on the fly during the drive in 
order to pick up low wattage AM stations, which operated with a 50 to 75 mile range, that were 
broadcasting MLB games during the daytime. Afternoon ballgames were a common occurrence 
in that era. For example, a 1960 drive from Walla Walla to my dad’s next assignment at Fort 
Monroe, Virginia corresponded with the Yankees — Pirates World Series, which took place from 
October 5 to October 13, all day games. My role on game days during that trip was to find 
stations on the car radio that were carrying the game, and when the signal started to fade after 
45 minutes or so, quickly find another station ahead of us (i.e., in a town that we were driving 
toward) that was broadcasting the game, and if one couldn’t be found, alert my mom, so she 
could unfold her roadmap in the backseat and chart an alternate route toward a town big 
enough to have a station with the game. Much of that trip was spent zigzagging all over the 


347 


map in search of a signal until we got to the Chicago area and the other big cities of the east 
with high wattage AM stations. As evident from the dates of that particular trip, Shirley and | 
were not in school before or during the trip. In fact, we missed nearly two months of the fall 
semester that year, which was not an unusual occurrence. Between the ane grade and my 
senior year in high school, we received a geographic education versus a classroom education at 
least four times as our family crossed the country in un-air-conditioned cars in September and 
October. 


My dad also initiated ball game trips when we were not on extended, between assignment, 
road trips, but were ensconced in our current place of residence. At an early age, | learned that 
these trips usually were scheduled in advance of an upcoming announcement of a relocation to 
another Army base. So, if my dad and | drove up to New York to see the Yankees or Mets play 
(and not one game, but an entire 3-4 game series) or to Philadelphia for an Army-Navy football 
game, or to Chicago and Washington D.C. to see MLB All-Star Games, or to Munich in Germany 
to see the Harlem Globetrotters or barnstorming post-season MLB teams play, it was 
reasonably certain that an imminent departure to a new army base, a new town and a new 
school would soon be forthcoming. To be honest, from my perspective, it was a good trade-off. 
By the 3" grade, my normal expectation already was: new year, new school, new classmates. 
Getting to see the Yankees in their 1950s prime at the original Yankee Stadium, getting to see 
Sandy Koufax of the LA Dodgers, in his almost unhittable prime, pitch against the Mets in the 
old Polo Grounds, getting to watch Wilt Chamberlain dunk up close from a baseline seat, or 
soaking up the pageantry that accompanied Army-Navy games were galvanizing experiences for 
me, and undoubtedly forged my lifelong love of sports, in spite of my limited athletic capacities. 


There are moments in your life that that make such an impression that they literally create their 
own little synaptic network in your brain; i.e., they crystallize a moment that is forever captured 
in a way that enables retrieval of visual images (photographs in your brain), but also sounds and 
even a sense of one’s own emotions in that moment. (Feldman DH. Beyond Universals in 
Cognitive Development. New York: Ablex Publishing Corporation. 1994) For me, one such 
crystallizing moment occurred during one of the aforementioned Mets-Dodgers game. Sandy 
Koufax was cruising toward his 19" win in what would ultimately be a 25-5 season for him, 
allowing just 3 hits with one out in the 9", and the Dodgers up 3-0. With much of the crowd 
heading already heading for exits, the Mets Rod Kanehl, a .240 hitter across his brief, three-year 
MLB career, managed to bloop a single just over the second baseman’s glove, which fluttered 
to the turf as paper debris from the departing crowd swirled in the Polo Grounds outfield. The 
next batter, Ron Hunt, who had hit only 38 homeruns across a 14 year MLB career, did just that 
— he ripped Koufax’s first pitch deep into the right field bleachers, and suddenly it was 3-2. That 
was 52 years ago, and | still carry the crystallized remembrance with me: the eerie silence that 
ensued as if fans were silently pondering the likelihood of what they just saw rather than 
viscerally reacting, the dust swirls kicked up by Hunt as he excitedly raced around the bases, 
tripping over third base, stumbling, and righting himself to literally dance to the plate, and 
perhaps most poignantly, looking over and seeing my Dad with the biggest grin and his hands 
raised high over his head, oddly enough in the classic touchdown display. The pathetic Mets, 
who lost 120 games the year before, and would eventually lose 111 that year, had a chance to 
beat the mighty Dodgers. The next batter also got a hit, the following guy walked, and Koufax 


348 


was pulled from the game, a very rare circumstance, but the Dodgers reliever managed to get 
the second and third outs, and the Mets rally ended in yet another defeat. I’ve always 
associated that particular moment with my lifelong predilection for rooting for inept, 
perpetually losing teams, and out-of-favor causes or viewpoints. 


In addition to road trips to games, Harold Hendricson closely followed local teams wherever we 
lived, especially in baseball, and purchased season tickets, even for lowly minor league teams. 
When we lived in Hampton, Virginia, near his assignment at Fort Monroe, my dad and | 
attended countless games of the Peninsula Grays, a Class A affiliate of the Washington Senators 
with our spool of one dollar per game season tickets, which we tore off and handed to the 
gatekeeper when entering the park, much like the coupons exchanged for turkey legs and hot 
dogs at a carnival food booth. Seating was first come, first serve, so we always arrived way early 
as my dad loved to sit in the front row near the Grays dugout. He had an agenda. 


Each game, Harold would pick out a Grays player, and heckle him for the entire evening, 
starting with batting practice before the game, and continuing through the contest. Whenever 
the anointed player came to the plate, he would hear it from Harold, until ... my dad fell asleep, 
which usually occurred in the 6'" or 7‘ inning, after about 90 minutes of play (games were 
faster in the 60s). His heckles were not especially original or creative, but delivered with gusto:, 
Unser ... you’re a bum, Brinkman .. you’re a bum, or for slight variety, Casanova .. you can’t hit, 
or Epstein .. go back to Class B (a lower league). But for his primary target who received a 
Harold heckle every game, a big slugger by the name of Brant Alyea, he yelled: “Alyea .. can you 
do it tonight?” After Alyea had heard that somewhat ambiguous query a few times early in the 
season, he walked over to the stands between innings and asked my dad, “so, what does that 
mean? My dad responded, “we’re just hoping for a homer, big guy.” Alyea, a pleasant sort, 
replied that he would try to oblige. By mid-season, Alyea and my dad would banter back and 
forth almost every game, unless my dad was asleep when the Grays slugger wandered over to 
our seats. In that case, Alyea would say to me something like, “don’t want to mess up the old 
guy’s sleep, but you might nudge him when | come up this inning,” followed by observations 
that “he was feeling lucky this time”, or “I got this guy (i.e., the pitcher) figured out,” or “the 
wind turned and is blowing out now”, or other hopeful proclamations. | was always dumbstruck 
that a very large professional baseball player was talking to me, and probably only mustered a 
nod, or at best, “okay,” but do remember being quizzical, if not concerned, about his 
observation that my dad was an old man; he was barely 40 at the time. 


| remember my mom commenting on more than one occasion that baseball games relaxed my 
dad, or “let him unspool and forget his worries”. The shoebox that contained the 259 letters 
that my mom wrote to her parents during WWII (see pages 330-346) also contained several 
letters she wrote to her parents during 1951-1952 when Harold was training at Fort Knox, 
Kentucky to serve as a tank commander in the Korean War. Apparently, it was a stressful 
training, full of exams and tank maneuvering or gunnery assessments in the field. She 
commented a couple of times that she encouraged Harold to drive the family to Cincinnati and 
Chicago to take in ballgames in order to “just get away and relax.” After returning from these 
ballpark jaunts, she commented in subsequent letters, “that was such a good idea”, or “what a 
relaxing weekend.” Something about the vibe of the ballpark and the game itself was 
apparently calming for my dad, a man known for his intensity.

A side note: All of the Peninsula Grays players that heard the Hendricson heckle at the little 
ballpark in Hampton, Virginia made it to the major leagues. Del Unser was an outfielder for the 
Senators and Philadelphia Phillies for 14 years and played in the 1980 World Series. Eddie 
Brinkman was a shortstop that played 14 years for the Senators and the Detroit Tigers, won 
Golden Glove awards (for fielding skill) and was named to All-Star teams. Paul Casanova was a 
Cuban catcher who experienced much racism as a minor league player in the small southern 
towns that comprised the Carolina League where the Grays played. After a season in the Negro 
League, Casanova had a successful 10-year career in the majors with the Senators and the 
Atlanta Braves. Mike Epstein, one of the few Jewish players in the MLB in that era, had a nine 
year career in MLB with five teams, once hitting 30 homers in a season with Senators and 
played in the 1972 World Series with the Oakland Athletics. Brant Alyea made it to MLB with the 
Senators in 1965 and hit a home run on the first pitch thrown to him in a major league game, 
one of only nine players ever to do so. He played seven MLB seasons with four teams.

And so, in the spring of 1961 while we were living in Hampton, my dad read that the Baltimore 
Colts, a perennial top team in the 1950s and 1960s NFL and the Washington Redskins, a 
perennial bottom-feeder in the league, but the local favorite as the NFL’s “Squad of the South” 
had signed a contract with the city of Norfolk, Virginia to stage a preseason exhibition game. 
The data of the game, August 26, 1961, was marked on our family events calendar, and he 
announced that we were going. At first, the plan was for all four of us to attend the game, but 
for reasons lost to me, only my dad and | made the journey across the Hampton Roads Bridge — 
Tunnel Highway to Norfolk and the stadium located on the campus of William and Mary — South 
Division, now Old Dominion University. Hampton is on the north side and Norfolk is on the 
south side of the large bay known as Hampton Roads, which serves as the mouth of the James 
River and two smaller rivers in southern Virginia. 


A bit of stage setting is needed at this point as a lead-in to the events of August 26, 1961. On 
drives to and from the ball games, the conversation was typically limited to expectations for the 
upcoming game, discussion of the game we just saw, my school work, and my efforts on 
whatever athletic team | was currently playing on, not my favorite topic as my successes were 
episodic. Or, we just listened to the radio. Sometimes, my dad had an agenda for the trip. For 
example, on one drive to New York in 1960 to see an Army (West Point) football game against 


350 


Syracuse, he spent considerable time talking about Syracuse’s star player, Ernie Davis, had how 
he had been mistreated in the previous years Cotton Bowl game by University of Texas players 
that yelled racial taunts at him, and hit him late after the ref’s whistle stopped the play. 
Throughout the game, Texas players also spit at other Black players on the Syracuse team, and 
yelled racial slurs at the line of scrimmage to try to get Syracuse players to jump offside. 
(Cosgrove B. LIFE at the 1960 Cotton Bowl: “Battle of the Hardnoses.” Time. www.time.com. 
January 2, 2014. Accessed: September 29, 2024). My dad seemed to be particularly offended by 
this behavior because Davis was a member of the Syracuse ROTC, and had been selected by the 
Syracuse ROTC Director to serve as corps commander. Davis was commissioned as a Second 
Lieutenant the day before his Syracuse graduation, wore his army uniform at graduation, and 
pledged to only sign with an NFL team that would help him fulfill his military commitment after 
graduation, all of which obviously impressed my dad. (Syracuse University News. Stories of 
Service: Ernie Davis ‘62. www.news.syr.edu. November 24, 2020. Accessed: September 28, 2024)

Contextual note: my dad always wore his dress green uniform to Army games. As my dad

After standing around on the edge of their conversation, | eventually was introduced to Davis, 
shook his hand, and recall thinking that he was not decidedly taller than | was but ever so much 
larger in every other way, and | probably managed to mumble a barely coherent greeting. 
During a bit of conversation about the freshmen game unfolding before us, the punter for the 
Army plebes miss-hit his kick and the ball waffled to our side of the field and landed with a 
splush in a muddy puddle, not too far from our little group. | recall jogging over to the ball, 
perhaps imaging myself hurling it back to the approaching referee in a tight spiral, impressing 
one and all, especially Mr. Davis. I’m speculating here as | do not remember my thoughts as | 
picked up the muddy football, but | undoubtedly also visualized throwing a wobbly, “wounded 
duck” that twirled over the ref’s head or landed far to his side. Then, as now, | didn’t have the 
capacity to throw a football that didn’t flutter and tumble. So, instead of a majestic heave, | 
scooped up the ball and walked it over to the ref, handing it to him with a glob of mud on the 
top, which | tried to wipe off at the last moment, and managed to fling the goop onto the top of 
my shoe, leaving myself with muddy fingers. The reaction of the All-American and my dad when 
| rejoined them is a thankfully lost memory. At the very least, | suppose they shared some level 
of bemusement. 


Soon after, Davis found an excuse to move away from us and strolled back toward the Syracuse 
bench. During the game that afternoon played in a steady and cold rain, the Army defenders 
swarmed all over Ernie Davis, but he had a strong game, rushing for 111 yards, intercepting a 
pass and making numerous tackles. In that era, the best players played both offense and 
defense. In an upset, Army won the game 9-6. On the way home, the point was made several 
times that the military was way ahead of society in treating everybody equally, and my dad bet 
that those Texas boys were not ROTC material like Ernie Davis. | was also questioned about 
going to an all-White school for the first time, which probably did not elicit a response laced 
with insight. Hampton, Virginia schools were segregated in 1960, while the Department of 
Defense schools | attended previously were integrated. | also learned how my dad knew Ernie 
Davis would be at the Plebe game. He had read an article in the Army Times newsmagazine 
about Davis’ ROTC activities, which included supporting freshmen ROTC members who were 
football players at their games. 

A side note: In 1961, Ernie Davis was the first Black player to win the Heisman Trophy. He was 
selected first in the NFL draft by the Washington Redskins, who promptly traded him to 
Cleveland in a deal that will be visited later in this story. Cleveland and Davis worked out an 
arrangement for fulfillment of his military obligations while playing professional football, and 


352 


the team made provisions for him to room during training camp and road games with his idol, 
Jim Brown, the Hall-of-Fame running back, also a Syracuse graduate. However, Ernie Davis was 
diagnosed with leukemia shortly after and died at the age of 23 without ever playing in the NFL. 
(Gallagher RC. The Express: The Ernie Davis Story. New York: Ballantine Books. 2008) 


With the context of the Ernie Davis interaction in mind, let’s re-join the trip to the Redskins- 
Colts exhibition game in Norfolk on August 26, 1961, which was sponsored by the Norfolk 
Kiwanis Club and advertised as the Kiwanis Bowl. Soon after my dad and | began the drive over 
the Hampton Roads Causeway toward Norfolk and the game site, it became apparent that this 
would be another “agenda” trip. After no more then a few minutes on the road, we pulled up at 
an information center at the start of the five-mile bridge across the bay. Wandering around to 
the side of the building, my dad stood for an uncomfortable number of seconds staring at two 
side- by-side water fountains, both poorly maintained and gnarly looking. | remember thinking, 
“we’re not going to drink out of those are we,” not something that | would utter out loud to my 
dad, especially when he had an edgy demeanor as he did that night. However, his focus was 
elsewhere, as he eventually pointed to a sign above the rusty, stained fountains: “White”, and 
“Colored,” and offered, “Quite a world we live in, huh?” He then strolled over to the adjacent 
doors that had the same signs. After a few moments of silence, he asked: “you gotta whiz” to 
which | quickly demurred, eliciting, “suit yourself,” his standard, | hear your answer but don't 
necessarily like it or belief it, and we tromped back to the car and took off over the causeway 
toward Norfolk. I’ve always pondered what his game plan was for our restroom stroll, but my 
passivity may have sidetracked attainment of the teachable moment he hoped to create.

Arriving at the stadium, quite early per usual, dad steered his prized Mercedes 200c into the 
“White Only” sector of the parking lot and parked tail-in to a slot along the chain link fence 
dividing the White and Colored lots. He liked to watch the other cars rolling into ballgame park 
lots, and would relocate our car if he didn’t like the looks of somebody parking near us. During 
this observation, we settled in for his requisite pregame cig break, which turned into several 
smokes as we watched a steady stream of cars pull into the White lot to the point of being full, 
but no cars parked in Colored lot behind us. Finally, we left the 200C and headed for S.B. 
Ballard Stadium, as it was called then. The only thing | remember my dad saying was, and I’m 
paraphrasing here, something to the effect of, “this might be a scene on the way; stay near 
me.” Excited to see my first game between NFL teams, especially one involving the Baltimore 
Colts, a powerhouse team with many stars such as Johnny Unitas and Lenny Moore, and a 
famous coach, Don Shula, | probably assumed he meant the big crowd swarming toward the 
stadium. 


353 


And indeed, it was a large onslaught of people, who funneled into one fairly narrow walkway 
from the parking lot into the stadium. As we moved through the congestion, | stayed behind my 
dad who was effective at pushing and weaving his way through ballgame crowds, but this 
clump of people was moving particularly slowly that night, and was strangely quiet; no din of 
excited hub-bub that was the norm for fans heading to a ballgame. When the mass of people 
thinned out a bit, | popped around beside him, and saw one of those sights that are not 
forgotten, likely made more vivid by the fact that it was dark and the walkway was only 
illuminated by streetlamps, with moving shadows everywhere, which always seems to 
dramatize a memory, for me at least.

One the right side of the walkway was a two or three deep line of White people extending 
many yards all the way to the ticket gate, virtually all men, stone silent, intently staring across 
the walkway at a much smaller line of Black people, about equal numbers of men and women, 
and some of the later were holding hand-made signs with slogans about segregation. There was 
a small knot of people at the center of that line, dressed up in “church clothes”, chatting among 
themselves, just about the only ones on either side doing any talking. | remember no yelling or 
haranguing from either side, and the ballgame crowd plodded ahead solemnly at a snail’s pace 
much like cars slowing to check out a wreck on the side of a road. 


Dutifully trying to keep moving ahead as directed, | lost sight of my dad who had abruptly 
peeled off to the left. Realizing | was no longer with him, | did a 360 look-around and spotted 
him shaking hands with the well-dressed Black picketers. Moving against the crowd’s current, | 
made my way over to where the little clutch was huddled, now deep in amicable conversation. 
Standing outside a ring of conversing adults was my 12 year-old norm, and so | waiting until my 
dad acknowledged my presence and initiated the obligatory introductions. First, Marie Young, a 


354 


Black women about my dad’s age, identified as the organizer of the picket line, another women, 
whose last name was Butt, which likely registered a bit in my adolescent cognition, and a man 
introduced as a lawyer and the leader of an important organization | had never heard of. | 
didn’t hear the man’s name because at that exact moment, another kid ran by, a White boy 
about my age, and ripped a newly purchased Colts hat from head, running away into the crowd. 
Surprised into non-action other than rubbing my now hatless head, the group looked at me 
quizzically, until my dad finally said something like .. “Well, don’t just stand there, go get it 
back”, or words to that effect. 


This command at least got me to spin around and eyeball the crowd moving past us, as | 
probably pondered the almost certain failure of such an effort. A few moments of silence 
ensued. | remember the women named Butt observing, perhaps to add some levity to the 
moment, that “for sure, that boy didn’t run over to this side”, waving at the smallish entourage 
of Black sign holders. | likely remained sufficiently paralyzed that the man from the important 
organization offered that the young thief most likely was attending the game with his parents 
and perhaps it would be easier to spot him and my hat inside the stadium, which my dad 
agreed was reasonable. However, he directed me to at least go check “behind those guys on the 
other side” because he thought he saw a bunch of kids running around over there when we 
walked in. | recall that | did uncomfortably wedge my way through the line-up of White men 
who were doing their best to glare at the black protesters. Given my pre-teen approach to 
problem resolution, | undoubtedly did not want to find the kid with my swiped hat because that 
would lead to a confrontation | almost assuredly would not handle well. As in dreams where 
you jump from place to place without explanation or connections, | don’t remember how | 
reconnected with my dad and got into the stadium, but the purloined hat was not found 
outside the stadium, and no effort was expended that | can recall to locate the culprit or cap 
after we took our seats. | imagine my dad felt the theft was a distraction to his intended agenda 
for the evening, and | probably was more focused on how he knew those people on the 
sidewalk outside the stadium. 


The only memory | have of events inside the stadium that night was that my dad broke the 
silence code during the national anthem. While a band was playing, and a singer was belting 
out the verse, he asked me what | noticed about the Redskin and Colt players lined up on the 
opposite sides of the field. | remember him making a big left to right sweeting motion with his 
arm, | guess encouraging me to scan the line-ups. The anthem dialogue and gesturing were 
memorable because even when he was in his “civvies,” as he was that night, he always stood 
silently, ramrod erect, eyes fixated on the flag, with hand over heart ... except that night. | know 
| didn’t provide the response he expected, e.g., the Redskins are all White, or the Colts have 
Black players and the Redskins don’t. Instead, | think | offered that both teams looked kind of 
sloppy and some of the uniforms were dirty. We were sitting down low behind the Colts bench, 
which afforded a good view of their grooming and attire. Not hearing what he wanted, the 
response was filled in for me, with a comment | do recall, “that’s what all the fuss is about out 
there” punctuated with a rather aggressive thumb over his shoulder gesture in reference to the 
walk into the stadium. And, that’s the last thing | remember about the events of the night other 
than a vague notion that the Redskins got stomped, an accurate recollection; the Colts won 41-

7. The details of the game, the walk out of the stadium (were the Black protesters with signs 
still there?) and the drive home have regressed into the fog of unretrievable memory. 


| don't know if my dad was discontent with my naiveté and obliviousness to THE social issue of 
that era, or if he was reconciled to my preteen sensibilities. However, my experiences at that 
game did have an effect, in unexpected ways. Although | was a “baseball kid” up until that 
game, which occurred amidst America’s fixation on the great Home Run Chase between Maris 
and Mantle of the 1961 Yankees, my favorite team, | found myself attracted to the lowly, inept 
Redskins and followed them closely through their 1-12-1 season that year, the only victory on 
the final Sunday, over the newly franchised and equally pathetic Dallas Cowboys. Following the 
“Skins” as almost everybody called them back then, an ironic identifier given the team’s racial 
circumstances, led me to the person who helped me better understand the implications of my 
dad’s question during the national anthem: a sportswriter for 76 years (1922-1998) with the 
Washington Post newspaper by the name of Shirley Povich. 


This sportswriter, a guy BTW, covered the Senators and Skins intensely in his daily column, This 
Morning With Shirley Povich, which always appeared in the left column of the first page of the 
Post’s sports section. He was the Post’s Sports Editor-in-Chief for 48 years, and also was a lead 
editorial writer and essayist on Civil Rights and de-segregation in athletics and society in the 
paper’s Opinion and Editorial Section. In his seven decades with the Post, he wrote more than 
12,000 columns, feature articles and essays, and won a Pulitzer prize for literature. In 1947, 
Povich wrote a 15 article series on the societal impact of Major League Baseball’s failure to de- 
segregate, entitled, “No More Shutouts,” that is widely credited with prompting Branch Rickey 
to finally sign Jackie Robinson to a MLB contract with the Brooklyn Dodgers, and for shaming 
other foot-dragging owners into long overdue desegregation. On the day that Robinson played 
his first game for the Dodgers, Povich wrote: “Four hundred and fifty-five years after Columbus 
eagerly but accidently bumped into a little Caribbean island and discovered America, the Major 
Leagues reluctantly discovered the American Negro.” (Povich SL. All Those Mornings at the Post. 
New York: Perseus Books Group. 1994) 


Shirley Povich’s scathing attacks on the racist policies of the 
Washington Redskins franchise in the National Football League 
were instrumental in galvanizing public opinion against 
segregation in professional sports and forcing the federal 
government to take action. 

Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 9/30/2024 


ees &, 


One of the fortunate happenings in my young life was when my parents, tired of the ultra- 
conservative and segregation-supporting leanings of the local paper in Hampton, Virginia, 
elected to subscribe to the suburban edition of the Post, which led me to Povich’s no-hold’s 
barred criticism of the Skin’s shabby quality of play, delivered with humor and irony, and his all- 
out war with the segregationist owner of the team, George Preston Marshall. 


356 


A side note: Povich was one of the main catalysts for my fascination with writing. | remember 
trying to mimic his witty yet “these are the facts” style of writing in middle school reports, often 
with a net effect of pleasing myself with my clever narrative and enabling my perplexed 
teacher’s to write “C” on many of them, as in, “next time — try to address the main topic of the 
assignment.” Some of Povich’s observations about the “lily-white, segregated representatives of 
our nation’s capital,” as he often called them, appear below. 


Today, the Redskins took the field in their traditional colors — burgundy, gold and Caucasian. 
Jim Brown, born ineligible to play for the Redskins, integrated their end zone three times today. 
The Redskins’ end zone has frequently been integrated by Negro players, but never their lineup. 


At least the Redskins’ have one distinction — the whitest huddle of any team in the league, 
although they have the blackest future of any team. 


George Preston Marshall is an anachronism, as out of date as the drop kick. 
The Redskins’ are in an excellent no. 1 draft position because their record is unsullied by victory. 
Marshall is getting more publicity than any loser since Robert E. Lee. 


From 25 yards out, Jim Brown was served the football by Milt Plum on a pitchout, and he 
integrated the Redskins’ goal line with more than deliberate speed, perhaps exceeding the 
famous Supreme Court decree [Brown vs. the Board of Education of Topeka]. Brown fled 25 
yards like a man in an uncommon hurry and the Redskins’ goal line at least became 
momentarily interracial. Note: The phrases “deliberate speed” and “uncommon hurry” appear 
in the Supreme Court’s Brown vs. the Board of Education of Topeka judgment, which decreed 
that racially segregated, separate but equal, public schools were unconstitutional. 


After the NFL owners group reacted to newspaper criticism of the segregated Redskins by 
issuing a resolution praising George Marshall as “the greatest asset sports has ever known,” 
Povich wrote in his column: There are those who will contend that a more debatable statement 
has never been uttered in the entire history of the spoken word. 


Referring to the August 26, 1961 exhibition versus the Colts, Povich wrote: Perhaps Redskins 
management noted that all five of the Colts’ touchdowns that evening were scored by players 
deemed unsuitable to wear the Burgundy and Gold.

By December 1961, when the Skins’ desultory season came to an end, and after reading four 
months of Povich’s columns ravaging the impact of Marshall’s racial beliefs and segregation 
practices on the NFL squad based in the nation’s capital and upon the D.C community, | was 


357 


thoroughly engaged in the Fight to Integrate the Redskins, and appreciated the role that the 
exhibition game in Norfolk played in this high-stakes drama. It almost certainly was the first 
public affairs/social issue in my young life that | read about avidly in newspapers and the 
newsmagazines of the day, such as Sports Illustrated and Time. The key moments of this 
struggle are highlighted in the Notes on section below. 


Notes on George Preston Marshall and the Fight to Integrate the Washington Redskins. 
George Preston Marshall (1896-1969) was in the Laundromat business, owning more nearly 60 
self-service facilities in many East Coast communities, but his life long passions were 
professional sports, and promoting racial segregation in the U.S. He owned several semi-pro 
basketball teams in the D.C. area in the 1920s, and after they all folded, he turned his attention 
to the fledgling concept of professional football. Around 1930, college football was widely 
popular, challenging major league baseball and boxing as America’s favorite sport, but pro 
football was a secondary novelty. Marshall purchased the rights to a failing football club in 
Boston in 1932, and shortly after renamed it the Boston Redskins, in part because the coach he 
hired, Lone Star William Dietz, claimed 50% Sioux heritage. Dietz’s claim was likely untrue, but 
Marshall liked the concept, and personally drew the Indian-themed logos that the franchise 
used until recent years, and he also commissioned the Redskin’s fight song, Hail to the Redskins. 
The fact that he chose Redskins as the team name was an early indication of his racial 
sensibilities, and the fact that this name was not questioned for 50 years makes a statement 
about the sensibilities of the American public. To be candid, well into adulthood, | thought the 
name was unique, loved the team’s iconic yet racially insensitive fight song, and was fond of 
their 1960s helmets when they were adorned with a spear and feather. 


George Preston Marshall, left, and Amon Carter at a 
groundbreaking ceremony for a John Nance Garner memorial in 
Fort Worth, Texas. Marshall was an aggressive White 
supremacist and politically supported southern Democrats 
(Dixiecrats) who resisted federal efforts to desegregate public 
facilities.

After barely surviving five years of minimal attendance and press coverage in Boston within the 
newly re-constituted National Football League (NFL), Marshall moved the club to Washington 
D.C. and sought to market the squad to southern states, which had no professional baseball or 


358 


football teams in that era, as the Team of the South. Between 1937 and 1961, Marshall 
tenaciously built up the largest radio, and then combined radio and television network for his 
team in the NFL. Prior to 1962, none of the primary radio or television networks (i.e., ABC, CBC, 
NBC and Dumont until 1957) broadcast regular season NFL games. Fans that wanted to watch 
their favorite team had to hope that a local station was part of their team’s self-created 
broadcast network. Not surprisingly given his racial attitudes, Marshall also believed that 
southern fans would not support a team representing the Old South that had Black players or 
coaches, or in the case of the Redskins, any Black person in any capacity throughout the entire 
business enterprise. To fill his squad, Marshall drafted White payers who had played at 
southern universities and recruited a steady stream of older White NFL players, mostly past 
their prime, who previously had starred at southern schools. As a consequence, after WWII, the 
team sunk into mediocrity, and by 1961, Marshall’s all-White squad was the worst team in the 
NFL. Between 1957 and 1961, the team won just 16 of 62 games.

In spite of his team’s abysmal record, and equally abysmal home game attendance at their tiny, 
rundown stadium in D.C., Griffith Park, the Burgundy & Gold network and marketing of 
Redskin-themed paraphernalia throughout the southern states, generated huge revenues and 
made Marshall a wealthy man. His regional Redskins media network was the first of its kind in 
the U.S. and became the model for the many regional sports networks that dominate U.S. 
television today. Marshall played a major role in the organizational development of the NFL 
from a sports afterthought in the 1930s to the dominant professional sport in the U.S. by the 
1970s. Along with George Halas, he created many of the features of the game we know today, 


359 


especially related to offensive rules and passing, and his half-time shows featuring the Redskins 
Marching Band and celebrity singers at stadiums and expert commentators on radio and 
television were soon copied by other teams in the league. He established the 60-40 revenue 
sharing system between home and visiting teams that structured team and league finances for 
70 years, and created the concept of dividing teams into geographically constructed 
conferences to create rivalries. He also was the main promoter of the end-of-season Pro Bowl 
all-star game, which until the 1990s was taken seriously by players, who earned substantial 
extra cash for playing and even more money for winning the contest. 


But, Marshall is best known today for an odious contribution to the NFL during its formative 
years: the so-called “secret gentlemen’s agreement” among team owners to never employ 
Black players or coaches, which was put into place in 1934. Povich noted, “Marshall is one of 
the NFLs greatest innovators, but also its leading bigot.” (Smith TG. Civil Rights on the Gridiron. 
Page 2 Goes to Washington. ESPN Page 2. www.espn.com. 2014) Defending the notorious 
agreement in 1940, Marshall said “/’// start hiring Negroes for the Redskins when the Harlem 
Globetrotters start hiring White players.” (Shaw, 2015) The gentleman’s agreement held until 
1946 when an upstart new pro football league, the All-American Football Conference (AAFC), 
eagerly signed numerous Black Americans. Two of the AAFC teams were particularly successful, 
the San Francisco 49ers and the Cleveland Browns. Each team implementing an aggressive, 
passing-oriented offense that was exciting compared to the stodgy style of play in the ground- 
bound NFL. A substantial number of the star players on the 49ers and Browns were Black, 
including well-known college All-Americans who were blocked from the all-White NFL. 


Fearing that the NFL was losing ground to the AAFC, a merger was soon arranged and the 
owners of all of the teams in the expanded 12 team NFL opened their checkbooks to Black 
players, except one — George Marshall and the Redskins. The other NFL teams continued to 
slowly add Black players to their rosters throughout the 1950s. In 1961, a pivotal year in NFL 
and civil rights history, 20% of all NFL roster positions were filled by Black athletes, with some 
teams having a dramatically higher percentage. The two southernmost NFL teams had the least 
Black players: Baltimore, seven, and Washington, zero. Sam Lacy, the long-time head 
sportswriter for the Baltimore Afro-American newspaper, the only Black journalist who covered 
the Norfolk exhibition game between the Colts and Redskins in person, commented in his 
write-up of the contest: “17,008 people were inside the stadium for the August 26"" matchup. 
The only non-White souls in attendance were the seven Black players on the Colts team and me. 
| wrote my game notes from my perch on the highest row of the bleachers as they did not seem 
to have room for me in the press box.” (Smith TG, 2014) 


In 1961, Marshall was still adamant in his segregationist beliefs, but realized that his franchise 
was in trouble with the NFL, and he was barely keeping the team afloat with earnings diverted 
from the Burgundy & Gold Radio/Television Network. Washington D.C. had experienced 
massive “White Flight to the Suburbs” in the 1950s, and as a result, the population of the D.C. 
community was 70% Black by 1961. Black NFL fans in D.C. were not interested in paying money 
to the racist Marshall to watch the lily White Skins play a miserable brand of football in a 
dilapidated stadium. Instead, at least 10,000 fans on game days made the short drive from D.C. 
to Baltimore to root for the successful and integrated Colts. (Smith G, 2011). 


360 


From the perspective of the NFL’s new, young (33 years old), somewhat socially progressive but 
keenly media savvy commissioner, Pete Rozelle, Marshall’s rag-tag, segregated team in the 
Nation’s Capital was the leagues’ biggest headache. In his first week on the job, Rozelle 
received a telephone call from President-elect John Kennedy, telling him rather bluntly that 
integrating that team and getting rid of Marshall were high, immediate action, priorities for his 
new administration. (Smith G. 2011) Independent of the incoming President’s demand, Rozelle 
was attempting to manage intense behind-the-scenes negotiations between the ownership 
group and the nations’ three primary television networks to create a nationwide broadcast 
schedule of NFL games every Sunday afternoon throughout the season and the playoffs. The 
main sticking point — none of the networks were willing to broadcast Redskin games for two 
reasons: fear of being associated in any way with segregation, and disdain for broadcast images 
of the Skins’ largely empty and rundown little stadium, which made the league look “bush 
league.” Marshall, of course, was fighting the entire concept tooth and nail for fear that 
nationally televised games by NBC, CBS or ABC would destroy his carefully constructed 
southern regional network, and indeed, the networks’ were adamant that Marshall’s network 
could not compete with their broadcasts. (Leggett W. The 28 Million Dollar Deal. High Finance 
and Hard Infighting Went Into the Acquisition of an Unprecedented Pro Football TV Deal. Sports 
Illustrated. www.vault.si.com. January 1964. Accessed October 7, 2024) 


In an effort to resolve the television network’s distaste for the imagery of the Redskin’s dinky 
home field, and also to entice White fans nestled in the burgeoning D.C. suburbs to journey 
back into town to attend games, Marshall proposed to move his teams’ home games into the 
new 50,000 seat D.C. Stadium scheduled to open in the fall of 1961. The new stadium was 
largely funded with federal money and was located on federal property to serve as the home of 
the Washington Senators MLB expansion franchise. The new Senators team had been literally 
thrown together overnight to prevent a proposed alternative baseball league, the Continental 
League, from creating a franchise in D.C. The original and long-suffering “Nats” moved to 
Minnesota to become the Twins after the 1959 season, and angry U.S. congressmen demanded 
that MLB promptly replace them with a new D.C. based franchise, because “it just wasn’t 
American for D.C. not to have a MLB team” and, more importantly, they did not want to be 
bogged down with politically toxic legislative proposals filed by MLB and the fledgling 
Continental League to block each other from the D.C. territory. (Buhite RD. The Continental 
League: A Personal History. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press. 2014) Before D.C. city 
management even reviewed, let alone approved, Marshall’s request to lease the new stadium, 
he advertised on his radio/television network and in the print media that the Skins were moving 
into a “bright and shiny” modern stadium. 


The District of Columbia Stadium, renamed RFK stadium after 
5 his 1968 assassination, was the first multi-purpose arena built 


in the 1960s to accommodate baseball or football. Like many 
of these structures, RFK was a bland oval, lacked personality 
or uniqueness with particularly poor seating for football.

The Wolds Best Stadium 


361 


Because he had broken his lease with old Griffith Park in anticipation of moving into D.C. 
Stadium, Marshall decided to play several of the team’s 1961 preseason exhibition games on 
the road in southern cities to bolster support for his Team of the South concept, assuming he 
would find friendly crowds “down in Dixie.” Thus, the August 26" match with the Colts was 
scheduled for S.B. Ballard Stadium, a fully segregated facility with a designated and roped off 
section of bleachers for Black ticket-buyers, a segregated parking lot and segregated restrooms 
and water fountains. There were no concession stands within the stadium although vendors 
wandered through the White-designated seating areas selling drinks and food items. 
Unbeknownst to Marshall, in the summer of 1961, the NAACP (National Association for 
Advancement of Colored People) and the U.S. justice department, headed by Attorney General 
Robert F. Kennedy, independently, and then quasi-collaboratively decided to target NFL 
exhibition games in segregated stadiums for civil rights advocacy. (McKenna, 2011; Smith G, 
2011). The NAACP focused on protesting NFL games played at segregated facilities and Bobby 
Kennedy decided to go after George Marshall directly by attempting to block his plans to play 
Redskin games at the D.C. Stadium. 


Two NEL Exhibition Games in August 1961 Shine a Light on Southern Segregation 

Two protests at NFL exhibition games scheduled in Virginia in August 1961 contributed to the 
NAACP’s goals of shining a national spotlight on racial segregation at NFL sponsored events, and 
prodding the NFL Commissioner’s office to finally take a firm public stand against Jim Crow 
practices. The first game was scheduled for August 12 in the unlikely location of Roanoke, 
Virginia, a relatively small and isolated town tucked away in the western side of the state. The 
city council of Roanoke, sensing an opportunity to be perceived nationally as more than just a 
little farm town, had spent considerable money advertising the game, sprucing up the 
community’s aging Victory Stadium, and paying for a television broadcast of the exhibition 
game to other cities in Virginia and North Carolina. The city had also pledged that all ticket and 
concession revenue from the game would go directly to charity organizations. The mayor, 
Chamber of Commerce and City Council realized that active participation by Roanoke’s Black 
population (18%) was needed to fill-up the 24,000-seat stadium. (Linden A. More Than Just 
Victory on Paper: From Roanoke to Kaepernick. Sport in American History. 
www.ussporthistory.com. September 29, 2016. Accessed: September 26, 2024) 


In violation of Virginia’s stringent public facility segregation policies, the city advertised open 
seating for the game for anyone who desired to buy a $4.00 ticket. When Virginia’s Attorney 
General learned about the open seating plan, he filed an injunction to stop ticket sales and 
demanded that the game be conducted as a segregated event with threats of repercussions for 
the city. Roanoke reluctantly agreed to comply. The local NAACP chapter led by the charismatic 
and proactive Reverend Raymond Wilkinson, filed a racial discrimination suit against the city, 
threatened to picket the game, including forming a “wall of protest” that the Colts and Steelers 
players would have to walk through to enter the stadium. Next, Wilkinson contacted Black 
players on the Steelers directly by a telegram that summarized the situation and concluded 
with “won't you join us in our fight for freedom by refusing to play in a segregated situation.” 
He also placed articles in local newspapers urging Black citizens to boycott the game even if 
they had already purchased tickets. When the Steelers coach, Buddy Parker, a White man, read 


362 


a newspaper article about the turmoil preceding the game and read Wilkinson’s telegram, he 
called a team meeting during which “nearly 100% of the White and Black players voted not to 
cross an NAACP picket line to play in a stadium that segregates Negro fans.” Coach Parker called 
his counterpart at the Colts, Don Shula, who held a similar vote, with a similar result, among his 
players. (Linden, 2016) 


The players’ threatened boycott, well publicized locally, and the prospect of walking through a 
picket line to reach the stadium dampened enthusiasm for the game, and ticket sales were 
poor. Game promoters, the Roanoke Chamber of Commerce and the City Council hurriedly 
organized a meeting with representatives of Colts and Steelers players, Rev. Wilkinson and the 
local NAACP chapter, the NFL league office, participating by telephone, and lawyers from the 
Commonwealth of Virginia Attorney General’s office. The Commonwealth’s attorneys were 
strident about enforcing segregated seating and restroom facilities at the stadium, in deference 
to the “Massive Resistance” to federal desegregation of public schools and other facilities led 
by Virginia’s powerful senior Senator, Harry F. Byrd. (Ely JW. The Crises of Conservative Virginia: 
The Byrd Organization and the Politics of Massive Resistance. Knoxville, TN: University of 
Tennessee Press. 1976). 


No minutes of the meeting appear to exist, but in spite of the state’s segregation policies, the 
Roanoke City Council ultimately decided to go ahead with the game as a non-segregated event, 
perhaps hoping the Attorney General’s bark was bigger than his bite. Raymond Wilkinson 
dropped the NAACP suit, and canceled the public protest at the stadium. The Steelers and Colts 
both agreed to show up in full force for the exhibition with no player protests, and the city and 
Wilkinson ran ads in White and Black newspapers encouraging all NFL fans to attend this open 
seating event. (Casey D. 1961 Victory Stadium Protest Preceded Sweeping Changes in Pro 
Football. August 24, 2024. Roanoke Times. www.roanoke.com. Accessed: September 27, 2024)

The NAACP was pleased with the national exposure of the controversy surrounding the 
Roanoke exhibition game, and the city’s decision to at least theoretically defy Virginia 
segregation policies. There was no meaningful repercussion for Roanoke other than verbal 
condemnation by the Attorney General and state politicians. However, the NAACP and Attorney 
General Robert Kennedy were disappointed with NFL Commissioner Rozelle’s bland and 
cautiously worded statement about the circumstances of the game, which concluded with: 


“This incident has focused the attention of the National Football League on the unhealthy 
conditions existing in cities of this type. | am hopeful that in the future seasons, clubs of the 
National Football League will not play games to segregated audiences.” (Linden, 2016) 


Rather than addressing the segregation policies of the Commonwealth of Virginia, Rozelle 
threw the city of Roanoke under the bus, and issued a wistful hope for integrated audiences in 
the future. 


Which brings us back to the Redskins- Colts exhibition game in Norfolk on August 26, 1961, just 
two weeks after the events in Roanoke. | shared my personal recollections of the so-called 
Kiwanis Bowl earlier. Let’s take a look at that game from a broader perspective. The leader of 
the Black picketers | met that night was Marie Golden Young, a 40-year city of Norfolk 
employee who managed city parks and community recreation centers in Black neighborhoods. 
Marie had recently joined the Women of Virginia’s Third Force, a third party voter registration 
group established and financed by a national civil rights organization, the Congress of Racial 
Equality (CORE), created and directed by James Foreman, a prominent civil rights leader in the 
1960s. Prior to her involvement with the Third Force, Young had petitioned and picketed for 
desegregation of public schools, picketed and participated in a law suit against a grocery store 
chain that placed stores in Black neighborhoods but refused to hire Black employees, and also 
participating in protests against the Catholic Church Diocese in Norfolk, which operated a 
segregated hospital with inferior medical staffing, bedding and equipment for Black patients. 
The primary mission of the Women of Virginia’s Third Force was to challenge segregation in 
public schools and transportation, and protest Virginia’s onerous poll tax that was instituted 
after WWII to discourage voting by Blacks and Hispanics. People who had never voted before, 
which included a large percentage of the non-White population of Virginia, were required to 
pay a fee in order to register to vote. Whites who had previously voted were exempt from the 
tax or simply were never asked to pay it when registering. (McKenna, 2011) 


The man whose name | did not catch the night of the game due to the pilfering of my Colts hat 
was Joseph Jordan, a Black attorney and community activist. Several years later, he did the legal 


364 


work and courtroom presentations during a series of court challenges to overturn the Virginia 
poll tax as a violation of the 14" amendment, concluding with arguing the petition before the 
Supreme Court. (Joseph A, Jordan Jr., Civil Rights Advocate. Newport News Daily Press. June 16, 
1991. www.newspapers. Com. Accessed October 7, 2024) Joseph Jordan offered the suggestion 
to search for the hat thief and my hijacked lid inside the stadium. 


At a monthly meeting of the Third Force at Marie Young’s home on August 11, 1961, discussion 
turned to newspaper accounts of the NAACP protest in Roanoke, and ultimately the decision 
was made to add segregation at public stadiums to the groups’ activism agenda. Also in 
attendance at this meeting was a young seamstress, Evelyn Thomas Butts, who would 
ultimately have a long and successful career as an equal rights activist in Virginia, and evolved 
into a major player in Norfolk politics. She was the person who tried to inject levity into the 
discussion of my stolen hat on the stadium walkway. 


Independent of the Third Force, the Norfolk NAACP chapter was energized by the Roanoke 
protest, and was urged by the NAACP national headquarters to replicate that protest in hopes 
of eliciting a stronger reaction from the NFL. Pre-game protest actions in Norfolk paralleled 
those in Roanoke: articles in a newspaper serving the Black community recommended a 
boycott of the game because of segregated seating, parking and rest rooms as well as the 
segregated Redskins roster, articles in the city’s main municipal newspaper, the Norfolk Daily 
News, provided similar information, a racial discrimination suit was filed against the city and the 
Kiwanis Club, the NAACP and the Third Force threaten picket lines and other awareness raising 
activities outside the stadium, and the NAACP and James Forman of CORE sent telegrams to 
Baltimore’s Black players, urging them to boycott the game. (McKenna, 2011)

sponsored by the local Kiwanis Club, who argued that Virginia’s 
segregated seating laws had to be obeyed: “We have no 
alternative. This is the law, no matter how we might feel about 
it individually, until it is repealed or declared unconstitutional.”

As in Roanoke, publicity about the impending protest and a potential players boycott 
negatively impacted ticket sales. After a few days of accusations flying back and forth, the 
Kiwanis Club and Norfolk city officials arranged a meeting of the involved parties with a 
composition similar to Roanoke’s conclave: Chamber of Commerce and Kiwanis Club 
Presidents, the NFL Commissioner, again by telephone, the Colts’ attorney, the Norfolk NAACP 
leader, Robert Robertson, city attorneys, the stadium manager, a Commonwealth Assistant 
Attorney General, Joseph Jordan of the Third Force, and one group not included in the Roanoke 
negotiations: representatives from the military, thus my dad’s involvement in this affair. 


365 


Organizers of the Kiwanis Bowl had been in discussion with Army, Navy and Air Force bases in 
the Hampton roads area to arrange game attendance by groups of soldiers, a tactic used then, 
and still to this day, to fill out the crowd and avoid swaths of empty seats visible on television 
broadcasts. The military, wary of the segregationist policies of the Commonwealth, were 
reluctant to send soldiers, sailors and airmen, with a high percentage of these servicemen being 
Black, into a known segregated facility — bad look for the military and likely a bad experience for 
many of the servicemen involved. Yet, it was a leverage point for the military and the NAACP: 
desegregate the stadium and its facilities completely and we might consider sending some 
troops to make your game attendance look better. (Ross CK. Outside the Lines: African 
Americans and the Integration of the NFL. Chapter 7. The Integration of the Washington 
Redskins. New York: New York University Press. 2022) 


Much to his dismay, my dad’s stateside assignment after eight years in the field as a combat 
officer in Korea and Europe was in an intelligence unit with an assignment to gather 
information on foreign agents (i.e., communists; it was the Cold War, after all) who may have 
infiltrated U.S. civil rights groups. His job required interaction with local NAACP and CORE 
offices and other equal rights advocacy groups, including quite possibly, the Third Force. He 
apparently drew the short straw in his office, and was assigned to represent the Army at the 
Kiwanis Bowl negotiations. 


As in Roanoke, an agreement was reached. The city of Norfolk would desegregate all seating 
and stadium facilities, however just for the day of the game, and would guarantee that all Black 
and White servicemen attending the game could sit together. The issue of restroom use was 
left in limbo. The NFL agreed to issue a statement asserting its position about segregation. In 
return, the NAACP would withdraw its suit and not assemble picket lines outside the stadium 
that fans and players would have to pass through. Black players on the Colts, reluctantly this 
time, agreed not to boycott the game. Based on a strongly worded appeal sent by James 
Foreman at CORE, the city of Norfolk and the NAACP (with only mild enthusiasm; there was 
tension among the organizations), consented to a small, silent demonstration by the Virginia 
Women’s Third Force outside the stadium focusing on the Redskins’ segregation policy, but 
they were directed not to implement any voter registration activity. James Foreman designated 
Marie Golden Young to organize and lead the picketers. (Basen R. Fifty Years Ago, The Last 
Outpost of Segregation in the NFL Fell. New York Times. www.nytimes.com. October 6, 2012. 
Accessed October 2, 2024) After the agreement was announced, all three military services 
elected not to send troops to the game; the terms of the agreement were too tenuous. 
However, it was assumed that some enlisted men and officers were planning to attend the 
game, perhaps with family members, after purchasing tickets on their own. To observe and 
report if any privately attending servicemen encountered difficulties, representatives from each 
service attended the game, thus the primary reason for Harold and Bill being at the stadium. In 
later years, | recollect my dad talking about squads of SPS (Navy Shore Patrol) and Army MPs 
positioned nearby in case of difficulties, but | did not uncover any accounts of this in newspaper 
articles or other game reports, and, apparently, there were no racial incidents within the 
stadium involving servicemen and their families. 


Rozelle’s NFL office issued a slightly stronger comment after the contest in Norfolk, praising all 
parties for working out an agreement that allowed the game to take place and condemning 


366 


segregation in concept, but stopped short of a policy statement about the Redskins or future 
NFL games in segregated facilities. However, the Colts owner pledged to never again allow his 
team to play a game in front of segregated fans. Despite the NFL’s hesitancy to take a firm 
stance against segregation, the protests and threatened boycotts at the Roanoke and Norfolk 
games were covered in newspapers across the nation and received attention on network 
television news programs, which increased NAACP and CORE visibility within White and Black 
communities, and emboldened the leaders of both groups to pursue more assertive protests. 


Robert F. Kennedy and George Preston Marshall 

Robert F. Kennedy (RFK) had a direct path to desegregating the Washington Redskins. In 1961, 
as now, the department of the Interior was responsible for management of all public facilities 
operating on federally owned lands in the U.S. The D.C. Stadium, largely constructed with 
federal money and situated on federally controlled property, was under the jurisdiction of the 
Department of Interior. With the blessing of his older brother, President John F. Kennedy (JFK), 
who did not want to personally confront Dixiecrat Marshall for political reasons, RFK directed 
Secretary of Interior Stewart Udall to bar Marshall and the Redskins from the stadium. The 
basis: The governance charter of the District of Columbia, as well as the federal government, 
banned discrimination based on race, gender or religion and prohibited segregation in any 
public facility. Udall had interacted with Marshall often during the construction of the stadium, 
and was not a fan of the Redskins’ owner, telling Povich and other Post reporters, that, “for 
Marshall, the purpose of any meeting is for him to be the one and only center of attention,” 
and also observed, Marshall doesn’t only hate Negroes, he hates everybody and everything 
except his money and his whores.” (McKenna, 2011) Shortly after, Udall informed Marshall that 
unless the Redskin Football Club officially desegregated, demonstrated willingness to hire Black 
employees throughout the organization, and specifically hired Black players for the football 
squad, the team would be banned from the D.C. Stadium. Marshall, predictably, fussed, cussed 
and fumed, threatened legal action, and pledged political repercussions for JFK, RFK and Udall. 


But RFK had another strategy to place even more pressure on Marshall. With begrudging 
consent from NFL Commissioner Rozelle, Kennedy worked behind the scenes to promote a 
rumor that quickly evolved into a newspaper headline story that the American Football League 
(AFL), an alternative pro league that had started play in 1960, was planning to place an 
integrated franchise in Washington D.C. for the 1962 season and that the D.C government was 
willing to exclusively lease the D.C. Stadium to this new team. The AFL, founded by some of the 
wealthiest business tycoons in America, had opened its checkbook to a large number of Black 
athletes, including several dozen who jumped from the NFL to AFL. The AFL actually had no 
intention of moving into D.C. while the Redskins were still based in the city, but Marshall was 
rattled by the story, and finally agreed to Udall’s terms, just a few weeks before the 1961 
regular season was to commence. Marshall agreed to draft “at least one, but probably several” 
Black collegians in the spring 1962 NFL draft and also agreed to sign “other Afro-American 
players as they are available for positions of need on the squad.” (Ross, 2022) 


However, Marshall being Marshall, his capitulation had a caveat: he had not allocated budget to 
hire additional players this late in preseason training, and there was not sufficient time to blend 
these new players into the team, so he requested deferment of fielding an integrated squad 
until the 1962 season. RFK and Udall were reluctant, figuring Marshall would find a way to 


367 


slither off the hook, or put political pressure on President Kennedy, who won the 1960 election 
by the slimmest of margins. For his part, JFK didn’t want to be embroiled in an ugly backyard 
fight within D.C. with Marshall. And so, JFK okayed the deferment to 1962, hoping to 
backburner the issue. 

A side note: A Dixiecrat was a Democrat from a southern state who supported racial 
segregation, such as Senator Harry F. Byrd of Virginia, the Massive Resistance leader. The 
Dixiecrats were a splinter group within the Democratic party from 1948 when the U.S. military 
was integrated by President Truman until 1968 when Richard Nixon was elected President, in 
large part because former Dixiecrats had joined the conservative wing of the Republican Party 
after passage of civil rights legislation in 1965. (Buchanan SE. The Dixiecrat Rebellion: Long-term 
Partisan Implications in the Deep South. Politics and Policy. 33(4): 754-769. 2005) 


Somewhat surprisingly, Marshall honored his pledge to draft a Black player in the 1962 NFL 
draft, although he stated in advance that he would not allow himself to be photographed 
shaking the hand of any Black draftee. Also surprisingly, the Redskins selected Ernie Davis, 
recent Heisman Trophy winner, with the first pick in the draft even though Davis had stated on 
multiple occasions that he would never play for Marshall given his segregationist beliefs. To be 
fair, Davis had also identified several other NFL cities where he would not play, stating 
frequently pre-draft that he wanted to play with his idol and mentor, Jim Brown, on the 
Cleveland Browns. To salvage the situation, the head coaches of the Redskins and Cleveland 
Browns, initially unbeknownst to their owners, worked out a trade that sent Davis to Cleveland, 
his preferred destination, for star wide receiver Bobby Mitchell, who was willing to be an 
integration pioneer with the Redskins. In the trade, two other Black players went to the 
Redskins, and Marshall’s team selected two Black collegians in later rounds of the draft. 
Marshall also signed two Black free agents prior to the start of the 1962 season, which jumped 
his non-White player roster from zero in 1961 to seven in 1962.

We already know the sad outcome for Davis in Cleveland. As for the Skins, even with Mitchell’s 
stellar play, the team remained lackluster in 1962 and 1963, winning only eight games 
combined in those years, finishing at the bottom of the standings. However, two events turned 
the franchise around after the 1963 season: Marshall’s health precipitously declined as he 
suffered a series of major medical crises that eventually took his life in 1969. He played no 
meaningful role in team affairs after the 1963 season. Minority owners Edward Bennett 
Williams and Jack Kent Cook, took over day-to-day management with Cook eventually 
becoming majority owner a few years later. One of Williams and Cooks’ first actions was to 


368 


acquire from the Eagles in a very lopsided trade, All-Pro quarterback Sonny Jurgenson, the 
league’s leading passer. Jurgenson’s wide open, pass-heavy, offense (he functioned as his own 
offensive coordinator) turned the Skins into the NFL’s highest scoring team in the 60s, 
dramatically increased their win totals and attracting several talented Black players who desired 
to play in his innovative offense. When the new ownership group hired George Allen, a 
defensive specialist, as head coach in 1971, the Skin’s defense finally caught up to the offense, 
and the team commenced a 25 year period of excellence that led to five Super Bowl 
appearances and three Super Bowl victories in 1983, 1988 and 1992, the later victory 
engineered by a Black quarterback, Doug Williams. 


Marshall’s 1969 will set up a charitable foundation, but contained the stipulation that none of 
its money would ever be used for any purpose that supported the principle of racial integration 
in any form. In 2006, the Virginia legislature unanimously approved a resolution that 
commended Marie Golden Young’s “lifetime dedication to civil rights” and recognized her for 
“leading protests and picketing against the Washington Redskins when the team refused to sign 
African-American players.” (McKenna, 2011) 


Notes on Challenges to the Virginia Poll Tax. In November 1963, Evelyn Thomas Butts and 
Third Force attorney Joseph Jordan sued the Commonwealth of Virginia in Butts Versus 
Harrison, Governor of Virginia, for requiring citizens to pay a poll tax prior to registering to vote. 
Butts was the chief plaintiff and other plaintiffs included Marie Golden Young. Butts’ contended 
that the tax was not constitutional because it placed an undue financial burden in violation of 
the 14" amendment. That amendment guarantees equal protection under the law and 
citizenship to all people born or naturalized in the United States and was primarily added to the 
Constitution in 1868 to ensure citizenship and legal protections for former slaves whose status 
was in limbo after Civil War. In addition to ratification by northern states, the 11 states that 
formed the Confederacy were required to ratify the amendment to regain representation in 
Congress. The amendment’s many clauses include provisions related to due process of law, 
voting rights, and disqualification from public office for any person who engaged in insurrection 
against the United States. (United States Senate. Senate Historical Office. www.senate.gov. 
Landmark Legislation: The Fourteenth Amendment. Accessed: October 8, 2024) 


The poll tax case was dismissed by lower level state courts and by Virginia’s Court of Appeals, 
but Butts and Jordan filed a revised version of the suit, which, after more dismissals, was again 
heard upon appeal by the 4" U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. That court upheld the legitimacy of 
the Virginia pool tax. Jordan reworked the suit and it was filed again in 1965, dismissed without 
hearing by a state court, and appealed to the 4" Circuit Court, where, yet again, the poll tax 
was upheld. Butts and Jordan appealed that decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, which agreed 
to hear the case. The Supreme court had recently received a similar case, Harper Versus Virginia 
State Board of Elections, and it combined the two cases together into a single action. Jordan 
argued the case before the Supreme Court in October 1965. In March, 1966, the Supreme Court 
issued a 6-3 decision that declared the poll tax administered by the Board of Elections in 
Virginia to be unconstitutional because it made the “affluence of the voter or the payment of a 
fee an electoral standard; voter qualifications have no relation to wealth.” The decision made 
poll taxes illegal in the eleven southern states that had instituted the device early in the 20th 


369 


century in an effort to disenfranchise Blacks. (Alexander KC. Developing and Sustaining Political 
Citizenship for Poor and Marginalized People: The Evelyn T. Butts Story. Doctoral Dissertation. 
Antioch University. AURA: Antioch University Repository and Archives. www.AURA.antioch.edu. 
2019)

Epilogue —Dickinson College 1969 

In February 1969, the same month that Susan and | first met, | attended a symposium at 
Dickinson College that addressed the declining interest in civil rights issues on university 
campuses during the Vietnam War era. The main event was a panel discussion that included, 
most prominently, John Lewis (1940-2020), the second most visible U.S. civil rights activist in 
the 20" century, after Martin Luther King (MLK). Lewis planned and participated in the 
Freedom Rides, and helped organize the 1963 March on Washington where his passionate 
speech received equal acclaim in the days after the event as MLK’s “I Have a Dream” oration. 
Lewis organized and led the Selma to Montgomery, Alabama March where he and other 
marchers were beaten and jailed by police. Lewis was frequently called to testify before 
Congress on civil rights matters, wrote dozens of newspaper editorials, keynoted national voter 
registration and equal rights conferences and organized picketing, restaurant sit-ins, ride-ins on 
segregated public busses, and protest marches in dozens of cities. And pertinent to the 
Dickinson symposium that day, Lewis created and directed the Student Non-Violent 
Coordinating Committee (SNCC) to energize college student engagement in the civil right 
movement. (Greenberg D. John Lewis: A Life. New York: Simon and Schuster. 2024) 


| do not remember what any of the panelists said that evening, but | do vividly recall the first 
thing Lewis did when the microphone was passed to him. He stood and pointed right at me in 
my aisle seat about 20 rows back, and said: (I’m paraphrasing here as | don't remember the 
exact words) “/’m glad to see you are wearing a SNCC button.” And, indeed the little round 
SNCC button, pictured below, adorned my big grey winter coat. The Dickinson SNCC chapter 
president, a fraternity brother of mine, had given it to me after | recently attended a couple of 
SNCC meetings, mostly out of curiosity, but also looking for an activity that was more high tone 
than intramural sports and frat life. Going full Judas on Lewis, | demurred, and said, “well 
actually, it’s not SNCC, it’s about achieving racial tolerance,” or something to that effect. 
Naturally, many heads swiveled in my direction, and as | was verbalizing my denial, my inner 
voice was undoubtedly questioning, “what are you doing dummy, why are these words coming 
out of your mouth?” The fog of memory obscures Lewis’ response, but think it was, “oh, okay, it 
looked like one from here,” and he probably stared at me a bit, before moving to his remarks. 


370 


My SNCC pin from college. There were several versions of the SNCC pin, 
and the acronym, SNCC, was printed on most of them, but not this one. 
I could obfuscate, and say that is what confused me, but that would not 
be accurate; | knew what it was, but wavered in the spotlight. 

Image source: Hendricson family photo collection. 


Disconcerted by my wrongheaded response, | devoted the remainder of the panel discussion to 
planning my rush up to the stage as soon as the session concluded so | could try to make things 
right with Lewis. And so, even before the applause died down, | headed down the center aisle 
toward the stage, but so did other students. By the time | got to the vicinity of Lewis and the 
other panelists, several layers of people were flinging questions in their direction. Much like my 
adolescent days, | waited outside the ring of conversation for quite a while until the crowd 
thinned, and | finally found myself in front of Lewis and another older panelist. | have a visual 
memory of the moment but cannot recollect what | said to Lewis or exactly his response. | recall 
that he looked tired and ready to depart, his work done for that day. After whatever apology / 
rationalization | offered, he indicated that he normally doesn’t put audience members on the 
spot like that, suggesting that may have flustered me. And then came the only words | do 
remember distinctly from that moment: “Did you ever find your hat,” not spoken by Lewis, but 
by the panelist standing with him. Flummoxed, | likely stammered “huh” and squinted, my 
prototypical puzzlement reaction. The question came from Joseph Jordan, the Third Force 
attorney who was standing with my dad and other protestors outside the Colts-Redskins game 
in Norfolk. | didn’t recognize him that evening in 1969, and he actually had to explain our 
connection. Jordan said he noticed me hanging back tonight, waiting to approach Mr. Lewis, 
and coupled with my size, age and general demeanor, it reminded him of the young boy who 
had his Colts hat swiped in Norfolk. He said, “I took a gamble, but | was pretty sure it was you.” 


I'd like to report that | became actively engaged in the civil rights activities of the Dickinson 
SNCC chapter after my encounter with Lewis and Jordan, but | didn’t. Other than serving on a 
planning committee for a student march to the Army War College in Carlisle on October 15, 
1969 to protest the Vietnam War (per John Lewis’ concerns), and participating with Susan in 
that march, my college activism was limited to a bystander’s moral support of progressive 
causes. 


The Dickinson “peace now” march to the Army War College was two weeks before the infamous 
1969 Halloween Night Parade, previously discussed, that led to the banning of college fraternities 
and sororities from that event. The events represent a yin and yang of 60s’ college experience. 
Image source: Hendricson family photo collection

To further the yin and yang analogy, one week before the War College March, a caravan of 200 
cars with an estimated 800 Dickinson students including Susan and |, and two others squeezed 
into the tiny backseat of her Pontiac Firebird, headed for Lancaster, PA, home of Franklin and 
Marshall College, and site of a Blood, Sweat and Tears (BS&T) concert in the F & M gymnasium, 
pictured below. Most of the caravan, including us, managed to get lost, and we walked into the 
gym 45 minutes after the 9:00pm start time. Because Dickinsonians represented 1/3 of the 
tickets, BS&T, unhappily, agreed to wait for our caravan. Throughout the steamy night in an un- 
air conditioned gym, we enjoyed the music, but endured the lead singer’s (David Clayton 
Thomas) belittlement of “f .... ing Dickersons” and other scatological riffs on the college’s name, 
which were picked up and joyously re-chanted by F & M students.
