Becoming Who We Are (Susan and Bill Hendricson; 1971-1978) 

Other members of our immediate family are likely are familiar with the San Antonio phase of 
my life with Susan. In contrast, our eight years in metropolitan Chicago, i.e., Chicagoland (1971 
— 1978), the first chapter of early marriage challenges, relationship building, and moving toward 
who we would be as adults, may be less well known. Even for Susan and I, it’s easy to forget 
that we had a substantially different existence in that decade. The five intervening decades 
have left a fuzzy veil over the Chicagoland phase, almost as if other people lived those years, 
but it was indeed a much younger version of us, and it was a meaningful period of our life 
together, as we started to learn how to navigate life’s ups and downs, and lay the foundation 
for who we are today. 


After our marriage ceremony on a snowy morning in Susan’s parent’s church, the first Baptist 
Church of Sliver Spring, Maryland, and the reception near Susan’s home at the Manor Country 
Club in Rockville, Maryland during an even more intense snowfall, we ran off into the future. 


January 2, 1971 — Departing After Our Wedding Day 


The first stop was a honeymoon in Bermuda, which was excellent until the final day when we 
both were struck with a rather violent gastrointestinal bug. After an uncomfortable flight home, 
we spent several miserable days in bed at the Hendricson house in Fairfax Virginia on GE 
Haynesworth Place, named in an extreme piece of irony after George E. “Tuck” Haynesworth, 
the trigger-happy Citadel cadet we met in John Lienau’s story. But, our gastrointestinal systems 
finally re-balanced, and we headed back to Carlisle, Pennsylvania to finish our college careers at 
Dickinson, balancing academics with jobs; Bill, Montgomery Ward paint department manager, 
Susan, Teaching Assistant and care provider for children with Down Syndrome. 


373

Two days after graduation, | started my first post-college employment, working on a 
construction crew, installing doors, windows and bathtubs, for a new 50 acre Ramada Inn 
Resort in Mechanicsburg, PA, a suburb of Harrisburg, the state capital. Ramada at that time was 
embarking on an image upgrade campaign, building swankier facilities to attract higher dollar 
reservations, especially in communities adjacent to the nation’s rapidly expanding interstate 
highway system. For the grand opening in Mechanicsburg, Ramada Corporation hired none 
other than Jerry Lee Lewis, the famed “Killer,” the Rockabilly star second only to Elvis (Great 
Balls of Fire, Whole Lot of Shakin Going On’, High School Confidential, Breathless, Crazy Arms, 
and more than 30 other Billboard Top 10 hits) to perform at a gala in the resort’s ballroom. The 
Killer’s journey to the resort led to my most memorable day on that job, which involved figuring 
out a way to get his beloved white baby grand piano, not surprisingly known as “Baby” into his 
suite on the second floor of the facility. Rather than rehearsing in the ballroom, which Lewis 
and his traveling partner, an attractive women introduced as his agent and spokesperson, 
claimed would lead to much gawking, autograph seeking and disruptions, they demanded that 
the piano be transported upstairs to Lewis’s suite to allow solitary preparation, and, because 
Jerry Lee, having scoped out the setting, decided that playing from the balcony above the 
ballroom would be a majestic experience for the gala attendees. This was news to our hotel 
manager who had already set up a cordoned-off performance area for Lewis and Baby near an 
inexplicably large fireplace, which had the appearance of a grand hearth in a medieval castle, 
along one side of the parquet floor ballroom in the Mechanicsburg Ramada Resort. 


With five of us crew members standing around watching this conversation, happy to be indoors 
in air conditioning and out of the oppressive central PA heat and humidity, the hotel manager 
dug in his heels, saying he didn’t believe it was possible to move Baby upstairs. The 


374 


agent/spokesperson whipped out a folder from her large over the shoulder bag, flipped to a 
marked page and began loudly reading contract terms, “to include private rehearsal 
accommodation within Mr. Lewis’ assigned residence up until one hour before commencement 
of designated engagement.” After a awkward stare down between the agent and the Ramada 
manager, with Jerry Lee leaning up against a pillar, grinning, nodding and strumming his fingers 
on his pants leg, probably listening to music in his head, (maybe his big 1971 hit: Would You 
Take Another Chance on Me) the manager waved us over, and, trying to act gruff, not his core 
nature, said in effect, “try the elevator first, and if that won’t work, haul that thing up the 
stairs,” pointing at me — “you're in charge; don’t break his damn piano.”

When we started to tilt Baby on its side so we could unscrew the legs, Lewis broke out of his 
reverie and told us to stop tipping the piano because it “jangled up” the innards, throwing it out 
of tune, and then informed us that the legs could not be unscrewed anyway because were 
bolted on with metal plates for reinforcement, probably due to the Killer’s gymnastics on and 
off Baby during shows. And Lewis didn't want it rolled, more jangle avoidance, so the Ramada 
Five picked up Baby, which likely weighed 500 pounds, and shuffled it over to the nearest 
elevator. Given the direction of this story to this point, it’s probably no surprise that the roughly 
7 foot (long) and 6 foot (wide) baby grand did not fit into the standard Otis 6.5 by 5.5 elevator. 
It would not have fit even if Lewis allowed us to carry it sideways. The staff elevator for cleaning 
and maintenance crews was only inches larger, and also a no-go. So, we shuffled Baby back to 
the remaining option, a curving staircase ascending up from the ballroom parquet to a balcony 
area on the Ramada’s Executive-Suite Wing. Up we went with Jerry’s Baby; | foolishly allowed 
myself to be on the upside, and thus had to back up the winding stairs. Fortunately, the 
staircase was wide so we didn’t have to lift Baby higher than the side railings, but the curve was 
pronounced and their were a.. lot.. of.. stairs. Up close, Jerry’s piano was banged up and 
obviously had been recently touched up and lacquered. We knew this because sticky lacquer 
was rubbing off in our hands as we wrangled it upward, making Baby slippery, leading to 
several encounters with the metal railing that separated us from the floor 20 or so feet below. 
Despite the slippery surface and the cumbersome heft of the device, Baby and the Ramada 
crew survived the staircase climb. 


For some reason, Susan and | were not invited to the by-invitation only, VIP, concert, but | did 
get to listen to Lewis and his agent yelling at us not to scratch the white piano as we struggled 
up the staircase to the balcony. And, after carrying, not rolling, Baby down a long hallway to 
Lewis’ suite, no tips were doled out once we deposited it in the room. Instead, the

spokesperson, fussed at us for our dirty boots, the dusty soles of which were adding color

down to this — a Ramada Inn in some place called Mechanicsburg? But | don't know really what

not scheduled to work the day that Baby made the return trip down to ground level, and into a 
moving van, off to Killer’s next gig, just a few miles away at the Williams Grove Amusement 
Park.

Independent of the piano lifting, just a few days before the end of my summer employment, | 
was offered a managerial job at the Resort in charge of the linen and maintenance services and 
night operations twice a week. After a few days of consideration, | said no in favor of heading 
off to graduate school. | must say that | did consider it; the starting salary was tempting. It took 
eight years for me to earn a salary in the educational world equal to Ramada’s offer. 


In 1970, | thought | wanted to be a high school history teacher, “to be better than all the bad 
ones | endured”, but my mentor at Carlisle Middle School where | taught during the senior year 
in Dickinson’s teacher prep program emphasized two pieces of career advise over and over 
again: (1) interview for teaching jobs with an advanced degree already in hand; you’ll start with 
a higher salary, and you'll always be financially ahead of other teachers who start without a 
Masters, and (2) get an educational technology degree (in 1970, that meant mainframe 
computers or the emerging medium of video recording) so you can also be certified as a 
school’s technology specialist, leading to an even higher starting salary (“even more than 
coaches” he advised from experience because he was a long-time football coach). So off to 
graduate school we went to achieve those goals. Accepted by several schools, the choice came 
down to Boston University or Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, just north of 
Chicago. We visited both and concluded that the academics were equivalent, but the cost of 
living in Boston was exorbitant. The rental of marginally passable apartments located far away 
from the BU campus was more than double that of much nicer accommodations in Evanston. 


And, it must be admitted that the community of Evanston itself was as much or more of an 
attraction as NU. When we drove for the first time north on Sheridan Road, the suburban 
extension of the famed Lake Shore Drive along Chicago’s Lake Michigan Gold Coast and crossed 
into Evanston, the decision was made at that moment. Sheridan Road, like virtually every other 
street in the town, was canopied with stately Elm and Maple trees. Well-restored apartment 
buildings and private homes from the 1920s and 30s lined both sides of the street with glimpses 


376 


of the massive lake in between homes on a shoreline that ran the length of the town. There 
were parks, many along the lake, and beautiful 19" century churches, and a spectacular section 
of the Chicago Greenbelt System extended along both sides of the North Branch of the Chicago 
River curving through town. After several miles of gawking, we rounded another curve in the 
road, past a large sandy beach, and there was Northwestern, canopied by trees with the full 
length of the campus directly on the water. In our eyes, this was the place for us.

The All-American recognitions from the conservative-leaning Civic League were surprising 
because Evanston always has been a community with decided progressive tendencies, likely 
driven by the predominance of church-led social activism throughout its history. Evanston is 
known as the City of Churches, and when we lived there, it had the highest church to 
population ratio of any U.S. city over 50,000. In the 1850s, an offshoot of the third Great 
Awakening that WF Hendricson encountered during one of his wagon train journeys, known as 
the Eyes Open Movement, originated in the Methodist Church of Evanston. It was comprised of 
men and women “awake to social inequalities and indignities that burden and belittle our 
fellow humans.” (Kidd, 2007) During the 1970s, among the sequence of North Shore suburbs of 
Evanston, Willamette, Kenilworth, Winnetka, Glencoe, Highland Park and Lake Forest that 
become increasingly affluent/opulent as you drive north, Evanston was the only community 
with a diverse population at 55% White, 30% Black and 15% Asian or Hispanic. 


However, it’s important to recognize that Evanston’s Black population was largely restricted by 
racially motivated real estate practices to the southern edge of the city bordering Chicago until 
the 1950’s. White homeowners and real estate agents slowly became comfortable with the 


377 


concept of selling to Black buyers during the 1960s, but even when we lived in Evanston, there 
was an area of town primarily populated with Black families. As far back as the 1920’s Evanston 
city leadership desired to promote racial integration, which was inconsistent with prevailing 
trends in the U.S. during that era. City Hall and the School Board, fighting stiff opposition from 
White parent groups and law suits that went all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court, 
constructed a new 65 acre campus for the Evanston Township High School (ETHS) in 1924 
within a traditionally Black neighborhood of Evanston. The move is generally credited with 
slowly breaking down segregationist attitudes and real estate practices within the city. ETHS is 
considered to have the largest campus acreage of any high school in Illinois, is almost annually 
listed as a top U.S. high school in the U.S. News and World Report rankings, and maintains a 
diverse student body, economically and racially. Ironically, in spite of its role in the U.S. civil 
rights movement, the school is likely best known today as the site of the 2004 movie, and 
current Broadway play, Mean Girls, written by Northwestern alumni, Tina Fey.

To imagine what Evanston was like back then, think about any outdoor scene in these 1980s 
movies: Risky Business, Ferris Bueller, Sixteen Candles, Pretty in Pink, Breakfast Club, Weird 
Science, Say Anything (John Cusack with his boom box), Uncle Buck, and Home Alone. All of 
these movies implied that they were set in the vastly more posh villages of Kenilworth or 
Winnetka, but, in actuality, they were mostly filmed in Evanston to provide a less ostentatious 
backdrop that would better connect with movie audiences. (Gora S. You Couldn’t Ignore Me If 
You Tried: The Brat Pack, John Hughes and Their Impact on a Generation. New York: Three 
Rivers Press. 2011.) Indeed, Evanston was solidly middle income in the 1970s. Even a low- 
income couple like us could live there if residences were selected carefully.

Several vivid recollections remain from our early years in Evanston. One is Susan riding off to 
Tom Thumb on her bike, bundled in a heavy winter coat, plowing through the slushy snow ona 
gloomy winter morning with even more falling snow swirling around her, blown by lake wind 
and enveloping her in a cocoon as she peddled down the street. Another is our move into our 
first house in Evanston, accomplished DIY during a blazing hot week in July 1973. 


Moving Day 1973. 


After turning down a job to be a bodyguard at a school for emotionally challenged adolescents 
(a good decision in retrospect), | somehow managed to land a job at Lutheran General 
Healthcare (LGH), a teaching hospital in the University of Illinois-Chicago (UIC Med) Medical 
School system of affiliated institutions known as the Metro Eight. The upside of the Lutheran 
General job was their willingness to accommodate my class schedule at NU and the downside 
was arriving VERY early in the morning, typically 5:00am, to accomplish a substantial part of the 
job, which was videotaping and photographing surgeries for use in resident training and for 
publications. LGH was in a far west suburb, Park Ridge (near O’Hare Airport), 30-40 minutes 
from Evanston if traffic was light and it was not snowing or icy. So — a lot of early mornings. 
Other tasks at LGH included editing the surgical tapes into 15 minute training videos, 
broadcasting 8:00am M & M (Morbidity and Mortality) Conferences, where the MDs critiqued 
each other’s work, to the other Metro Eight hospitals, broadcasting the daily Noon Conferences 
(teaching sessions for Metro Eight residents and attendings sponsored by pharmaceutical reps 
(lots of good food!), and at least an hour a day of photocopying journal articles for UIC Med 
faculty that were writing manuscripts and preparing lectures. Reminder: this was 20 years pre- 
internet. One other notable moment at Lutheran General was participating in the first 
nationwide fax transmission in the U.S. in 1971. The National Library of Medicine (NLM) sent 
the inaugural fax to a hospital in each of the 50 states. Lutheran General represented Illinois. 
My job was to install the fax machine on the auditorium stage and hope that it worked at the 
big moment. It did! As large crowd full of physicians and nursing staff watched, a 8 X 11 inch 
image of George Washington noisily rolled out of the machine, which | handed to the hospital’s 
CEO, who held it up to the crowd to applause and cheers. | then faxed a page with our hospital 


379 


logo back to NLM, and received a confirmation fax with a big image of the NLM logo, eliciting 
more cheering. The hospital librarian, who was assigned responsibility for the machine, then 
launched into reading a long list of instructions and Fax usage guidelines, which thinned the 
audience considerably. 


| probably filmed and/or photographed over 100 surgeries in my time at LGH. When filming 
(this was still the pre-video era), | stood behind the surgeons, residents and scrub nurses at a 
console where | operated a 16mm camera mounted on a dolly positioned over the table. The 
surgeon or his resident would bark orders to zoom in or out, or ask me to come to move to the 
side, foot or head of the table to shoot at an angle with a secondary film camera. Within a 
week, | would edit film from the two camera into the final 15-minute product, typically with the 
guidance of the resident or sometimes, the surgeon himself. For still photography intended for 
journal articles of lecture slides, | stood next to the lead surgeon and snapped shots at his 
direction, often sliding around the table to get better sight lines, sometimes bumping or 
standing in front of residents or nurses, which annoyed them to no end. Certainly the most 
memorable surgery occurred very near the end of my time at LGH. The surgery that morning 
was a new approach, in 1973, for correcting hip dysplasia, which involved surgically cutting and 
realigning the upper area of the femur (thigh bone) to change its angle so that it meshed better 
with the hip socket. The surgeon, whose name | cannot recall (it might have been Franzblau), 
wanted full documentation by film and photography for a planned manuscript and a 
presentation at an upcoming surgical conference. 


For still photography, | most often used the Surgery Department’s Nikon, but prior to the 
surgery that morning, the lead surgeon presented me with his personal camera, a fabled 
Hasselblad 500cm, widely considered to be the ultimate camera of that era, the personal 
favorite of Ansel Adams and other noted photographers, and the camera that NASA sent into 
orbit with the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo astronauts. The iconic photo of the Earthrise from 
the moon was taken in 1969 by astronaut William Anders with a Hasselblad cm. (O’Hare M. 
How the Stunning Earthrise Became the World’s Most Famous Photograph. New Scientist. 
www.newscientist.com. December 18, 2018. Accessed January 5, 2025) In 1973, a Hasselblad 
500cm with a top of the line Zeiss lens system could cost as much as $3,000, equivalent to 
$15,000 today, and it also required expensive rolls of film specially made for that camera.

The surgeon handed me a half dozen rolls of the costly 500cm film, telling me to “get 
everything.” Unnerved, | used the 30 minutes before the patent was wheeling into the

admonished the group to “let the photographer get his shots.” The surgery and the shooting

moment when the electric saw the surgeon was applying to the patient’s femur decided to 
seize up and stop. Attempts to re-start the device failed. He handed the saw to a resident 
standing next to me and told him to go to an adjacent operatory and locate a functioning saw. 
The resident, whipped around with defunct saw in his hand and ... yep ... mashed it right into 
the Hasselblad. | apparently did not have an adequate grip on the camera because it flew out of 
my hands like a ball off a bat, bouncing hard off the tiled concrete floor, spewing parts as it 
tumbled to rest against an equipment cart. | recall the dead silence that enveloped the room 
and remember the resident and | staring at each other much too long, likely fearful of turning 
toward the surgeon. Our trance was broken by the surgeon’s calm voice, urging the resident to 
quickly retrieve a replacement saw, and telling me to go grab the Surgery Department’s Nikon 
and return ASAP. The resident and | scurried out of the OR to collect our respective 
replacement devices, both of us likely dreading the aftermath of the Hasselblad’s demise.

After our return, the femur re-alignment proceeded to a successful conclusion, after which, the 
patient and much of the surgical team moved away to other destinations, and those staff 
responsible for operatory clean-up and disinfection turned to their tasks. Awaiting the re- 
appearance of the surgeon, the resident and | collected the pieces of the camera and deposited 
them on a tray. Fortunately the main body of the camera was intact so it was likely that the film 
was not compromised. Eventually the surgeon returned and informed us that he didn’t consider 
either of us at fault: we were both carrying out tasks he had assigned, but, perhaps, we both 
should have had more situational awareness. He directed the resident to make sure the faulty 
saw was assessed, repaired and tested, and told me to get the Hasselblad and Nikon film 
processed promptly so we could schedule a photo review session. He motioned to the 
wounded Hasselblad on the tray and asked me to bring it to his administrative assistant after 
the film was extracted. And then he walked away. When we met to select photos for his 
manuscript and his conference presentation, he didn’t mention the Hasselblad, but said that 
the department chair had agreed to purchase a second Nikon as a back-up, and that residents 


381 


would do still photography in the future to reduce clutter around the table. A lesson learned for 
me: there always is consequence. 


In addition to my surgical photography duties in the portion of my job description that stated 
“and all other tasks as assigned by the Chair of the Surgery Department,” (who also was Chief of 
Staff and Director of Medical Education, the ultimate BMOC; Big Man On Campus), | routinely 
performed two other duties. During the school year, | drove his daughter from her middle 
school to a nearby equestrian center where she practiced dressage for 45 minutes every day in 
lieu of her PE class at school, and then returned her to school. | typically did this on my way 
back to Northwestern for afternoon classes, and not a few times was late arriving on campus 
due to the daughter’s casual approach to time management. A related task, but more pertinent 
to LGHs medical education mission, was assisting guest speakers who came to LGH to present 
Friday 8:00am seminars, called Grand Rounds in the medical world, and then driving them in 
the surgeon’s car, a Mercedes, not my VW bus, to other Metro 8 affiliated hospitals for similar 
presentations later in the day. An upside of this job was meeting and having time to chat with 
several luminaries in 1970s health care, including Dr. Elisabeth Kubler-Ross, author of Death 
And Dying (Kubler-Ross E. On Death and Dying. New York: Macmillan Publishing. 1969), which 
was named one of the 100 most important books of the 20" century by several organizations 
including the New York Public Library and Simon and Shuster Publishers, among many other 
literary entities. Time Magazine recognized her as Woman of the Year in 1977, and she is 
recognized on many lists of most influential people of the 20" century. 


Notes on Death and Dying Dr. Elisabeth Kubler-Ross (1926-2004) was commonly known as EKR 
at the peak of her fame, and the acronym is used to this day for her philanthropy — the ERK 
Foundation. ERK is best known for her elucidation of the stages of grief that individuals 
progress through emotionally and cognitively: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and 
acceptance, as they come to grips with the reality of an impending life-altering event. These 
events include one’s own death, the passing of a loved one, or major disruptions to life 
circumstances including divorce, loss of a job, or major work environment changes that 
dramatically alter a person’s role. By 1972 when she visited LGH, EKR was already 
internationally famous for her pioneering research on the experiences and emotions of the 
terminally ill as they approached death, data that she gathered by interviewing hundreds o 
dying people during their final months. Over the following decades, she would garner even 
more acclaim for her passionate pursuit of initiatives to improve the quality of medical and 
psychological care for dying persons, which triggered the hospice movement and the field o 
palliative medicine worldwide. Between 1969 until her death in 2004, EKR collaborated with 
health care systems in the U.S. and other nations to create hospice care facilities and develop 
palliative care training programs, and started several holistic health institutes. She also traveled 
the world conducting workshops to promote better understanding among health care providers 
of the emotional processes that the terminally ill experience, and to share strategies for 
enhancing quality of life of those approaching death (i.e., to make passage from this life a 
meaningful experience), which in her view, was one of several transition periods in a person’s 
existence, just as important as marriage, birth of children, career accomplishments and 


382 


retirement. (Chaban MCG. The life Work of Dr. Elisabeth Kubler-Ross and Its Impact on the 
Death Awareness Movement. New York: E. Mellen Press. 2000) 


Dr. Elisabeth Kubler-Ross about ten years after her visit to Lutheran 
General Hospital. 
Image source: Wikipedia. www.en.m.wikipedia.org. Accessed: 7/9/2023. 


Prior to entering medical school in her native Switzerland, EKR worked for refugee-aid 
organizations in Poland, Rumania, France and Germany in the years after World War Il, 
including an aid station for survivors of Nazi concentration camps. During her psychiatric 
residency training at hospitals in New York City and Long Island and later as a postdoctoral 
fellow in Denver, EKR was appalled by the treatment, or lack thereof, of those individuals 
labeled by physicians as “hopeless patients” (i.e., the terminally ill) who were neglected 
medically and psychologically, almost completely ignored for long periods of time by nursing 
staff and needlessly overly sedated to make management easier. These experiences triggered 
her lifelong dedication to restoring the dying patient’s sense of dignity and improving medical 
care during the final phase of life. 


Her rise to fame in palliative care began somewhat by accident. When her physician husband, 
Emanuel Ross, MD, was hired as Director of Neuropathology at Loyola University Medical 
School in Chicago, EKR took a job as a junior faculty member at the University of Chicago 
Pritzker School of Medicine in the Psychiatry Department. One day, the department chair had a 
scheduling complication that prevented him from delivering a lecture to medical students. With 
just a few hours notice, the chair directed EKR to step in and conduct the class, but provided no 
lecture notes, indicating she could select her own topic. With no time to adequately prepare a 
presentation, EKR asked one of her patients, a 19-year-old women in the final stages of her 
battle with cancer, if she would be willing to be interviewed in front of the class, and the 
patient agreed. 


The session was a riveting experience for the medical students; for many it was their first 
encounter with a dying patient and the first time they heard the patient’s perception of the 
dying process. (Chacon, 2000) Many students broke into tears during the interview, and others 
stayed long after the class concluded to speak with the patient and pepper EKR with questions 
or share personal experiences with grief. Based on this experience, EKR intensified her efforts 
to interview terminal patients, and based on these encounters, produced a brief article for 
publication in a limited circulation Chicago-based journal that reported her findings along with 
an early version of her five step grief model. (Kubler-Ross E. On Death and Dying — The Dying 
Patient As A Teacher. The Chicago Theological Seminary Register. 1966; 17(3): 2-18) The editor 
of this journal sensed that the article may attract a wider audience, and forwarded it to several 
major publishing houses in New York. After reading the article, Macmillan Publishing 
immediately offered EKR a contract with a lucrative advance payment for an expanded 250- 


383 


page manuscript that was ultimately published in December 1969. The book instantly became 
an international best seller. On Death and Dying remained on the New York Times Top Ten Best 
Seller list until 1977. 


After the Grand Rounds presentation at LGH, EKR was scheduled to repeat the presentation at 
11:00am and 2:00pm at other Metro Eight hospitals, and then return to LGH for a seminar open 
to the public at 5:00pm, followed by a reception, a busy day, but | learned that EKR experienced 
days like this at least weekly. My job was to chauffer her, in the Chief of Staff's Mercedes, to 
and from these events. Assuming that discussion of the five stages of grief would occur as we 
motored around North Suburban Chicago, | had read her book and come up with a few 
questions to ask. One of these questions, if | could work up the courage, was about my 
lingering, sequestered away, feelings (a cocktail of embarrassment, guilt and feigned 
indifference), evolving from the 1967 combat death of a cousin almost exactly my age, Billy 
Janes, in Vietnam while | was cavorting around my college campus. | never got a chance to ask 
any of these question — a lost opportunity, especially in regard to Billy, a conversation | never 
have had with anyone to this day. 


As soon as | exited the LGH parking lot, EKR asked if she could smoke in this car as she pulled a 
pack of Dunhills from her satchel. Caught off guard | said | didn’t know and let the query hang in 
the air a few beats, until she offered, “probably your boss would not appreciate it,” and asked if 
we could stop shortly before we reached her next destination on the days speaking tour, so she 
could smoke, commenting: “it’s part of my pre-talk ritual, you now.” And also her post-talk 
ritual as | learned a couple of hours later. Abruptly switching gears, she asked, “Well then, what 
should we talk about? While my thoughts went immediately to the pre-planned list of question, 
she followed the question with, surprisingly, “I’d like to pick your brain about automobiles.” 


She explained that she and her husband were debating the pros and cons of options for a new 
car. | gleaned that her husband was driving a Chrysler New Yorker, which she considered too 
flashy for her taste, and she offered that now he wants a car like the one Steve McQueen drove 
in Bullitt, rattling off the name without missing a beat, a Ford Mustang GTO 390 Fastback; “he 
even wants a green one, just like in the movie.” She then mumbled something unintelligible in 
the hybrid German that many Swiss speak, and said “that’ll turn some heads at Loyola,” 
followed by a silent interlude of staring out the window, while | tried to visualize EKR and her 
husband in a movie theatre watching Bullitt. 


In a moment or two she became present again, and returned to her own car situation. She was 
driving a two door 1962 Ford Fairlane, which was “well used and abused.” EKR related that she 
was ready for something new and “a bit more classy” but not so much that people would think 
it ostentatious, or stereotypical of a doctor. EKR ran through a number of options, often 
commenting she had seen this or that car in a movie or on TV, and asked my impressions of 
each. She had far more knowledge of car models, custom features, engine types and prices 
than | did then or now, so it was largely a one-sided conversation. By the time we arrived back 
at LGH, she had seemingly settled on a station wagon, such as a Buick Estate, which would be 
helpful for shuttling her eight and 11 year old kids and their friends to their events, (“so many 
parties, practices and competitions” she muttered), and because it would not look like a 


384 


wealthy doctor’s automobile, offering that her husband had the flashy doctor’s car stereotype 
well covered. 


As we pulled up to the main entry of LGH where the administrative assistants of the CEO and 
Chief of Staff were waiting to escort Dr. Kubler-Ross to her next destination, | felt compelled to 
say something about the grief stages before she exited the car, so | said that | enjoyed her talk 
and observed that her model applied to a lot of life events, to which she replied, “well .. I’m 
glad you think so; it’s still taking shape in my own mind; the acceptance) phase might be too 
much of a happy Hollywood ending, don’t you think,” followed by shrug and quizzical facial 
expression. And then she was out of the car, striding quickly to yet another Death and Dying 
presentation, and later in life to a fascination with spirituality, life after death scenarios, and 
ultimately disillusionment with her model as her own health declined after a series of strokes. 
(Lattin D. Expert on Death Faces Her Own Death. Kubler-Ross Now Questions Her Life’s Work. 
SFGate. www.sfgate.com. May 31, 1997. Accessed January 6, 2025) | don’t remember my 
thoughts as | returned the Mercedes to the Chief of Staff’s parking slot, other than a general 
recollection that EKR was not what | expected: chain smoker, surprisingly deep knowledge of 
cars, movie-goer, harried working mom often on the road chauffeuring her kids, maybe signs of 
spousal friction (Manny and ERK separated fairly soon after, and divorced seven years later), 
and uncertain about the veracity of her famous grief model, but perhaps she was just pulling 
my leg. However, EKR didn’t strike me as a joker. 


While employed at Lutheran General, | earned a Masters from the NU School of Education and 
Social Policy in 1973 after bouncing from program to program to get the specific degree and list 
of courses desired by UIC Med to be considered for an academic appointment at the medical 
center. Teaching at the high school level was now a discarded goal. | interviewed and showed 
one of my LGH surgical training tapes during the oral presentation to the faculty. Something 
must have clicked because the job was offered and | started work at UIC Med as an Assistant 
Professor of Health Professions Education in a medical school department known as the Center 
for Educational Development (CED), now known as the Department of Medical Education. 
(www.chicago.medicine.ic.edu/medical-education) Work in CED over the next five years 
involved teaching courses in a Masters of Health Professions Education for international 
medical educators operated in conjunction with the World Health Organization, and directing 
the UIC Med Instructional Television Unit (ITU). During these five years, the ITU produced more 
than 100 training videos and films for medical, dental, pharmacy and _ nursing 
students/residents, including a four-part series commissioned by the UIC Medical Sociology 
Department, funded by a HUD (Department of Housing and Urban Development) grant on the 
social and behavioral impact of living in high rise urban housing. The series focused on the 
controversial Cabrini Green Development, a mile from the UIC Medical Center. 


This series was triggered by the closing of a McDonald’s Restaurant that was placed, with great 
fanfare, within the Cabrini Green High Rise Complex. It was the first McDonald’s anywhere in 
Chicagoland to be closed for any reason. The urban myth is that this McDonald’s site was shut 
down after rumored incidents of people shooting at the neon McDonalds Arches sign from the 
walkways of the housing project, which was never verified. It is known that the sign was hit 
several times by gunfire or objects thrown from passing cars. The actual reason for the closing 
is less dramatic — the economics of families in the project limited their capacity to use the 


385 


restaurant. Additionally, and more chilling, a young child was killed by a stray bullet, apparently 
fired from a passing car during a road rage incident, while waiting with her parents in the 
McDonald’s drive through lane. This incident, often confabulated with the sign shooting 
rumors, fueled the perception that the Cabrini Green Complex was dangerous. (Chatelain M. 
The Intertwined History of McDonald’s and Black America. BunkHistory (www.bunkhistory.org). 
University of Richmond, New American History Initiative. January 6, 2020. Accessed: November 
17, 2023) 


We filmed onsite in Cabrini Green in the winter of 1975-76, interviewing 15 resident families 
about life in Cabrini Green. It was often below zero and our cameras locked up when shooting 
exterior scenes because the internal lubricating oil sludged up. Residents who agreed to be 
interviewed drew the ire of other residents. Little boxes that looked like coffins were left on 
their doorsteps with dead rats inside, with a chilling effect on participation. To clarify project 
goals with the Cabrini Green community, the supervising UIC faculty member arranged for two 
cast members (Esther Rolle and John Amos) of the TV series Good Times, which depicted a 
family living in Cabrini Green-like development in Chicago, to speak to residents in a town hall 
meeting. Rolle and Amos stressed the uses and benefits of the film, and resistance declined, 
although the camera crew was harassed a few times by teenagers looking to show off, and 
hoping to appear in the film. The film was shown on the Chicago PBS affiliate and in other U.S. 
cities in the 1970s. 


Built in stages between 1942 and 1962 and fully 
demolished by 2011, the 70-acre Cabrini Green Homes 
became a national symbol of urban blight and failed 
low-income high rise housing policies. In addition to the 
main 16 story building pictured here, the Green 
included nearly 150 two-story row houses and two 
eight floor apartment buildings, with a population of 
15,000 at its peak.

| also learned from my UIC - CED colleagues that there were opportunities to supplement a 
university salary via consulting and outside contract work. My consulting career, which 
paralleled university work, started in 1975 after signing a contract with the media arm of 
Chicago-based Aldine Publishing Company, which had a strong academic orientation. The job 
was to produce training videos for allied health fields such as radiological technology, 
respiratory therapy and clinical lab science. Aldine became the first of 211 consulting clients | 
had in my career; about 2/3s were other universities and 1/3 were professional associations 
and educationally oriented businesses. 


| wrote the scripts for these videos in conjunction with allied health faculty at the College of 
DuPage in suburban Glen Ellyn, Illinois, and we taped the programs at a commercial television 
production facility at Naval Air Station Glenview. During World War II, Glenview Station was a 
naval aviation training site, but in the 1970s, operations were limited to search and rescue on 
Lake Michigan via seaplanes, with many buildings leased to commercial ventures including the 
television studio. The Glenview Station Studio (GSS) was heavily scheduled for shooting 


386 


commercials, and used by Chicago ABC, CBS and NBC affiliates for post-production editing. It 
was also used by national networks for pre and postproduction work on sports programming, 
including the tape-delayed Sunday night broadcast of the Indianapolis 500 on ABC. 


A side note: During the 1970s, major sporting events were often broadcast in the evening in a 
tape-delayed format, usually edited to fit a two-hour time slot. This was done to avoid 
preempting popular prime time shows. Even the NBA and NHL finals were tape delayed, starting 
at 10:30pm, to avoid disrupting regular programming and the local news. There was no way 
that CBS, for example, was going show an NBA Finals game instead of All in the Family, MASH, 
The Mary Tyler Moore, Bob Newhart and Carol Burnett on a Saturday evening. (Brooks T, 
Marsh E. Complete Directory to Prime Time Network TV Shows. (29"" ed.). New York: Ballantine. 
2007; Gross E. Saturday Nights on CBS in 1970s: The Greatest TV Line-Up Ever. Woman’s World. 
October 8, 2023. www.womansworld.com. Accessed: December 4, 2023) 


Aldine purchased studio time at GSS whenever it was available, which often involved evenings 
and Sunday afternoons. We were taping a show on a Sunday afternoon in late May 1977 on 
positioning patients with musculoskeletal injuries for radiographic imaging. The GSS manager 
told us we had to absolutely vacate the facility by 4:00pm because he had a new and important 
client from ABC scheduled at 5:30pm for a live broadcast. Unfortunately, our production 
proceeded slowly. The on-camera demonstrator often misspoke his lines, and some of the 
camera angles | envisioned in the script did not work, requiring re-writes. At 3:45pm, we were 
setting up to shoot the final sequence when an entourage of people sauntered into the control 
room including Jim McKay, host of ABCs Wide World of Sports, Jackie Stewart, a famous race 
car driver of the 60s transitioning to TV commentary, and Howard Cosell of Monday Night 
Football. (Holliman R. Indy 500 Comes Alive on ABC. St. Petersburg Times. May 30, 1976. 
Accessed: April 3, 2023 via www.newspapers.com.) McKay was friendly but also looked 
bemused at our instructional television production, Stewart leaned against the wall and looked 
bored, and Cosell, surprisingly given his caustic TV persona, asked questions about what we 
were doing, and then launched into a lengthy anecdote about instructional television programs 
he once did for little leaguers on batting, throwing, fielding and base running. 


A side note: Cosell, a practicing attorney in the 1950s and 60s, was chief counsel for the 
corporate entity that operates Little League Baseball. He was largely responsible for creating 
the infrastructure and bylaws of Little League America and Little League International, the 
operating policies that leagues and teams follow to this day, and revised several rules of the 
game including all players must participate in each game and the ten run mercy rule. (Bloom J. 
There You Have It: The Life, Legacy and Legend of Howard Cosell. Amherst MA: University of 
Massachusetts Press. 2010) 


Cosell’s little league story pushed us past the 4:00pm deadline, but McKay chimed in and said 
they had plenty of time, so go ahead and finish the production, and even offered a camera 
position suggestion. We re-racked the tape and managed to get thru the final script page 
without incident. When we were done, McKay explained what they were going to do, which 
was to pretend to live broadcast the middle of the Indy 500 race, joking “don’t tell anybody that 
this is how we actually do it.” He invited us to stay and watch if we had time. The Indy 500 Race 
was shown on the Sunday evening before Memorial Day starting at 9:00pm Eastern time. 
McKay, the lead announcer, and Stewart, the racing commentator, recorded their call of the 


387 


10:00 am start and the initial 12 laps (30 miles) of the race from the track broadcast booth in 
Indianapolis. As the race progressed, they walked around the track and taped interviews with 
pit crews and racing VIPs, and then returned to the broadcast booth to record their 
commentary for the final 12 laps. 


As soon as the race was over and the top finishers were interviewed, the announcers were 
hustled off to an awaiting private jet that whisked them to Glenview Naval Air Station. While 
the announcers were in the air, ABC producers edited the 3.5-hour race down to 90 minutes. At 
GSS, McKay, Stewart and Cosell, who just happened to be in Chicago and agreed to add color 
perspective, watched the condensed footage displayed on 70s style RBG (i.e., red, green, blue) 
big screen projectors and announced the race as if it was a live event. They did a rehearsal from 
5:30 to 7:00pm, worked out kinks for 30 minutes, ate a quick dinner, and went live at 8:00pm 
Chicago time, 9:00pm in the East. | watched the rehearsal. It was amazing how fast they 
switched from idle chitchat to on-camera professional announcer mode. 


With the UIC job and consulting, our income was finally sufficient to turn our attention to family 
building. During her pregnancy, | learned about Susan’s inner strength, the core element of who 
she has been throughout our five decade marriage. The pregnancy experience was indeed a 
trial for Susan. During her first trimester, Susan was exposed to Rubella at her school, had to 
resign her position, and per the medical norm of that era, was confined to home, and largely to 
bed rest, for the remaining six months of her pregnancy. She kept both of us as calm and 
optimistic as possible given the real risk for miscarriage or birth defects. However, as the 
months proceeded, signs increasingly pointed to a normal birth. By September 1974, Susan had 
gone two weeks past the due date and was developing a concerning uremic condition 
impacting kidney function, not uncommon in overly long pregnancies. Her Ob-Gyn told her 
“deliver in two days or we are inducing”. I'll always remember Susan’s rather emphatic 
response: “I definitely did not want that. | was determined to do it on my own terms.” She told 
me, “we’re going to Orchard Plaza, (a large shopping mall and home to the theatre where we 
saw Jaws and Star Wars), and I’m walking until contractions start.” And that’s what we did. We 
arrived at Orchard Plaza at opening time, 10:00am, and started walking, around and around. By 
5:00pm, Susan was in labor and we drove straight to Evanston Hospital. Showing her 
confidence in the mall walk-around, Susan had packed the VW van with everything we would 
need at the hospital. Once there, it took a while, 12 hours, but Adam Charles Hendricson was 
born at 5:30am Sunday, September 22, 1974.

f 1 Sees 

A tradition started the summer after Adam’s birth. In July 1975, the three of us went to 
Whidbey Island for a two-week holiday at Harold and Mildred’s beachfront home on the Puget 
Sound. The Hendricson’s traveled to Whidbey every year until 1988, and periodically thereafter. 
Activities on the beach or on the water abounded. It was especially memorable when we visited 
over July 4th. Adam and Aaron’s granddad Harold enjoyed nothing better than driving to the 
Swinomish Tribal Reservation at the north end of Whidbey Island, buying hundreds of dollars of 
fireworks, stoking a big bonfire on the beach and firing the rockets and boomers (M80s, M100s, 
and others now illegal) out over the water, encouraging us to shoot at boats anchored in 
Mutiny Bay that annoyed him, particularly his frenemy neighbor’s 80 foot teak hulled cruiser. 
Of course, he knew that the anchorages were far beyond reach of our fireworks. 


389 


Summers at Whidbey Island started during the Evanston years and continued after our move to

defended by Aunt Shirley while Adam and Dillon rush in to break up the play. 


During our Evanston years, we had adventures in both of our VW vans. The first van was not 
technically a camper, but we attempted to use it that way by pulling out the two rows of back 
seats, covering the floor with sofa cushions and topped them with sleeping bags. Weekend trips 
were relatively close range: Ravinia Park, site of hiking trails and outdoor concerts on-the lawn 
where we saw performances by Chicago’s Joffrey Ballet, Gray’s Lake on the Wisconsin border or 
Geneva, the first city in the Wisconsin Dells recreational area. In 1972, we went off on our first 
extended journey in the pseudo camper, driving 3,800 miles round trip from Evanston to Walla 
Walla to see Grandma and Grandpa Dennis, roughly paralleling at least the route, if not the 
duress, of the wagon train journeys by the Dennis, Goodman, Morgan and Hendricson families. 
Looking back on it now, it seems rather reckless. The 1965 bus obviously had a lot of miles on it, 
but the odometer was broken so we didn’t know how many. It was probably for the best that 
we did not know. We didn’t have the engine checked before we departed, and we had never 
driven it more than 200 miles on a trip. But we completed the two-week round trip without 
major mechanical incident. 


However, other issues arose. One night we camped next to the Great Salt Lake, which we drove 
far off the logical path to see. While eating outside, we were set upon by a swarm of 
mosquitoes so gigantic (both the swarm and the Skeeters) that they must have escaped from a 
genetic mutation experiment. We raced inside the van, slammed the door and cranked all the 
windows shut, assuming we would be safe. Not so. The mutant mosquitoes slithered into the 
van, and things were tense until we decided to abandon the VW for several hours. When we 
returned, the mosquitoes were somewhere else, and we got on the road as fast as we could. 


On the way home while driving east on 1-84 just past Boise, Idaho and listening to music on a 
local radio station, | spied a very bright object in the sky with a pronounced multi-color contrail. 
The radio announcer cut in suddenly and started fielding telephone calls from listeners who 
saw the same flaming object. One after another, callers described with increasingly levels of 
alarm and high levels of certainty that the flight path of this UFO or even worse, a Russian 


390 


ICBM, was aimed directly at Mountain Home, the next town along 1-84, location of a major Air 
Force base, and as everyone in that area seemingly knew, the home to nuclear missile silos. The 
escalating call-in hysteria, egged on by the radio announcer, continued until the streaking 
object (described in subsequent, less histrionic reports as a trash-can sized meteor) descended 
and incinerated in the atmosphere. The decimation of Idaho averted, | looked over at Susan 
who was staring out her window at a disturbingly large tornado moving at an angle toward the 
road. We considered options, and concluded that moving forward was better than sitting on 
the shoulder of the Interstate. That turned out to be the correct call; the twister kept moving 
toward us, but suddenly popped upward and flew the other direction. The remainder of the 
drive back to Chicago was devoid of atmospheric events. 


The next summer (1973), on a camping trip to Door County Wisconsin (i.e., Sturgeon Bay, fish 
boil capital of the U.S.A.), we endured an incredibly violent wind and hailstorm huddled inside 
the van, made especially disturbing because it occurred In the middle of the night. We waited 
for the roof to be punctured, windows shattered, and the van to be blown over, but somehow 
the tin can held together, only to be virtually totaled in a collision about a month later. That 
incident occurred when we were driving to Galena, Illinois to look for antiques. While stopped 
at a red light on the outskirts of Galena on a rainy day, the driver of the car behind us hit the 
accelerator instead of the brakes and plowed into the van at high speed, knocking us 20 yards 
down the road into a culvert and pancaking the back half of the VW. We were fortunate to 
escape without injury, but that was the end of van # 1, which we eventually sold for parts. We 
then traded Susan’s Firebird, which had a transmission problem (would not shift out of second 
gear) for VW van # 2, which was a legitimate camper, relatively new (1969) and had a 
functioning odometer. We don’t want to imply that we pulled a fast one on the car dealer, but 
for the test drive on the streets around the dealership in Chicago, we were counting on the fact 
that mid-day traffic would keep the speed below 30 MPH, which it did. We may have failed an 
ethical check on that transaction. When we relocated to Texas, we drove that camper to San 
Antonio, and soon after traded it for an AMC Pacer (i.e. the George Jetson car), for reasons that 
| do not remember, but it strikes us now as an odd decision. 


Susan and the 1969 VW van, the camper with sink, fridge, 
fold out table, and mini sofa, which made the journey to 
San Antonio in 1978. 


Although Susan and | enjoyed living in Evanston, and took advantage of restaurants, theatres, 
world class museums, shopping and sporting events in Chicago, three factors compelled us to 
consider other places to live: (1) we could afford to rent decent places to live, but purchasing a 
home was beyond our capacity, (2) | was informed that | would not be eligible for promotion 
within the UIC Medical School above Assistant Professor without an M.D., and my seven year 


391 


tenure clock was ticking toward a 1980 terminal date, and (3) there’s no sugar coating it — the 
weather in the Chicago area is brutal seven months a year. | fared less well in the winter than 
Susan. My asthma was triggered by the sudden change from pleasant fall weather to full-on 
harsh winter at the end of October, which frequently left me sick in bed on my birthday 
(November 4) with bronchitis or pneumonia. When a newly opened health science center in the 
University of Texas System dangled an offer in 1978, we decided to take the leap. 


Chicago Retrospective 

What was it about the Chicagoland area that Susan and | liked so much? It certainly was not the 
weather for more than half the year, and we paid a winter tax by living in Evanston right on the 
water. Nobody told us about Lake Effect Snow! If it snowed 9 inches at O’Hare Airport 15 miles 
inland, it snowed 18 inches in Evanston. In summing up our experience in the Second City, the 
main attribute that sticks with us is the lack of pretentiousness; there was no “look at us — 
we’re so special, we’re so lucky to live here” attitude that oozes from some coastal cities; not 
naming names, but you know what coastal cities and regions I’m talking about. 


When living in Chicagoland, the vibe was “we’re doing our thing here, and we don't care if 
anybody knows it.” That attitude may still apply. In 2023, Chicago had 35 restaurants with 
Michelin stars, second only to NYC (49), but few people elsewhere realize this and people in 
Chicago likely don’t care that others don’t know. Chicagoland in 2023 had three universities 
ranked by the Academic Ranking of World University (ARWU) System in the top 50 worldwide: 
University of Chicago (10), Northwestern University (29), and the University of Illinois, multiple 
campuses including UIC and its Medical Center (49), the only American city to achieve this 
recognition. (2023 Academic Ranking of World Universities. www.shanghairanking.com. 
Accessed: December 13, 2023). Chicago is the only U.S. city to have three universities in the 
AWRU Top 50. Depending on the ranking system, Chicago’s Institutes of Art, Shedd Aquarium, 
Field Museum of Natural History, and Adler Planetarium are ranked from first to third in the 
nation, and top 20 worldwide. Chicago has 159 two and four year colleges, 3 to LA County 
(230) and the greater NYC region (209), both of which have more than double the population, 
but 30 to 50 more universities than Boston, Philadelphia, Washington DC, Dallas, and Houston. 
In 2023, Chicago was fifth in the world for theatre companies (207) that have existed for ten 
consecutive years following New York at 430, Paris with 353, Tokyo with 231, and London at 
214. The Chicago Public Library has 82 branches (2"¢ only to New York) and has been ranked top 
five in the U.S. by the American Librarian Association since 1984. The University of Chicago 
Library is the 9" largest academic library in the world, and second largest in the U.S. after 
Stanford University. (Data in preceding paragraph primarily obtained from: Beard J. 50 Best 
Cities in the World in 2024. January 23, 2024. TimeOut Magazine. www.timeout.com. Accessed 
March 8, 2024, and McCann A. Wallethub. City-Data.com. Best Big Cities to Live In, 2021. 
www.wallethub.com/edu/best-worst.. Live-in/14358/. Accessed: March 8, 2024) 


Back to the preceding coastal comments. Actually, Chicago is quite coastal; the city has 29 miles 
of public access Lake Michigan shoreline and the North Shore communities have 38 miles of 
largely public access beaches. Only New York, Seattle and Los Angeles have more public access 
shoreline in the U.S. (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Office for 
Coastal and Shoreline Management. Shoreline Mileage of the United States. 
www.coast.noaa.gov. July 2022. Accessed: December 5, 2023). Among major coastal cities, only 


392 


San Diego, with a substantially smaller population, has more acres of beaches per 100,000 
residents than Chicago, although much of San Diego’s beach acreage is not accessible to the 
public. (Source: Statistica. Cities With the Largest Expanse of Beaches per 100,000 Residents in 
the United States. 2022. www.statistica.com. Accessed: March 8, 2024). 


One Chicago attachment has provided more frustration than joy. My emotional investment in 
the Chicago White Sox started in 1971, and has managed to stay with me ever since, for 
inconceivable reasons. When my former favorite team, the Washington Senators, cowardly 
skulked away to the Dallas suburbs to become the Texas Rangers in 1971, | was in need of a 
new team when Susan and | arrived in Chicago. Having always been an American League fan 
(Yankees until mid-60s and then the Senators), | went with the ChiSox over the more lovable 
and accessible Cubs. Wrigley Field is a few stops south of Evanston on the L (Chicago’s rapid 
transit system named for its elevated loop around the downtown core). Susan and | attended 
games in Wrigleyville out of convenience, because getting to Comiskey Park (now known as 
Rate Field) was a hassle, and honestly, could be dangerous in the 1970s. 


To catch ChiSox games, | often drove directly from work at the UIC Medical Center, also located 
on the Southside over to Comiskey, only 8 miles, but between 6:00 and 7:00pm, often was a 45 
minute drive, depending on traffic flow on Wells Avenue as | rolled between stop lights through 
Chicago’s Chinatown to avoid the evening rush hour log jam on the I-90 Expressway. The last 
time | can remember making that journey to Comiskey, | was held over at work with a jinxed 
television production, where everything that could go wrong, did go wrong, with precision. 
Fighting through early evening traffic, | arrived at the private pay lot | typically used at least 30 
minutes after the game started. White Sox fans, myself included, who attended night games in 
person during that era routinely hired teenagers from neighborhoods near the ballpark to 
watch our cars during games. 


On this evening, eager to meet up with several UIC Med colleagues already in their seats, | 
rushed off from the lot without paying the young man who collected the parking fee, the usual 
$10.00 to have one of his younger cohorts, probably a sibling, to watch over my vehicle, the 
aforementioned 1969 VW camper. | don't remember any details about the game, but | do 
remember the brick that had been thrown through the driver’s side fly window of the camper, 
which facilitated easy access to the inner door handle, and then convenient access to the 
inexplicably upscale Blaupunkt radio that VW installed in their 1960s era campers, which by the 
time of my postgame arrival at the lot, no longer resided in the VW. To cap off the evening, | 
managed to cut my hand rather severely while brushing the glass shards off the drivers seat, 
permanently imbuing the faded tan cloth seat cover with a profound reddish hue, which was 
fun to explain when we sold the camper several years later. To date, my loyalty to the ChiSox 
has been rewarded by only one World Series victory (2005) in five decades, and during the 2024 
season, | cringed my way through an all-time MLB record for ineptitude — 121 losses in a single 
season! My unflinching blind loyalty to the Sox remains, even with the upcoming 2025 season 
representing a highly likely continuation of a bleak re-building cycle.

Chapter V — Post Script, San Antonio 


On the day that our Evanston life concluded, the final act of clearing out the Noyes Street house 
on a sunny but bruisingly cold day was to run Susan’s favorite houseplants out to the VW 
camper. It had been idling for quite a while to get the internal temperature up to 50. The 
camper’s heater was not the greatest. That feat accomplished, we headed south toward our 
new life, with Adam sitting in a spare tire in the camper’s kitchen nook wrapped in blankets. 


A side note: Rear seat belts were not really a thing in 1978, especially when your rear seats are 
removed to allow room for boxes. When we arrived in San Antonio three days later, it was still 
sunny, but 80 degrees rather the five degrees below zero, and it did not get cooler until October. 


One my first day of work at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio 
(UTHSCA; pronounced You — Tuss — Cah) | wore my academic uniform: a three piece wool suit, 
suited for spring in Chicago, but not so much for San Antonio. It was 95 degrees that day. On 
day two at UTHSCSA, Susan called my office phone around lunchtime, the first phone call in my 
45 year career at the University, with the following information, (Susan speaking here) — “Bill, 
there are a bunch of men in our backyard and they built a bonfire and they’re cooking 
something over the fire.” Turns out they were the landscape crew hired by the builder to plug 
our yard with sod, which would ultimately grow into a rather thick Bermuda grass lawn. They 
were cooking lunch — roasted chickens on a spit. 


And so, Susan, Adam and | spent our first year in San Antonio adjusting to a different climate, 
different landscape (i.e., short trees, no lake, sticky clay-like caliche instead of dirt, different 
grass and plants) different ways of doing things (i.e., the landscape crew), new critters (close 
encounters with water moccasins and rattlers, regular backyard visits by coyotes and bobcats), 
central air conditioning (not a thing in Chicago) and new wardrobes. We knew it would be hot, 
but the impact of five straight months of 95 degrees did not register until we lived through that 
first summer. And nobody mentioned the humidity during the recruitment process. Yikes! In 
spite of moving into a neighborhood in the little suburb of Leon Valley with a lot of young 
children and friendly neighbors, it’s safe to say we experienced considerable transitional shock 
during year one in San Antonio, and were not convinced that this was the place for us — at first! 


> ' Nae Our first home in San Antonio, purchased for $37,500, 


and sold for twice as much four years later. 


But life moves forward, and a new and different home gradually becomes the home you know. 
Likely the cementing event that made us into the San Antonio Hendricson’s was the December 
1978 birth of our second son, Aaron Charles Hendricson. Susan speaking here: “When | received 
the due date, | was determined that this child would not have a birthday right before Christmas 


395 


that would be overshadowed by Christmas activities and presents.” The first week of December 
came and passed with no sign of impending delivery, so a specific inducement date was set, 
December 15 at 1:00pm, and that is when Aaron joined the clan. Our first winter in San Antonio 
was especially joyous with Aaron’s arrival, and with Susan’s mother and Bill’s parents visiting. 
With extra people in the house, we almost immediately realized that our nice little starter 
home was not going to work for very long. Plans were laid for moving ahead into the next 
house in San Antonio where our children would hopefully grow up. 


One of my parenteral goals was to allow Adam and Aaron to move completely through one 
school system, grades 1-12, with the same set of peers; in other words to feel rooted in the 
community where they lived and connected to their friends and classmates, the opposite of 
what my sister and | experienced growing up. That goal was accomplished with the exception of 
one year. Adam completed first grade in Leon Valley Elementary prior to moving to our second 
house in the Churchill Estates neighborhood. Except for that single year, Adam completed 11 
years in the public schools that were closest to our neighborhood, which were Larkspur 
Elementary (grades 2-5), Eisenhower Middle School (grades 6-8) and Winston Churchill High 
School (grades 9-12). Aaron ran the gauntlet of 12 straight years in Larkspur, Eisenhower and 
Churchill. Both of our sons graduated from Churchill with peers they first met in the lower 
levels of elementary school. We hope this continuity made a difference in their lives. 


Baby Aaron with brother Adam, Grandpa Harold and

After selling the starter home on Sunlight Drive (aptly named) in Leon Valley, which did its job 
well during our initial years in San Antonio (SA hereafter), we have purchased three more 
houses in the city. In this sequence, the homes were in the subdivisions of Churchill Estates (13 
years), Deerfield (15 years) and Point Bluff, our current home (14 years). We have unique 
memories from all three, but the home on Reigh Count will always be place where the boys 
experienced their childhood, and where Susan and | have the most emotional investment. We 
bought that house in 1982 as a HUD House, meaning the government had taken it over after 


396 


the previous owner failed to make payments on an FHA loan. The 3,000-foot house and an acre 
of property, which had stood empty for two years, REALLY needed a lot of TLC to bring it up to

for the Lincoln log play set that we constructed in the back yard (only God knows how). The logs 
you see in the photo below each weighted a hundred pounds.

Susan’s Work in San Antonio 

After a brief stint at an early childhood development center near UTHSCSA, Susan began work 
at Coker Methodist Day School, a few miles from our Reigh Count home. It became a home 
away from home. She worked at Coker for 30 years, forming life-long friendship with a large 
cohort of fellow teachers who still get together to this day. Many hundreds of young children 
took their educational first steps in Susan’s classroom, and she loved each one of them, no 
matter what ... and there was a lot of happenings to challenge “the no matter what” adage. 
After ten years at Coker, the “Mrs. Hendricson, you probably don’t remember me ...” 
phenomenon began. No matter where we went, especially grocery stores, restaurants, theatres 
and big box stores, Susan was approached by teenagers, and/or child and parent combos who 
would approach timidly and lead off with the Mrs. Hendricson, you probably don’t remember 
me line. Most of the time, she did remember them, even after 10-20 years, especially if a 
parent was nearby. And if she didn’t right away, Susan learned to ask subtle questions to pin 
down the year or a memorable event to help a name pop into her head. Extra time on outings 
was allocated to accommodate former student approaches and the ensuing conversations. 


With students and an assistant in 1995. Halloween was a

role expanded far beyond that. During Susan’s time at Larkspur, the student population was 
largely from families with challenging economic circumstances, and many children had limited 
English language skills. The school was resource-challenged to the nth degree, requiring 
creativity to implement the curriculum. From 2013 through the onset of COVID in 2020, every 
day posed new challenges and excitement as Susan rotated among the seven Kindergarten 
classrooms assisting teachers and students with a wide variety of tasks.

program known as Operation School Bus (OSB) and clothes and supplies for infant care through

2023, ALSA was recognized as the philanthropic organization of the year by the San Antonio 
Express News. In 2024, Susan was recognized as ALSA Volunteer of the Year. Since 2018, Susan 
also has served on the Board of Directors of our neighborhood’s (Point Bluff) Women’s Club, a 
large and active group sponsoring more than 20 events annually for our community.

My Work in San Antonio 

For the initial 20 years at UTHSCSA, | functioned as a Project Manager for accreditation, 
curriculum, educational research and professional development. In 1998, | was appointed Chair 
of the Educational Research and Development (ERD) Department comprised of 12 educational, 
evaluation and technology specialists who supported and staffed the academic programs of the 
five health professions schools at UTHSCSA. In 2005, | became Assistant Dean for Education and 
Faculty Development of the UTHSCSA School of Dentistry, remaining in that position until 
retirement 2017. As Assistant Dean, | directed a top to bottom curriculum revision, managed 
honors programs and fellowships in research, community service and teaching for students and 
residents, coordinated the School’s monthly faculty development program, served as Co-I on six 
federally funded faculty development and Center of Excellence grants, conducted 10 selective 
courses for students and directed the first year training for newly hired faculty known as TEXAS 
(Teaching Excellence and Academic Skills). From 1998 to 2009, | also served as Associate Editor 
of the Journal of Dental Education, working for the American Dental Education Association, 
which was an evening and weekend job.

| stayed retired in 2017 for two weeks, and then returned to a joint appointment in the

dissertation and thesis completion for Doctoral and Masters level students, conduct scientific 
communication courses for graduate students and postdoc fellows, and serve as Co-director of 
UTEC (University Teaching Excellence Consortium), which helped PhD candidates and postdocs 
prepare for careers in science teaching at undergraduate-focused universities. During my five 
years with UTEC, an NIH funded initiative, 47 PhDs and postdocs in UTEC obtained university 
level faculty appointments with emphasis on teaching.

Our Sons 

Susan and | are blessed with marvelous sons who have brought indescribable joy and pride to 
our lives. Adam and Aaron both excelled academically, artistically and athletically in high 
school, graduated from Tulane University (Adam) and Emory University (Aaron) with honors, 
where each played a collegiate sport, (Adam, rugby; Aaron, swimming), and completed 
postgraduate education in Neuropharmacology (Adam, PhD) and law (Aaron, JD). Both have 
enjoyed successful professional careers over the past twenty years in their respective fields of 
endeavor. 


Adam and Aaron in 2010. 


Susan and | plan to spend the rest of our days in San Antonio, our home for the past 47 years. 
Although we were initially uncertain about San Antonio, and still find the many months of 
searing summer heat to be challenging, we cannot imagine living anywhere else. It is where we 
fully became who we are.

About The Author 


Bill Hendricson is 76 years old, and has been married to Susan Lienau Hendricson for 53 years. 
Their hobbies include gardening, finding art for their home, reading, photography, crossword 
and jigsaw puzzles, and walking. Bill and Susan are longstanding fans of University of Texas 
Longhorn football and San Antonio Spurs basketball. Bill has published 123 papers on health 
professions education during his academic career, which have been purchased or downloaded 
from access sites in 188 of the 193 nations recognized by the United Nations, and cited by 
authors in 162 nations. Although not a dentist, he has written several of the most referenced 
publications pertinent to dental education over the past 100 years. (Yeung AWK, Tanaka R, 
Leung WK. Current Dentistry. 2021) In retirement, he reviews approximately 100 manuscripts 
annually for six academic journals.
